P0000.meaning: No trouble code is stored. This is the ECU's pass code, meaning its self-diagnosis found nothing wrong.
causes: No fault; this is the ECU's pass code.
The ECU reports it when its fault memory is empty.
It is also shown after codes were cleared or a repair was completed.
fixes: No repair is needed.
If the check engine light is on anyway, re-read the codes with the engine running and look at pending codes too.
If there is a symptom but no code, use live data (fuel trims, coolant temp, MAF, knock correction) to track it down.

P0011.meaning: The intake camshaft on bank 1 (the right side: cylinders 1 and 3, plus 5 on six-cylinders) is more advanced than the AVCS variable cam timing system commanded, or is not responding to its commands. The engine may idle rough, stall or feel down on power; it is usually safe to drive gently to a repair, but check the oil level straight away.
causes: Low engine oil level or pressure, since AVCS is moved by oil pressure.
Old, sludgy or wrong-viscosity oil.
Clogged AVCS oil filter screen feeding the bank 1 oil control valve (a common cause on turbo EJ engines).
Sticking or failed AVCS oil control valve (OCV) on bank 1.
Faulty AVCS cam sprocket, or timing belt or chain out by a tooth.
Camshaft or crankshaft position sensor giving a poor signal.
fixes: Check the oil level and condition first; top up or change the oil and filter using the grade in the owner's manual.
If live data shows AVCS values for your ECU, compare the bank 1 intake cam target with the actual advance: actual should follow target within a few degrees.
Remove and clean the AVCS oil filter screen for the bank 1 oil control valve; replace it if torn or caked.
Unplug the oil control valve and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value; briefly powering it with 12 V should give a clear click.
If the code appeared after timing belt or chain work, verify the cam and crank timing marks.
Replace the oil control valve or AVCS sprocket if the screen is clean, the valve tests good and timing still does not follow target.

P0014.meaning: The exhaust camshaft on bank 1 (the right side: cylinders 1 and 3, plus 5 on six-cylinders) is not where the exhaust AVCS system commanded it (over-advanced, or not responding). Only engines with dual AVCS set this code, such as the FB and FA engines, the EZ36 and some later EJ engines. The engine may idle rough, lack power or stall; check the oil level right away and drive gently until it is fixed.
causes: Low engine oil level or pressure, since AVCS is moved by oil pressure.
Old, sludgy or wrong-viscosity oil.
Clogged oil filter screen feeding the bank 1 exhaust oil control valve.
Sticking or failed exhaust AVCS oil control valve (OCV) on bank 1.
Faulty exhaust cam sprocket (AVCS actuator), or timing belt or chain out by a tooth.
Exhaust camshaft or crankshaft position sensor giving a poor signal.
fixes: Check the oil level and condition first; top up or change the oil and filter using the grade in the owner's manual.
If live data shows AVCS values for your ECU, compare the bank 1 exhaust cam target with the actual position: actual should follow target within a few degrees.
Remove and clean the oil filter screen for the exhaust oil control valve; replace it if torn or caked.
Unplug the exhaust oil control valve and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value; briefly powering it with 12 V should give a clear click.
If the code appeared after timing belt or chain work, verify the cam and crank timing marks.
Replace the oil control valve or exhaust cam sprocket if the screen is clean, the valve tests good and timing still does not follow target.

P0016.meaning: The ECU found that the intake camshaft position on bank 1 (the right side: cylinders 1 and 3, plus 5 on six-cylinders) does not line up with the crankshaft position as it should. This can mean the timing belt or chain has jumped a tooth, so avoid hard driving until it is checked: most Subaru engines are interference engines and a slipped belt can bend valves.
causes: Timing belt or chain has jumped a tooth, or was installed a tooth off during a belt job.
Stretched timing chain or worn tensioner on chain-driven engines (FB, FA, EZ30, EZ36).
AVCS cam sprocket stuck away from its base position, often from low or dirty oil or a clogged intake oil control valve screen.
Faulty bank 1 intake camshaft position sensor or crankshaft position sensor, or poor wiring to them.
Damaged reluctor (tone) teeth on the cam sprocket or crank sprocket.
fixes: Check the oil level and condition, and note any AVCS or cam/crank sensor codes stored with this one.
Inspect the cam and crank sensor connectors and wiring for oil, corrosion and chafing.
If the code appeared after timing belt or chain work, remove the covers and verify every timing mark lines up.
Check the timing belt or chain and its tensioner for wear, slack or missing teeth.
Test the cam and crank sensors as the service manual describes; a scope of the signals is the best check.
Clean the intake oil control valve screen, then replace the sensor, sprocket, belt or chain as the checks indicate.

P0026.meaning: The oil switching valve (OSV) that switches intake valve lift on bank 1 (the right side: cylinders 1 and 3, plus 5 on six-cylinders) is not giving the result the ECU expects. It belongs to Subaru's AVLS variable valve lift system, used on some SOHC EJ25 and EZ30 engines; the engine usually runs, but may lack power at higher rpm or idle unevenly.
causes: Low oil level, low oil pressure or dirty oil, since valve lift is switched by oil pressure.
Clogged oil filter screen for the OSV.
Sticking or failed oil switching valve on bank 1.
Wiring or connector fault at the OSV.
Sticking lift-switching rocker arm parts in the cylinder head (less common).
fixes: Check the oil level and condition; change the oil and filter if overdue or the wrong grade.
Inspect the OSV connector and harness for oil contamination, corrosion and loose pins.
Unplug the OSV and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value.
Remove the OSV and its oil screen, clean the screen, and check the valve moves freely (a clear click) when briefly powered with 12 V.
Replace the OSV if it sticks or is out of spec, then clear and re-test with a drive through the rpm range where lift switches.

It belongs to Subaru's AVLS variable valve lift system, used on some SOHC EJ25 and EZ30 engines; the engine usually runs, but may lack power at higher rpm or idle unevenly.

P0030.meaning: The heater in the front oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single front A/F sensor) is not drawing the current, or reaching the temperature, the ECU expects. Without a working heater the sensor warms up slowly and the ECU stays in open-loop fueling longer; the car is safe to drive, but economy and emissions suffer.
causes: Weak or failed heater element inside the sensor, the most common cause.
Corroded, loose or water-logged sensor connector.
Wiring chafed or melted against the exhaust or turbo.
Blown fuse or poor power supply to the heater.
Connector or extension harness damaged or left loose during downpipe, J-pipe or header work.
ECU heater driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check the fuse for the oxygen sensor heaters, and check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Inspect the sensor connector and harness for corrosion, melting or chafing against the exhaust.
Unplug the sensor and measure resistance across the two heater pins; compare with the service manual value (open or near zero means a failed heater).
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the heater feed pin of the harness side, and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if the heater is out of spec, then clear and re-test.

P0031.meaning: The ECU sees a low voltage in the heater circuit of the front oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single front A/F sensor). This usually means the heater has burnt out or lost its power feed, or the control wire is shorted to ground. Without a working heater the sensor warms up slowly and the ECU stays in open-loop fueling longer; the car is safe to drive, but economy and emissions suffer.
causes: Heater element inside the sensor has burnt out (open circuit), the most common cause.
Blown fuse or missing power feed to the heater.
Broken wire, corroded pin or unplugged connector.
Connector or extension harness damaged or left loose during downpipe, J-pipe or header work.
Heater control wire shorted to ground, or an ECU heater driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check the fuse for the oxygen sensor heaters, and check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Inspect the sensor connector and harness for corrosion, melting or chafing against the exhaust.
Unplug the sensor and measure resistance across the two heater pins; compare with the service manual value (an open reading means the heater has burnt out).
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the heater feed pin of the harness side, and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if the heater is out of spec, then clear and re-test.

P0032.meaning: The ECU sees a high voltage (or excessive current) in the heater circuit of the front oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single front A/F sensor). This usually means the heater is shorted or its control wire is shorted to power. Without a working heater the sensor warms up slowly and the ECU stays in open-loop fueling longer; the car is safe to drive, but economy and emissions suffer.
causes: Heater element shorted inside the sensor, the most common cause.
Heater control wire shorted to battery voltage.
Damaged or water-logged connector with pins bridging.
Wrong replacement sensor with a different heater rating.
ECU heater driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check the fuse for the oxygen sensor heaters, and check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Inspect the sensor connector and harness for corrosion, melting or chafing against the exhaust.
Unplug the sensor and measure resistance across the two heater pins; compare with the service manual value (a near-zero reading means the heater is shorted).
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the heater feed pin of the harness side, and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if the heater is out of spec, then clear and re-test.

P0034.meaning: The ECU sees a low voltage in the control circuit of the turbo bypass valve solenoid (the recirculating blow-off valve that vents boost when you lift off). This applies to engines with an electrically controlled bypass valve, such as the FA20DIT; you may hear compressor surge (fluttering) on lift-off and the ECU may reduce boost.
causes: Unplugged, loose or corroded connector at the bypass valve solenoid (often disturbed during intake or turbo work).
Open circuit in the solenoid coil or its wiring.
Missing power feed to the solenoid (blown fuse or broken wire).
Control wire shorted to ground.
Aftermarket bypass valve fitted without the factory solenoid connected.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the bypass valve connector is plugged in and locked, especially after any intake or bypass valve work.
Inspect the harness near the turbo for heat damage and chafing.
Unplug the solenoid and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the power feed and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test with a few gentle boost-and-lift cycles.

P0035.meaning: The ECU sees a high voltage in the control circuit of the turbo bypass valve solenoid (the recirculating blow-off valve that vents boost when you lift off). This applies to engines with an electrically controlled bypass valve, such as the FA20DIT; you may hear compressor surge (fluttering) on lift-off and the ECU may reduce boost.
causes: Solenoid coil shorted internally.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage.
Damaged or water-logged connector with pins bridging.
Aftermarket bypass valve or wiring that does not match the factory solenoid.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the bypass valve connector is plugged in and locked, especially after any intake or bypass valve work.
Inspect the harness near the turbo for heat damage and chafing.
Unplug the solenoid and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the power feed and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test with a few gentle boost-and-lift cycles.

Blown fuse or missing power feed to the heater.
Broken wire, corroded pin or unplugged connector.
Sensor unplugged, damaged or relocated during aftermarket downpipe or exhaust work (common on WRX, STI and other turbo models).
Heater control wire shorted to ground, or an ECU heater driver fault (rare).

With the key on, check for battery voltage on the heater feed pin of the harness side, and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.

P0046.meaning: The boost control solenoid circuit, or its effect on boost, is outside the range the ECU expects. On petrol turbos this is the wastegate boost control solenoid; on the EE20 diesel it is the control for the variable-geometry turbo. Expect overboost, underboost or the ECU cutting power to protect the engine; avoid full throttle until it is fixed.
causes: Split, loose or wrongly routed hoses between the turbo, the solenoid and the wastegate actuator.
Sticking or failed boost control solenoid.
Wiring or connector fault at the solenoid.
Wastegate flapper or turbo vanes sticking (seized wastegate on petrol turbos, sooted vanes on the EE20 diesel).
Aftermarket boost controller or solenoid that does not match the ECU's tune.
fixes: Inspect every boost control hose for cracks, loose ends and correct routing (compare with the hose diagram under the hood or in the service manual).
Check the solenoid connector and compare the coil resistance with the service manual value.
In live data, watch boost and wastegate duty during a safe, steady pull: boost should follow the duty changes smoothly, without spikes or a sudden drop.
With the engine off, check that the wastegate arm (or VGT actuator on the diesel) moves freely through its full travel.
Replace the solenoid if it sticks or tests out of spec, and make sure any aftermarket setup matches the tune.

ECU heater driver fault (rare).

Check the fuse for the oxygen sensor heaters, and check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.

With the key on, check for battery voltage on the heater feed pin of the harness side, and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.

This usually means the heater is shorted or its control wire is shorted to power. Bank 2 oxygen sensors are only fitted where each cylinder bank has its own sensor, mainly some six-cylinder (EZ30, EZ36) models. Without a working heater the sensor warms up slowly and the ECU stays in open-loop fueling longer; the car is safe to drive, but economy and emissions suffer.
causes: Heater element shorted inside the sensor, the most common cause.
Heater control wire shorted to battery voltage.
Damaged or water-logged connector with pins bridging.
Wrong replacement sensor with a different heater rating.
ECU heater driver fault (rare).
fixes: If your car has no such sensor, confirm the code with a generic OBD-II scanner first, as it may be a misread rather than a real fault.
Check the fuse for the oxygen sensor heaters, and check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Inspect the sensor connector and harness for corrosion, melting or chafing against the exhaust.
Unplug the sensor and measure resistance across the two heater pins; compare with the service manual value (a near-zero reading means the heater is shorted).
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the heater feed pin of the harness side, and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if the heater is out of spec, then clear and re-test.

P0057.meaning: The ECU sees a low voltage in the heater circuit of the rear oxygen sensor for bank 2 (bank 2 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; bank 2 is the left side, cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders). This usually means the heater has burnt out or lost its power feed, or the control wire is shorted to ground. Bank 2 oxygen sensors are only fitted where each cylinder bank has its own sensor, mainly some six-cylinder (EZ30, EZ36) models. Driving is safe, but the ECU cannot properly monitor the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Heater element inside the sensor has burnt out (open circuit), the most common cause.
Blown fuse or missing power feed to the heater.
Broken wire, corroded pin or unplugged connector.
Sensor unplugged, damaged or relocated during aftermarket downpipe or exhaust work (common on WRX, STI and other turbo models).
Heater control wire shorted to ground, or an ECU heater driver fault (rare).
fixes: If your car has no such sensor, confirm the code with a generic OBD-II scanner first, as it may be a misread rather than a real fault.
Check the fuse for the oxygen sensor heaters, and check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Inspect the sensor connector and harness for corrosion, melting or chafing against the exhaust.
Unplug the sensor and measure resistance across the two heater pins; compare with the service manual value (an open reading means the heater has burnt out).
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the heater feed pin of the harness side, and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if the heater is out of spec, then clear and re-test.

P0058.meaning: The ECU sees a high voltage (or excessive current) in the heater circuit of the rear oxygen sensor for bank 2 (bank 2 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; bank 2 is the left side, cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders). This usually means the heater is shorted or its control wire is shorted to power. Bank 2 oxygen sensors are only fitted where each cylinder bank has its own sensor, mainly some six-cylinder (EZ30, EZ36) models. Driving is safe, but the ECU cannot properly monitor the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Heater element shorted inside the sensor, the most common cause.
Heater control wire shorted to battery voltage.
Damaged or water-logged connector with pins bridging.
Wrong replacement sensor with a different heater rating.
ECU heater driver fault (rare).

Inspect the sensor connector and harness for corrosion, melting or chafing against the exhaust.
Unplug the sensor and measure resistance across the two heater pins; compare with the service manual value (a near-zero reading means the heater is shorted).
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the heater feed pin of the harness side, and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if the heater is out of spec, then clear and re-test.

P0063.meaning: The ECU sees a low voltage in the heater circuit of oxygen sensor 3 for bank 2 (a third sensor further down the exhaust, typically after a second catalytic converter; bank 2 is the left side). This usually means the heater has burnt out or lost its power feed, or the control wire is shorted to ground. Bank 2 oxygen sensors are only fitted where each cylinder bank has its own sensor, mainly some six-cylinder (EZ30, EZ36) models. Most Subarus have no sensor 3. Driving is safe, but the ECU cannot properly monitor the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Heater element inside the sensor has burnt out (open circuit), the most common cause.
Blown fuse or missing power feed to the heater.
Broken wire, corroded pin or unplugged connector.
Sensor unplugged, damaged or relocated during aftermarket downpipe or exhaust work (common on WRX, STI and other turbo models).
Heater control wire shorted to ground, or an ECU heater driver fault (rare).
fixes: If your car has no such sensor, confirm the code with a generic OBD-II scanner first, as it may be a misread rather than a real fault.

Inspect the sensor connector and harness for corrosion, melting or chafing against the exhaust.
Unplug the sensor and measure resistance across the two heater pins; compare with the service manual value (an open reading means the heater has burnt out).

P0064.meaning: The ECU sees a high voltage (or excessive current) in the heater circuit of oxygen sensor 3 for bank 2 (a third sensor further down the exhaust, typically after a second catalytic converter; bank 2 is the left side). This usually means the heater is shorted or its control wire is shorted to power. Bank 2 oxygen sensors are only fitted where each cylinder bank has its own sensor, mainly some six-cylinder (EZ30, EZ36) models. Most Subarus have no sensor 3. Driving is safe, but the ECU cannot properly monitor the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Heater element shorted inside the sensor, the most common cause.
Heater control wire shorted to battery voltage.
Damaged or water-logged connector with pins bridging.
Wrong replacement sensor with a different heater rating.
ECU heater driver fault (rare).
fixes: If your car has no such sensor, confirm the code with a generic OBD-II scanner first, as it may be a misread rather than a real fault.
Check the fuse for the oxygen sensor heaters, and check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Inspect the sensor connector and harness for corrosion, melting or chafing against the exhaust.
Unplug the sensor and measure resistance across the two heater pins; compare with the service manual value (a near-zero reading means the heater is shorted).
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the heater feed pin of the harness side, and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if the heater is out of spec, then clear and re-test.

P0065.meaning: The air assisted injection (AAI) system, which uses a solenoid valve to feed a little intake air to the injector tips to help the fuel atomize (mainly at cold start and idle), is not performing as expected. Only some engines have this system; the car is normally safe to drive, but cold starts and idle may be rougher and emissions higher.
causes: Cracked, disconnected or blocked AAI air hoses.
Sticking or failed AAI solenoid valve.
Carbon or dirt blocking the air passages at the injectors.
Vacuum leak in the intake affecting the air supply.
Wiring or connector fault at the solenoid.
fixes: Inspect the AAI hoses from the intake to the solenoid and injectors for cracks and loose ends.
Check the solenoid connector and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value.
Remove the solenoid and check that it opens and closes cleanly (a clear click) when briefly powered with 12 V.
Clean any blocked passages, replace the solenoid if faulty, then clear and re-test from a cold start.

P0066.meaning: The ECU sees a low voltage in the control circuit of the air assisted injection (AAI) solenoid valve, which feeds a little intake air to the injector tips to help the fuel atomize, mainly at cold start and idle. Only some engines have this system. The car is normally safe to drive, but cold starts and idle may be rougher.
causes: Open circuit in the solenoid coil or its wiring.
Missing power feed (blown fuse or broken wire).
Control wire shorted to ground.
Unplugged or corroded connector.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the AAI solenoid connector is plugged in and inspect the pins for corrosion.
Unplug the solenoid and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the power feed and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0067.meaning: The ECU sees a high voltage in the control circuit of the air assisted injection (AAI) solenoid valve, which feeds a little intake air to the injector tips to help the fuel atomize, mainly at cold start and idle. Only some engines have this system. The car is normally safe to drive, but cold starts and idle may be rougher.
causes: Solenoid coil shorted internally.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage.
Damaged or water-logged connector with pins bridging.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the AAI solenoid connector is plugged in and inspect the pins for corrosion.
Unplug the solenoid and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the power feed and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0068.meaning: The manifold pressure reading does not agree with what the ECU expects from throttle position and airflow. The engine may hesitate or idle poorly, and drive-by-wire models may go into a reduced-power mode.
causes: Vacuum or boost leak after the throttle body (PCV and breather hoses, intake manifold gasket, brake booster hose).
Faulty, contaminated or poorly connected MAP sensor.
Dirty or faulty MAF sensor making airflow disagree with pressure.
Carbon build-up or a fault in the throttle body or throttle position sensor.
Split or loose hose to the MAP sensor, where it is hose-fed.
fixes: Key on, engine off: MAP and atmospheric pressure in live data should match, about 100 kPa at sea level (lower at altitude).
At warm idle MAP should sit well below atmospheric (typically around 30 to 40 kPa absolute) and rise smoothly with throttle; a high idle reading points to a leak or a bad sensor.
Inspect all vacuum, PCV and breather hoses; a smoke test finds hidden leaks.
Clean the MAF sensor with MAF cleaner and check the MAP sensor connector and hose.
Replace the MAP sensor if it disagrees with atmospheric pressure or does not change smoothly, with no leaks present.

P0076.meaning: The ECU sees a low voltage in the control circuit of the bank 1 oil switching valve (OSV), which switches intake valve lift on bank 1 (the right side: cylinders 1 and 3, plus 5 on six-cylinders). It belongs to Subaru's AVLS variable valve lift system, used on some SOHC EJ25 and EZ30 engines. The ECU cannot switch valve lift, so power at higher rpm may be down, but the engine is normally safe to drive.
causes: Open circuit in the OSV coil or its wiring.
Missing power feed to the valve (blown fuse or broken wire).
Control wire shorted to ground.
Unplugged, oily or corroded OSV connector.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the OSV connector is fully plugged in and inspect the pins for oil and corrosion.
Unplug the OSV and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the power feed at the harness side.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for shorts to ground or to power.
Replace the OSV or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0077.meaning: The ECU sees a high voltage in the control circuit of the bank 1 oil switching valve (OSV), which switches intake valve lift on bank 1 (the right side: cylinders 1 and 3, plus 5 on six-cylinders). It belongs to Subaru's AVLS variable valve lift system, used on some SOHC EJ25 and EZ30 engines. The ECU cannot switch valve lift, so power at higher rpm may be down, but the engine is normally safe to drive.
causes: OSV coil shorted internally.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage.
Damaged or oil-soaked connector with pins bridging.
Chafed harness touching another powered circuit.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the OSV connector is fully plugged in and inspect the pins for oil and corrosion.
Unplug the OSV and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the power feed at the harness side.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for shorts to ground or to power.
Replace the OSV or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0082.meaning: The ECU sees a low voltage in the control circuit of the bank 2 oil switching valve (OSV), which switches intake valve lift on bank 2 (the left side: cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders). It belongs to Subaru's AVLS variable valve lift system, used on some SOHC EJ25 and EZ30 engines. The ECU cannot switch valve lift, so power at higher rpm may be down, but the engine is normally safe to drive.
causes: Open circuit in the OSV coil or its wiring.
Missing power feed to the valve (blown fuse or broken wire).
Control wire shorted to ground.
Unplugged, oily or corroded OSV connector.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the OSV connector is fully plugged in and inspect the pins for oil and corrosion.
Unplug the OSV and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the power feed at the harness side.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for shorts to ground or to power.
Replace the OSV or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0083.meaning: The ECU sees a high voltage in the control circuit of the bank 2 oil switching valve (OSV), which switches intake valve lift on bank 2 (the left side: cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders). It belongs to Subaru's AVLS variable valve lift system, used on some SOHC EJ25 and EZ30 engines. The ECU cannot switch valve lift, so power at higher rpm may be down, but the engine is normally safe to drive.
causes: OSV coil shorted internally.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage.
Damaged or oil-soaked connector with pins bridging.
Chafed harness touching another powered circuit.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the OSV connector is fully plugged in and inspect the pins for oil and corrosion.
Unplug the OSV and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the power feed at the harness side.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for shorts to ground or to power.
Replace the OSV or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0088.meaning: Fuel rail pressure is above the target. This applies to direct-injection engines: the EE20 diesel and direct-injection petrol engines such as the FA20DIT and the FA20D in the BRZ. The ECU may limit power, and real overpressure stresses injectors and pipes, so get it checked soon.
causes: Faulty fuel rail pressure sensor reading too high.
Sticking pressure regulating valve on the high-pressure pump (the suction control valve on the EE20 diesel).
Pressure limiter or relief valve on the rail stuck closed.
Wiring fault in the rail pressure sensor or regulating valve circuit.
Contaminated fuel affecting the pump valves.
fixes: If your ECU reports it, compare fuel rail pressure with target in live data at idle and during gentle acceleration: actual should stay close to target.
After the engine has sat for a while, the rail pressure reading should drop close to zero; a high reading on a cold, rested engine points to the sensor or its wiring.
Inspect the rail pressure sensor and regulating valve connectors for corrosion and fuel or oil contamination.
Compare the regulating valve's coil resistance with the service manual value.
Replace the sensor, regulating valve or pressure limiter as the checks indicate, then clear and re-test.

P0089.meaning: The ECU is commanding the pressure regulating valve on the high-pressure fuel pump (the suction control valve on the EE20 diesel), but rail pressure is not responding as expected, as if the valve is stuck open. Applies to direct-injection engines; expect hard starting, low power or limp mode.
causes: Sticking pressure regulating valve on the high-pressure pump (the suction control valve on the EE20 diesel), the most common cause.
Dirt or water in the fuel, or a clogged fuel filter.
Low supply pressure from the in-tank fuel pump.
Worn high-pressure fuel pump.
Wiring or connector fault at the regulating valve.
fixes: Replace the fuel filter if it is due, and drain any water from it on the diesel.
Check the regulating valve connector and wiring, and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value.
If your ECU reports it, compare fuel rail pressure with target in live data at idle and during gentle acceleration: actual should stay close to target.
Check the low-pressure supply: the tank pump should prime for a couple of seconds at key on, and lines should not be kinked or blocked.
Replace the regulating valve, or the high-pressure pump if the valve is not sold separately or the pump is worn.

P0091.meaning: The ECU sees a low voltage in the control circuit of fuel pressure regulator 1, which is the pressure regulating valve on the high-pressure fuel pump (the suction control valve on the EE20 diesel) on direct-injection engines. The ECU cannot control rail pressure properly, so expect limp mode, poor running or a no-start.
causes: Open circuit in the regulating valve coil or its wiring.
Missing power feed to the valve (blown fuse or broken wire).
Control wire shorted to ground.
Unplugged, corroded or fuel-soaked connector.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the regulating valve connector is fully seated and the pins are clean.
Unplug the valve and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the power feed and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Inspect the harness around the pump for chafing and heat damage.
Replace the regulating valve (or the pump assembly if the valve is not sold separately) or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0092.meaning: The ECU sees a high voltage in the control circuit of fuel pressure regulator 1, which is the pressure regulating valve on the high-pressure fuel pump (the suction control valve on the EE20 diesel) on direct-injection engines. The ECU cannot control rail pressure properly, so expect limp mode, poor running or a no-start.
causes: Regulating valve coil shorted internally.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage.
Damaged or contaminated connector with pins bridging.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the regulating valve connector is fully seated and the pins are clean.
Unplug the valve and compare its coil resistance with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the power feed and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Inspect the harness around the pump for chafing and heat damage.
Replace the regulating valve (or the pump assembly if the valve is not sold separately) or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0093.meaning: Fuel rail pressure is dropping faster than the ECU can account for, which it treats as a large leak in the high-pressure fuel system. This is mainly an EE20 diesel code. Check for leaking fuel before driving further: fuel spraying onto a hot engine is a fire risk, and the ECU may cut power or stop the engine.
causes: Leaking or cracked high-pressure fuel pipe, or a loose fitting between pump, rail and injectors.
Injector leaking internally and returning too much fuel (excess back-leak).
Rail pressure limiter valve stuck open.
Running very low on fuel, or air in the system after a filter change.
Clogged fuel filter or weak supply starving the high-pressure pump.
Faulty rail pressure sensor.
fixes: With the engine off, look and smell for fuel around the pump, rail, injector pipes and return lines; do not run the engine if fuel is leaking.
Make sure the tank has fuel, and bleed air from the system after any filter change.
Replace the fuel filter if it is due.
Have an injector back-leak (leak-off) test done to find an injector returning too much fuel.
Check whether the rail pressure limiter is returning fuel when it should not, following the service manual procedure.
Replace the leaking pipe, injector, limiter or sensor, then clear and re-test.

P0096.meaning: The reading from the second intake air temperature sensor (IAT 2), which on turbo and diesel engines usually sits after the intercooler, often built into the manifold pressure sensor does not make sense compared with other temperatures, or does not change as expected. It mainly affects fueling and timing accuracy; the car is normally driveable.
causes: Faulty sensor with a stuck or drifting reading.
Sensor tip coated in oil from the PCV system.
Poor connector contact or corroded pins.
Heat soak after short trips or long idling exposing a marginal sensor.
Intercooler or intake leak disturbing the air around the sensor.
fixes: Inspect the sensor connector for corrosion and loose pins, and the sensor tip for oil.
After an overnight cold soak, compare IAT 2 with the main IAT and coolant temp in live data (if your ECU reports it): all should read close to outside air temperature.
Measure the sensor's resistance at a known temperature and compare with the service manual table.
Replace the sensor (on combined units, the whole manifold pressure and temperature sensor) if the reading is wrong.

P0097.meaning: The signal voltage from the second intake air temperature sensor (IAT 2), which on turbo and diesel engines usually sits after the intercooler, often built into the manifold pressure sensor is too low, so it reads implausibly hot. The ECU uses a backup value and may pull timing or boost; the car is normally driveable.
causes: Signal wire shorted to ground.
Sensor shorted internally.
Water or corrosion in the connector.
Chafed harness near the intake or intercooler.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the connector and harness for water, corrosion and chafing.
Unplug the sensor: the live data reading should jump to very cold; if it still reads hot, the wiring is shorted to ground.
Measure the sensor's resistance at a known temperature and compare with the service manual table.
Replace the sensor (on combined units, the whole manifold pressure and temperature sensor) or repair the wiring.

P0098.meaning: The signal voltage from the second intake air temperature sensor (IAT 2), which on turbo and diesel engines usually sits after the intercooler, often built into the manifold pressure sensor is too high, so it reads implausibly cold (often around -40°C, a sign of an open circuit). The ECU uses a backup value; the car is normally driveable.
causes: Sensor unplugged or connector loose.
Broken signal or ground wire.
Open circuit inside the sensor.
Corroded connector pins.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the connector is fully seated and locked.
Inspect the pins and harness for corrosion and breaks.
Unplug the sensor and briefly bridge the two harness pins: live data should jump to very hot; if not, the wiring is open.
Measure the sensor's resistance and compare with the service manual table; replace it if it is open.

P0101.meaning: The airflow reading from the mass airflow (MAF) sensor does not match what the ECU expects for the current rpm, throttle and manifold pressure. The engine may hesitate, idle rough or run lean; drive gently, and on turbo models avoid full boost until it is fixed.
causes: Dirty or oil-contaminated MAF sensor (oiled aftermarket air filters are a common cause).
Unmetered air leak after the MAF: cracked PCV or breather hoses, or a loose turbo inlet or intake coupler (common on EJ turbos).
Aftermarket intake or MAF housing that changes the sensor's calibration.
Blocked or badly fitted air filter.
Faulty MAF sensor.
Wiring or connector fault.
fixes: Check the air filter and air box, and make sure the MAF sensor is seated and clipped in properly.
Clean the MAF element with dedicated MAF cleaner only (do not touch it) and let it dry fully.
Check MAF in live data: a warm engine at idle typically shows a few g/s (roughly 2.5 to 5 g/s), rising smoothly with rpm; also watch fuel trims.
Inspect every intake hose, PCV and breather hose and the turbo inlet for cracks; a smoke test finds hidden leaks.
If an aftermarket intake is fitted, refit the stock intake or make sure the tune matches it.
Replace the MAF sensor if the reading is still wrong after cleaning and fixing leaks.

P0102.meaning: The MAF sensor signal voltage is lower than possible, as if the sensor were unplugged or had lost power. The ECU falls back to estimated airflow, so expect poor running or stalling; drive gently.
causes: MAF connector unplugged, loose or corroded (often after air filter or intake work).
Blown fuse or missing power feed to the MAF sensor.
Broken signal or ground wire, or signal wire shorted to ground.
Intake hose off after the MAF, so little air passes the sensor.
Failed MAF sensor.
fixes: Check that the MAF connector is fully seated and inspect the pins.
Make sure every intake hose after the MAF is connected and clamped.
Check the MAF fuse, and with the key on check for battery voltage on the power feed and a good ground (compare with the service manual pinout).
Check MAF in live data: a warm engine at idle typically shows a few g/s (roughly 2.5 to 5 g/s), rising smoothly with rpm; also watch fuel trims.
Replace the MAF sensor if power and ground are good but the signal stays low.

P0103.meaning: The MAF sensor signal voltage is higher than possible. The ECU falls back to estimated airflow, so expect rough running, rich fueling or stalling; drive gently.
causes: Signal wire shorted to a power wire.
Poor or open ground at the MAF sensor.
Failed or contaminated MAF sensor.
Water or corrosion in the connector.
Aftermarket wiring spliced into the MAF circuit (for example some piggyback tuning devices).
fixes: Inspect the MAF connector and harness for water, corrosion and chafing.
Check the ground wire for continuity to a good body ground.
Check MAF in live data: a warm engine at idle typically shows a few g/s (roughly 2.5 to 5 g/s), rising smoothly with rpm; also watch fuel trims.
Remove any aftermarket devices spliced into the MAF circuit and re-test.
Replace the MAF sensor if the wiring is good and the reading stays high.

P0106.meaning: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor reading is outside the range the ECU expects for current conditions, or does not change as it should (it may be flagged as reading too low). On turbo models this sensor also measures boost, so the ECU may limit boost or power.
causes: Vacuum or boost leak: cracked PCV or breather hoses, loose intercooler couplers, intake manifold gasket.
Split, loose or blocked hose to the MAP sensor, where it is hose-fed.
Faulty or contaminated MAP sensor.
Poor connector contact or corrosion.
Faulty atmospheric pressure reading making the comparison fail.
fixes: Key on, engine off: MAP and atmospheric pressure in live data should match, about 100 kPa at sea level (lower at altitude).
At warm idle MAP should sit well below atmospheric (typically around 30 to 40 kPa absolute) and rise smoothly with throttle; a high idle reading points to a leak or a bad sensor.
Inspect the MAP sensor hose and connector, plus all vacuum, PCV and breather hoses.
On turbo models, pressure-test the intake and intercooler piping for boost leaks.
Replace the MAP sensor if its reading is wrong with no leaks present.

P0107.meaning: The MAP sensor signal voltage is lower than possible, as if the manifold held a near-perfect vacuum. The ECU substitutes a fixed value, so expect poor running and, on turbo models, limited boost.
causes: Unplugged or loose MAP sensor connector.
Open 5 V reference wire, or signal wire shorted to ground.
Failed MAP sensor.
Corroded pins or water in the connector.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the connector is fully seated and inspect the pins for corrosion.
With the key on, check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground at the connector.
Key on, engine off: MAP and atmospheric pressure in live data should match, about 100 kPa at sea level (lower at altitude).
Wiggle-test the harness while watching the MAP reading in live data.
Replace the sensor if reference and ground are good but the signal stays low.

P0108.meaning: The MAP sensor signal voltage is higher than possible, as if there were extreme boost. The ECU substitutes a fixed value, so expect poor running and, on turbo models, limited boost.
causes: Open ground wire at the MAP sensor.
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage.
Failed MAP sensor.
Water or corrosion in the connector.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the connector and harness for water, corrosion and chafing.
With the key on, check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground at the connector.
Key on, engine off: MAP and atmospheric pressure in live data should match, about 100 kPa at sea level (lower at altitude).
Wiggle-test the harness while watching the MAP reading in live data.
Replace the sensor if reference and ground are good but the signal stays high.

P0111.meaning: The reading from the intake air temperature (IAT) sensor, which on most Subarus is built into the MAF sensor does not make sense compared with other temperatures, or does not change as expected. It affects fueling and timing slightly; the car is normally fine to drive.
causes: Faulty IAT sensor (usually part of the MAF sensor assembly).
Dirty or oil-coated sensor element.
Poor connector contact or corroded pins at the MAF sensor.
Heat soak from an aftermarket intake that draws hot engine bay air.
Wiring fault.
fixes: After an overnight cold soak, compare IAT with coolant temp in live data: both should read close to outside air temperature.
While driving, IAT should fall towards ambient and change smoothly, without jumps.
Inspect and clean the MAF/IAT connector and check the pins.
Measure IAT resistance at a known temperature and compare with the service manual table.
Replace the MAF/IAT sensor assembly (or the separate IAT sensor on models that have one) if the reading is wrong.

P0112.meaning: The signal voltage from the intake air temperature (IAT) sensor, which on most Subarus is built into the MAF sensor is too low, so it reads implausibly hot. The ECU uses a backup value and may retard timing; the car is normally driveable.
causes: Signal wire shorted to ground.
Sensor shorted internally.
Water or corrosion in the MAF/IAT connector.
Chafed harness near the air box or intake.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the MAF/IAT connector and harness for water, corrosion and chafing.
Unplug the sensor: the live data reading should jump to very cold; if it still reads hot, the wiring is shorted to ground.
Measure IAT resistance at a known temperature and compare with the service manual table.
Replace the MAF/IAT sensor assembly (or the separate IAT sensor on models that have one) if the reading is wrong.

P0113.meaning: The signal voltage from the intake air temperature (IAT) sensor, which on most Subarus is built into the MAF sensor is too high, so it reads implausibly cold (often around -40°C, a sign of an open circuit). The ECU uses a backup value; the car is normally driveable.
causes: MAF/IAT sensor unplugged or connector loose (common after air filter or intake work).
Broken signal or ground wire.
Open circuit inside the sensor.
Corroded connector pins.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the MAF/IAT connector is fully seated and locked.
Inspect the pins and harness for corrosion and breaks.
Check the IAT reading in live data: it should show roughly ambient temperature, not around -40°C.
Measure IAT resistance and compare with the service manual table.
Replace the MAF/IAT sensor assembly (or the separate IAT sensor on models that have one) if the reading is wrong.

P0116.meaning: The engine coolant temperature (ECT) sensor reading does not match what the ECU expects: it may change too slowly, jump, or disagree with intake air temperature after a cold soak. The ECU relies on it for fueling, idle and fans, so fix it soon, and watch the temperature gauge for real overheating.
causes: Faulty or drifting ECT sensor.
Low coolant or air trapped around the sensor (common on boxers after a coolant change if not bled properly).
Thermostat stuck open, so coolant warms up too slowly.
Corroded connector or poor ground.
Wiring fault.
fixes: Check the coolant level with the engine cold, and bleed air from the system as the service manual describes.
After an overnight cold soak, compare coolant temp and IAT in live data: they should be within a few degrees of each other.
On a drive, coolant temp should climb smoothly to roughly 85 to 95°C and stay there.
Inspect the sensor connector for corrosion, and compare the sensor's resistance with the service manual table.
Replace the thermostat (genuine Subaru recommended) or the ECT sensor as the checks indicate.

P0117.meaning: The coolant temperature sensor signal voltage is too low, so it reads implausibly hot. The ECU uses a backup value and may run the radiator fans continuously; the engine may run lean or start poorly when cold. Check the temperature gauge and coolant level to rule out real overheating.
causes: Signal wire shorted to ground.
ECT sensor shorted internally.
Water or corrosion in the connector.
Chafed harness under the intake manifold.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Confirm the engine is not actually overheating: check the gauge, coolant level and for leaks.
Inspect the ECT connector and harness for water, corrosion and chafing.
Unplug the sensor: live data coolant temp should jump to very cold; if it still reads hot, the wiring is shorted to ground.
Compare the sensor's resistance at a known temperature with the service manual table.
Replace the ECT sensor or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0118.meaning: The coolant temperature sensor signal voltage is too high, so it reads implausibly cold (often around -40°C, a sign of an open circuit). The ECU uses a backup value and may run the radiator fans continuously; expect rich running and poor hot starts.
causes: ECT sensor unplugged or connector loose.
Broken signal or ground wire.
Open circuit inside the sensor.
Corroded connector pins.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the ECT connector is fully seated and locked.
Inspect the pins and harness for corrosion and breaks.
Unplug the sensor and briefly bridge the two harness pins: live data should jump to very hot; if not, the wiring is open.
Compare the sensor's resistance with the service manual table; replace it if it is open.
On a drive, coolant temp should climb smoothly to roughly 85 to 95°C and stay there.

P0121.meaning: The throttle position sensor (TPS) signal does not agree with what the ECU expects from engine load and airflow, or the two sensor tracks on an electronic throttle disagree. On drive-by-wire models (most Subarus from the mid 2000s on) this usually triggers limp mode with limited throttle; drive gently to a repair.
causes: Worn or dirty TPS track causing dropouts (common on older cable-throttle models).
Loose or corroded throttle body connector.
Carbon build-up or a sticking throttle plate.
Wiring fault in the 5 V reference, ground or signal wire.
Faulty electronic throttle body on drive-by-wire models.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the throttle body connector, checking for corrosion or bent pins.
Watch throttle position in live data while slowly pressing the pedal with the key on and engine off: it should rise smoothly from about 0% to near 100% with no jumps or dropouts.
Clean carbon from the throttle bore and plate with throttle body cleaner (key off on drive-by-wire models).
With the key on, check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground at the connector.
Replace the TPS or throttle body if the signal is erratic; some drive-by-wire models need a throttle relearn afterwards.

P0122.meaning: The throttle position sensor (TPS) A signal voltage is lower than possible, below the closed-throttle value. On drive-by-wire models (most Subarus from the mid 2000s on) this usually triggers limp mode with limited throttle; drive gently to a repair.
causes: Throttle body connector unplugged or loose.
Open 5 V reference wire.
Signal wire shorted to ground.
Failed TPS or electronic throttle body.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check that the throttle body connector is fully seated and inspect the pins.
With the key on, check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground at the connector.
Watch throttle position in live data while slowly pressing the pedal with the key on and engine off: it should rise smoothly from about 0% to near 100% with no jumps or dropouts.
Wiggle-test the harness while watching throttle position in live data.
Replace the TPS or throttle body if reference and ground are good but the signal stays low.

P0123.meaning: The throttle position sensor (TPS) A signal voltage is higher than possible, above the wide-open-throttle value. On drive-by-wire models (most Subarus from the mid 2000s on) this usually triggers limp mode with limited throttle; drive gently to a repair.
causes: Open ground wire at the TPS.
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage.
Failed TPS or electronic throttle body.
Water or corrosion in the connector.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the throttle body connector and harness for water, corrosion and chafing.
With the key on, check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground at the connector.
Watch throttle position in live data while slowly pressing the pedal with the key on and engine off: it should rise smoothly from about 0% to near 100% with no jumps or dropouts.
Wiggle-test the harness while watching throttle position in live data.
Replace the TPS or throttle body if reference and ground are good but the signal stays high.

P0125.meaning: The engine took too long to warm up enough for closed-loop fuel control (where the ECU starts using the oxygen sensors). It is not harmful in itself, but fuel use goes up and cabin heat may be weak.
causes: Thermostat stuck open or opening too early (non-genuine thermostats are a common cause on Subarus).
Low coolant level or air in the cooling system.
Faulty or drifting coolant temperature sensor.
Radiator fans running when they should not (fan relay or sensor fault).
Very cold weather combined with long idling or short trips.
fixes: Check the coolant level with the engine cold, and bleed the system as the service manual describes.
On a normal drive, coolant temp should climb smoothly to roughly 85 to 95°C within about 10 to 15 minutes and stay there.
Check that the radiator fans stay off while the engine is cold.
After an overnight cold soak, compare coolant temp and IAT in live data: they should be within a few degrees of each other.
Replace the thermostat with a genuine Subaru part (correct temperature rating, with the air bleed valve at the top), bleed the system, then clear and re-test.

P0126.meaning: Coolant temperature stayed too low for too long for the ECU to consider the engine warmed up for stable operation. It is not harmful in itself, but fuel use goes up and some self-tests will not run.
causes: Thermostat stuck open or opening too early (non-genuine thermostats are a common cause on Subarus).
Low coolant level or air in the cooling system.
Faulty or drifting coolant temperature sensor.
Radiator fans running when they should not.
Very cold weather combined with long idling or short trips.
fixes: Check the coolant level with the engine cold, and bleed the system as the service manual describes.
On a normal drive, coolant temp should climb smoothly to roughly 85 to 95°C within about 10 to 15 minutes and stay there.
Check that the radiator fans stay off while the engine is cold.
After an overnight cold soak, compare coolant temp and IAT in live data: they should be within a few degrees of each other.
Replace the thermostat with a genuine Subaru part (correct temperature rating, with the air bleed valve at the top), bleed the system, then clear and re-test.

P0128.meaning: Coolant temperature stays below the thermostat's regulating temperature, so the ECU suspects the thermostat. It is safe to drive, but fuel economy, emissions and cabin heat suffer.
causes: Thermostat stuck open or opening too early, the most common cause.
Non-genuine thermostat with the wrong rating or no air bleed valve (Subarus are sensitive to this).
Low coolant or air trapped in the system.
Coolant temperature sensor reading low.
Radiator fans running constantly.
fixes: Watch coolant temp in live data on a drive: it should climb smoothly to roughly 85 to 95°C within about 10 to 15 minutes and stay there, even at highway speed.
Check the coolant level with the engine cold, and bleed the system as the service manual describes.
Feel the upper radiator hose from a cold start: it should stay cool until the engine is warm, then get hot quickly; early warmth means the thermostat is open.
After an overnight cold soak, compare coolant temp and IAT in live data: they should be within a few degrees of each other.
Replace the thermostat with a genuine Subaru part (correct temperature rating, with the air bleed valve at the top), bleed the system, then clear and re-test.

P0129.meaning: The atmospheric (barometric) pressure reading is out of range or disagrees with the manifold pressure sensor with the engine off. On many Subarus this sensor is built into the ECU; it is used to correct fueling and boost for altitude, so drivability is usually only mildly affected.
causes: Faulty atmospheric pressure sensor inside the ECU (or the separate sensor on models that have one).
MAP sensor reading wrong, so the two disagree.
Water damage or corrosion affecting the ECU.
Low or unstable system voltage.
Wiring or connector fault on an externally mounted sensor.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Key on, engine off: MAP and atmospheric pressure in live data should match, about 100 kPa at sea level (lower at altitude).
If MAP is the odd one out, fix the MAP sensor first (see its codes); if atmospheric pressure is wrong, check the ECU and its connectors for water damage.
Replace or repair the ECU (or the separate sensor) if the reading stays wrong.

P0130.meaning: The ECU found a fault in the signal circuit of the front oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single front A/F sensor): the signal is out of range or stuck, often reading lean. The ECU falls back to open-loop fueling, so economy and emissions suffer, but it is normally safe to drive.
causes: Aged or contaminated sensor.
Wiring or connector fault (corrosion, or chafing near the exhaust or turbo).
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor letting in outside air (cracked up-pipe or header gaskets on EJ engines).
Genuine lean condition from an intake or vacuum leak.
Sensor heater fault (look for heater codes too).
fixes: Check for other stored codes, especially heater and fuel trim codes, and fix those first.
Watch the front A/F sensor in live data: at warm idle it should hover around 14.7:1 (lambda 1.0), go fully lean when you lift off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and swing rich when you open the throttle.
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring for corrosion, melting or damage.
Check for exhaust leaks before the sensor (listen for ticking at cold start, check gaskets and flanges).
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if wiring and exhaust are good, then clear and re-test.

P0131.meaning: The signal from the front oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single front A/F sensor) is below the range the ECU accepts. The ECU falls back to open-loop fueling, so economy and emissions suffer, but it is normally safe to drive.
causes: Signal wire shorted to ground or chafed through near the exhaust.
Failed or contaminated sensor.
Water or corrosion in the sensor connector.
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor pulling in outside air.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the connector and harness for corrosion, melting or chafing.
Watch the front A/F sensor in live data: at warm idle it should hover around 14.7:1 (lambda 1.0), go fully lean when you lift off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and swing rich when you open the throttle.
Check the wiring between sensor and ECU for continuity and shorts to ground, using the service manual wiring diagram.
Check for exhaust leaks before the sensor.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if the wiring is sound, then clear and re-test.

P0132.meaning: The signal from the front oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single front A/F sensor) is above the range the ECU accepts. The ECU falls back to open-loop fueling, so economy and emissions suffer, but it is normally safe to drive.
causes: Signal wire shorted to a voltage source, sometimes to the heater circuit inside a damaged sensor.
Failed or contaminated sensor (oil, coolant or fuel additives).
Water or corrosion in the sensor connector.
Engine running very rich (leaking injector, high fuel pressure).
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the connector and harness for corrosion, melting or chafing.
Watch the front A/F sensor in live data: at warm idle it should hover around 14.7:1 (lambda 1.0), go fully lean when you lift off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and swing rich when you open the throttle.
Check the wiring between sensor and ECU for shorts to power, using the service manual wiring diagram.
Check fuel trims and look for signs of rich running (black smoke, fuel smell).
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if the wiring is sound, then clear and re-test.

P0133.meaning: The front oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single front A/F sensor) responds too slowly to changes in the air/fuel mixture. Fuel control becomes less precise, so economy and emissions suffer, but it is normally safe to drive.
causes: Aged sensor, the most common cause on high-mileage cars.
Sensor contaminated by oil burning, coolant (for example from a leaking EJ25 head gasket) or silicone sealant.
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor.
Weak sensor heater, so the sensor runs too cool.
Wiring or connector resistance from corrosion.
fixes: Check for heater, misfire or fuel trim codes and fix those first.
Watch the front A/F sensor in live data: at warm idle it should hover around 14.7:1 (lambda 1.0), go fully lean when you lift off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and swing rich when you open the throttle.
Check for exhaust leaks before the sensor.
Inspect the connector for corrosion, and look for signs of oil or coolant consumption.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part, then clear and re-test with a drive that includes some coasting in gear.

P0134.meaning: The signal from the front oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single front A/F sensor) is not changing, as if the sensor were dead or disconnected. The ECU falls back to open-loop fueling, so economy and emissions suffer, but it is normally safe to drive.
causes: Failed sensor.
Sensor heater not working, so the sensor never gets hot enough to switch.
Open circuit in the signal wiring or an unplugged connector.
Exhaust leak or severe contamination masking the reading.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check for heater codes, and make sure the connector is plugged in and clean.
Watch the front A/F sensor in live data: at warm idle it should hover around 14.7:1 (lambda 1.0), go fully lean when you lift off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and swing rich when you open the throttle.
Check the wiring between sensor and ECU for continuity, using the service manual wiring diagram.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if the wiring is sound, then clear and re-test.

P0135.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the heater circuit of the front oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single front A/F sensor): the heater is not drawing the expected current. Some tools label this code 'rear', but bank 1 sensor 1 is the front sensor. Without a working heater the sensor warms up slowly and the ECU stays in open-loop fueling longer; the car is safe to drive, but economy and emissions suffer.
causes: Heater element inside the sensor has burnt out, the most common cause.
Blown fuse or missing power feed to the heater.
Corroded, loose or water-logged connector.
Connector or extension harness damaged or left loose during downpipe, J-pipe or header work.
Heater control wire open or shorted, or an ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check the fuse for the oxygen sensor heaters, and check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Inspect the sensor connector and harness for corrosion, melting or chafing against the exhaust.
Unplug the sensor and measure resistance across the two heater pins; compare with the service manual value (open or near zero means a failed heater).
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the heater feed pin of the harness side, and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if the heater is out of spec, then clear and re-test.

P0136.meaning: The ECU found a fault in the signal circuit of the rear oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single rear sensor). Some tools label this code 'front', but sensor 2 is always the one after the converter. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Failed or aged sensor.
Wiring or connector fault (corrosion, chafing against the exhaust).
Sensor unplugged, damaged or relocated during aftermarket downpipe or exhaust work (common on WRX, STI and other turbo models).
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor.
Heater fault affecting the sensor (look for heater codes too).
fixes: Check for heater codes and fix those first.
Inspect the sensor connector and harness for corrosion, melting or damage.

Watch the rear O2 sensor voltage in live data on a warm engine: it usually sits fairly steady around 0.6 to 0.8 V at cruise, drops below about 0.2 V within a few seconds of lifting off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and rises again when you get back on the throttle.
Check for exhaust leaks between the engine and the sensor.
Replace the sensor if wiring and exhaust are good, then clear and re-test.

P0137.meaning: The voltage from the rear oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single rear sensor) stays too low, so it reads lean all the time. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (flange gaskets, flex joint, cracked pipe) letting in air.
Aged or contaminated sensor.
Signal wire shorted to ground, or a damaged connector.
Engine genuinely running lean (vacuum leak, misfire); check fuel trims.
O2 sensor spacer or aftermarket exhaust changing the reading.
fixes: Watch the rear O2 sensor voltage in live data on a warm engine: it usually sits fairly steady around 0.6 to 0.8 V at cruise, drops below about 0.2 V within a few seconds of lifting off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and rises again when you get back on the throttle.
Snap the throttle open briefly: a good sensor should rise above about 0.6 V as the mixture goes rich.
Check for exhaust leaks between the engine and the sensor.
Inspect the connector and wiring for damage and shorts to ground, and check fuel trims for a real lean condition.
Replace the sensor if it will not respond, then clear and re-test.

P0138.meaning: The voltage from the rear oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single rear sensor) stays too high, so it reads rich all the time. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Signal wire shorted to a voltage source, sometimes to the heater circuit inside a damaged sensor.
Sensor contaminated by oil, coolant or fuel additives.
Engine genuinely running rich (leaking injector, faulty front A/F sensor, high fuel pressure).
Water or corrosion in the connector.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Watch the rear O2 sensor voltage in live data on a warm engine: it usually sits fairly steady around 0.6 to 0.8 V at cruise, drops below about 0.2 V within a few seconds of lifting off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and rises again when you get back on the throttle.
On a lift-off at 2500 to 3000 rpm the voltage should drop below about 0.2 V; if it stays high, suspect the sensor or wiring.
Check fuel trims and the front A/F sensor for a real rich condition.
Inspect the connector and wiring for shorts to power.
Replace the sensor if the engine is not running rich, then clear and re-test.

P0139.meaning: The rear oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single rear sensor) responds too slowly to changes in the air/fuel mixture. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Aged rear sensor, the most common cause.
Exhaust leak near the sensor.
Sensor contaminated by oil, coolant or silicone.
Wiring or connector resistance from corrosion.
Weak sensor heater, so the sensor runs too cool.
fixes: Check for heater and misfire codes and fix those first.

Watch the rear O2 sensor voltage in live data on a warm engine: it usually sits fairly steady around 0.6 to 0.8 V at cruise, drops below about 0.2 V within a few seconds of lifting off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and rises again when you get back on the throttle.
Check for exhaust leaks around the sensor and its flanges.
Inspect the connector for corrosion.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part, then clear and re-test with a drive that includes some coasting in gear.

P013A.meaning: The rear oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single rear sensor) responds too slowly when the mixture changes from rich to lean. The ECU usually runs this test during deceleration fuel cut and the following re-acceleration. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Aged rear sensor, the most common cause.
Exhaust leak near the sensor.
Sensor contaminated by oil, coolant or silicone.
Wiring or connector resistance from corrosion.
Weak sensor heater, so the sensor runs too cool.
fixes: Check for heater and misfire codes and fix those first.

Watch the rear O2 sensor voltage in live data on a warm engine: it usually sits fairly steady around 0.6 to 0.8 V at cruise, drops below about 0.2 V within a few seconds of lifting off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and rises again when you get back on the throttle.
Check for exhaust leaks around the sensor and its flanges.
Inspect the connector for corrosion.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part, then clear and re-test with a drive that includes some coasting in gear.

P013B.meaning: The rear oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single rear sensor) responds too slowly when the mixture changes from lean to rich. The ECU usually runs this test during deceleration fuel cut and the following re-acceleration. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Aged rear sensor, the most common cause.
Exhaust leak near the sensor.
Sensor contaminated by oil, coolant or silicone.
Wiring or connector resistance from corrosion.
Weak sensor heater, so the sensor runs too cool.
fixes: Check for heater and misfire codes and fix those first.

Watch the rear O2 sensor voltage in live data on a warm engine: it usually sits fairly steady around 0.6 to 0.8 V at cruise, drops below about 0.2 V within a few seconds of lifting off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and rises again when you get back on the throttle.
Check for exhaust leaks around the sensor and its flanges.
Inspect the connector for corrosion.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part, then clear and re-test with a drive that includes some coasting in gear.

P013C.meaning: The rear oxygen sensor for bank 2 (bank 2 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; bank 2 is the left side, cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders) responds too slowly when the mixture changes from rich to lean. The ECU usually runs this test during deceleration fuel cut and the following re-acceleration. Bank 2 oxygen sensors are only fitted where each cylinder bank has its own sensor, mainly some six-cylinder (EZ30, EZ36) models. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Aged rear sensor, the most common cause.
Exhaust leak near the sensor.
Sensor contaminated by oil, coolant or silicone.
Wiring or connector resistance from corrosion.
Weak sensor heater, so the sensor runs too cool.
fixes: If your car has no such sensor, confirm the code with a generic OBD-II scanner first, as it may be a misread rather than a real fault.
Check for heater and misfire codes and fix those first.

Watch the bank 2 rear O2 sensor voltage in live data on a warm engine: it usually sits fairly steady around 0.6 to 0.8 V at cruise, drops below about 0.2 V within a few seconds of lifting off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and rises again when you get back on the throttle.
Check for exhaust leaks around the sensor and its flanges.
Inspect the connector for corrosion.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part, then clear and re-test with a drive that includes some coasting in gear.

P013D.meaning: The rear oxygen sensor for bank 2 (bank 2 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; bank 2 is the left side, cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders) responds too slowly when the mixture changes from lean to rich. The ECU usually runs this test during deceleration fuel cut and the following re-acceleration. Bank 2 oxygen sensors are only fitted where each cylinder bank has its own sensor, mainly some six-cylinder (EZ30, EZ36) models. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.

Exhaust leak near the sensor.
Sensor contaminated by oil, coolant or silicone.
Wiring or connector resistance from corrosion.
Weak sensor heater, so the sensor runs too cool.

Check for heater and misfire codes and fix those first.

Watch the bank 2 rear O2 sensor voltage in live data on a warm engine: it usually sits fairly steady around 0.6 to 0.8 V at cruise, drops below about 0.2 V within a few seconds of lifting off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and rises again when you get back on the throttle.
Check for exhaust leaks around the sensor and its flanges.
Inspect the connector for corrosion.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part, then clear and re-test with a drive that includes some coasting in gear.

P013E.meaning: The rear oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single rear sensor) is too slow to start responding when the mixture changes from rich to lean. The ECU usually runs this test during deceleration fuel cut and the following re-acceleration. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.

Exhaust leak near the sensor.
Sensor contaminated by oil, coolant or silicone.

Watch the rear O2 sensor voltage in live data on a warm engine: it usually sits fairly steady around 0.6 to 0.8 V at cruise, drops below about 0.2 V within a few seconds of lifting off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and rises again when you get back on the throttle.
Check for exhaust leaks around the sensor and its flanges.
Inspect the connector for corrosion.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part, then clear and re-test with a drive that includes some coasting in gear.

P013F.meaning: The rear oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single rear sensor) is too slow to start responding when the mixture changes from lean to rich. The ECU usually runs this test during deceleration fuel cut and the following re-acceleration. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.

Exhaust leak near the sensor.

Weak sensor heater, so the sensor runs too cool.

Check for exhaust leaks around the sensor and its flanges.
Inspect the connector for corrosion.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part, then clear and re-test with a drive that includes some coasting in gear.

P0140.meaning: The signal from the rear oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single rear sensor) is outside its expected range or not changing, as if the sensor were dead or disconnected. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Failed sensor.
Open circuit in the signal wiring or an unplugged connector.
Sensor unplugged, damaged or relocated during aftermarket downpipe or exhaust work (common on WRX, STI and other turbo models).
Sensor heater not working, so the sensor never gets hot enough.
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor.
fixes: Check for heater codes, and make sure the connector is plugged in and clean.

Watch the rear O2 sensor voltage in live data on a warm engine: it usually sits fairly steady around 0.6 to 0.8 V at cruise, drops below about 0.2 V within a few seconds of lifting off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and rises again when you get back on the throttle.
Check the wiring between sensor and ECU for continuity, using the service manual wiring diagram.
Replace the sensor if the wiring is sound, then clear and re-test.

P0141.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the heater circuit of the rear oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single rear sensor): the heater is not drawing the expected current. On Subarus this code points at the rear sensor's heater rather than its signal. Driving is safe, but the ECU cannot properly monitor the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Heater element inside the sensor has burnt out, the most common cause.
Blown fuse or missing power feed to the heater.
Corroded, loose or water-logged connector.
Sensor unplugged, damaged or relocated during aftermarket downpipe or exhaust work (common on WRX, STI and other turbo models).
Heater control wire open or shorted, or an ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check the fuse for the oxygen sensor heaters, and check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Inspect the sensor connector and harness for corrosion, melting or chafing against the exhaust.
Unplug the sensor and measure resistance across the two heater pins; compare with the service manual value (open or near zero means a failed heater).
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the heater feed pin of the harness side, and check the control wire to the ECU for breaks or shorts.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if the heater is out of spec, then clear and re-test.

P0142.meaning: The ECU found a fault in the signal circuit of oxygen sensor 3 for bank 1 (a third sensor further down the exhaust, typically after a second catalytic converter). Most Subarus have no sensor 3. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.

Wiring or connector fault (corrosion, chafing against the exhaust).

Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor.
Heater fault affecting the sensor (look for heater codes too).
