Check for exhaust leaks between the engine and the sensor.
Replace the sensor if wiring and exhaust are good, then clear and re-test.

P0143.meaning: The voltage from oxygen sensor 3 for bank 1 (a third sensor further down the exhaust, typically after a second catalytic converter) stays too low, so it reads lean all the time. Most Subarus have no sensor 3. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (flange gaskets, flex joint, cracked pipe) letting in air.
Aged or contaminated sensor.
Signal wire shorted to ground, or a damaged connector.
Engine genuinely running lean (vacuum leak, misfire); check fuel trims.

fixes: If your car has no such sensor, confirm the code with a generic OBD-II scanner first, as it may be a misread rather than a real fault.

On a lift-off at 2500 to 3000 rpm the voltage should drop below about 0.2 V; if it stays high, suspect the sensor or wiring.

P0145.meaning: Oxygen sensor 3 for bank 1 (a third sensor further down the exhaust, typically after a second catalytic converter) responds too slowly to changes in the air/fuel mixture. Most Subarus have no sensor 3. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Aged rear sensor, the most common cause.
Exhaust leak near the sensor.
Sensor contaminated by oil, coolant or silicone.
Wiring or connector resistance from corrosion.

Watch the sensor 3 voltage (if your ECU reports it) in live data on a warm engine: it usually sits fairly steady around 0.6 to 0.8 V at cruise, drops below about 0.2 V within a few seconds of lifting off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and rises again when you get back on the throttle.

Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part, then clear and re-test with a drive that includes some coasting in gear.

Most Subarus have no sensor 3. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.

P014A.meaning: The rear oxygen sensor for bank 2 (bank 2 sensor 2, after the catalytic converter; bank 2 is the left side, cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders) is too slow to start responding when the mixture changes from rich to lean. The ECU usually runs this test during deceleration fuel cut and the following re-acceleration. Bank 2 oxygen sensors are only fitted where each cylinder bank has its own sensor, mainly some six-cylinder (EZ30, EZ36) models. It does not hurt the engine, but the ECU cannot properly check the catalytic converter until it is fixed.
causes: Aged rear sensor, the most common cause.
Exhaust leak near the sensor.
Sensor contaminated by oil, coolant or silicone.
Wiring or connector resistance from corrosion.
Weak sensor heater, so the sensor runs too cool.

Watch the bank 2 rear O2 sensor voltage in live data on a warm engine: it usually sits fairly steady around 0.6 to 0.8 V at cruise, drops below about 0.2 V within a few seconds of lifting off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and rises again when you get back on the throttle.
Check for exhaust leaks around the sensor and its flanges.
Inspect the connector for corrosion.

P014C.meaning: The front oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single front A/F sensor) responds too slowly when the mixture changes from rich to lean. Fuel control becomes less precise, so economy and emissions suffer, but it is normally safe to drive.
causes: Aged sensor, the most common cause on high-mileage cars.
Sensor contaminated by oil burning, coolant (for example from a leaking EJ25 head gasket) or silicone sealant.
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor.
Weak sensor heater, so the sensor runs too cool.
Wiring or connector resistance from corrosion.
fixes: Check for heater, misfire or fuel trim codes and fix those first.
Watch the front A/F sensor in live data: at warm idle it should hover around 14.7:1 (lambda 1.0), go fully lean when you lift off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and swing rich when you open the throttle.
Check for exhaust leaks before the sensor.
Inspect the connector for corrosion, and look for signs of oil or coolant consumption.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part, then clear and re-test with a drive that includes some coasting in gear.

P014D.meaning: The front oxygen sensor (bank 1 sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinders this is the single front A/F sensor) responds too slowly when the mixture changes from lean to rich. Fuel control becomes less precise, so economy and emissions suffer, but it is normally safe to drive.

Watch the front A/F sensor in live data: at warm idle it should hover around 14.7:1 (lambda 1.0), go fully lean when you lift off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and swing rich when you open the throttle.
Check for exhaust leaks before the sensor.
Inspect the connector for corrosion, and look for signs of oil or coolant consumption.

Bank 2 oxygen sensors are only fitted where each cylinder bank has its own sensor, mainly some six-cylinder (EZ30, EZ36) models. P0150.meaning: The ECU found a fault in the signal circuit of the front oxygen sensor for bank 2 (bank 2 sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; bank 2 is the left side, cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders): the signal is out of range or stuck, often reading lean. Bank 2 oxygen sensors are only fitted where each cylinder bank has its own sensor, mainly some six-cylinder (EZ30, EZ36) models. The ECU falls back to open-loop fueling, so economy and emissions suffer, but it is normally safe to drive.
causes: Aged or contaminated sensor.
Wiring or connector fault (corrosion, or chafing near the exhaust or turbo).
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor letting in outside air (cracked up-pipe or header gaskets on EJ engines).
Genuine lean condition from an intake or vacuum leak.
Sensor heater fault (look for heater codes too).
fixes: If your car has no such sensor, confirm the code with a generic OBD-II scanner first, as it may be a misread rather than a real fault.
Check for other stored codes, especially heater and fuel trim codes, and fix those first.

Watch the bank 2 front A/F sensor in live data: at warm idle it should hover around 14.7:1 (lambda 1.0), go fully lean when you lift off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and swing rich when you open the throttle.
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring for corrosion, melting or damage.
Check for exhaust leaks before the sensor (listen for ticking at cold start, check gaskets and flanges).
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if wiring and exhaust are good, then clear and re-test.

P0151.meaning: The signal from the front oxygen sensor for bank 2 (bank 2 sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; bank 2 is the left side, cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders) is below the range the ECU accepts. Bank 2 oxygen sensors are only fitted where each cylinder bank has its own sensor, mainly some six-cylinder (EZ30, EZ36) models. The ECU falls back to open-loop fueling, so economy and emissions suffer, but it is normally safe to drive.
causes: Signal wire shorted to ground or chafed through near the exhaust.
Failed or contaminated sensor.
Water or corrosion in the sensor connector.
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor pulling in outside air.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: If your car has no such sensor, confirm the code with a generic OBD-II scanner first, as it may be a misread rather than a real fault.
Inspect the connector and harness for corrosion, melting or chafing.

Watch the bank 2 front A/F sensor in live data: at warm idle it should hover around 14.7:1 (lambda 1.0), go fully lean when you lift off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and swing rich when you open the throttle.
Check the wiring between sensor and ECU for continuity and shorts to ground, using the service manual wiring diagram.
Check for exhaust leaks before the sensor.
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if the wiring is sound, then clear and re-test.

P0152.meaning: The signal from the front oxygen sensor for bank 2 (bank 2 sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; bank 2 is the left side, cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders) is above the range the ECU accepts. Bank 2 oxygen sensors are only fitted where each cylinder bank has its own sensor, mainly some six-cylinder (EZ30, EZ36) models. The ECU falls back to open-loop fueling, so economy and emissions suffer, but it is normally safe to drive.
causes: Signal wire shorted to a voltage source, sometimes to the heater circuit inside a damaged sensor.
Failed or contaminated sensor (oil, coolant or fuel additives).

Engine running very rich (leaking injector, high fuel pressure).
ECU fault (rare).

Inspect the connector and harness for corrosion, melting or chafing.

Watch the bank 2 front A/F sensor in live data: at warm idle it should hover around 14.7:1 (lambda 1.0), go fully lean when you lift off at 2500 to 3000 rpm, and swing rich when you open the throttle.
Check the wiring between sensor and ECU for shorts to power, using the service manual wiring diagram.
Check fuel trims and look for signs of rich running (black smoke, fuel smell).
Replace the sensor with an OEM-spec part if the wiring is sound, then clear and re-test.

P0153.meaning: The ECU found that the bank 2 upstream sensor (bank 2 sensor 1: before the catalytic converter on the left side, cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders) reacts too slowly to changes in the mixture. It is safe to drive short term, but fuel economy and emissions suffer and the catalytic converter can be stressed over time.
causes: An aged or contaminated sensor (oil burning, coolant from a head gasket leak, or silicone sealant can coat the tip).
An exhaust leak ahead of the sensor, such as a leaking header or up-pipe gasket, pulling in outside air.
A weak sensor heater, so the sensor runs too cold to respond quickly.
A mixture problem on bank 2, such as a vacuum leak or a lazy injector, that upsets the test.
Damaged wiring or a corroded connector adding resistance to the signal.
fixes: Check for other codes first (misfire, fuel trim, heater codes) and fix those before condemning the sensor.
Inspect the exhaust from the head to the sensor for leaks: listen for ticking at cold start and look for soot trails at the gaskets.
Inspect the sensor connector and harness for heat damage, chafing and corrosion.
Watch the bank 2 A/F sensor in live data while blipping the throttle and lifting off: the reading should swing rich and lean quickly and smoothly, not lag or sit flat.
Replace the sensor with the correct OEM-type part (on most Subarus sensor 1 is a wideband A/F sensor, not a simple switching O2 sensor), then clear and re-test.

P0154.meaning: The ECU sees no usable signal from the bank 2 upstream sensor (bank 2 sensor 1: before the catalytic converter on the left side, cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders), as if the circuit were open. The engine falls back to less precise fuel control, so it is drivable but economy and emissions suffer and it should be fixed soon.
causes: An unplugged, loose or corroded connector at the sensor or along the harness.
A broken signal wire, often heat-damaged or chafed near the exhaust.
A failed sensor element with an internal open circuit.
A dead sensor heater, keeping the sensor too cold to produce a signal.
Rarely, a fault in the ECU input.
fixes: Check that the sensor connector is fully seated and locked, and look for green corrosion or pushed-back pins.
Inspect the harness from the sensor to the main loom for melted insulation or breaks, especially where it runs near the exhaust.
Check the heater: with the key on there should be battery voltage (about 12 V) on the heater feed, and the heater resistance should match the service manual value.
Watch the bank 2 A/F sensor in live data: a reading stuck at one value that never moves points to an open circuit or a dead sensor.
With the battery disconnected, check continuity of each wire from the sensor connector to the ECU connector; expect close to 0 ohms.
Replace the sensor if the wiring checks out, then clear and re-test.

P0156.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the circuit of the bank 2 downstream oxygen sensor (bank 2 sensor 2: after the catalytic converter on the left side). This sensor mainly checks the catalytic converter, so the car usually drives normally, but the catalyst monitor cannot run and an emissions test will fail.
causes: A failed oxygen sensor.
A damaged, corroded or unplugged connector, or wiring chafed or melted near the exhaust.
An exhaust leak near the sensor.
A sensor heater fault keeping the sensor too cold.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the sensor connector and harness under the car for damage from heat, road debris or corrosion, and reseat the connector.

Watch the rear O2 sensor voltage in live data once the engine is fully warm: it should move within about 0.1 to 0.9 V and, with a healthy cat, sit fairly steady around 0.5 to 0.8 V at a steady cruise.
Check for exhaust leaks at the flanges and flex joint near the sensor.
Check the heater resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Replace the sensor if the wiring and exhaust are good, then clear and re-test.

P0157.meaning: The bank 2 downstream oxygen sensor (bank 2 sensor 2: after the catalytic converter on the left side) has read lower than expected for too long, as if the exhaust were always lean. It is often a sensor or wiring fault, but a real lean condition or an exhaust leak can cause it too; the car usually drives normally.
causes: A failed sensor stuck at a low voltage.
The signal wire shorted to ground or a damaged harness.
An exhaust leak ahead of the sensor letting in outside air.
A real lean condition, such as a vacuum leak or weak fuel delivery.
A contaminated sensor.
fixes: Check fuel trims first: if A/F learning is strongly positive (more than about +10%), chase the lean condition before replacing the sensor.
Inspect the exhaust near the sensor for leaks at gaskets, flanges and the flex joint.
Inspect the sensor wiring for chafing against the body or exhaust where it could short to ground.
Watch the rear O2 sensor in live data: during a firm acceleration it should rise above about 0.8 V; one that stays near 0.1 V while the front A/F sensor shows a normal mixture is faulty.
Replace the sensor if the wiring and exhaust are good, then clear and re-test.

P0158.meaning: The bank 2 downstream oxygen sensor (bank 2 sensor 2: after the catalytic converter on the left side) is reading higher than it should, as if the exhaust were always rich or the signal were shorted to voltage. The car usually drives normally, but check that the engine is not really running rich.
causes: A failed sensor with an internal short.
The signal wire shorted to a voltage source, for example melted against the heater wire in the harness.
The engine really running rich (leaking injector, high fuel pressure, faulty front A/F sensor).
A sensor contaminated by fuel, oil or coolant.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check fuel trims: if A/F learning is strongly negative (beyond about -10%), fix the rich condition first.
Inspect the sensor harness for melted or fused sections, especially where it passes near the exhaust.
Watch the rear O2 sensor in live data during a lift-off from about 3000 rpm: a good sensor drops toward 0.1 V during fuel cut; one stuck above 0.9 V is faulty or shorted.
Unplug the sensor with the key on and see if the ECU reading changes; if it still reads high, the fault is in the wiring.
Replace the sensor if the wiring is good, then clear and re-test.

P0159.meaning: The ECU found that the bank 2 downstream oxygen sensor (bank 2 sensor 2: after the catalytic converter on the left side) responds too slowly to changes in the exhaust. The car usually drives normally, but the catalyst monitor becomes unreliable and emissions checks can fail.
causes: An aged or worn sensor.
A sensor contaminated by oil burning, coolant or silicone.
An exhaust leak near the sensor.
A weak sensor heater.
Extra resistance in the wiring or connector.
fixes: Check for other codes (misfire, fuel trim, heater) and fix those first.
Inspect the connector and wiring, and check for exhaust leaks near the sensor.
Watch the rear O2 sensor in live data: on a lift-off from about 3000 rpm it should drop to near 0.1 V within a few seconds, and rise above about 0.8 V on a firm acceleration.
Check the heater resistance against the service manual value.
Replace the sensor, then clear and re-test.

P015A.meaning: The ECU found that the bank 1 upstream air/fuel sensor (bank 1 sensor 1: before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinder Subarus this single front sensor covers the whole engine) reacts too slowly when the mixture goes from rich to lean, for example when fuel is cut on deceleration. It is safe to drive short term, but fuel control and emissions suffer.
causes: An aged or contaminated A/F sensor (oil burning or coolant from a head gasket leak coat the tip).
An exhaust leak before the sensor, such as the up-pipe or header gaskets on EJ turbos or a cracked flange.
A weak sensor heater.
A corroded connector or damaged wiring.
A mixture problem, such as a leaking injector, that keeps the exhaust rich longer than expected.
fixes: Check for other codes (misfire, fuel trim, A/F heater) and fix those first.
Inspect the exhaust from the heads to the sensor for leaks: listen for ticking at cold start and look for soot trails.
Inspect and reseat the sensor connector, and check the harness for heat damage.
Watch the A/F sensor #1 reading in live data on a lift-off from about 3000 rpm: when fuel cut starts it should jump to a very lean reading almost immediately, not drift there slowly.
Replace the A/F sensor with an OEM-type wideband sensor, then clear and re-test.

P015B.meaning: The ECU found that the bank 1 upstream air/fuel sensor (bank 1 sensor 1: before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinder Subarus this single front sensor covers the whole engine) reacts too slowly when the mixture goes from lean to rich, for example when fuel returns after deceleration. It is safe to drive short term, but fuel control and emissions suffer.

Watch the A/F sensor #1 reading in live data: after a lift-off, when you press the throttle again the reading should return to around 14.7:1 (or richer under load) almost immediately.
Replace the A/F sensor with an OEM-type wideband sensor, then clear and re-test.

Replace the A/F sensor with an OEM-type wideband sensor, then clear and re-test.

It is safe to drive short term, but fuel control and emissions suffer.
causes: An aged or contaminated A/F sensor (oil burning or coolant from a head gasket leak coat the tip).

A weak sensor heater.
A corroded connector or damaged wiring.
A vacuum leak or weak injector on bank 2 that keeps the mixture lean longer than expected.
fixes: Check for other codes (misfire, fuel trim, A/F heater) and fix those first.
Inspect the bank 2 exhaust from the head to the sensor for leaks: listen for ticking at cold start and look for soot trails.
Inspect and reseat the sensor connector, and check the harness for heat damage.
Watch the bank 2 A/F sensor in live data: after a lift-off, when you press the throttle again the reading should return to around 14.7:1 (or richer under load) almost immediately, just like bank 1.
Replace the A/F sensor with an OEM-type wideband sensor, then clear and re-test.

P0160.meaning: The bank 2 downstream oxygen sensor (bank 2 sensor 2: after the catalytic converter on the left side) gives a signal that is out of the expected range or does not behave as expected for the driving conditions. The car usually drives normally, but the catalyst monitor cannot be trusted until it is fixed.
causes: An aged or failed sensor.
An exhaust leak near the sensor.
Damaged wiring or a corroded connector.
A mixture problem (rich or lean running) that pushes the reading outside the expected range.
A sensor heater fault.
fixes: Check for other codes and look at fuel trims; fix any rich or lean condition first.
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring, and check for exhaust leaks near the sensor.
Watch the rear O2 sensor in live data once fully warm: it should move within about 0.1 to 0.9 V, drop low on a lift-off and rise high on a firm acceleration.
Check the heater resistance against the service manual value.
Replace the sensor if the checks point to it, then clear and re-test.

P0161.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the heater circuit of the bank 2 downstream oxygen sensor (bank 2 sensor 2: after the catalytic converter on the left side). The heater brings the sensor up to working temperature quickly; without it the catalyst monitor is delayed, but the car drives normally.
causes: A burned-out heater element inside the sensor (the most common cause).
A blown fuse on the heater supply.
A corroded connector or broken wire in the heater circuit.
Rarely, a faulty heater driver in the ECU.
fixes: Check the fuse that feeds the oxygen sensor heaters (see the fuse box label or owner's manual).
Inspect and reseat the sensor connector, and look for heat damage on the harness.
Measure resistance across the heater terminals of the sensor and compare with the service manual value; an open reading means the heater is dead.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the heater feed on the harness side.
Replace the sensor if the heater is open, then clear and re-test.

P0162.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the circuit of the bank 2 sensor 3 oxygen sensor, a third sensor further down the exhaust (after a second catalytic converter) on the left side. Only a few Subaru variants have a sensor 3, so confirm which sensor is meant in the service manual for your model; the car usually drives normally.
causes: A failed oxygen sensor.
Damaged, corroded or unplugged wiring or connector.
An exhaust leak near the sensor.
A sensor heater fault.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Identify the sensor 3 location for your model in the service manual.
Inspect the connector and harness under the car for damage from heat, road debris or corrosion, and reseat the connector.
Check for exhaust leaks near the sensor.
Check the heater resistance against the service manual value.
Replace the sensor if the wiring and exhaust are good, then clear and re-test.

P0165.meaning: The ECU found that the bank 2 sensor 3 oxygen sensor (a third sensor further down the exhaust, after a second catalytic converter, on the left side) responds too slowly. Only a few Subaru variants have a sensor 3; the car usually drives normally, but emissions monitoring is affected.
causes: An aged or worn sensor.
A sensor contaminated by oil burning, coolant or silicone.
An exhaust leak near the sensor.
A weak sensor heater.
Extra resistance in the wiring or connector.
fixes: Check for other codes (misfire, fuel trim, heater) and fix those first.
Identify the sensor 3 location for your model, then inspect its connector and wiring.
Check for exhaust leaks near the sensor.
Check the heater resistance against the service manual value.
Replace the sensor, then clear and re-test.

P0170.meaning: The ECU's fuel trim for bank 1 has hit its limit, meaning it can no longer correct the mixture; this general code can mean either too lean or too rich. On four-cylinder Subarus bank 1 covers the whole engine; the car usually drives, but find the cause soon, especially on turbo engines where a lean mixture risks knock.
causes: Unmetered air: cracked PCV or breather hoses, a split intake boot, or (on EJ turbos) a cracked turbo inlet hose.
A dirty or faulty MAF sensor, or an aftermarket intake that changes the MAF reading.
Weak fuel delivery: failing fuel pump, clogged filter or faulty pressure regulator.
Leaking or clogged injectors.
A faulty front A/F sensor, or an exhaust leak before it.
An EVAP purge valve stuck open (rich).
fixes: Check A/F correction and A/F learning (Subaru's short and long term fuel trims) in live data at idle and at a steady 2500 rpm: combined within about +/-10% is normal; a large positive number means lean, a large negative number means rich.
Inspect the intake boot, PCV and breather hoses and all vacuum lines for cracks; squeeze hoses, since cracks often hide on the underside.
Clean the MAF sensor with dedicated MAF cleaner and check that MAF g/s rises smoothly with rpm.
Have the intake smoke tested for leaks you cannot see.
Check fuel pressure with a gauge and compare with the service manual value.
After the repair, clear and re-test, and check that fuel trims settle near zero.

P0171.meaning: The ECU is adding more fuel than it is allowed to because the engine is getting more air than the MAF sensor measured, or too little fuel. On four-cylinder Subarus this covers the whole engine; on turbo engines, running lean under boost can cause detonation, so drive gently until it is fixed.
causes: Unmetered air: cracked PCV or breather hoses, a split intake boot, a leaking intake manifold gasket or brake booster hose.
On EJ turbos, a cracked turbo inlet hose or leaking breather hoses at the turbo inlet, letting in air the MAF never saw.
A dirty or faulty MAF sensor, or an aftermarket intake that changes the MAF reading.
Weak fuel delivery: failing fuel pump, clogged filter or faulty fuel pressure regulator.
Clogged or dirty injectors.
An exhaust leak before the front A/F sensor, which makes the mixture look lean.
fixes: Check fuel trims in live data: if A/F learning is high at idle but closer to normal at 2500 rpm, suspect a vacuum leak; if it is high everywhere, suspect fuel delivery or the MAF.
Inspect every vacuum and breather hose, the intake boot and (on turbos) the turbo inlet for cracks; squeeze hoses, since cracks often hide on the underside.
Clean the MAF sensor with dedicated MAF cleaner and check live MAF g/s: it should rise smoothly with rpm; compare with a known-good value for your engine.
Have the intake smoke tested to find leaks you cannot see.
Check fuel pressure with a gauge and compare with the service manual value.
Check the exhaust for leaks ahead of the A/F sensor, then clear and re-test after repairs.

P0172.meaning: The ECU is pulling out more fuel than it is allowed to because the mixture keeps reading rich. On four-cylinder Subarus this covers the whole engine; it can foul plugs and overheat the catalytic converter, so fix it soon.
causes: A leaking or stuck-open injector.
Fuel pressure too high: a faulty pressure regulator or a blocked return line.
A MAF sensor over-reading, or on turbos an atmospheric blow-off valve venting air the MAF already measured.
An EVAP purge valve stuck open, sending extra fuel vapour into the intake.
A coolant temperature sensor reading too cold, so the ECU adds fuel.
A faulty front A/F sensor, or fuel-diluted oil feeding vapour through the PCV system.
fixes: Check live data: A/F learning strongly negative (beyond about -10%) confirms the ECU is pulling fuel; also check that coolant temperature reads roughly 85 to 100 °C once warm.
On turbo cars with an aftermarket blow-off valve, fit a recirculating valve or have the tune adjusted.
Test the purge valve: with no power it should not let air through when you blow into it.
Clean or test the MAF sensor and compare MAF g/s with a known-good value.
Check fuel pressure against the service manual value, and look for fuel in the regulator vacuum hose (a sign of a leaking diaphragm).
Smell the oil for fuel, and have the injectors leak-down and flow tested if the other checks pass.

P0174.meaning: The ECU is adding more fuel than it is allowed to on bank 2 (the left side, cylinders 2, 4 and 6), which usually means extra air or too little fuel on that side. This code mainly appears on six-cylinder EZ30/EZ36 engines; drive gently until it is fixed.
causes: A vacuum leak on the bank 2 side, such as a leaking intake manifold gasket or cracked hose.
Shared causes if bank 1 is lean too: cracked PCV hoses, a split intake boot, or a dirty or faulty MAF sensor.
Weak fuel delivery: failing fuel pump, clogged filter or faulty pressure regulator.
Clogged injectors on bank 2.
An exhaust leak before the bank 2 A/F sensor, or a faulty bank 2 A/F sensor.
fixes: Compare fuel trims for both banks in live data: if both are lean, look at shared causes (MAF, fuel pressure, PCV); if only bank 2 is lean, focus on that side.
Inspect the vacuum hoses, PCV hoses and intake boot for cracks.
Clean the MAF sensor with dedicated MAF cleaner and check that MAF g/s rises smoothly with rpm.
Have the intake smoke tested, paying attention to the bank 2 runners.
Check fuel pressure against the service manual value.
Check the bank 2 exhaust for leaks before the A/F sensor, then clear and re-test after repairs.

P0175.meaning: The ECU is pulling out more fuel than it is allowed to on bank 2 (the left side, cylinders 2, 4 and 6) because the mixture keeps reading rich. This code mainly appears on six-cylinder EZ30/EZ36 engines; fix it soon to protect the plugs and catalytic converter.
causes: A leaking or stuck-open injector on bank 2.
Shared causes if bank 1 is rich too: high fuel pressure, a MAF sensor over-reading, or an EVAP purge valve stuck open.
A coolant temperature sensor reading too cold.
A faulty bank 2 A/F sensor.
Fuel-diluted oil feeding vapour through the PCV system.
fixes: Compare fuel trims for both banks in live data: if both are rich, look at shared causes; if only bank 2 is rich, focus on its injectors and A/F sensor.
Check that coolant temperature reads roughly 85 to 100 °C once warm.
Test the purge valve: with no power it should not let air through when you blow into it.
Check fuel pressure against the service manual value.
Check the bank 2 A/F sensor response in live data, then have the bank 2 injectors leak-down and flow tested if needed.

P0181.meaning: The fuel temperature sensor (on most Subarus part of the fuel pump and sender unit in the tank) gives a reading that does not make sense, for example it does not match other temperatures after the car has stood overnight. The ECU uses it mainly for EVAP leak testing, so the car drives normally but EVAP monitoring is affected.
causes: A failing sensor inside the fuel pump assembly.
A corroded or loose connector at the top of the fuel pump, usually under the rear seat access cover.
Damaged wiring between the tank and the ECU.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: After the car has stood overnight, compare fuel temperature (if your ECU reports it) with intake air and coolant temperature in live data: they should be within a few degrees.
Remove the access cover under the rear seat and inspect the fuel pump connector for corrosion and loose pins.
Measure the sensor resistance at a known temperature and compare with the service manual value.
Check the wiring from the pump connector to the ECU for damage.
Replace the sensor or fuel pump assembly if the sensor is out of spec, then clear and re-test.

P0182.meaning: The fuel temperature sensor (on most Subarus part of the fuel pump and sender unit in the tank) signal voltage is too low, which the ECU reads as an impossibly hot fuel temperature. The car drives normally, but EVAP monitoring is affected.
causes: The signal wire shorted to ground, for example pinched or chafed.
An internally shorted sensor.
Water or corrosion in the connector at the fuel pump.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the fuel temperature reading in live data if your ECU reports it; a very high value on a cold car confirms the fault.
Inspect the connector at the fuel pump (under the rear seat access cover) for water and corrosion.
Unplug the sensor: if the reading jumps to very cold, the wiring is fine and the sensor is shorted.
Check the harness for a short to ground between the tank and the ECU.
Replace the sensor or fuel pump assembly, or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0183.meaning: The fuel temperature sensor (on most Subarus part of the fuel pump and sender unit in the tank) signal voltage is too high, which the ECU reads as an impossibly cold fuel temperature, usually from an open circuit. The car drives normally, but EVAP monitoring is affected.
causes: An unplugged or loose connector at the fuel pump.
A broken signal or ground wire.
An open circuit inside the sensor.
A signal wire shorted to a voltage source.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the fuel temperature reading in live data if your ECU reports it; a very low value on a warm car confirms the fault.
Inspect the connector at the fuel pump (under the rear seat access cover), especially if the pump was recently replaced.
Measure the sensor resistance and compare with the service manual value; an open reading means a failed sensor.
Check continuity of the signal and ground wires from the pump connector to the ECU.
Replace the sensor or fuel pump assembly, or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0191.meaning: The fuel rail pressure sensor reading does not match what the ECU expects for the conditions. This sensor is used on direct injection petrol engines (FA20 and FA20DIT) and the common-rail EE20 diesel; the ECU may limit power, so fix it soon.
causes: A low-pressure supply problem: weak in-tank pump, clogged fuel filter or (on the diesel) air in the fuel.
A weak or faulty high-pressure pump, or on the diesel a sticking suction control valve.
A faulty rail pressure sensor.
Damaged wiring or a corroded connector.
Running the tank very low, or poor quality fuel.
fixes: Top up the tank; on the diesel, replace the fuel filter if it is due and bleed any air from the system.
Inspect the rail pressure sensor connector and harness for damage, oil contamination and corrosion.
Compare actual and target rail pressure in live data if your ECU reports them: actual should track target closely at idle and during acceleration.
Check for a stable 5 V reference and a good ground at the sensor connector with the key on.
Have the low-pressure supply measured; if it is good, suspect the high-pressure pump, the suction control valve (diesel) or the sensor, then clear and re-test after repair.

P0192.meaning: The fuel rail pressure sensor signal is below its valid range, usually a wiring or sensor fault. This sensor is used on direct injection petrol engines (FA20 and FA20DIT) and the common-rail EE20 diesel; expect limp mode, poor running or a no-start.
causes: A signal wire open or shorted to ground.
Loss of the 5 V reference to the sensor, sometimes pulled down by another shorted sensor on the same supply.
A corroded or loose connector.
A failed rail pressure sensor.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the rail pressure sensor connector, looking for corrosion and bent pins.
With the key on, check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground at the connector.
Watch rail pressure in live data while wiggling the harness; dropouts point to a wiring fault.
Check the signal wire for continuity to the ECU and for shorts to ground.
Replace the sensor (on some engines it is part of the rail) if the wiring is good, then clear and re-test.

P0193.meaning: The fuel rail pressure sensor signal is above its valid range, usually a wiring or sensor fault. This sensor is used on direct injection petrol engines (FA20 and FA20DIT) and the common-rail EE20 diesel; expect limp mode, poor running or a no-start.
causes: A signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage.
An open ground wire to the sensor.
A corroded or loose connector.
A failed rail pressure sensor.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the rail pressure sensor connector, looking for corrosion and bent pins.
With the key on, check the reference wire is about 5 V (not higher) and the ground wire has good continuity to ground.
Check the rail pressure reading in live data with the engine off after it has stood for a while: a high or jumping value points to the sensor or wiring.
Check the signal wire for shorts to other wires in the harness.
Replace the sensor (on some engines it is part of the rail) if the wiring is good, then clear and re-test.

P0196.meaning: The engine oil temperature sensor reading is implausible, for example it does not warm up along with the coolant or it jumps around. The ECU uses oil temperature for AVCS cam timing and engine protection on engines that have this sensor, so cam timing may be less precise; the car is usually drivable.
causes: A failing oil temperature sensor.
A corroded or loose connector, or damaged wiring.
Low engine oil level.
A thermostat stuck open, so the engine and oil warm up too slowly.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the oil level and top up if needed.
After the car has stood overnight, compare oil temperature with coolant and intake air temperature in live data: they should be within a few degrees.
Warm the engine and watch both temperatures: oil should rise steadily and end up near or a little above coolant temperature; coolant that stays well below about 80 °C points to the thermostat.
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring.
Measure the sensor resistance at a known temperature against the service manual value, and replace the sensor if it is out of spec.

P0197.meaning: The engine oil temperature sensor signal voltage is too low, which the ECU reads as an impossibly hot oil temperature. The ECU may use a substitute value, so cam timing and engine protection strategies can be affected; the car is usually drivable.
causes: The signal wire shorted to ground, for example chafed on the engine.
An internally shorted sensor.
Oil or water inside the connector.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the oil temperature reading in live data on a cold engine: a very high value confirms the fault.
Inspect the connector for oil or water inside and clean or replace it.
Unplug the sensor: if the reading jumps to very cold, the wiring is fine and the sensor is shorted.
Check the harness for a short to ground between the sensor and the ECU.
Replace the sensor or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0198.meaning: The engine oil temperature sensor signal voltage is too high, which the ECU reads as an impossibly cold oil temperature, usually from an open circuit. The ECU may use a substitute value, so cam timing and engine protection strategies can be affected; the car is usually drivable.
causes: An unplugged or loose connector.
A broken signal or ground wire.
An open circuit inside the sensor.
A signal wire shorted to a voltage source.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the oil temperature reading in live data on a warm engine: a very low value confirms the fault.
Inspect and reseat the sensor connector, especially after recent engine work.
Measure the sensor resistance and compare with the service manual value; an open reading means a failed sensor.
Check continuity of the signal and ground wires from the sensor to the ECU.
Replace the sensor or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0201.meaning: The ECU detected an electrical fault in the injector circuit for cylinder 1 (front right, bank 1). That cylinder may not be getting fuel, which causes a misfire, rough running and possible catalytic converter damage, so avoid hard driving until it is fixed.
causes: A loose or corroded connector on the cylinder 1 injector.
Damaged wiring to the injector (chafing, heat or rodent damage).
An injector with an open or shorted coil.
A problem with the injector power supply (fuse or relay), which usually affects several injectors.
Rarely, a failed injector driver in the ECU, sometimes caused by a shorted injector.
fixes: Unplug the cylinder 1 injector connector, inspect for corrosion or bent pins, and reseat it until it clicks.
Measure injector resistance across its two pins and compare with the service manual value; it should closely match the other injectors, and an open or much lower reading means a bad injector.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the supply side of the injector connector.
Plug a noid light into the connector and crank the engine: it should flash steadily, the same as on another cylinder.
Check the harness between the injector and the ECU, then repair the wiring or replace the injector, and clear and re-test.

P0202.meaning: The ECU detected an electrical fault in the injector circuit for cylinder 2 (front left, bank 2). That cylinder may not be getting fuel, which causes a misfire, rough running and possible catalytic converter damage, so avoid hard driving until it is fixed.
causes: A loose or corroded connector on the cylinder 2 injector.
Damaged wiring to the injector (chafing, heat or rodent damage).
An injector with an open or shorted coil.
A problem with the injector power supply (fuse or relay), which usually affects several injectors.
Rarely, a failed injector driver in the ECU, sometimes caused by a shorted injector.
fixes: Unplug the cylinder 2 injector connector, inspect for corrosion or bent pins, and reseat it until it clicks.
Measure injector resistance across its two pins and compare with the service manual value; it should closely match the other injectors, and an open or much lower reading means a bad injector.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the supply side of the injector connector.
Plug a noid light into the connector and crank the engine: it should flash steadily, the same as on another cylinder.
Check the harness between the injector and the ECU, then repair the wiring or replace the injector, and clear and re-test.

P0203.meaning: The ECU detected an electrical fault in the injector circuit for cylinder 3 (bank 1, right side: rear on four-cylinders, middle on six-cylinders). That cylinder may not be getting fuel, which causes a misfire, rough running and possible catalytic converter damage, so avoid hard driving until it is fixed.
causes: A loose or corroded connector on the cylinder 3 injector.
Damaged wiring to the injector (chafing, heat or rodent damage).
An injector with an open or shorted coil.
A problem with the injector power supply (fuse or relay), which usually affects several injectors.
Rarely, a failed injector driver in the ECU, sometimes caused by a shorted injector.
fixes: Unplug the cylinder 3 injector connector, inspect for corrosion or bent pins, and reseat it until it clicks.
Measure injector resistance across its two pins and compare with the service manual value; it should closely match the other injectors, and an open or much lower reading means a bad injector.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the supply side of the injector connector.
Plug a noid light into the connector and crank the engine: it should flash steadily, the same as on another cylinder.
Check the harness between the injector and the ECU, then repair the wiring or replace the injector, and clear and re-test.

P0204.meaning: The ECU detected an electrical fault in the injector circuit for cylinder 4 (bank 2, left side: rear on four-cylinders, middle on six-cylinders). That cylinder may not be getting fuel, which causes a misfire, rough running and possible catalytic converter damage, so avoid hard driving until it is fixed.
causes: A loose or corroded connector on the cylinder 4 injector.
Damaged wiring to the injector (chafing, heat or rodent damage).
An injector with an open or shorted coil.
A problem with the injector power supply (fuse or relay), which usually affects several injectors.
Rarely, a failed injector driver in the ECU, sometimes caused by a shorted injector.
fixes: Unplug the cylinder 4 injector connector, inspect for corrosion or bent pins, and reseat it until it clicks.
Measure injector resistance across its two pins and compare with the service manual value; it should closely match the other injectors, and an open or much lower reading means a bad injector.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the supply side of the injector connector.
Plug a noid light into the connector and crank the engine: it should flash steadily, the same as on another cylinder.
Check the harness between the injector and the ECU, then repair the wiring or replace the injector, and clear and re-test.

P0205.meaning: The ECU detected an electrical fault in the injector circuit for cylinder 5 (rear right, bank 1; six-cylinder EZ30/EZ36 engines only). That cylinder may not be getting fuel, which causes a misfire, rough running and possible catalytic converter damage, so avoid hard driving until it is fixed.
causes: A loose or corroded connector on the cylinder 5 injector.
Damaged wiring to the injector (chafing, heat or rodent damage).
An injector with an open or shorted coil.
A problem with the injector power supply (fuse or relay), which usually affects several injectors.
Rarely, a failed injector driver in the ECU, sometimes caused by a shorted injector.
fixes: Unplug the cylinder 5 injector connector, inspect for corrosion or bent pins, and reseat it until it clicks.
Measure injector resistance across its two pins and compare with the service manual value; it should closely match the other injectors, and an open or much lower reading means a bad injector.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the supply side of the injector connector.
Plug a noid light into the connector and crank the engine: it should flash steadily, the same as on another cylinder.
Check the harness between the injector and the ECU, then repair the wiring or replace the injector, and clear and re-test.

P0206.meaning: The ECU detected an electrical fault in the injector circuit for cylinder 6 (rear left, bank 2; six-cylinder EZ30/EZ36 engines only). That cylinder may not be getting fuel, which causes a misfire, rough running and possible catalytic converter damage, so avoid hard driving until it is fixed.
causes: A loose or corroded connector on the cylinder 6 injector.
Damaged wiring to the injector (chafing, heat or rodent damage).
An injector with an open or shorted coil.
A problem with the injector power supply (fuse or relay), which usually affects several injectors.
Rarely, a failed injector driver in the ECU, sometimes caused by a shorted injector.
fixes: Unplug the cylinder 6 injector connector, inspect for corrosion or bent pins, and reseat it until it clicks.
Measure injector resistance across its two pins and compare with the service manual value; it should closely match the other injectors, and an open or much lower reading means a bad injector.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the supply side of the injector connector.
Plug a noid light into the connector and crank the engine: it should flash steadily, the same as on another cylinder.
Check the harness between the injector and the ECU, then repair the wiring or replace the injector, and clear and re-test.

P0219.meaning: The ECU recorded engine speed above its safe maximum, usually from a missed shift into too low a gear or a clutch dropped at high rpm. A brief over-rev may do no harm, but a big one can bend valves or damage bearings, so check the engine if it now runs or sounds different.
causes: A missed shift, for example selecting 2nd instead of 4th at speed.
Dropping the clutch or wheelspin at high rpm.
On automatics, a transmission slipping or dropping into neutral under load.
Rarely, a false rpm reading from crank sensor signal noise.
fixes: Think back to how the car was driven: if a missed shift happened and the engine runs smoothly with no new noises, it may have escaped damage.
Look for other stored codes (misfire, cam or crank sensor) and check for smooth idle and the roughness monitor values in live data if your ECU supports them.
Listen for ticking or knocking from the valvetrain or bottom end, and watch oil pressure if you have a gauge.
If it runs rough or makes noise, do a compression test and a leak-down test; bent valves show as low compression or leakage past the valves.
If there was no over-rev, inspect the crank sensor wiring for damage or routing near ignition parts, and on automatics have the transmission checked for slipping.

P0222.meaning: On electronic throttle engines the throttle body has two position sensors (main and sub) as a safety check; the ECU sees sensor B (the sub sensor) reading below its valid range. The ECU usually limits throttle opening in a fail-safe mode, so drive carefully to where it can be repaired.
causes: A corroded or loose throttle body connector.
The sensor B signal wire open or shorted to ground.
Loss of the 5 V reference, sometimes pulled down by another shorted sensor on the same supply.
A worn or failed sensor inside the throttle body.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the throttle body connector for corrosion and bent pins, and reseat it firmly.
With the key on, check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground at the connector.
In live data, watch both throttle position signals while slowly opening the throttle (key on, engine off): both should move smoothly with no dropouts.
Wiggle the harness while watching live data to find intermittent breaks.
Replace the throttle body if the sensor is faulty (the sensors are usually not sold separately), follow the service manual's learning procedure, then clear and re-test.

P0223.meaning: On electronic throttle engines the throttle body has two position sensors (main and sub) as a safety check; the ECU sees sensor B (the sub sensor) reading above its valid range. The ECU usually limits throttle opening in a fail-safe mode, so drive carefully to where it can be repaired.
causes: A corroded or loose throttle body connector.
The sensor B signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage.
An open ground wire to the sensor.
A worn or failed sensor inside the throttle body.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the throttle body connector for corrosion and bent pins, and reseat it firmly.
With the key on, check that the reference wire reads about 5 V (not higher) and the sensor ground has good continuity to ground.
In live data, watch both throttle position signals while slowly opening the throttle (key on, engine off): both should move smoothly with no jumps to full scale.
Wiggle the harness while watching live data to find intermittent shorts.
Replace the throttle body if the sensor is faulty (the sensors are usually not sold separately), follow the service manual's learning procedure, then clear and re-test.

P0230.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the circuit that powers the fuel pump, on the relay or pump control side. Depending on the fault the engine may stall, run poorly under load or not start, so treat it as urgent.
causes: A faulty fuel pump relay or a blown fuse.
A failing fuel pump controller, on models that have one.
Corroded or burned pins at the fuel pump connector under the rear seat, or a poor ground.
A worn or seizing fuel pump drawing too much current.
Damaged wiring between the relay, controller and pump.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the fuel pump fuse, and swap the fuel pump relay with an identical relay from another circuit.
Turn the key on and listen for the pump priming for a few seconds.
Remove the rear seat access cover and inspect the pump connector for corrosion, melted plastic or loose pins, and check the ground point.
Check the voltage at the pump connector while priming or cranking and compare with the service manual value; it should be close to battery voltage when the pump is commanded to full speed.
Inspect the fuel pump controller connectors if fitted, then replace the controller, relay or pump as the tests indicate, and clear and re-test.

P0234.meaning: Boost pressure went above the ECU's safe limit. The ECU usually cuts fuel or reduces power to protect the engine, and repeated overboost can damage it, so avoid full throttle until it is fixed.
causes: A boost control solenoid stuck, failed or unplugged.
A wastegate actuator hose split, disconnected or routed wrong, so the wastegate never sees boost.
A wastegate flapper or actuator arm seized by rust and carbon.
An aftermarket boost controller or tune set above the ECU's limit.
On the EE20 diesel, variable geometry turbo vanes sticking from soot.
A faulty boost (MAP) sensor reading high.
fixes: Log boost (manifold relative pressure) and wastegate duty in live data during a full-throttle run and compare with stock values for your model.
Inspect the hoses between the turbo, boost control solenoid and wastegate actuator for splits and correct routing, using the underhood or service manual diagram.
With the engine cold and off, check that the wastegate arm moves freely by hand.
Test the boost control solenoid: it should click when commanded, and its coil resistance should match the service manual value.
Compare the MAP reading with barometric pressure at key on, engine off: they should read almost the same.
Remove any aftermarket boost controller or have the tune checked; on the diesel, have the VGT actuator and vanes checked and cleaned.

P0244.meaning: The ECU found that the boost control (wastegate) solenoid A circuit is outside its expected operating range, with the reading on the high side. Boost control may be erratic or the ECU may limit boost, so drive gently until it is fixed.
causes: A failing boost control solenoid, with a partly shorted coil or a sticking valve.
A corroded connector or damaged wiring adding resistance or causing a partial short.
Split or wrongly routed solenoid or wastegate hoses.
An aftermarket boost controller interfering with the solenoid.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the boost control solenoid connector, and check the wiring for damage.
Measure the solenoid coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Inspect the solenoid and wastegate hoses for splits and correct routing.
Log boost and wastegate duty in live data: boost should follow the duty smoothly without spikes or hunting.
Replace the solenoid if it is out of spec or sticking, then clear and re-test.

P0245.meaning: The ECU sees the boost control (wastegate) solenoid A circuit reading low, usually a short to ground or an open circuit. The ECU can no longer control boost properly and may limit power; drive gently until it is fixed.
causes: An unplugged, loose or corroded solenoid connector.
A control wire shorted to ground or broken.
A failed solenoid coil.
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the boost control solenoid connector.
Measure the solenoid coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; open or near zero means a bad solenoid.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the solenoid supply wire.
Check the control wire for continuity to the ECU and for shorts to ground.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test while watching wastegate duty and boost in live data.

P0246.meaning: The ECU sees the boost control (wastegate) solenoid A circuit reading high, usually a short to power or an open circuit in the control side. The ECU can no longer control boost properly and may limit power; drive gently until it is fixed.
causes: A control wire shorted to battery voltage.
An open circuit in the solenoid or its wiring.
An internally shorted solenoid coil.
A corroded or loose connector.
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the boost control solenoid connector.
Measure the solenoid coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the control wire for shorts to other wires in the harness, especially where it runs near hot or sharp parts.
With the key on, confirm the supply wire has battery voltage and the control wire behaves as the service manual describes.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test while watching wastegate duty and boost in live data.

P0249.meaning: The ECU sees the circuit for boost control (wastegate) solenoid B reading low, usually a short to ground or an open circuit. Solenoid B is a second boost control solenoid fitted only on some turbo engines, so check the service manual for which part your engine calls B; the ECU may limit boost until it is fixed.
causes: An unplugged, loose or corroded solenoid connector.
A control wire shorted to ground or broken.
A failed solenoid coil.
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Identify solenoid B for your engine in the service manual, then inspect and reseat its connector.
Measure the solenoid coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the solenoid supply wire.
Check the control wire for continuity to the ECU and for shorts to ground.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test while watching boost in live data.

P0250.meaning: The ECU sees the circuit for boost control (wastegate) solenoid B reading high, usually a short to power or an open circuit in the control side. Solenoid B is a second boost control solenoid fitted only on some turbo engines, so check the service manual for which part your engine calls B; the ECU may limit boost until it is fixed.
causes: A control wire shorted to battery voltage.
An open circuit in the solenoid or its wiring.
An internally shorted solenoid coil.
A corroded or loose connector.
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Identify solenoid B for your engine in the service manual, then inspect and reseat its connector.
Measure the solenoid coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the control wire for shorts to other wires in the harness.
With the key on, confirm the supply wire has battery voltage and the control wire behaves as the service manual describes.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test while watching boost in live data.

P0261.meaning: The ECU sees the control circuit for the cylinder 1 injector (front right, bank 1) reading too low, usually a short to ground or a shorted injector coil. A shorted control wire can hold the injector open and flood the cylinder, so if the engine runs very rough or smells strongly of fuel, stop driving.
causes: The injector control wire chafed through and shorted to ground.
An injector with an internally shorted coil (resistance too low).
Water or corrosion in the injector connector.
Rarely, a damaged injector driver in the ECU.
fixes: Unplug the cylinder 1 injector connector, inspect for water, corrosion or bent pins, and reseat it.
Measure injector resistance and compare with the service manual value and the other injectors; a much lower reading means a shorted injector.
With the ECU and injector unplugged, check the control wire for continuity to ground: there should be none.
Plug a noid light into the connector and crank the engine: it should flash, not stay lit.
Replace the injector or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0264.meaning: The ECU sees the control circuit for the cylinder 2 injector (front left, bank 2) reading too low, usually a short to ground or a shorted injector coil. A shorted control wire can hold the injector open and flood the cylinder, so if the engine runs very rough or smells strongly of fuel, stop driving.
causes: The injector control wire chafed through and shorted to ground.
An injector with an internally shorted coil (resistance too low).
Water or corrosion in the injector connector.
Rarely, a damaged injector driver in the ECU.
fixes: Unplug the cylinder 2 injector connector, inspect for water, corrosion or bent pins, and reseat it.
Measure injector resistance and compare with the service manual value and the other injectors; a much lower reading means a shorted injector.
With the ECU and injector unplugged, check the control wire for continuity to ground: there should be none.
Plug a noid light into the connector and crank the engine: it should flash, not stay lit.
Replace the injector or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0267.meaning: The ECU sees the control circuit for the cylinder 3 injector (bank 1, right side: rear on four-cylinders, middle on six-cylinders) reading too low, usually a short to ground or a shorted injector coil. A shorted control wire can hold the injector open and flood the cylinder, so if the engine runs very rough or smells strongly of fuel, stop driving.
causes: The injector control wire chafed through and shorted to ground.
An injector with an internally shorted coil (resistance too low).
Water or corrosion in the injector connector.
Rarely, a damaged injector driver in the ECU.
fixes: Unplug the cylinder 3 injector connector, inspect for water, corrosion or bent pins, and reseat it.
Measure injector resistance and compare with the service manual value and the other injectors; a much lower reading means a shorted injector.
With the ECU and injector unplugged, check the control wire for continuity to ground: there should be none.
Plug a noid light into the connector and crank the engine: it should flash, not stay lit.
Replace the injector or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0270.meaning: The ECU sees the control circuit for the cylinder 4 injector (bank 2, left side: rear on four-cylinders, middle on six-cylinders) reading too low, usually a short to ground or a shorted injector coil. A shorted control wire can hold the injector open and flood the cylinder, so if the engine runs very rough or smells strongly of fuel, stop driving.
causes: The injector control wire chafed through and shorted to ground.
An injector with an internally shorted coil (resistance too low).
Water or corrosion in the injector connector.
Rarely, a damaged injector driver in the ECU.
fixes: Unplug the cylinder 4 injector connector, inspect for water, corrosion or bent pins, and reseat it.
Measure injector resistance and compare with the service manual value and the other injectors; a much lower reading means a shorted injector.
With the ECU and injector unplugged, check the control wire for continuity to ground: there should be none.
Plug a noid light into the connector and crank the engine: it should flash, not stay lit.
Replace the injector or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0299.meaning: Boost pressure stayed below what the ECU was asking for. The car will feel down on power; it is usually safe to drive gently, but find the cause, since a boost leak after the MAF can also cause lean running.
causes: A boost leak: loose or split intercooler or throttle body couplers, or a leaking bypass or blow-off valve.
A wastegate stuck open or a boost control solenoid fault.
An exhaust leak before the turbo (on EJ turbos, failed up-pipe gaskets or a cracked up-pipe are common).
A worn turbo (excess shaft play, damaged compressor wheel) or a cracked turbo inlet hose.
On the EE20 diesel, variable geometry turbo vanes stuck open, split boost hoses or a clogged DPF restricting the exhaust.
A faulty boost (MAP) sensor reading low.
fixes: Log boost (manifold relative pressure) and wastegate duty in live data during a full-throttle pull in a safe place and compare with stock values for your model.
Inspect all intercooler hoses and clamps for oil film, splits or loose clamps.
Listen for exhaust ticking near the turbo at cold start and check the up-pipe gaskets.
Pressure test the intake tract with a boost leak tester and listen or spray soapy water to find leaks.
Check that the wastegate arm moves freely and that the solenoid hoses are routed correctly.
Remove the turbo inlet and check the compressor wheel: slight shaft play is normal, but the wheel must not touch the housing or show damaged blades.

P0301.meaning: The ECU counted misfires on cylinder 1 (front right, bank 1). A flashing check engine light means the misfire is severe enough to damage the catalytic converter: reduce speed and load, and avoid driving further than needed.
causes: A worn or fouled spark plug.
A failing ignition coil or cracked coil boot (or a bad plug wire on engines with a coil pack and wires).
A clogged or failing cylinder 1 injector.
A vacuum leak near the cylinder 1 intake runner.
Low compression: a burnt valve, a head gasket leak (a known EJ25 weak point) or worn rings.
A wiring or connector fault at the coil or injector.
fixes: Note whether the check engine light flashes, and look for companion codes (coil, injector, lean, cam or crank).
Pull the cylinder 1 spark plug and inspect it for wear, oil fouling, cracks or a fuel-soaked tip; replace plugs as a set if they are due.
Swap the cylinder 1 coil with a neighbouring cylinder, clear and re-test: if the misfire moves, replace the coil.
Watch the roughness monitor for cylinder 1 in live data if your ECU supports it, and check fuel trims for a lean condition.
Check the injector: its resistance should match the other cylinders and it should click with the engine running.
Do a compression test (all cylinders within about 10% of each other) and a leak-down test if cylinder 1 is low.

P0302.meaning: The ECU counted misfires on cylinder 2 (front left, bank 2). A flashing check engine light means the misfire is severe enough to damage the catalytic converter: reduce speed and load, and avoid driving further than needed.
causes: A worn or fouled spark plug.
A failing ignition coil or cracked coil boot (or a bad plug wire on engines with a coil pack and wires).
A clogged or failing cylinder 2 injector.
A vacuum leak near the cylinder 2 intake runner.
Low compression: a burnt valve, a head gasket leak (a known EJ25 weak point) or worn rings.
A wiring or connector fault at the coil or injector.
fixes: Note whether the check engine light flashes, and look for companion codes (coil, injector, lean, cam or crank).
Pull the cylinder 2 spark plug and inspect it for wear, oil fouling, cracks or a fuel-soaked tip; replace plugs as a set if they are due.
Swap the cylinder 2 coil with a neighbouring cylinder, clear and re-test: if the misfire moves, replace the coil.
Watch the roughness monitor for cylinder 2 in live data if your ECU supports it, and check fuel trims for a lean condition.
Check the injector: its resistance should match the other cylinders and it should click with the engine running.
Do a compression test (all cylinders within about 10% of each other) and a leak-down test if cylinder 2 is low.

P0303.meaning: The ECU counted misfires on cylinder 3 (bank 1, right side: rear on four-cylinders, middle on six-cylinders). A flashing check engine light means the misfire is severe enough to damage the catalytic converter: reduce speed and load, and avoid driving further than needed.
causes: A worn or fouled spark plug.
A failing ignition coil or cracked coil boot (or a bad plug wire on engines with a coil pack and wires).
A clogged or failing cylinder 3 injector.
A vacuum leak near the cylinder 3 intake runner.
Low compression: a burnt valve, a head gasket leak (a known EJ25 weak point) or worn rings.
A wiring or connector fault at the coil or injector.
fixes: Note whether the check engine light flashes, and look for companion codes (coil, injector, lean, cam or crank).
Pull the cylinder 3 spark plug and inspect it for wear, oil fouling, cracks or a fuel-soaked tip; replace plugs as a set if they are due.
Swap the cylinder 3 coil with a neighbouring cylinder, clear and re-test: if the misfire moves, replace the coil.
Watch the roughness monitor for cylinder 3 in live data if your ECU supports it, and check fuel trims for a lean condition.
Check the injector: its resistance should match the other cylinders and it should click with the engine running.
Do a compression test (all cylinders within about 10% of each other) and a leak-down test if cylinder 3 is low.

P0304.meaning: The ECU counted misfires on cylinder 4 (bank 2, left side: rear on four-cylinders, middle on six-cylinders). A flashing check engine light means the misfire is severe enough to damage the catalytic converter: reduce speed and load, and avoid driving further than needed.
causes: A worn or fouled spark plug.
A failing ignition coil or cracked coil boot (or a bad plug wire on engines with a coil pack and wires).
A clogged or failing cylinder 4 injector.
A vacuum leak near the cylinder 4 intake runner.
Low compression: a burnt valve, a head gasket leak (a known EJ25 weak point) or worn rings; on EJ257 STI engines, a cracked ringland on cylinder 4 is a known failure.
A wiring or connector fault at the coil or injector.
fixes: Note whether the check engine light flashes, and look for companion codes (coil, injector, lean, cam or crank).
Pull the cylinder 4 spark plug and inspect it for wear, oil fouling, cracks or a fuel-soaked tip; replace plugs as a set if they are due.
Swap the cylinder 4 coil with a neighbouring cylinder, clear and re-test: if the misfire moves, replace the coil.
Watch the roughness monitor for cylinder 4 in live data if your ECU supports it, and check fuel trims for a lean condition.
Check the injector: its resistance should match the other cylinders and it should click with the engine running.
Do a compression test (all cylinders within about 10% of each other) and a leak-down test if cylinder 4 is low.

P0305.meaning: The ECU counted misfires on cylinder 5 (rear right, bank 1; six-cylinder EZ30/EZ36 engines only). A flashing check engine light means the misfire is severe enough to damage the catalytic converter: reduce speed and load, and avoid driving further than needed.
causes: A worn or fouled spark plug.
A failing ignition coil or cracked coil boot.
A clogged or failing cylinder 5 injector.
A vacuum leak near the cylinder 5 intake runner.
Low compression: a burnt valve, a head gasket leak or worn rings.
A wiring or connector fault at the coil or injector.
fixes: Note whether the check engine light flashes, and look for companion codes (coil, injector, lean, cam or crank).
Pull the cylinder 5 spark plug and inspect it for wear, oil fouling, cracks or a fuel-soaked tip; replace plugs as a set if they are due.
Swap the cylinder 5 coil with another cylinder, clear and re-test: if the misfire moves, replace the coil.
Check fuel trims for bank 1 in live data for a lean condition.
Check the injector: its resistance should match the other cylinders and it should click with the engine running.
Do a compression test (all cylinders within about 10% of each other) and a leak-down test if cylinder 5 is low.

P0306.meaning: The ECU counted misfires on cylinder 6 (rear left, bank 2; six-cylinder EZ30/EZ36 engines only). A flashing check engine light means the misfire is severe enough to damage the catalytic converter: reduce speed and load, and avoid driving further than needed.
causes: A worn or fouled spark plug.
A failing ignition coil or cracked coil boot.
A clogged or failing cylinder 6 injector.
A vacuum leak near the cylinder 6 intake runner.
Low compression: a burnt valve, a head gasket leak or worn rings.
A wiring or connector fault at the coil or injector.
fixes: Note whether the check engine light flashes, and look for companion codes (coil, injector, lean, cam or crank).
Pull the cylinder 6 spark plug and inspect it for wear, oil fouling, cracks or a fuel-soaked tip; replace plugs as a set if they are due.
Swap the cylinder 6 coil with another cylinder, clear and re-test: if the misfire moves, replace the coil.
Check fuel trims for bank 2 in live data for a lean condition.
Check the injector: its resistance should match the other cylinders and it should click with the engine running.
Do a compression test (all cylinders within about 10% of each other) and a leak-down test if cylinder 6 is low.

P0325.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the knock sensor 1 circuit (on four-cylinder boxers the single knock sensor sits on top of the crankcase under the intake manifold). Without a working knock sensor the ECU retards ignition timing as a precaution, so the car feels sluggish; on turbo engines avoid full boost until it is fixed.
causes: A cracked, corroded or loose knock sensor connector or pigtail (the plastic gets brittle from engine heat on EJ engines).
Damaged wiring under the intake manifold.
A failed knock sensor.
A sensor that is loose or over-tightened, so it misreads engine vibration.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check knock correction and, on turbo ECUs, IAM (ignition advance multiplier) in live data; a dropped IAM or constant timing retard fits this code.
Inspect the knock sensor connector and pigtail for cracks, corrosion or a broken latch.
Measure the sensor resistance and compare with the service manual value, and check harness continuity to the ECU.
Make sure the sensor is clean where it seats and tightened to the torque in the service manual.
Replace the sensor (and the pigtail or connector if damaged), then clear and re-test; on turbo models, watch IAM recover over the next drives.

P0327.meaning: The knock sensor 1 signal is below its valid range, usually from an open circuit, a disconnected connector or a short to ground (on four-cylinder boxers the single knock sensor sits on top of the crankcase under the intake manifold). The ECU retards ignition timing as a precaution, so the car feels sluggish; on turbo engines avoid full boost until it is fixed.
causes: A disconnected, cracked or corroded knock sensor connector or pigtail.
A broken signal wire or one shorted to ground under the intake manifold.
A failed knock sensor.
A loose sensor with poor contact to the block.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check knock correction and, on turbo ECUs, IAM in live data; a dropped IAM or constant timing retard fits this code.
Inspect the knock sensor connector and pigtail for cracks, corrosion or a broken latch, and reseat it.
Measure the sensor resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the signal wire for continuity to the ECU and for shorts to ground.
Replace the sensor or repair the wiring, torque the sensor to the service manual value, then clear and re-test.

P0328.meaning: The knock sensor 1 signal is above its valid range, usually from a short to voltage or a damaged sensor or pigtail (on four-cylinder boxers the single knock sensor sits on top of the crankcase under the intake manifold). The ECU retards ignition timing as a precaution, so the car feels sluggish; on turbo engines avoid full boost until it is fixed.
causes: A damaged or corroded knock sensor pigtail or connector.
A signal wire shorted to a voltage source.
A failed knock sensor.
Electrical noise from damaged wiring or a nearby ignition fault.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check knock correction and, on turbo ECUs, IAM in live data; a dropped IAM or constant timing retard fits this code.
Inspect the knock sensor connector and pigtail for cracks, corrosion or a broken latch, and reseat it.
Measure the sensor resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the signal wire for shorts to other wires in the harness.
Replace the sensor or repair the wiring, torque the sensor to the service manual value, then clear and re-test.

P0330.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the knock sensor 2 circuit, fitted on engines with two knock sensors (such as the six-cylinders), where it usually covers bank 2 (left side). Without a working knock sensor the ECU retards ignition timing as a precaution, so the car feels sluggish.
causes: A cracked, corroded or loose knock sensor 2 connector or pigtail.
Damaged wiring to the sensor.
A failed knock sensor.
A sensor that is loose or over-tightened, so it misreads engine vibration.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check knock correction in live data; constant timing retard fits this code.
Inspect the knock sensor 2 connector and pigtail for cracks, corrosion or a broken latch.
Measure the sensor resistance and compare with the service manual value, and check harness continuity to the ECU.
Make sure the sensor is clean where it seats and tightened to the torque in the service manual.
Replace the sensor (and the pigtail or connector if damaged), then clear and re-test.

P0332.meaning: The knock sensor 2 signal is below its valid range, usually from an open circuit, a disconnected connector or a short to ground; knock sensor 2 is fitted on engines with two knock sensors (such as the six-cylinders) and usually covers bank 2 (left side). The ECU retards ignition timing as a precaution, so the car feels sluggish.
causes: A disconnected, cracked or corroded knock sensor 2 connector or pigtail.
A broken signal wire or one shorted to ground.
A failed knock sensor.
A loose sensor with poor contact to the block.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check knock correction in live data; constant timing retard fits this code.
Inspect the knock sensor 2 connector and pigtail for cracks, corrosion or a broken latch, and reseat it.
Measure the sensor resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the signal wire for continuity to the ECU and for shorts to ground.
Replace the sensor or repair the wiring, torque the sensor to the service manual value, then clear and re-test.

P0333.meaning: The knock sensor 2 signal is above its valid range, usually from a short to voltage or a damaged sensor or pigtail; knock sensor 2 is fitted on engines with two knock sensors (such as the six-cylinders) and usually covers bank 2 (left side). The ECU retards ignition timing as a precaution, so the car feels sluggish.
causes: A damaged or corroded knock sensor 2 pigtail or connector.
A signal wire shorted to a voltage source.
A failed knock sensor.
Electrical noise from damaged wiring or a nearby ignition fault.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check knock correction in live data; constant timing retard fits this code.
Inspect the knock sensor 2 connector and pigtail for cracks, corrosion or a broken latch, and reseat it.
Measure the sensor resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the signal wire for shorts to other wires in the harness.
Replace the sensor or repair the wiring, torque the sensor to the service manual value, then clear and re-test.

P0335.meaning: The ECU is not getting a usable signal from the crankshaft position sensor, which tells it engine speed and piston position. This can cause stalling or a crank-no-start, so do not rely on the car until it is fixed.
causes: A failed crankshaft position sensor.
An oil-soaked, corroded or damaged connector or wiring.
Damaged or missing teeth on the crank reluctor, sometimes after a timing belt job.
A loose sensor or metal debris stuck to the sensor tip.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Watch the tachometer or the rpm reading in live data while cranking; if it stays at zero, the ECU is not seeing the crank signal.
Inspect the crank sensor connector and wiring for oil contamination, corrosion and damage.
Check that the sensor bolt is tight and the sensor tip is clean.
Measure the sensor resistance (on magnetic types) and compare with the service manual value; with an oscilloscope, the signal should be a clean, regular pattern while cranking.
If the timing belt was recently replaced, check the crank sprocket and reluctor for damage and correct installation.
Replace the sensor with a quality OEM part, then clear and re-test.

P0336.meaning: The crankshaft position sensor signal is present but irregular: the ECU sees missing or extra pulses, or a pattern that does not match the cam sensor. Symptoms include stumbling, stalling or a hard start; fix it soon, as the engine could cut out while driving.
causes: A failing crankshaft position sensor with an intermittent signal.
Electrical noise from damaged wiring or wiring routed near ignition parts or the alternator.
Damaged reluctor teeth, or metal debris on the sensor tip.
A timing belt that has jumped a tooth, so crank and cam signals no longer line up.
A loose sensor.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the crank sensor connector, and check the wiring for damage and correct routing away from ignition parts.
Check that the sensor is tight and its tip is clean.
Check for cam sensor codes as well; if both appear, inspect the timing belt and check the timing marks line up per the service manual.
Scope the sensor signal while cranking or idling: it should be a clean, regular pattern with no dropouts.
