Replace the sensor with a quality OEM part, then clear and re-test.

P0340.meaning: The ECU is not getting a valid signal from camshaft position sensor A (the bank 1 intake cam sensor on AVCS engines, or the only cam sensor on older engines). The engine may be hard to start, run rough or stall, and a no-start is possible.
causes: A failed camshaft position sensor.
A corroded or loose connector, or damaged wiring.
A timing belt that has slipped, jumped or broken.
A damaged cam reluctor or sensor plate.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the cam sensor connector, and check the wiring for oil contamination and damage.
If the engine is hard to start or will not start, check the timing belt before cranking repeatedly: many Subaru engines are interference engines, so a jumped belt can damage valves.
Measure the sensor resistance (on magnetic types) and compare with the service manual value.
Scope the sensor signal while cranking: it should be a clean, regular pattern.
Replace the sensor with a quality OEM part, then clear and re-test.

P0341.meaning: The camshaft position sensor A signal (the bank 1 intake cam sensor on AVCS engines, or the only cam sensor on older engines) is present but does not line up with the crank signal as expected. This can cause rough running and poor power, and it can point to cam timing problems, so fix it soon.
causes: A timing belt that has jumped a tooth or was installed one tooth off.
AVCS problems: a sticking oil control valve or clogged AVCS oil filter screens holding the cam at the wrong angle.
Low or dirty engine oil affecting AVCS.
A failing cam sensor or electrical noise in its wiring.
A damaged cam reluctor.
fixes: Check the oil level and condition; change it if it is low, sludgy or overdue.
On AVCS engines, watch intake cam advance angle and its target in live data: actual should follow target closely at idle and when revving.
Inspect and reseat the cam sensor connector, and check the wiring routing.
Remove and clean the AVCS oil filter screens and check the oil control valve for sticking.
If the timing belt was recently serviced or cam timing is clearly off, check the timing marks against the service manual.
Replace the sensor if the timing and AVCS are correct, then clear and re-test.

P0345.meaning: The ECU is not getting a valid signal from camshaft position sensor A on bank 2 (the intake cam sensor on the left head, cylinders 2 and 4, on AVCS engines). The engine may run rough, lose AVCS cam timing control or be hard to start.
causes: A failed camshaft position sensor.
A corroded or loose connector, or damaged wiring.
A timing belt that has jumped, so bank 2 cam timing is off.
A damaged cam reluctor.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the bank 2 cam sensor connector, and check the wiring for oil contamination and damage.
If the engine is hard to start, check the timing belt and timing marks before cranking repeatedly.
Measure the sensor resistance (on magnetic types) and compare with the service manual value.
Watch the bank 2 cam angle in live data if your ECU reports it: it should be steady and follow its target.
Replace the sensor with a quality OEM part, then clear and re-test.

P0350.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in an ignition coil circuit, without naming a specific coil. Expect misfires or rough running; drive gently, since misfires can damage the catalytic converter.
causes: A failed ignition coil.
A loose or corroded coil connector.
Damaged wiring to a coil, or a problem with the coil power supply (fuse or relay).
A failed igniter, on older engines that have a separate one.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check for misfire codes that point to a specific cylinder.
Inspect and reseat all coil connectors, looking for corrosion and broken latches.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) at the coil power supply.
Swap a suspect coil with another cylinder, clear and re-test: if the fault moves, replace the coil.
Measure coil resistance and compare with the service manual value, then replace the faulty coil and clear and re-test.

P0351.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the circuit for ignition coil A (normally the cylinder 1 coil; on older engines with a single coil pack, one of its circuits). Expect misfires or rough running; drive gently, since misfires can damage the catalytic converter.
causes: A failed coil A.
A loose or corroded coil connector.
Damaged wiring between the coil and the ECU.
A problem with the coil power supply (fuse or relay).
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the coil A connector, looking for corrosion and a broken latch.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) at the coil power supply.
On coil-on-plug engines, swap coil A with another cylinder, clear and re-test: if the fault moves, replace the coil.
Measure coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the control wire for continuity to the ECU, then replace the coil or repair the wiring and clear and re-test.

P0352.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the circuit for ignition coil B (normally the cylinder 2 coil; on older engines with a single coil pack, one of its circuits). Expect misfires or rough running; drive gently, since misfires can damage the catalytic converter.
causes: A failed coil B.
A loose or corroded coil connector.
Damaged wiring between the coil and the ECU.
A problem with the coil power supply (fuse or relay).
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the coil B connector, looking for corrosion and a broken latch.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) at the coil power supply.
On coil-on-plug engines, swap coil B with another cylinder, clear and re-test: if the fault moves, replace the coil.
Measure coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the control wire for continuity to the ECU, then replace the coil or repair the wiring and clear and re-test.

P0353.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the circuit for ignition coil C (normally the cylinder 3 coil). Expect misfires or rough running; drive gently, since misfires can damage the catalytic converter.
causes: A failed coil C.
A loose or corroded coil connector.
Damaged wiring between the coil and the ECU.
A problem with the coil power supply (fuse or relay).
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the coil C connector, looking for corrosion and a broken latch.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) at the coil power supply.
On coil-on-plug engines, swap coil C with another cylinder, clear and re-test: if the fault moves, replace the coil.
Measure coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the control wire for continuity to the ECU, then replace the coil or repair the wiring and clear and re-test.

P0354.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the circuit for ignition coil D (normally the cylinder 4 coil). Expect misfires or rough running; drive gently, since misfires can damage the catalytic converter.
causes: A failed coil D.
A loose or corroded coil connector.
Damaged wiring between the coil and the ECU.
A problem with the coil power supply (fuse or relay).
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the coil D connector, looking for corrosion and a broken latch.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) at the coil power supply.
On coil-on-plug engines, swap coil D with another cylinder, clear and re-test: if the fault moves, replace the coil.
Measure coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the control wire for continuity to the ECU, then replace the coil or repair the wiring and clear and re-test.

P0355.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the circuit for ignition coil E (the cylinder 5 coil, six-cylinder EZ30/EZ36 engines only). Expect misfires or rough running; drive gently, since misfires can damage the catalytic converter.
causes: A failed coil E.
A loose or corroded coil connector.
Damaged wiring between the coil and the ECU.
A problem with the coil power supply (fuse or relay).
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the coil E connector, looking for corrosion and a broken latch.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) at the coil power supply.
Swap coil E with another cylinder, clear and re-test: if the fault moves, replace the coil.
Measure coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the control wire for continuity to the ECU, then replace the coil or repair the wiring and clear and re-test.

P0356.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the circuit for ignition coil F (the cylinder 6 coil, six-cylinder EZ30/EZ36 engines only). Expect misfires or rough running; drive gently, since misfires can damage the catalytic converter.
causes: A failed coil F.
A loose or corroded coil connector.
Damaged wiring between the coil and the ECU.
A problem with the coil power supply (fuse or relay).
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the coil F connector, looking for corrosion and a broken latch.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) at the coil power supply.
Swap coil F with another cylinder, clear and re-test: if the fault moves, replace the coil.
Measure coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the control wire for continuity to the ECU, then replace the coil or repair the wiring and clear and re-test.

P0365.meaning: The ECU has a problem with the signal from camshaft position sensor B on bank 1, the exhaust cam sensor on the right head (cylinders 1 and 3, plus 5 on six-cylinders). It is fitted on engines with exhaust cam timing (dual AVCS), such as FB and FA engines and the EZ36; expect rough running, lost AVCS control or a hard start.
causes: A failed camshaft position sensor.
A corroded or loose connector, or damaged wiring.
Exhaust AVCS problems: a sticking oil control valve or clogged oil screens.
Cam timing off from a jumped timing belt or a stretched timing chain (FB and FA engines use chains).
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the oil level and condition; change it if it is low, sludgy or overdue.
Inspect and reseat the bank 1 exhaust cam sensor connector, and check the wiring for oil contamination and damage.
Watch the bank 1 exhaust cam angle and its target in live data if your ECU reports them: actual should follow target closely.
Measure the sensor resistance (on magnetic types) or scope its signal, and compare with the service manual.
Replace the sensor if the timing and AVCS are correct, then clear and re-test; if cam timing is clearly off, check the belt or chain timing marks per the service manual.

P0390.meaning: The ECU has a problem with the signal from camshaft position sensor B on bank 2, the exhaust cam sensor on the left head (cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders). It is fitted on engines with exhaust cam timing (dual AVCS), such as FB and FA engines and the EZ36; expect rough running, lost AVCS control or a hard start.
causes: A failed camshaft position sensor.
A corroded or loose connector, or damaged wiring.
Exhaust AVCS problems: a sticking oil control valve or clogged oil screens.
Cam timing off from a jumped timing belt or a stretched timing chain (FB and FA engines use chains).
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the oil level and condition; change it if it is low, sludgy or overdue.
Inspect and reseat the bank 2 exhaust cam sensor connector, and check the wiring for oil contamination and damage.
Watch the bank 2 exhaust cam angle and its target in live data if your ECU reports them: actual should follow target closely.
Measure the sensor resistance (on magnetic types) or scope its signal, and compare with the service manual.
Replace the sensor if the timing and AVCS are correct, then clear and re-test; if cam timing is clearly off, check the belt or chain timing marks per the service manual.

P0400.meaning: The ECU detected that exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) flow is not what it expects. On petrol Subarus EGR is fitted only to some older engines; on the EE20 diesel EGR is used heavily, and a fault can mean reduced power or limp mode.
causes: Carbon build-up clogging the EGR valve or passages.
An EGR valve stuck open or closed.
A blocked EGR cooler or pipe (EE20 diesel).
A fault in the EGR control (solenoid, vacuum hose or electric motor) or its wiring.
A MAP or MAF sensor giving a wrong reading, which the ECU uses to judge EGR flow.
fixes: Inspect the EGR valve connector and any vacuum hoses for damage.
On the diesel, compare EGR position with its target in live data: actual should follow target smoothly.
Remove the EGR valve and check for heavy carbon; clean it with carburettor or intake cleaner and check it moves freely.
Clean the EGR passages in the intake (petrol) or inspect the EGR cooler, pipe and intake manifold for carbon (diesel).
Replace the EGR valve if it is sticking or faulty, then clear and re-test.

P0401.meaning: The ECU detected less EGR flow than commanded, usually because carbon has clogged the valve or passages. On petrol engines this can cause pinging (knock) under load; on the EE20 diesel it raises emissions and may reduce power.
causes: Carbon build-up in the EGR passages or intake.
An EGR valve stuck closed.
A blocked EGR cooler or pipe (EE20 diesel).
A split vacuum hose or faulty control solenoid on vacuum-operated systems.
A MAP or MAF sensor reading inaccurately.
fixes: Inspect vacuum hoses and the EGR valve connector.
On the diesel, compare EGR position with its target in live data; also check knock correction on petrol engines for extra knock.
Remove and clean the EGR valve, and check that it opens and closes freely.
Clean the EGR passages (petrol) or inspect the EGR cooler, pipe and intake manifold for carbon (diesel).
Replace the EGR valve if it still sticks, then clear and re-test.

P0402.meaning: The ECU detected more EGR flow than commanded, usually an EGR valve stuck partly open. This causes a rough idle, hesitation or stalling on petrol engines, and smoke and low power on the EE20 diesel.
causes: Carbon holding the EGR valve partly open.
A failed EGR valve.
A control solenoid stuck on, or a vacuum hose routed wrong (vacuum-operated systems).
A faulty EGR position sensor reading wrong (EE20 diesel).
A MAP or MAF sensor reading inaccurately.
fixes: Inspect the EGR vacuum hoses and connector.
On the diesel, compare EGR position with its target in live data at idle: it should be nearly closed when commanded closed.
Remove the EGR valve and check that it seals fully when closed; clean off carbon.
Test the control solenoid or motor and compare with the service manual.
Replace the EGR valve if it does not seal, then clear and re-test.

P0403.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the circuit that drives the EGR valve or its control solenoid. EGR control is lost, which can cause knock or rough running on petrol engines and reduced power on the EE20 diesel.
causes: A loose or corroded EGR connector.
Damaged wiring between the EGR valve or solenoid and the ECU.
A failed EGR solenoid or motor coil.
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the EGR connector, looking for corrosion and bent pins.
Measure the solenoid or motor coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for supply voltage at the connector as the service manual describes.
Check the wiring to the ECU for continuity and shorts.
Replace the EGR valve or solenoid, or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0404.meaning: The EGR valve is not following the ECU's commands correctly, so its operation is out of the expected range. Expect rough running, hesitation or reduced power, especially on the EE20 diesel.
causes: A sticking EGR valve from carbon build-up.
A worn EGR motor or position sensor.
A poor connection in the EGR wiring.
Low supply voltage to the valve.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the EGR connector, and check the wiring for damage.
Compare EGR position with its target in live data: actual should follow target smoothly without lagging or jumping.
Remove the EGR valve and clean off carbon; check that it moves freely.
Check battery and charging voltage: about 12.6 V engine off and 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Replace the EGR valve if it still does not follow commands, then clear and re-test.

P0405.meaning: The EGR valve position sensor signal is below its valid range; this sensor is built into the electronic EGR valve, mainly on the EE20 diesel. The ECU can no longer confirm EGR position and may limit power.
causes: A signal wire open or shorted to ground.
Loss of the 5 V reference to the sensor.
A corroded or loose EGR valve connector.
A failed position sensor inside the EGR valve.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the EGR valve connector.
With the key on, check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground at the connector.
Check the signal wire for continuity to the ECU and for shorts to ground.
Watch EGR position in live data while wiggling the harness; dropouts point to a wiring fault.
Replace the EGR valve (the sensor is usually part of it) if the wiring is good, then clear and re-test.

P0406.meaning: The EGR valve position sensor signal is above its valid range; this sensor is built into the electronic EGR valve, mainly on the EE20 diesel. The ECU can no longer confirm EGR position and may limit power.
causes: A signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage.
An open ground wire to the sensor.
A corroded or loose EGR valve connector.
A failed position sensor inside the EGR valve.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the EGR valve connector.
With the key on, check the reference wire is about 5 V (not higher) and the ground wire has good continuity to ground.
Check the signal wire for shorts to other wires in the harness.
Watch EGR position in live data while wiggling the harness; jumps point to a wiring fault.
Replace the EGR valve (the sensor is usually part of it) if the wiring is good, then clear and re-test.

P0409.meaning: The EGR valve position sensor reading does not match what the ECU expects, for example it does not change when the valve is commanded to move. This is mainly seen on the EE20 diesel; expect reduced power or poor running until fixed.
causes: A sticking EGR valve from carbon, so the position does not change as commanded.
A worn or failing position sensor inside the EGR valve.
A poor connection in the sensor wiring.
A worn EGR motor.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the EGR valve connector.
Compare EGR position with its target in live data: it should follow smoothly and return to closed.
Remove the EGR valve and clean off carbon; check that it moves freely through its full travel.
Check the sensor supply, ground and signal wiring against the service manual.
Replace the EGR valve if it still does not track, then clear and re-test.

P0410.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the secondary air injection system, which pumps fresh air into the exhaust for a short time after a cold start to heat the catalytic converter faster. It does not affect how the car drives once warm, but emissions tests will fail.
causes: Air switching (combination) valves stuck from moisture and carbon, a common Subaru failure.
A failed secondary air pump, often from water getting in.
Cracked or disconnected secondary air hoses.
A blown fuse or failed secondary air pump relay.
A faulty secondary air pressure sensor or wiring.
fixes: Listen at a cold start (engine fully cooled): the pump should run with an obvious whirring sound for a short time.
Check the secondary air pump fuse and relay.
Inspect the air hoses from the pump to the valves for cracks and loose connections.
Remove and inspect the air switching (combination) valves for sticking, carbon or corrosion.
Test the pump by powering it directly with 12 V; replace the pump or valves as needed, then clear and re-test from a cold start.

P0411.meaning: The ECU measured the wrong amount of airflow from the secondary air injection system during its test after a cold start. It does not affect how the car drives once warm, but emissions tests will fail.
causes: Air switching (combination) valves stuck open or closed.
A weak or failed secondary air pump.
Cracked, disconnected or blocked secondary air hoses.
A faulty secondary air pressure sensor.
Carbon build-up in the air passages to the exhaust.
fixes: Listen at a cold start: the pump should run with an obvious whirring sound for a short time.
Inspect the air hoses for cracks, loose connections and blockages.
Remove and inspect the air switching (combination) valves for sticking or carbon.
Check the secondary air pressure sensor and its wiring against the service manual.
Replace the faulty valves or pump, then clear and re-test from a cold start.

P0413.meaning: The ECU detected an open circuit in secondary air injection control circuit A. RomRaider calls it pump A, but in the standard code definition this is air switching valve A (on Subaru, one of the electric combination valves that let pump air into the exhaust); it only affects cold-start emissions.
causes: An unplugged or corroded connector on the valve.
A broken wire in the valve circuit.
A valve coil that has gone open circuit.
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Identify component A for your model in the service manual, then inspect and reseat its connector.
Measure the coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; an open reading means a failed valve.
With the key on, check for supply voltage at the connector as the service manual describes.
Check the wiring to the ECU for continuity.
Replace the valve or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test from a cold start.

P0414.meaning: The ECU detected a short circuit in secondary air injection control circuit A. RomRaider calls it pump A, but in the standard code definition this is air switching valve A (on Subaru, one of the electric combination valves that let pump air into the exhaust); it only affects cold-start emissions.
causes: A valve coil that has shorted internally, often after water or corrosion gets in.
A wire shorted to ground or to power.
Water or corrosion in the connector.
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Identify component A for your model in the service manual, then inspect its connector for water and corrosion.
Measure the coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; a much lower reading means a shorted coil.
Check the wiring for shorts to ground or to other wires.
Replace the valve or repair the wiring.
Clear and re-test from a cold start.

P0416.meaning: The ECU detected an open circuit in secondary air injection control circuit B. RomRaider calls it pump B, but in the standard code definition this is air switching valve B (on Subaru, the second electric combination valve that lets pump air into the exhaust); it only affects cold-start emissions.
causes: An unplugged or corroded connector on the valve.
A broken wire in the valve circuit.
A valve coil that has gone open circuit.
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Identify component B for your model in the service manual, then inspect and reseat its connector.
Measure the coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; an open reading means a failed valve.
With the key on, check for supply voltage at the connector as the service manual describes.
Check the wiring to the ECU for continuity.
Replace the valve or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test from a cold start.

P0417.meaning: The ECU detected a short circuit in secondary air injection control circuit B. RomRaider calls it pump B, but in the standard code definition this is air switching valve B (on Subaru, the second electric combination valve that lets pump air into the exhaust); it only affects cold-start emissions.
causes: A valve coil that has shorted internally, often after water or corrosion gets in.
A wire shorted to ground or to power.
Water or corrosion in the connector.
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Identify component B for your model in the service manual, then inspect its connector for water and corrosion.
Measure the coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; a much lower reading means a shorted coil.
Check the wiring for shorts to ground or to other wires.
Replace the valve or repair the wiring.
Clear and re-test from a cold start.

P0418.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the secondary air pump relay circuit, so the pump may not run (or may not switch off) after a cold start. It does not affect how the car drives once warm, but a pump that never switches off can burn out.
causes: A failed secondary air pump relay.
A blown fuse in the pump circuit.
Damaged wiring or a corroded connector at the relay or pump.
A seized pump drawing too much current and damaging the relay.
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Check the secondary air pump fuse.
Swap the relay with an identical one from another circuit and re-test.
Listen at a cold start: the pump should run for a short time, then stop; if it runs continuously, the relay is sticking.
Check the relay control wire from the ECU and the pump wiring for damage.
Test the pump by powering it directly with 12 V and replace it if it is seized, then clear and re-test.

P0420.meaning: The ECU compared the front A/F sensor with the rear oxygen sensor and found the catalytic converter is no longer storing oxygen as well as it should. On four-cylinder Subarus this code covers the whole exhaust; the car drives normally, but it will fail emissions and a failing cat can eventually restrict flow.
causes: An aging or damaged catalytic converter, often after a misfire or oil or coolant burning.
An exhaust leak near the rear O2 sensor or at the up-pipe or downpipe flanges.
A slow or faulty rear O2 sensor.
An aftermarket downpipe or high-flow cat (common on EJ turbos), which often cannot pass the ECU's test.
The engine running rich or lean, or burning oil, for example from a head gasket leak or worn rings.
fixes: Fix any misfire, fuel trim or O2 sensor codes first; they can cause or mimic this code.

Watch the rear O2 sensor in live data at a steady 2500 rpm once fully warm: a healthy cat gives a fairly steady voltage around 0.5 to 0.8 V, while a reading that swings up and down rapidly suggests a worn cat.
Inspect the exhaust for leaks before and around the rear O2 sensor (gaskets, flex joints, cracked pipes).
Test or replace the rear O2 sensor if it responds slowly.
Replace the catalytic converter with an OEM or legally compliant unit, after fixing whatever damaged the old one (oil burning, misfire).

P0441.meaning: The ECU found that the EVAP purge system, which draws fuel vapour from the charcoal canister into the engine, is not flowing as expected. It has little effect on driving, but emissions tests will fail.
causes: A purge control solenoid valve stuck open or closed.
Cracked, disconnected or blocked purge hoses (on turbo models, also the hoses and check valves toward the turbo inlet).
A clogged charcoal canister or blocked canister vent.
A faulty fuel tank pressure sensor.
Wiring or connector problems at the purge valve.
fixes: Inspect the purge hoses from the canister to the intake for cracks, loose ends and blockages.
Test the purge valve: with no power it should not let air through when you blow into it; with 12 V applied it should click and open.
Inspect and reseat the purge valve connector.
Check the fuel tank pressure reading in live data if your ECU reports it: with the fuel cap off it should read close to zero.
Replace the purge valve or damaged hoses, then clear and re-test (the EVAP monitor may need a few drive cycles).

P0442.meaning: The ECU's EVAP self-test found a small leak in the fuel vapour system (fuel tank, filler, hoses or canister). It does not affect driving, but it will fail an emissions test.
causes: A fuel cap that is loose, cross-threaded or has a worn seal.
A rusted or cracked fuel filler neck (common on older Subarus in salted-road regions).
Cracked or loose EVAP hoses near the tank, canister or engine bay.
A faulty canister drain or vent valve, or pressure control solenoid.
A leaking purge valve or fuel tank pressure sensor seal.
fixes: Remove the fuel cap, inspect the seal, refit it and tighten until it clicks; replace it with an OEM cap if the seal is cracked.
Inspect the filler neck for rust holes, especially near the fuel door and where it joins the tank.
Inspect all EVAP hoses and connections you can reach, including at the canister under the rear of the car.
Check the canister drain valve for sticking or debris.
Have a smoke test done: it is the most reliable way to find small leaks.
After the repair, clear and re-test; the EVAP test needs specific conditions (fuel level, cold start), so allow a few days of normal driving.

P0444.meaning: The ECU sees the circuit that drives the EVAP purge control solenoid valve reading low, usually an open circuit or a short to ground. Purge control is lost; the car normally drives fine, but a stuck valve can cause a rough idle and emissions tests will fail.
causes: An unplugged, loose or corroded connector on the purge valve.
A broken wire in the purge valve circuit.
A purge valve coil that has gone open circuit.
A blown fuse on the valve supply.
Rarely, an ECU driver fault.
fixes: Inspect and reseat the purge valve connector, looking for corrosion and bent pins.
Measure the purge valve coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; an open reading means a failed valve.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the valve supply wire.
Check the control wire for continuity to the ECU and for shorts to ground.
Replace the purge valve or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0445.meaning: The ECU detected a short in the EVAP purge control solenoid valve circuit, either inside the valve coil or in the wiring. Purge control is lost; the car normally drives fine, but a stuck valve can cause a rough idle and emissions tests will fail.
causes: A purge valve coil that has shorted internally.
A control wire chafed and shorted to ground or to power.
Water or corrosion in the connector.
Rarely, an ECU driver damaged by a shorted valve.
fixes: Inspect the purge valve connector for water and corrosion, and reseat it.
Measure the purge valve coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; a much lower reading means a shorted coil.
Check the control wire for shorts to ground or to other wires in the harness.
Replace the purge valve or repair the wiring.
Clear and re-test; if the code returns with a good valve and wiring, have the ECU driver checked.

P0447.meaning: The ECU detected an open circuit in the EVAP canister vent valve (Subaru calls it the drain valve), the solenoid near the charcoal canister that opens and seals the canister to fresh air. The engine runs normally and it is safe to drive, but the EVAP leak tests cannot run until it is fixed.
causes: Corroded or loose connector at the vent (drain) valve, which sits under the car near the fuel tank and canister and is exposed to water and road salt.
Broken or chafed wire between the ECU and the vent valve.
Failed vent valve solenoid coil (open winding).
Blown fuse or missing power feed to the valve.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the vent valve connector under the car for corrosion, green deposits or a broken lock tab; clean it and apply dielectric grease.
With the key on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) at the valve's power pin.
Unplug the valve and measure the coil resistance; an open reading (OL) means the coil is broken. Compare a normal reading with the service manual value.
Check the wire from the valve back to the ECU for continuity and for chafing where it runs along the underbody.
Replace the vent valve or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0448.meaning: The ECU detected a short circuit in the EVAP canister vent valve (drain valve) circuit. The engine runs normally, but the EVAP tests are disabled, and a valve stuck closed can make the fuel nozzle click off early when refuelling.
causes: Water intrusion or corrosion in the vent valve connector under the car, near the canister and fuel tank.
Wire chafed through and shorting to the body or to another wire along the underbody.
Vent valve solenoid with a shorted coil (very low resistance).
Harness damaged by road debris, jacking or bodywork.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the vent valve connector and nearby harness under the car for corrosion, water and crushed or rubbed-through wires.
Unplug the valve and measure the coil resistance; a reading near 0 ohms means a shorted coil. Compare with the service manual value.
With the valve and ECU unplugged, check the control wire for a short to ground and to other wires.
Check that the valve clicks when powered briefly from a 12 V source and that air flows through it when unpowered.
Replace the vent valve or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0451.meaning: The fuel tank pressure sensor gives readings that do not make sense for the conditions, for example no change when the EVAP system is sealed or vented. Driveability is not affected, but the EVAP leak tests are disabled.
causes: Kinked, cracked, disconnected or blocked hose between the pressure sensor and the tank or canister.
Liquid fuel or water in the sensor or its hose, often from topping off the tank past the first nozzle click.
Faulty fuel tank pressure sensor.
Vent (drain) valve or purge valve stuck, so pressure does not change as the ECU expects.
Poor connection at the sensor connector.
fixes: Stop topping off after the nozzle clicks off; overfilling can push fuel into the EVAP lines.
Locate the fuel tank pressure sensor (on or near the tank or canister) and inspect its hose for kinks, cracks and liquid; clear it if it is blocked.
Check the sensor connector for corrosion and a firm fit.
With the key on, check the sensor has about 5 V reference and a good ground, and that the signal voltage with the fuel cap off matches the service manual value.
Check that the vent and purge valves click when activated and are not stuck.
Replace the pressure sensor if the hose and wiring are good, then clear and re-test.

P0452.meaning: The fuel tank pressure sensor signal is below its normal range, which usually means an electrical fault rather than real vacuum in the tank. The car drives normally, but EVAP monitoring is disabled.
causes: Signal wire shorted to ground or chafed.
Missing 5 V reference supply to the sensor (open or shorted reference wire).
Corroded or loose sensor connector.
Faulty fuel tank pressure sensor.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the sensor connector and the harness near the tank for corrosion and damage.
With the key on, measure the reference voltage at the sensor connector: about 5 V is good. If other sensor codes are also stored, a shared 5 V reference may be shorted.
Back-probe the signal with the connector plugged in; a reading stuck near 0 V points to a shorted signal wire or a bad sensor.
Check the signal and ground wires for continuity to the ECU and for shorts to ground.
Replace the sensor if supply and ground are good but the signal stays low, then clear and re-test.

P0453.meaning: The fuel tank pressure sensor signal is above its normal range, which usually means an electrical fault rather than real pressure in the tank. The car drives normally, but EVAP monitoring is disabled.
causes: Open sensor ground wire.
Signal wire open or shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage.
Corroded or loose sensor connector.
Faulty fuel tank pressure sensor.
Blocked sensor hose trapping pressure (less common).
fixes: Inspect the sensor connector and the harness near the tank for corrosion and damage.
With the key on, check about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground (under 0.1 V between the ground pin and battery negative).
Back-probe the signal; a reading stuck near 5 V points to an open ground, a short to voltage or a bad sensor.
Check the sensor hose is not blocked and that the reading changes when you remove the fuel cap.
Replace the sensor if supply and ground are good but the signal stays high, then clear and re-test.

P0455.meaning: The EVAP leak test found a large leak in the fuel vapour system. The engine runs normally and it is safe to drive, but fuel vapour is escaping, so you may smell fuel near the car.
causes: Fuel cap missing, loose, not clicked, or with a damaged seal.
Cracked or disconnected EVAP hose, for example at the purge valve on the intake manifold or along the underbody to the canister.
Rusted fuel filler neck, a well-known problem on Subarus in areas that salt the roads.
Vent (drain) valve stuck open or a cracked charcoal canister.
Purge valve stuck open.
fixes: Check the fuel cap: it must click when tightened. Replace it with an OEM cap if the seal is cracked or flattened.
Inspect the EVAP hoses at the purge valve and intake manifold for cracks and loose ends.
Inspect the filler neck, the canister and the vent valve near the tank for rust, cracks and loose clamps.
Check the purge valve holds vacuum when not powered (it should be closed).
Have a smoke test done; it is the fastest way to find the exact leak.
After the repair, clear the code and drive several cycles so the ECU can re-run the EVAP test.

P0456.meaning: The EVAP system has a very small leak, about the size of a pinhole (roughly 0.5 mm or 0.02 inch). It does not affect the engine and is safe to drive, but the car will fail an emissions inspection with this code.
causes: Worn or hardened fuel cap seal.
Hairline cracks in aged EVAP hoses or at hose ends.
Rusted or pinholed fuel filler neck.
Purge valve that leaks slightly when closed.
Leaking charcoal canister or vent (drain) valve seal.
fixes: Replace the fuel cap with an OEM cap; it is cheap and fixes a lot of P0456 codes.
Inspect the filler neck, especially the top where it meets the body and the lower hose joints, for rust.
Check all EVAP hoses and clamps from the purge valve back to the canister.
Test the purge valve: apply vacuum with a hand pump, it should hold when unpowered.
Have a smoke test done; very small leaks are hard to find by eye.
After the repair, clear and let the ECU re-run the EVAP test over several drive cycles (it usually needs a cold soak overnight).

P0457.meaning: The ECU found an EVAP leak and concluded that the fuel cap is loose or missing, usually right after refuelling. It is safe to drive.
causes: Fuel cap not tightened until it clicks after refuelling.
Fuel cap left off or lost.
Damaged, cracked or dirty cap seal.
Wrong or poor-quality aftermarket cap.
Damaged or rusty filler neck opening where the cap seals.
fixes: Check the cap is fitted and tighten it until it clicks.
Inspect the cap's rubber seal and the neck opening for dirt, cracks or damage; wipe both clean.
Replace the cap with an OEM cap if the seal is worn.
If the code returns with a good cap, inspect the filler neck for rust and check for other EVAP leaks as for P0455.
Clear and re-test over a few drive cycles.

P0458.meaning: The ECU detected a low voltage (open or short to ground) in the EVAP purge control solenoid circuit. This valve, on or near the intake manifold, lets fuel vapour from the canister into the engine; the car drives normally, but purging and the EVAP tests are disabled.
causes: Damaged or corroded connector at the purge solenoid on the intake manifold.
Open or grounded wire between the ECU and the purge solenoid.
Failed purge solenoid coil.
Missing power feed to the solenoid (blown fuse or main relay issue).
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the purge valve connector and harness on the intake manifold; engine heat often makes these connectors brittle.
With the key on, check for battery voltage at the solenoid's power pin.
Measure the solenoid coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; open or near 0 ohms means the valve is bad.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for a short to ground.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0459.meaning: The ECU detected a high voltage in the EVAP purge control solenoid circuit, typically an open coil or a control wire shorted to power. The car drives normally, but purging and the EVAP tests are disabled.
causes: Open purge solenoid coil.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage or to another powered wire.
Damaged or corroded connector at the purge solenoid on the intake manifold.
Harness damage near hot engine parts.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the purge valve connector and harness on the intake manifold for heat damage and corrosion.
Measure the solenoid coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; an open reading (OL) means the valve is bad.
With the ECU and solenoid unplugged, check the control wire for a short to battery voltage.
Power the solenoid briefly from 12 V; it should click and let air through.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0461.meaning: The fuel level reading does not change the way the ECU expects as fuel is used, for example it stays the same over a long drive. Subaru tanks are saddle-shaped with a main and a sub level sender, so a problem in either half can cause this; the engine is not affected, but the gauge may be wrong.
causes: Sticking float arm or worn resistor track on the main or sub fuel level sender.
Poor contact at the sender connectors under the rear seat access covers.
Fuel not moving from the sub tank side to the main side (jet pump problem), so one sender reading stops changing.
Wiring fault between the senders, the combination meter and the ECU.
Faulty combination meter input on models where the meter reads the senders.
fixes: Note whether the gauge sticks, jumps or reads wrong at certain levels; if your ECU reports fuel level, watch it in the app's live data while driving.
Remove the rear seat cushion and access covers and check both sender connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
With the sender removed, measure its resistance while moving the float from empty to full; it should change smoothly with no dead spots. Compare with the service manual range.
Check the wiring between the senders, the meter and the ECU for continuity.
Replace the faulty sender (main or sub), then clear and re-test.

P0462.meaning: The fuel level sensor signal is below its normal range, usually an electrical fault (short to ground) rather than a truly empty or full tank. The fuel gauge may read wrong or stick at one end; the engine is not affected.
causes: Signal wire shorted to ground between the sender and the meter or ECU.
Faulty main or sub fuel level sender (shorted or worn resistor track).
Damaged harness under the rear seat or along the tank.
Faulty combination meter input on models where the signal passes through the meter.
fixes: Compare the gauge with the actual fuel in the tank (fill up and note the reading).
Remove the rear seat cushion and access covers and inspect both sender connectors and wires for damage.
Unplug the senders and check the signal wire for a short to ground.
Measure each sender's resistance and compare with the service manual range for the current fuel level.
Replace the faulty sender or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0463.meaning: The fuel level sensor signal is above its normal range, usually an open circuit rather than a truly full or empty tank. The fuel gauge may read wrong or stick at one end; the engine is not affected.
causes: Open circuit in the sender signal or ground wire.
Corroded or unplugged connector at the main or sub sender under the rear seat.
Faulty sender with a broken resistor track or a float arm that has fallen off.
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source.
Faulty combination meter input on models where the signal passes through the meter.
fixes: Compare the gauge with the actual fuel in the tank.
Remove the rear seat cushion and access covers and check that both sender connectors are plugged in and clean.
Check the sender ground to the body and the signal wire for continuity to the meter and ECU.
Measure each sender's resistance; an open reading (OL) means a broken sender. Compare a normal reading with the service manual range.
Replace the faulty sender or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0464.meaning: The fuel level sensor signal is jumping around or dropping out intermittently. The fuel gauge may flicker or suddenly change; the engine is not affected, but do not rely on the gauge until it is fixed.
causes: Worn spot on the resistor track of the main or sub sender, often at the level you usually drive at.
Loose or corroded sender connector under the rear seat.
Chafed wire that intermittently loses contact or shorts.
Poor ground at the sender or meter.
fixes: Note at which fuel level the gauge misbehaves; if your ECU reports fuel level, watch it in the app's live data while driving over bumps.
Remove the rear seat cushion and access covers, wiggle the sender connectors and check them for corrosion.
With the sender removed, sweep the float slowly while watching the resistance on a multimeter; any jump or dropout means the sender is worn.
Check the harness for chafing and the grounds for a clean connection.
Replace the faulty sender, then clear and re-test.

P0480.meaning: The ECU detected a fault (low voltage, open or short to ground) in the control circuit of radiator fan relay 1, which switches the main cooling fan. The fan may not run, so watch the temperature gauge closely, especially in traffic and with the A/C on.
causes: Failed fan relay (coil open or shorted).
Blown fuse feeding the relay coil.
Open or grounded wire between the ECU and the relay.
Corroded relay socket or connector in the engine bay relay box.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check the fan fuses and swap fan relay 1 with an identical relay in the box to see if the fault moves.
Idle the engine warm with the A/C on; the fans should run. Watch coolant temperature in the app's live data: fans normally switch on in the mid to high 90s °C (compare with the service manual).
Inspect the relay socket for corrosion or heat damage and measure the relay coil resistance.
Check the relay control wire back to the ECU for continuity and shorts.
Replace the relay or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0483.meaning: The ECU commanded the radiator fan on but did not see the expected result, typically coolant temperature not dropping as it should. Overheating is possible, so watch the temperature gauge and stop if it climbs.
causes: Fan motor worn, seized or spinning slowly.
Fan relay or fuse fault so the fan does not actually run.
Low coolant or air trapped in the cooling system (boxer engines are prone to air pockets after a coolant change).
Thermostat stuck closed or partly closed.
Radiator fins clogged or radiator blocked internally.
Coolant temperature sensor giving a misleading reading.
fixes: Check the coolant level in the reservoir and radiator with the engine cold.
Turn the A/C on at idle and confirm both fans run at full speed; with the engine off, spin each fan by hand to feel for rough or stiff bearings.
Watch coolant temperature in the app's live data and compare it with the gauge; a reading that jumps or does not fit the real temperature points to the sensor.
Bleed the cooling system properly (use the radiator bleed screw where fitted and run the heater on hot).
Clean blocked radiator fins and test the thermostat; replace the fan motor, thermostat or radiator as needed.

P0500.meaning: The ECU is not getting a valid vehicle speed signal. Depending on the model it comes from a sensor on the transmission or from the ABS/VDC wheel speed sensors, so the speedometer, cruise control and automatic shifting may also be affected.
causes: Faulty vehicle speed sensor on the transmission (older models) or a failed wheel speed sensor feeding the ABS/VDC unit (later models).
Damaged wiring or corroded connector at the sensor.
ABS/VDC unit fault; check for ABS or VDC warning lights and codes.
Communication fault between the combination meter, ABS/VDC unit, TCM and ECU (CAN on later models).
Damaged or dirty tone ring or reluctor at the sensor.
fixes: Check whether the speedometer works; if it does not, the fault is in the sensor or its signal path to the meter.
Watch vehicle speed in the app's live data on a test drive; it should match the speedometer and change smoothly.
Check for ABS, VDC and TCM codes; a wheel speed sensor fault often sets codes in several modules.
Inspect the speed sensor connector and harness for damage and corrosion.
Test or replace the speed sensor and repair wiring as needed, then clear and re-test.

P0501.meaning: The vehicle speed signal was implausible at low speed, for example reading zero or jumping while engine load and rpm show the car is moving. Speedometer, cruise control and shifting may be affected.
causes: Faulty vehicle speed sensor on the transmission (older models) or a failed wheel speed sensor feeding the ABS/VDC unit (later models).
Damaged wiring or corroded connector at the sensor.
ABS/VDC unit fault; check for ABS or VDC warning lights and codes.
Communication fault between the combination meter, ABS/VDC unit, TCM and ECU (CAN on later models).
Damaged or dirty tone ring or reluctor at the sensor.
fixes: Watch vehicle speed in the app's live data while pulling away and driving slowly; it should rise smoothly from zero with no dropouts.
Check whether the speedometer needle is steady at low speed.
Check for ABS, VDC and TCM codes and fix any wheel speed sensor faults first.
Inspect the speed sensor connector and wiring for looseness and corrosion.
Remove the sensor, clean metal debris from its tip, or replace it if faulty, then clear and re-test.

P0502.meaning: The vehicle speed signal is missing or too low while the car is clearly moving, usually an open or shorted sensor circuit. Speedometer, cruise control and shifting may be affected.
causes: Faulty vehicle speed sensor on the transmission (older models) or a failed wheel speed sensor feeding the ABS/VDC unit (later models).
Damaged wiring or corroded connector at the sensor.
ABS/VDC unit fault; check for ABS or VDC warning lights and codes.
Communication fault between the combination meter, ABS/VDC unit, TCM and ECU (CAN on later models).
Damaged or dirty tone ring or reluctor at the sensor.
fixes: Check whether the speedometer works.
Watch vehicle speed in the app's live data on a test drive; a reading stuck at zero confirms no signal.
Check for ABS, VDC and TCM codes.
Inspect the sensor connector and check the wiring to the ECU (or meter/ABS unit) for continuity and shorts to ground.
Replace the speed sensor if the wiring is good, then clear and re-test.

P0503.meaning: The vehicle speed signal was implausible at high speed, for example dropping out or jumping erratically at motorway speeds. Speedometer, cruise control and shifting may be affected.
causes: Faulty vehicle speed sensor on the transmission (older models) or a failed wheel speed sensor feeding the ABS/VDC unit (later models).
Damaged wiring or corroded connector at the sensor.
ABS/VDC unit fault; check for ABS or VDC warning lights and codes.
Communication fault between the combination meter, ABS/VDC unit, TCM and ECU (CAN on later models).
Damaged or dirty tone ring or reluctor at the sensor.
fixes: Watch vehicle speed in the app's live data at a steady high speed; it should be steady and match the speedometer.
Check whether the speedometer needle bounces at speed.
Check for ABS, VDC and TCM codes.
Inspect the sensor connector and harness for loose pins, chafing, or wires routed near ignition parts that could pick up interference.
Replace the speed sensor if the wiring is good, then clear and re-test.

P0506.meaning: The engine idles below its target speed and the idle control (a separate idle air control valve on older engines, the electronic throttle on newer ones) cannot bring it up. Expect a low or rough idle and possible stalling, especially with the A/C on.
causes: Carbon buildup in the throttle body or idle air control valve passage.
Idle air control valve sticking (older engines with a separate IAC valve).
Electronic throttle body dirty or not re-learned after cleaning or a battery disconnect.
Extra engine load, such as a dragging alternator or A/C compressor.
Clogged air filter or restricted intake.
fixes: Watch engine speed and, if available, target idle speed in the app's live data at warm idle, with and without the A/C.
Replace a clogged air filter.
Clean the throttle body and IAC passage with throttle body cleaner; on electronic throttles do it with the key off and do not force the plate.
Perform an idle relearn: after cleaning or a battery disconnect, let the engine idle fully warm with all loads off for about 10 minutes.
Check the IAC valve operation and wiring, and replace it if it sticks.

P0507.meaning: The engine idles above its target speed and the idle control cannot bring it down. It is usually caused by extra air getting in; it is safe to drive, but a high idle makes the car creep and shifts harsher on automatics.
causes: Vacuum leak, often a cracked PCV or breather hose or intake boot on EJ engines.
Idle air control valve stuck open or sticky from carbon.
Throttle plate not closing fully (binding cable, dirt or a disturbed stop screw).
Brake booster vacuum hose leak.
Coolant temperature sensor reading too cold, which raises the idle target.
fixes: Watch idle speed, coolant temperature and fuel trims in the app's live data; high positive trims at idle point to a vacuum leak.
Listen for hissing and inspect the PCV and breather hoses, intake boot and brake booster hose for cracks.
Check the throttle closes fully and the cable (on cable throttles) is not binding.
Clean the throttle body and IAC valve.
Have a smoke test done on the intake to find hidden leaks, then perform an idle relearn.

P0508.meaning: The ECU detected a low voltage (open or short to ground) in the idle air control valve circuit. Idle speed may be erratic, too high or too low, and the engine may stall when coming to a stop.
causes: Corroded or loose connector at the idle air control valve on the throttle body or intake.
Damaged wire between the ECU and the IAC valve, shorted to ground.
Failed IAC valve coil.
Heavy carbon buildup jamming the valve.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the IAC connector and harness for damage and corrosion.
Measure the IAC coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; near 0 ohms means a shorted coil.
With the ECU and valve unplugged, check the wires for a short to ground.
Clean the IAC valve and its passage.
Replace the IAC valve if it is electrically faulty, then clear and re-test.

P0509.meaning: The ECU detected a high voltage (open coil or short to power) in the idle air control valve circuit. Idle speed may be erratic, too high or too low, and the engine may stall when coming to a stop.
causes: Open IAC valve coil.
Broken wire or corroded connector at the IAC valve.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage.
Heavy carbon buildup jamming the valve.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the IAC connector and harness for damage and corrosion.
Measure the IAC coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; an open reading (OL) means a broken coil.
With the ECU and valve unplugged, check the wires for continuity and for a short to battery voltage.
Clean the IAC valve and its passage.
Replace the IAC valve if it is electrically faulty, then clear and re-test.

P050A.meaning: During the first seconds after a cold start, the ECU raises idle speed to heat the catalytic converter quickly, and the actual idle did not follow its target. This code is fairly common on later Subarus; the car usually runs fine, but it stops the emissions monitors from completing.
causes: Dirty throttle body, so the throttle cannot meter the extra airflow accurately.
Intake air leak after the MAF sensor, such as a cracked PCV hose or loose intake boot.
Weak battery or a recent battery disconnect that reset the learned idle values.
Wrong coolant or intake air temperature reading, so the ECU picks the wrong idle target.
ECU software; some models received updated software for cold start codes.
fixes: Check battery voltage first: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Clean the throttle body and check the intake tract and PCV hoses for leaks.

After a cold soak (overnight), watch engine speed, coolant temperature and intake air temperature in the app's live data for the first minute after start; coolant and intake temperatures should start close to each other and to the outside air.
Perform an idle relearn after cleaning or battery work.
Ask a Subaru dealer whether an ECU software update or service bulletin applies to your model and year.

P050B.meaning: During cold start the ECU retards ignition timing to heat the catalytic converter, and the actual timing did not follow its target, usually because the ECU had to add timing to hold idle speed. It often appears together with P050A; the car usually runs fine but will not complete the emissions monitors.
causes: Idle speed problems during cold start (see P050A): a dirty throttle body or an air leak.
Extra engine drag from heavy electrical load or oil that is too thick for the temperature.
Poor-quality or wrong-octane fuel.
Misfire or weak spark during warm-up.
ECU software; some models received updated software for cold start codes.
fixes: Check for other codes, especially P050A and misfire codes, and fix those first.
Use the recommended oil grade and fresh fuel of the correct octane.
Clean the throttle body and check the intake for leaks.
After a cold soak, watch ignition timing and engine speed in the app's live data for the first minute; timing should stay low (well retarded) for a short time and then rise as idle settles.
Ask a Subaru dealer whether an ECU software update or service bulletin applies to your model and year.

P0512.meaning: The ECU detected a problem with the starter request signal, which tells it the driver is cranking the engine with the key or start button. The engine may not crank, or may crank without the ECU recognising it.
causes: Faulty start contacts in the ignition switch, or a faulty push-button start switch.
Starter relay or starter cut relay fault.
Clutch pedal switch (manual) or inhibitor switch (automatic) not closing.
Damaged wiring or poor connector between the switch, the relays and the ECU.
Keyless access or body control module fault on push-button models.
fixes: Check battery voltage first: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. A weak battery can upset the start circuit.
On manuals, press the clutch fully and check the clutch switch adjustment; on automatics, try starting in Neutral as well as Park.
Check the starter-related fuses and swap the starter relay with an identical relay.
Check for battery voltage on the starter request wire at the ECU while cranking; compare with the service manual.
Repair the wiring or replace the switch that does not send the signal, then clear and re-test.

P0513.meaning: The immobilizer did not recognise the key, so the ECU will not let the engine run. The engine may crank but not start, or start and die after a second or two, and the security indicator may flash.
causes: Key not registered to the car (new, copied or aftermarket key).
Damaged transponder chip in the key, for example after a drop.
Interference from another transponder key or keyless card on the same key ring.
Faulty immobilizer antenna ring around the ignition cylinder, or its connector.
ECU or immobilizer module replaced without registering the keys.
Low battery voltage during the key check.
fixes: Remove other keys and cards from the key ring and try again.
Try the spare key; if it works, the first key is faulty or not registered.
Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V with the engine off.
Inspect the antenna ring connector around the ignition cylinder.
Have the keys registered (or the ECU and immobilizer paired) by a dealer or locksmith with Subaru immobilizer tools.

P0516.meaning: The ECU detected a low voltage in the battery temperature sensor circuit. On models with alternator charge control the ECU uses battery temperature to set the charging voltage; with this fault it falls back to a default strategy, so the battery may be under- or overcharged.
causes: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground.
Faulty battery temperature sensor (internally shorted).
Harness near the battery damaged by acid corrosion or chafing.
Faulty battery sensor unit on models where it is combined with the battery current sensor.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the sensor and its wiring around the battery for acid corrosion, chafing and pinched wires.
Clean corroded battery terminals and the area around the battery tray.
Unplug the sensor and measure its resistance; it should change smoothly with temperature. Compare with the service manual value.
With the sensor and ECU unplugged, check the signal wire for a short to ground.
Replace the sensor or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0517.meaning: The ECU detected a high voltage in the battery temperature sensor circuit, usually an open circuit or unplugged sensor. On models with alternator charge control the ECU falls back to a default charging strategy, so the battery may be under- or overcharged.
causes: Sensor unplugged, for example after a battery replacement.
Open circuit in the signal or ground wire.
Faulty battery temperature sensor (open internally).
Corroded connector near the battery.
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source.
fixes: Check the sensor is plugged in and fitted in its place, especially after battery work.
Inspect the connector and harness around the battery for corrosion and damage.
Unplug the sensor and measure its resistance; an open reading (OL) means a failed sensor. Compare a normal reading with the service manual value.
Check the signal and ground wires for continuity to the ECU.
Replace the sensor or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0519.meaning: The ECU could not control idle speed and has switched to a fail-safe idle strategy. Idle may be high or unstable and the engine may stall; on electronic throttle models it is often linked to a throttle body problem.
causes: Dirty or sticking throttle body or idle air control valve.
Large vacuum leak (PCV hose, intake boot, brake booster hose).
Electronic throttle body or throttle motor fault (look for P0638 or P2101 as well).
Throttle position sensor fault.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check for other codes, especially throttle, IAC and throttle position codes, and deal with those first.
Watch idle speed, throttle position and fuel trims in the app's live data; high positive trims at idle suggest a vacuum leak.
Clean the throttle body and IAC valve and check the intake hoses for leaks.
Perform an idle relearn after repairs.
Test or replace the throttle body or IAC valve if idle still cannot be controlled.

P0545.meaning: The ECU detected a low voltage in the exhaust gas temperature (EGT) sensor circuit. This sensor is used mainly on the EE20 boxer diesel to protect the turbo, catalyst and DPF; with it faulty the ECU may reduce power (limp mode) and stop DPF regeneration.
causes: Sensor wire shorted to ground, often where the harness runs close to the hot exhaust.
Faulty EGT sensor (they fail from repeated heat cycling).
Melted or damaged harness or connector.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the sensor harness near the exhaust and turbo for melted insulation and chafing.
Check the connector for corrosion and a firm fit.
Unplug the sensor and measure its resistance with the exhaust cold; compare with the service manual value.
With the sensor and ECU unplugged, check the signal wire for a short to ground.
Replace the sensor (anti-seize on the thread) or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test; a forced DPF regeneration may be needed afterwards if the soot load is high.

P0546.meaning: The ECU detected a high voltage in the exhaust gas temperature (EGT) sensor circuit, usually an open circuit. This sensor is used mainly on the EE20 boxer diesel to protect the turbo, catalyst and DPF; with it faulty the ECU may reduce power (limp mode) and stop DPF regeneration.
causes: Open EGT sensor element (burnt out).
Broken wire or unplugged connector, often near the hot exhaust.
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source.
Corroded connector pins.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the sensor harness near the exhaust and turbo for melted insulation and broken wires.
Check the connector is fully plugged in and free of corrosion.
Unplug the sensor and measure its resistance with the exhaust cold; an open reading (OL) means the sensor has failed. Compare a normal reading with the service manual value.
Check the signal and ground wires for continuity to the ECU and for a short to voltage.
Replace the sensor (anti-seize on the thread) or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test; a forced DPF regeneration may be needed afterwards if the soot load is high.

P0558.meaning: The ECU detected a high voltage in the brake booster pressure sensor circuit. This sensor, fitted on some later models and the EE20 diesel, tells the ECU how much vacuum is in the brake booster; the brakes still work, but check that the pedal does not feel hard.
causes: Open circuit or broken wire in the sensor ground or signal circuit.
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage.
Corroded or loose sensor connector.
Faulty brake booster pressure sensor.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check the brake pedal feel with the engine running; if the pedal is hard, inspect the booster vacuum hose and check valve before driving far.
Inspect the sensor connector and harness for damage and corrosion.
With the key on, check about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground at the sensor connector.
Back-probe the signal with the engine running; it should change when you pump the brake pedal. Compare with the service manual value.
Replace the sensor if supply and ground are good but the signal stays high, then clear and re-test.

P0559.meaning: The ECU detected a high voltage in the alternator control or monitoring circuit. On models where the ECU controls alternator output (charge control), charging may become uncontrolled or fall back to a fixed voltage; watch for the battery light and lights that dim or flare.
causes: Open or damaged wire in the alternator control or feedback circuit.
Corroded or loose connector at the alternator.
Faulty voltage regulator inside the alternator.
Battery current sensor fault on models with charge control.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check battery voltage first: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Watch battery voltage in the app's live data with loads switched on and off.
Inspect the alternator connector and main output cable for corrosion and a tight fit.
Check the alternator control and feedback wires to the ECU for continuity and shorts.
Have the alternator tested and replace it (or its regulator) if the output is wrong.
Clear and re-test after the repair.

P0562.meaning: The ECU saw its supply voltage drop below the normal range while running. Low voltage can cause poor running, electronic throttle faults and a string of other codes; if the battery light is on, the car will eventually stall once the battery is drained.
causes: Weak or failing battery.
Alternator not charging (worn brushes, failed regulator, slipping belt).
Loose or corroded battery terminals or ground straps (engine to body, body to battery).
Poor connection in the alternator output cable or a main fuse.
High electrical load from aftermarket accessories.
fixes: Check battery voltage first: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Watch battery voltage in the app's live data with the lights, blower and rear demister on.
Clean and tighten the battery terminals and check the engine and body ground straps.
Check the alternator drive belt for tension and wear.
Load test the battery (many parts stores do this for free) and replace it if weak.
Have the alternator tested and replace it if the output is low.

P0563.meaning: The ECU saw its supply voltage go above the normal range. Overcharging can boil or swell the battery and damage electronics, so find the cause soon.
causes: Faulty voltage regulator in the alternator (overcharging).
Poor ground or poor alternator sense connection making the regulator raise output.
Jump-starting or charging with a booster set to a high voltage.
Aftermarket charging or electrical equipment wired incorrectly.
Charge control fault on models where the ECU sets alternator output.
fixes: Check running voltage: 13.5 to 14.7 V is normal, above about 15 V points to overcharging. Watch battery voltage in the app's live data.
Clean and tighten the battery terminals, ground straps and the alternator connector.
Check the battery for swelling, hissing or a hot case, and replace it if damaged.
Have the alternator and regulator tested and replace them if they overcharge.
Clear and re-test after the repair.

P0565.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the cruise control SET switch signal, for example the switch reading as pressed for too long or a signal that does not make sense. Cruise control is disabled until it is fixed; the car is otherwise safe to drive.
causes: Worn or sticking cruise control switch on the steering wheel or stalk.
Faulty clock spring (spiral cable) behind the steering wheel on models with wheel-mounted cruise buttons; it can also affect the horn and airbag light.
Damaged wiring or poor connector between the switch and the ECU.
Moisture or dirt inside the switch.
fixes: Press and release SET several times to see if it sticks, and check the other cruise buttons.
Check whether the horn and other steering wheel controls work and whether the airbag light is on; if they also misbehave, suspect the clock spring.
If the app shows cruise switch states in live data, watch the SET signal while pressing the button.
Inspect the switch connector at the steering column for corrosion and a firm fit.
Replace the cruise switch or clock spring as needed; airbag work needs the battery disconnected and a wait before removal, so follow the service manual.

P0579.meaning: The cruise control switch signal is out of its expected range (too high), so the ECU cannot tell which button is pressed. Cruise control is disabled; the car is otherwise safe to drive.
causes: Open circuit in the cruise switch wiring or its ground.
Worn or dirty cruise switch contacts changing the signal voltage (many cruise switches send a different voltage per button on one wire).
Faulty clock spring (spiral cable) on models with cruise buttons on the steering wheel.
Corroded connector at the switch or steering column.
fixes: Check whether the horn and other steering wheel controls work and whether the airbag light is on; if not, suspect the clock spring.
If the app shows cruise switch states in live data, press each button and check that each one registers.
Inspect the switch connector at the steering column for corrosion and a firm fit.
Measure the switch output or resistance for each button and compare with the service manual values.
Replace the cruise switch or clock spring as needed; airbag work needs the battery disconnected and a wait before removal, so follow the service manual.

P0600.meaning: The ECU lost communication, or received bad data, on its link to another control module, most often the automatic transmission control module (TCM). Shift quality may suffer and the transmission may go into fail-safe.
causes: Damaged wiring or corroded connectors on the communication lines between the ECU and TCM (CAN bus on later models).
TCM without power or ground (for example a blown fuse), so it does not answer.
Faulty TCM or another module disrupting the network.
Aftermarket device spliced into the communication lines.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check for codes in the TCM and other modules; communication codes in several modules point to wiring.
Check the TCM and ECU fuses and ground connections.
Inspect the connectors at the ECU and TCM for corrosion or water entry.
On CAN models, with the battery disconnected, measure resistance between CAN high and CAN low at the OBD-II connector (pins 6 and 14); about 60 ohms is typical for a healthy bus.
Remove aftermarket devices from the network and re-test.

P0601.meaning: The ECU's self-check found that the contents of its program memory do not match the stored checksum. The engine may not start or may run badly; this often follows an interrupted or incorrect reflash.
causes: Interrupted or failed reflash, for example a tune flash where the power dropped or the cable came loose.
Tuned ROM written with an incorrect checksum.
Low battery voltage during programming.
Internal ECU memory failure.
fixes: Check battery voltage and connect a battery maintainer before any flashing: at least about 12.6 V with the engine off.
If the ECU was recently tuned or reflashed, reflash a known-good ROM (the stock ROM or your tuner's map) with a tool that corrects checksums.
Have a Subaru dealer reflash the latest factory software.
If the code returns after a clean reflash, replace the ECU (a replacement needs immobilizer registration).

P0602.meaning: The ECU reports that it is not programmed, or that its programming is incomplete or does not match the car. The engine may not run correctly, or at all.
causes: Replacement ECU fitted without being programmed for the car.
Interrupted reflash.
Wrong software or ROM for the car (for example a ROM from a different model or transmission).
Internal ECU fault.
fixes: Check battery voltage and connect a battery maintainer before any programming: at least about 12.6 V with the engine off.
Confirm the ROM or calibration ID matches your exact model, engine and transmission.
Reflash the correct software, either a known-good ROM or the latest factory software at a dealer.
If the code returns after a correct reflash, replace the ECU (a replacement needs immobilizer registration).

P0604.meaning: The ECU's self-test found a fault in its working memory (RAM). The ECU may behave unpredictably: stalling, poor running or a no-start are possible.
causes: Internal ECU fault.
Unstable supply voltage or voltage spikes (bad battery, loose terminals, faulty alternator).
Poor ECU ground connection.
Water or corrosion inside the ECU or its connectors.
fixes: Check battery voltage first: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Clean and tighten the battery terminals and check the engine and body ground straps.
Check the ECU and its connectors for water, corrosion or signs of damage.
Reflash the ECU software.
If the code returns, replace the ECU (a replacement needs immobilizer registration).

P0605.meaning: The ECU's self-test found a fault in its program memory (ROM or flash). The engine may not start or may run badly; it can follow an interrupted or incorrect reflash.
causes: Interrupted or failed reflash.
Corrupted or incorrect ROM image written to the ECU.
Low battery voltage during programming.
Internal ECU memory failure.
fixes: Check battery voltage and connect a battery maintainer before any flashing: at least about 12.6 V with the engine off.
If the ECU was recently tuned or reflashed, reflash a known-good ROM with a tool that verifies the write and corrects checksums.
Have a Subaru dealer reflash the latest factory software.
If the code returns after a clean reflash, replace the ECU (a replacement needs immobilizer registration).

P0606.meaning: The ECU's processor failed its internal self-check, or its main and monitoring processors disagree. On electronic throttle models the ECU usually enters limp mode with reduced power; have it checked soon.
causes: Internal ECU fault.
Unstable supply voltage or voltage spikes.
Poor ECU ground connection.
Water or corrosion inside the ECU or its connectors.
Corrupted software after a failed reflash.
fixes: Check battery voltage first: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Clean and tighten the battery terminals and check the engine and body ground straps.
Check the ECU and its connectors for water, corrosion or damage.
Reflash the ECU software.
If the code returns, replace the ECU (a replacement needs immobilizer registration).

P0607.meaning: The ECU detected that it is not performing correctly internally, for example a failed watchdog or internal timing check. Symptoms range from none to stalling or limp mode.
causes: Internal ECU fault.
Unstable supply voltage or voltage spikes.
Poor ECU ground connection.
Water or corrosion inside the ECU or its connectors.
Corrupted software after a failed reflash.
fixes: Check battery voltage first: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Clean and tighten the battery terminals and check the engine and body ground straps.
Check the ECU and its connectors for water, corrosion or damage.
Reflash the ECU software.
If the code returns, replace the ECU (a replacement needs immobilizer registration).

P0628.meaning: On the EE20 diesel, the ECU detected a short to ground in the suction control valve circuit. This valve on the high-pressure fuel pump meters how much fuel is pumped into the common rail, so expect limp mode, poor power or stalling; the engine may not restart.
causes: Chafed or pinched wire between the ECU and the suction control valve, shorted to ground.
Faulty suction control valve coil (shorted).
Corroded, damaged or fuel-soaked connector at the high-pressure pump.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the connector at the high-pressure pump and the nearby harness for rubbing, damage and corrosion.
Unplug the valve and measure the coil resistance; compare with the service manual value (near 0 ohms means a shorted coil).
With the valve and ECU unplugged, check each wire for continuity and for a short to ground.
Replace the suction control valve or repair the wiring; check the service manual for any learning procedure after replacement.
Clear and re-test, checking in live data that rail pressure follows its target.

P0629.meaning: On the EE20 diesel, the ECU detected a short to positive (battery voltage) in the suction control valve circuit. This valve on the high-pressure fuel pump meters how much fuel is pumped into the common rail, so expect limp mode, poor power or stalling; the engine may not restart.
causes: Control wire shorted to battery voltage or another powered wire.
Faulty suction control valve coil.
Damaged or corroded connector at the high-pressure pump.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the connector at the high-pressure pump and the nearby harness for rubbing, damage and corrosion.
Unplug the valve and measure the coil resistance; compare with the service manual value.
With the valve and ECU unplugged, check the control wire for a short to battery voltage.
Replace the suction control valve or repair the wiring; check the service manual for any learning procedure after replacement.
Clear and re-test, checking in live data that rail pressure follows its target.

P0638.meaning: The electronic throttle motor could not move the throttle plate to the position the ECU asked for within the allowed time. The ECU usually switches to limp mode with reduced power and a fixed or raised idle; drive gently and get it checked.
causes: Carbon or dirt buildup making the throttle plate stick.
Worn throttle motor or gears inside the throttle body.
Poor connection at the throttle body connector.
Low system voltage from a weak battery or charging fault.
Ice in the throttle body in freezing weather.
Faulty throttle position sensors inside the throttle body (often also sets P2101 or P2135).
fixes: Check battery voltage first: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
