With the key off, inspect the throttle plate for carbon and clean it gently with throttle body cleaner, without forcing the plate against the motor.
Inspect the throttle body connector and harness for corrosion and bent pins.
With the key on and engine off, press the pedal slowly while watching throttle position in the app's live data; it should move smoothly with no jumps or hesitation.
Perform an idle relearn after cleaning, and replace the throttle body if the code returns.

P0661.meaning: The ECU detected a low voltage (open or short to ground) in the intake manifold tuning valve circuit. This solenoid switches the intake runner path for better torque on engines that have one (for example some six-cylinder models); you may notice weaker mid-range or top-end power, but it is safe to drive.
causes: Corroded or loose connector at the tuning valve solenoid.
Open or grounded wire between the ECU and the solenoid.
Failed solenoid coil.
Missing power feed (blown fuse or main relay problem).
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Locate the tuning valve solenoid on the intake manifold and inspect its connector and vacuum hoses.
With the key on, check for battery voltage at the solenoid's power pin.
Measure the coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; near 0 ohms means a shorted coil.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for a short to ground.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0662.meaning: The ECU detected a high voltage (open coil or short to power) in the intake manifold tuning valve circuit. This solenoid switches the intake runner path for better torque on engines that have one (for example some six-cylinder models); you may notice weaker mid-range or top-end power, but it is safe to drive.
causes: Open solenoid coil.
Broken wire or corroded connector at the tuning valve solenoid.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage.
Harness damage near hot engine parts.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Locate the tuning valve solenoid on the intake manifold and inspect its connector and vacuum hoses.
Measure the coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; an open reading (OL) means a broken coil.
With the ECU and solenoid unplugged, check the control wire for continuity and for a short to battery voltage.
Power the solenoid briefly from 12 V; it should click.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0687.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in its main relay control circuit; the ECU keeps this relay on for a short time after key-off to finish tasks such as throttle checks and saving learned values. Symptoms range from none to a no-start, or a flat battery if the relay stays on.
causes: Faulty ECU main relay (sticking contacts or open coil).
Corroded relay socket or connector.
Open or shorted wire in the relay control circuit.
Blown fuse feeding the relay.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check the related fuses and swap the main relay with an identical relay to see if the fault moves.
After switching off, listen for the main relay clicking off within a short time; if it never clicks off, the relay or its control is stuck.
If the battery keeps going flat, measure the parasitic drain overnight or after the car has gone to sleep.
Inspect the relay socket and check the control wire to the ECU for continuity and shorts.
Replace the relay or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0691.meaning: The ECU detected a low voltage (open or short to ground) in the radiator fan control circuit. The fan may not run, or may run all the time; watch the temperature gauge, especially in traffic and with the A/C on.
causes: Failed fan relay or fan control module.
Control wire shorted to ground or open between the ECU and the relay.
Blown fan fuse.
Corroded relay socket or fan connector.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check the fan fuses and swap the fan relays with identical relays to see if the fault moves.
Idle the engine warm with the A/C on; the fans should run. Watch coolant temperature in the app's live data: fans normally switch on in the mid to high 90s °C (compare with the service manual).
Inspect the relay sockets and fan motor connectors for corrosion and heat damage.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for a short to ground.
Replace the relay or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0692.meaning: The ECU detected a high voltage (open circuit or short to power) in the radiator fan control circuit. The fan may run all the time or not at all; watch the temperature gauge, especially in traffic and with the A/C on.
causes: Fan relay stuck on or with an open coil.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage.
Broken wire or corroded connector in the fan control circuit.
Aftermarket fan switch or wiring changes.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check whether the fan runs with the key on and a cold engine; if it does, the relay is stuck or the control wire is shorted.
Swap the fan relays with identical relays to see if the fault moves.
Idle the engine warm with the A/C on and check the fans run; watch coolant temperature in the app's live data.
With the ECU and relay unplugged, check the control wire for a short to battery voltage.
Replace the relay or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0700.meaning: This is a flag, not the fault itself: the transmission control module (TCM) has stored its own code and asked the engine ECU to turn on the check engine light. The transmission may be in fail-safe mode, with harsh shifts or held in one gear.
causes: Any fault stored in the TCM: sensors, solenoids, fluid temperature or gear ratio problems.
Low or degraded ATF.
Wiring or connector problems at the transmission or TCM.
Low battery voltage causing the TCM to log faults.
fixes: Read the codes stored in the transmission control module (TCM) with a tool that can access it; the AT OIL TEMP light flashing after start-up on many Subaru automatics also means a TCM code is stored.
Check the ATF level with the transmission hot, the engine idling and the car on level ground, using the HOT mark on the dipstick; top up if low and look for leaks.
Check battery voltage first: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Inspect the transmission harness connectors for oil, water and corrosion.
Repair the underlying TCM fault, then clear the codes in both modules and re-test.

P0703.meaning: The ECU or TCM saw an implausible signal from the brake light switch, for example no change while the car speeds up and stops. This can affect cruise control, torque converter lock-up and the brake lights, so check that the brake lights work.
causes: Brake light switch misadjusted or failed (on the brake pedal bracket).
Blown brake light fuse.
Broken wire or poor connector at the switch.
Missing or worn rubber pedal stop, so the switch plunger is not pressed correctly.
fixes: Have someone watch the brake lights while you press the pedal: they should come on with light pressure and go off when released.
Check the brake light fuse.
Inspect the switch and its adjustment at the pedal, and replace a missing rubber pedal stop.
Measure the switch with a multimeter: it should switch cleanly between open and closed as the pedal moves.
Replace the switch if faulty, then clear and re-test.

P0704.meaning: The ECU saw an implausible signal from the clutch pedal switch on a manual transmission, for example no change during gear changes. It can affect cruise control, idle behaviour during shifts and, on some models, starting.
causes: Clutch switch misadjusted or failed at the clutch pedal.
Broken or disconnected wire at the switch.
Pedal assembly problem, such as a broken return spring or missing pedal stop.
Aftermarket clutch pedal, stop or switch modifications.
fixes: Check the clutch switch connector at the pedal is plugged in and undamaged.
If the app shows the clutch switch in live data, watch it change as you press and release the pedal.
Measure the switch with a multimeter: it should switch cleanly between open and closed as the pedal moves.
Adjust the switch per the service manual so it operates within the pedal travel.
Replace the switch if faulty, then clear and re-test.

P0705.meaning: The TCM or ECU received an invalid or conflicting signal from the transmission range sensor (the inhibitor switch on the automatic transmission), for example two positions at once or none. The car may not start in Park or Neutral, the gear display may be wrong, and the transmission may go into fail-safe.
causes: Inhibitor switch out of adjustment.
Shift cable out of adjustment or stretched.
Corroded or damaged inhibitor switch connector on the side of the transmission.
Worn or failed inhibitor switch.
Wiring fault to the TCM or ECU.
fixes: Check the gear display matches the lever in every position, the reversing lights come on only in R, and the engine starts only in P and N.
Inspect the inhibitor switch connector and wiring on the transmission for corrosion and damage.
Check the shift cable adjustment so each lever position matches the detent at the transmission.
Adjust the inhibitor switch per the service manual procedure.
Check each position with a multimeter and replace the switch if it does not switch cleanly, then clear and re-test.

P0710.meaning: The TCM detected a fault in the transmission fluid (ATF) temperature sensor circuit. Without it the TCM cannot adapt shifts and lock-up to fluid temperature, so shifts may be harsh or lock-up may not engage; the AT OIL TEMP light may flash.
causes: Damaged wiring or poor connection in the transmission harness (the sensor is inside the transmission).
Faulty ATF temperature sensor (often part of the internal harness).
Corroded or oil-soaked transmission connector.
TCM fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the transmission connectors for oil, water and corrosion.
If ATF temperature is available in live data, check that it starts close to the outside air temperature on a cold car and rises smoothly as it warms.
Measure the sensor resistance at the transmission connector and compare with the service manual value for the current fluid temperature.
Check the wiring to the TCM for continuity and shorts.
Replace the sensor or internal harness (on most Subaru automatics this means dropping the pan), then clear and re-test.

P0711.meaning: The ATF temperature reading does not make sense for the conditions, for example it does not rise after a long drive or does not fit the engine temperature. Shifts may be harsh or lock-up may not engage; the AT OIL TEMP light may flash.
causes: Faulty ATF temperature sensor reading inaccurately.
High resistance from a corroded or oil-soaked connector.
Low ATF level, so the sensor is not properly immersed.
ATF cooler or thermostat problem making the fluid temperature unusual.
Intermittent wiring fault.
fixes: Check the ATF level with the transmission hot, the engine idling and the car on level ground, using the HOT mark on the dipstick; top up if low and look for leaks.
If ATF temperature is available in live data, check that it starts close to the outside air temperature on a cold car and rises smoothly as it warms.
Inspect the transmission connectors for oil, water and corrosion.
Measure the sensor resistance cold and hot and compare with the service manual values.
Replace the sensor or internal harness if it reads wrong, then clear and re-test.

P0712.meaning: The ATF temperature sensor signal is below its normal range, which usually means a short to ground (it can also read as extremely hot fluid). Shifts may be harsh or lock-up may not engage; the AT OIL TEMP light may flash.
causes: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground inside or outside the transmission.
Faulty ATF temperature sensor (internally shorted).
Damaged internal harness in the valve body.
Genuinely overheated ATF (heavy towing, slipping transmission).
TCM fault (rare).
fixes: Check the ATF level and condition; burnt-smelling fluid suggests real overheating.
If ATF temperature is available in live data, check that it starts close to the outside air temperature on a cold car and rises smoothly as it warms.
Inspect the transmission connectors and harness for damage.
Measure the sensor resistance and check for a short to ground; compare with the service manual value.
Replace the sensor or internal harness, then clear and re-test.

P0713.meaning: The ATF temperature sensor signal is above its normal range, which usually means an open circuit (it can also read as extremely cold fluid). Shifts may be harsh or lock-up may not engage; the AT OIL TEMP light may flash.
causes: Open circuit in the sensor wiring or connector.
Faulty ATF temperature sensor (open internally).
Corroded or unplugged transmission connector.
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source.
TCM fault (rare).
fixes: Check the transmission connectors are fully plugged in and free of corrosion.
If ATF temperature is available in live data, check that it starts close to the outside air temperature on a cold car and rises smoothly as it warms.
Measure the sensor resistance at the transmission connector; an open reading (OL) means a broken circuit. Compare a normal reading with the service manual value.
Check the wiring to the TCM for continuity.
Replace the sensor or internal harness, then clear and re-test.

P0715.meaning: The TCM is not getting a valid signal from the torque converter turbine (input) speed sensor. It uses this signal to control shifts and lock-up, so expect harsh or delayed shifts and possible fail-safe mode.
causes: Faulty turbine speed sensor on the transmission case.
Damaged wiring or corroded connector.
Metal debris on the sensor tip.
TCM fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the sensor connector and wiring for damage and corrosion.
Remove the sensor and clean metal debris from the tip; heavy debris points to internal wear.
Measure the sensor resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the wiring back to the TCM for continuity and shorts.
Replace the sensor if faulty, then clear and re-test.

P0716.meaning: The torque converter turbine (input) speed sensor signal is present but erratic or implausible. Expect harsh or flared shifts and possible fail-safe mode.
causes: Loose or corroded sensor connector causing an intermittent signal.
Metal debris on the sensor tip.
Faulty turbine speed sensor.
Low ATF level or internal slipping that makes the speed reading unexpected.
Wiring picking up interference or chafed insulation.
fixes: Check the ATF level with the transmission hot, the engine idling and the car on level ground, using the HOT mark on the dipstick; top up if low and look for leaks.
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring and wiggle them with the engine running while watching for changes.
Remove the sensor and clean any metal debris from the tip.
Measure the sensor resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Replace the sensor if faulty, then clear and re-test.

P0719.meaning: The TCM saw the brake switch signal stay low (off) when it should have changed. It uses this signal to release torque converter lock-up when you brake; with a fault, the engine may stumble or stall when stopping, and cruise control may not work.
causes: Brake light switch misadjusted or failed.
Blown brake light fuse.
Open wire or poor connector between the switch and the TCM.
Burnt-out brake light bulbs on models that sense the signal through the lamp circuit.
fixes: Have someone watch the brake lights while you press the pedal: they should come on with light pressure.
Check the brake light fuse and bulbs.
Inspect the switch, its adjustment and connector at the pedal.
Measure the switch with a multimeter: it should switch cleanly between open and closed as the pedal moves.
Replace the switch or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0720.meaning: The TCM detected a problem with the output (vehicle) speed sensor signal from the automatic transmission, reported as a high or implausible signal. Shifts may be harsh or wrong, and the transmission may go into fail-safe.
causes: Faulty output speed sensor on the transmission or transfer case.
Damaged wiring or corroded connector.
Metal debris on the sensor tip.
Wiring picking up interference or shorted to another signal.
TCM fault (rare).
fixes: Compare vehicle speed in the app's live data with the speedometer on a test drive.
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring for damage and corrosion.
Remove the sensor and clean metal debris from the tip.
Measure the sensor resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Replace the sensor if faulty, then clear and re-test.

P0722.meaning: The TCM is getting no signal, or too low a signal, from the output (vehicle) speed sensor on the automatic transmission. Shifts may be harsh or wrong, the speedometer may be affected, and the transmission may go into fail-safe.
causes: Faulty output speed sensor.
Open wire or corroded connector at the sensor.
Signal wire shorted to ground.
Metal debris on the sensor tip.
TCM fault (rare).
fixes: Compare vehicle speed in the app's live data with the speedometer on a test drive.
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring for damage and corrosion.
Measure the sensor resistance and check the wiring to the TCM for continuity and shorts to ground; compare with the service manual value.
Remove the sensor and clean metal debris from the tip.
Replace the sensor if faulty, then clear and re-test.

P0724.meaning: The TCM saw the brake switch signal stay high (on) when it should have changed, as if the brake pedal were always pressed. Torque converter lock-up and cruise control may not work, and the brake lights may stay on.
causes: Brake light switch misadjusted or stuck closed.
Missing or worn rubber pedal stop, so the switch plunger hangs free.
Signal wire shorted to battery voltage.
Faulty switch.
fixes: Check whether the brake lights stay on with the pedal released.
Inspect the switch and rubber pedal stop at the brake pedal and adjust the switch.
Measure the switch with a multimeter: it should be open with the pedal released and closed when pressed (or the reverse, per the service manual).
Check the signal wire for a short to battery voltage.
Replace the switch or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0725.meaning: The TCM is not getting a valid engine speed signal from the engine ECU. Shift and lock-up control fall back to defaults, so shifts may feel harsh.
causes: Wiring or connector fault on the engine speed signal line or CAN link between the ECU and TCM.
Crankshaft position sensor problem (check for engine codes such as P0335).
ECU or TCM communication fault.
Poor ground at the ECU or TCM.
fixes: Check for engine codes, especially crank sensor codes, and fix those first.
Watch engine speed in the app's live data; it should be steady at idle and follow the tachometer.
Inspect the ECU and TCM connectors for corrosion and loose pins.
Check the engine speed signal wire (or CAN wires) between the ECU and TCM for continuity.
Repair the wiring or connectors, then clear and re-test.

P0726.meaning: The engine speed signal received by the TCM is present but implausible, for example jumping or not matching turbine speed. Shifts may be harsh or erratic.
causes: Intermittent wiring or connector fault between the ECU and TCM.
Crankshaft position sensor giving an erratic signal (check for engine codes).
Electrical interference from ignition parts or aftermarket wiring.
Poor ground at the ECU or TCM.
fixes: Check for engine codes, especially crank sensor or misfire codes.
Watch engine speed in the app's live data for dropouts or spikes.
Inspect the ECU and TCM connectors and grounds.
Check the wiring between the ECU and TCM for chafing and loose pins.
Repair as needed, then clear and re-test.

P0731.meaning: The TCM compared input (turbine) speed with output speed and found the wrong ratio while in 1st gear, which means the transmission is slipping or not fully engaged in that gear. Driving on a slipping transmission can quickly make the damage worse, so drive gently and get it checked.
causes: Low, burnt or degraded ATF.
Worn clutch or brake for 1st gear.
Sticking shift solenoid or valve body fault.
Faulty turbine or output speed sensor giving a wrong reading.
Low line pressure (line pressure duty solenoid or pump wear).
fixes: Check the ATF level with the transmission hot, the engine idling and the car on level ground, using the HOT mark on the dipstick; top up if low and look for leaks.
Check the fluid condition: dark brown colour, a burnt smell or metal particles point to internal wear.
Read the TCM codes for speed sensor or solenoid faults and fix those first.
If the fluid is old but not burnt, a drain and refill with the correct Subaru ATF may help.
If the slipping continues, have a transmission specialist check line pressure and the valve body, or overhaul the transmission.

P0732.meaning: The TCM compared input (turbine) speed with output speed and found the wrong ratio while in 2nd gear, which means the transmission is slipping or not fully engaged in that gear. Driving on a slipping transmission can quickly make the damage worse, so drive gently and get it checked.
causes: Low, burnt or degraded ATF.
Worn clutch or brake for 2nd gear.
Sticking shift solenoid or valve body fault.
Faulty turbine or output speed sensor giving a wrong reading.
Low line pressure (line pressure duty solenoid or pump wear).
fixes: Check the ATF level with the transmission hot, the engine idling and the car on level ground, using the HOT mark on the dipstick; top up if low and look for leaks.
Check the fluid condition: dark brown colour, a burnt smell or metal particles point to internal wear.
Read the TCM codes for speed sensor or solenoid faults and fix those first.
If the fluid is old but not burnt, a drain and refill with the correct Subaru ATF may help.
If the slipping continues, have a transmission specialist check line pressure and the valve body, or overhaul the transmission.

P0733.meaning: The TCM compared input (turbine) speed with output speed and found the wrong ratio while in 3rd gear, which means the transmission is slipping or not fully engaged in that gear. Driving on a slipping transmission can quickly make the damage worse, so drive gently and get it checked.
causes: Low, burnt or degraded ATF.
Worn clutch or brake for 3rd gear.
Sticking shift solenoid or valve body fault.
Faulty turbine or output speed sensor giving a wrong reading.
Low line pressure (line pressure duty solenoid or pump wear).
fixes: Check the ATF level with the transmission hot, the engine idling and the car on level ground, using the HOT mark on the dipstick; top up if low and look for leaks.
Check the fluid condition: dark brown colour, a burnt smell or metal particles point to internal wear.
Read the TCM codes for speed sensor or solenoid faults and fix those first.
If the fluid is old but not burnt, a drain and refill with the correct Subaru ATF may help.
If the slipping continues, have a transmission specialist check line pressure and the valve body, or overhaul the transmission.

P0741.meaning: The torque converter lock-up clutch is slipping or not engaging when commanded, so engine speed stays higher than expected at steady cruise. This wastes fuel and heats the ATF; drive gently until it is checked.
causes: Low or degraded ATF.
Lock-up duty solenoid sticking.
Valve body fault.
Worn lock-up clutch inside the torque converter.
Brake switch signal wrongly releasing lock-up.
fixes: Check the ATF level with the transmission hot, the engine idling and the car on level ground, using the HOT mark on the dipstick; top up if low and look for leaks.
Read the TCM codes and fix any lock-up solenoid or brake switch faults first.
Watch engine speed in the app's live data at a steady 80 to 100 km/h on a flat road; when lock-up engages, rpm should drop slightly and hold steady.
If the fluid is old, a drain and refill with the correct Subaru ATF may cure shudder or slip.
If it persists, have the lock-up solenoid, valve body or torque converter checked by a transmission specialist.

P0743.meaning: The TCM detected an electrical fault (open or short) in the torque converter lock-up duty solenoid circuit. Lock-up will not work, so fuel economy drops and the ATF runs hotter; the car is drivable but should be checked.
causes: Corroded, oil-soaked or loose transmission connector.
Damaged wiring between the TCM and the transmission.
Failed lock-up duty solenoid coil.
Damaged internal harness in the valve body.
TCM fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the transmission connectors and harness for damage, oil and corrosion.
Measure the solenoid resistance at the transmission connector and compare with the service manual value; open or near 0 ohms is a fault.
Check the wires from the transmission to the TCM for continuity and shorts to ground.
If the external wiring is good, drop the pan and check the internal harness and solenoid.
Replace the faulty part, then clear and re-test.

P0748.meaning: The TCM detected an electrical fault in the line pressure duty solenoid circuit; this solenoid sets the main hydraulic pressure in the automatic transmission. Expect harsh shifts, and the transmission will usually go into fail-safe, held in one gear.
causes: Corroded, oil-soaked or loose transmission connector.
Damaged wiring between the TCM and the transmission.
Failed line pressure duty solenoid coil.
Damaged internal harness in the valve body.
TCM fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the transmission connectors and harness for damage, oil and corrosion.
Measure the solenoid resistance at the transmission connector and compare with the service manual value; open or near 0 ohms is a fault.
Check the wires from the transmission to the TCM for continuity and shorts to ground.
If the external wiring is good, drop the pan and check the internal harness and solenoid.
Replace the faulty part, then clear and re-test.

P0751.meaning: The TCM commanded shift solenoid A but the gear change did not happen as expected, so it believes the solenoid is stuck off or not working mechanically. Shifts may be missing or wrong, and the transmission may go into fail-safe.
causes: Low or dirty ATF, or debris sticking shift solenoid A or its valve.
Shift solenoid A stuck mechanically.
Valve body fault (sticking shift valve).
Internal clutch wear that makes the shift look like a solenoid problem.
Intermittent electrical connection.
fixes: Check the ATF level with the transmission hot, the engine idling and the car on level ground, using the HOT mark on the dipstick; top up if low and look for leaks.
Read all TCM codes; an electrical code for the same solenoid (P0753) points to wiring first.
Measure the solenoid resistance at the transmission connector and compare with the service manual value.
Drop the pan, check for debris, and test the solenoid by applying battery voltage briefly (it should click).
Replace the solenoid or have the valve body serviced, then clear and re-test.

P0753.meaning: The TCM detected an electrical fault (open or short) in the shift solenoid A circuit. The transmission will usually go into fail-safe, held in one gear with harsh engagement, until it is repaired.
causes: Corroded, oil-soaked or loose transmission connector.
Damaged wiring between the TCM and the transmission.
Failed shift solenoid A coil (open or shorted).
Damaged internal harness in the valve body.
TCM fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the transmission connectors and harness for damage, oil and corrosion.
Measure the solenoid resistance at the transmission connector and compare with the service manual value; open or near 0 ohms is a fault.
Check the wires from the transmission to the TCM for continuity and shorts to ground.
If the external wiring is good, drop the pan and check the internal harness and solenoid.
Replace the faulty part, then clear and re-test.

P0778.meaning: The TCM detected an electrical fault (open or short) in pressure control solenoid B, a duty solenoid in the valve body that controls the pressure to a clutch or brake during shifts. Expect harsh or slipping shifts and possible fail-safe mode.
causes: Corroded, oil-soaked or loose transmission connector.
Damaged wiring between the TCM and the transmission.
Failed pressure control solenoid B coil.
Damaged internal harness in the valve body.
TCM fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the transmission connectors and harness for damage, oil and corrosion.
Measure the solenoid resistance at the transmission connector and compare with the service manual value; open or near 0 ohms is a fault.
Check the wires from the transmission to the TCM for continuity and shorts to ground.
If the external wiring is good, drop the pan and check the internal harness and solenoid.
Replace the faulty part, then clear and re-test.

P0785.meaning: The TCM detected a fault in a shift timing solenoid, which controls exactly when clutches and brakes apply and release during a shift (on the 4EAT these include the low clutch and 2-4 brake timing solenoids). Expect harsh or flared shifts and possible fail-safe mode.
causes: Corroded, oil-soaked or loose transmission connector.
Damaged wiring between the TCM and the transmission.
Failed timing solenoid coil, or a solenoid stuck by debris.
Damaged internal harness in the valve body.
TCM fault (rare).
fixes: Check the ATF level with the transmission hot, the engine idling and the car on level ground, using the HOT mark on the dipstick; top up if low and look for leaks.
Inspect the transmission connectors and harness for damage, oil and corrosion.
Measure the solenoid resistance at the transmission connector and compare with the service manual value; open or near 0 ohms is a fault.
Check the wires from the transmission to the TCM for continuity and shorts to ground.
If the external wiring is good, drop the pan, check for debris and test the solenoid; replace the faulty part, then clear and re-test.

P0801.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the reverse inhibit control circuit, which prevents reverse from being selected while the car is moving forward. Reverse may be blocked, or allowed when it should not be, so never select reverse while rolling forward.
causes: Faulty reverse inhibit solenoid or actuator.
Open or shorted wire in the control circuit.
Corroded or loose connector at the transmission.
Missing or wrong vehicle speed signal used to decide when to block reverse.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check for vehicle speed codes and confirm vehicle speed reads correctly in the app's live data.
Inspect the connector and wiring at the reverse inhibit solenoid on the transmission.
Measure the solenoid resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and shorts.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0817.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the circuit it uses to allow or block the starter (for example the starter cut relay linked to the immobilizer, clutch switch or inhibitor switch). The engine may not crank, or may crank when it should not.
causes: Faulty starter cut relay.
Open or shorted wire in the starter disable circuit.
Clutch switch (manual) or inhibitor switch (automatic) fault.
Immobilizer fault blocking the starter.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check battery voltage first: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Check the starter-related fuses and swap the starter cut relay with an identical relay.
On manuals, check the clutch switch operates at full pedal travel; on automatics, try starting in both Park and Neutral.
Check for immobilizer codes such as P0513.
Check the control wiring between the ECU and the relay for continuity and shorts, then repair and re-test.

P0850.meaning: The ECU saw an implausible signal from the neutral position switch (on manuals a switch on the gearbox, on automatics part of the inhibitor switch), for example no change between driving and stopping in neutral. The ECU uses it for idle control and on some models for starting, so idle may dip or rise oddly.
causes: Faulty neutral position switch on the transmission.
Corroded, loose or damaged switch connector.
Broken or shorted wire between the switch and the ECU.
Inhibitor switch out of adjustment on automatics.
fixes: If the app shows the neutral switch in live data, watch it change as you move the lever into and out of neutral.
Inspect the switch connector on the transmission for corrosion and damage.
Measure the switch with a multimeter: it should change state cleanly between neutral and in gear.
Check the wire to the ECU for continuity and shorts; on automatics, check the inhibitor switch adjustment.
Replace the switch or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0851.meaning: The neutral position switch signal stays low, so the ECU sees the transmission as always in (or never in) neutral depending on the circuit design. Idle control may be affected and, on some models, starting.
causes: Signal wire shorted to ground.
Faulty neutral position switch stuck in one state.
Damaged or corroded switch connector.
Inhibitor switch out of adjustment on automatics.
fixes: If the app shows the neutral switch in live data, watch it as you move the lever into and out of neutral.
Inspect the switch connector and wiring on the transmission for damage and corrosion.
Measure the switch with a multimeter in neutral and in gear; it should change state cleanly.
With the switch and ECU unplugged, check the signal wire for a short to ground.
Replace the switch or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P0852.meaning: The ECU reads the neutral position switch input as stuck high, so it may think the car is in neutral (or park) while it is actually in gear; on manuals this is the neutral switch on the gearbox, on automatics the inhibitor (range) switch. It is usually safe to drive, but idle control and starting can be affected.
causes: Faulty neutral position switch (manual) or inhibitor switch (automatic).
Inhibitor switch out of adjustment after transmission or shifter work (automatics).
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source, or an open ground at the switch.
Corroded, oily or loose connector at the switch on the transmission.
Rarely, an ECU input fault.
fixes: In the app's live data, watch the neutral position switch while moving the lever: it should read on only in neutral (and park on automatics).
Check the switch connector on the transmission for corrosion, oil contamination and a secure latch.
On automatics, check that the starter only works in P and N and that the gear indicator matches the lever; adjust the inhibitor switch if not.
With the connector unplugged, test the switch with a multimeter: continuity should change as you move in and out of neutral.
Check the wiring back to the ECU for chafing or a short to power, then replace the switch if it tests faulty.

P0864.meaning: The engine ECU and the automatic transmission control unit (TCM) exchange data such as engine torque and shift status, and the ECU found that link out of its normal range. The transmission may go into a fail-safe mode with harsh or limited shifting (on older models the AT OIL TEMP light may flash), so drive gently until it is fixed.
causes: Loose, corroded or water-damaged connector at the ECU or TCM.
Damaged wiring between the ECU and TCM (chafed harness, rodent damage).
Low or unstable battery voltage, or a poor ground connection.
A fault inside the TCM.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Clean the battery terminals and main grounds.
Read the codes stored in the transmission control unit as well, since they often point to the same fault.
Inspect the ECU and TCM connectors for corrosion, water and bent pins, and reseat them with the battery disconnected.

Check the communication wires between the two modules for continuity and for shorts to ground or power. On CAN-bus models, about 60 ohms between CAN high and CAN low with the battery disconnected is normal.
If the wiring and power supply are good, have the TCM tested or replaced.

P0865.meaning: The ECU saw the communication line to the automatic transmission control unit (TCM) stuck at a low voltage, which usually means a short to ground or an open circuit. The transmission may go into fail-safe mode with harsh or limited shifting (on older models the AT OIL TEMP light may flash), so drive gently until it is fixed.
causes: Communication wire shorted to ground (chafed harness).
Open wire or unplugged connector between the ECU and TCM.
Corroded or water-damaged connector at either module.
TCM not powered (blown fuse) or a fault inside the TCM.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Check the TCM fuses and read the TCM's own codes to confirm it is powered and responding.
Inspect the ECU and TCM connectors for corrosion, water and bent pins, and reseat them with the battery disconnected.
With both modules unplugged, check the communication wire for continuity end to end and for a short to ground (it should read open to ground).
If the wiring and power supply are good, have the TCM tested or replaced.

P0866.meaning: The ECU saw the communication line to the automatic transmission control unit (TCM) stuck at a high voltage, which usually means a short to a voltage source or a lost ground. The transmission may go into fail-safe mode with harsh or limited shifting (on older models the AT OIL TEMP light may flash), so drive gently until it is fixed.
causes: Communication wire shorted to a power wire in the harness.
Poor or open ground at the TCM or ECU.
Corroded or water-damaged connector at either module.
A fault inside the TCM.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Clean and tighten the engine and body ground connections.
Read the TCM's own codes, since they often point to the same fault.
Inspect the ECU and TCM connectors for corrosion, water and bent pins, and reseat them with the battery disconnected.
With both modules unplugged and the key on, check the communication wire for voltage: it should not show battery voltage.
If the wiring and grounds are good, have the TCM tested or replaced.

P0880.meaning: The ignition-switched power supply to the transmission control unit (TCM), shown as PIVGN, is outside its expected range. Without stable power the TCM can drop into fail-safe mode with harsh shifts or the transmission held in one gear, so drive gently until it is fixed.
causes: Weak battery or a charging system problem.
Blown, loose or corroded fuse in the TCM or ignition supply.
Poor ground connection at the TCM or at the engine and body grounds.
Worn ignition switch contacts or a faulty ignition relay.
Wiring or connector fault in the supply to the TCM.
Rarely, a TCM fault.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Check the fuses that feed the TCM and ignition circuits, and look for corrosion in the fuse box.
With the key on, measure the supply voltage at the TCM connector; it should be within about 0.5 V of battery voltage.
Do a voltage drop test on the TCM ground with the engine running: well under 0.2 V is good.
Wiggle the harness and ignition switch while watching the voltage to find an intermittent connection.

P0882.meaning: The ignition-switched power supply to the transmission control unit (TCM), shown as PIVGN, is reading too low. The TCM may drop into fail-safe mode with harsh shifts or the transmission held in one gear, so drive gently until it is fixed.
causes: Weak or discharged battery, or a failing alternator.
High resistance in a fuse, fuse holder or connector in the TCM supply.
Poor ground connection at the TCM or at the engine and body grounds.
Worn ignition switch contacts or a faulty ignition relay.
Damaged supply wire to the TCM.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Have the battery load tested and the charging system checked if the voltages are low.
Check the fuses that feed the TCM and ignition circuits for corrosion and a tight fit.
With the key on, measure the supply voltage at the TCM connector; it should be within about 0.5 V of battery voltage.
Do a voltage drop test on the TCM ground and supply with the engine running: well under 0.2 V on the ground side is good.

P0883.meaning: The ignition-switched power supply to the transmission control unit (TCM), shown as PIVGN, is reading too high. This usually points to overcharging or a wiring fault, and high voltage can damage electronics, so fix it promptly.
causes: Alternator voltage regulator overcharging (above about 15 V).
Jump start or battery charger with too high a voltage.
Supply wire shorted to another circuit.
Loose battery connection causing voltage spikes.
Rarely, a TCM input fault.
fixes: Check charging voltage with the engine running: 13.5 to 14.7 V is normal; above about 15 V points to the alternator regulator.
Clean and tighten the battery terminals and main grounds.
Measure the supply voltage at the TCM connector and compare it with battery voltage.
Check the harness for chafing where the supply wire could touch another circuit.
Replace the alternator or regulator if it overcharges, then clear and re-test.

P0955.meaning: The control unit that switches the backup (reversing) light relay found an open circuit in the relay control line. The reversing lights may not come on in reverse; driving is not affected, but fix it for safety and inspections.
causes: Failed backup light relay (open coil).
Relay loose or not fully seated in its socket.
Broken wire or unplugged connector in the relay control circuit.
Blown fuse feeding the relay.
Rarely, a fault in the control unit.
fixes: With the ignition on and the lever in R, check whether the reversing lights come on.
Check the fuse for the backup light circuit.
Swap the relay with an identical one and see whether the lights and the code change.
Measure the relay coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; an infinite reading means an open coil.
Check the control wire between the relay socket and the control unit for continuity.

P0957.meaning: The control unit that switches the backup (reversing) light relay found the relay control line reading low, which usually means a short to ground. The reversing lights may not work correctly; driving is not affected, but fix it for safety and inspections.
causes: Relay control wire shorted to ground (chafed harness).
Relay coil shorted internally.
Corroded or wet relay socket or connector.
Blown fuse feeding the relay.
Rarely, a fault in the control unit.
fixes: With the ignition on and the lever in R, check whether the reversing lights come on.
Check the fuse for the backup light circuit.
Swap the relay with an identical one and see whether the lights and the code change.
With the relay removed and the control unit unplugged, check the control wire for a short to ground (it should read open).
Inspect the harness for chafing, especially where it passes body panels and brackets.

P0958.meaning: The control unit that switches the backup (reversing) light relay found the relay control line reading high, which usually means a short to a voltage source. The reversing lights may not work correctly; driving is not affected, but fix it for safety and inspections.
causes: Relay control wire shorted to a power wire.
Relay coil shorted or relay contacts stuck.
Corroded or wet connector bridging terminals.
Harness damage where wires rub against the body.
Rarely, a fault in the control unit.
fixes: With the ignition on, check whether the reversing lights come on only in R.
Swap the relay with an identical one and see whether the lights and the code change.
Measure the relay coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
With the relay removed and the key on, check the control wire for voltage where there should be none.
Inspect the harness and connectors for water, corrosion and chafing, and repair as needed.

P1009.meaning: The ECU found the circuit of the swirl control valve reading low; this valve sits in the intake and adds swirl to the incoming air at low load, and is fitted mainly to the EE20 boxer diesel. Expect higher emissions and possibly rougher running at low load; it is usually safe to drive while you diagnose it.
causes: Unplugged, corroded or loose connector at the swirl valve actuator.
Wiring open or shorted to ground, often from chafing near hot engine parts.
Failed swirl valve actuator (motor or solenoid).
Actuator jammed by soot and oil build-up in the intake.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the actuator connector for corrosion, oil and a secure latch.
Check the harness between the actuator and the ECU for chafing or melted insulation.
Measure the actuator resistance and compare with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for supply voltage at the actuator connector.
If the valve is vacuum operated on your model, also check its vacuum hose and control solenoid, then replace the actuator if it still fails.

P1026.meaning: The variable valve lift system on system 1 (normally bank 1: right side, cylinders 1 and 3) did not switch between its low-lift and high-lift intake cam profiles as expected; this is i-AVLS on EJ25 SOHC engines from about 2005 on, and AVLS on some JDM EJ20s. The engine may feel flat at higher rpm or idle roughly; it is safe to drive gently, but check the oil level first.
causes: Low engine oil level, or old and sludgy oil (the system switches with oil pressure).
Clogged filter screen on the oil switching solenoid valve for system 1.
Sticking or failed oil switching solenoid valve for system 1.
Wiring or connector fault at the solenoid.
Sticking lift-switching pins in the rocker arms (less common, internal).
fixes: Check the oil level and condition, and top up or change the oil with the grade Subaru specifies.
Inspect the solenoid connector and wiring for oil ingress, corrosion or damage.
Measure the solenoid coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Remove the oil switching solenoid and clean or replace its filter screen and seals.
Replace the solenoid if it tests bad; if the code returns with a good solenoid and clean oil, have the oil pressure and rocker assembly checked.

P1028.meaning: The variable valve lift system on system 2 (normally bank 2: left side, cylinders 2 and 4) did not switch between its low-lift and high-lift intake cam profiles as expected; this is i-AVLS on EJ25 SOHC engines from about 2005 on, and AVLS on some JDM EJ20s. The engine may feel flat at higher rpm or idle roughly; it is safe to drive gently, but check the oil level first.
causes: Low engine oil level, or old and sludgy oil (the system switches with oil pressure).
Clogged filter screen on the oil switching solenoid valve for system 2.
Sticking or failed oil switching solenoid valve for system 2.
Wiring or connector fault at the solenoid.
Sticking lift-switching pins in the rocker arms (less common, internal).
fixes: Check the oil level and condition, and top up or change the oil with the grade Subaru specifies.
Inspect the solenoid connector and wiring for oil ingress, corrosion or damage.
Measure the solenoid coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.

P1086.meaning: The position sensor for tumble generator valve (TGV) 2, on the left side (bank 2, cylinders 2 and 4), is reading below its normal voltage range. The TGVs are flaps in the intake runners that close at cold idle for better mixing; the engine usually still runs fine, but cold idle and emissions may suffer.
causes: Corroded, oil-soaked or loose connector at the TGV motor under the intake manifold (very common on EJ engines).
Sensor signal wire open, or shorted to ground.
Lost 5 V reference to the sensor.
Failed position sensor inside the TGV motor assembly.
TGVs removed or deleted without the ECU being tuned to disable the TGV codes.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: In the app's live data, check the left TGV position voltage: it should sit between the extremes and change when the valve moves, not stay near 0 V.
Inspect the connector at the left TGV motor for corrosion, oil and bent pins; clean it with contact cleaner and reseat it.
With the key on, check for the 5 V reference and a good ground at the sensor connector, and compare with the service manual.
Check the signal wire back to the ECU for breaks and for a short to ground.
Replace the TGV motor and sensor assembly if the wiring is good. If the TGVs have been deleted, the ECU must be tuned to disable these codes.

P1087.meaning: The position sensor for tumble generator valve (TGV) 2, on the left side (bank 2, cylinders 2 and 4), is reading above its normal voltage range. The TGVs are flaps in the intake runners that close at cold idle for better mixing; the engine usually still runs fine, but cold idle and emissions may suffer.
causes: Corroded, oil-soaked or loose connector at the TGV motor under the intake manifold (very common on EJ engines).
Sensor signal wire shorted to a voltage source.
Open sensor ground wire.
Failed position sensor inside the TGV motor assembly.
TGVs removed or deleted without the ECU being tuned to disable the TGV codes.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: In the app's live data, check the left TGV position voltage: it should sit between the extremes and change when the valve moves, not stay near 5 V.
Inspect the connector at the left TGV motor for corrosion, oil and bent pins; clean it with contact cleaner and reseat it.
With the key on, check for the 5 V reference and a good ground at the sensor connector, and compare with the service manual.
Check the signal wire for a short to voltage and the sensor ground wire for continuity back to the ECU.
Replace the TGV motor and sensor assembly if the wiring is good. If the TGVs have been deleted, the ECU must be tuned to disable these codes.

causes: Corroded, oil-soaked or loose connector at the TGV motor under the intake manifold (very common on EJ engines).

The TGVs are flaps in the intake runners that close at cold idle for better mixing; the engine usually still runs fine, but cold idle and emissions may suffer.

P1090.meaning: When the ECU commanded tumble generator valve (TGV) 1 on the right side (bank 1, cylinders 1 and 3) to open, the position sensor did not confirm that it opened. A TGV that stays closed restricts airflow and can cost noticeable power at higher load; it is safe to drive gently while you diagnose it.
causes: TGV shaft or flap sticking from carbon and oil build-up in the intake runner.
Failing TGV motor, or worn gears in the motor assembly.
Corroded or loose connector at the TGV motor under the intake manifold.
Faulty position sensor reporting the wrong position even though the valve moves.
Wiring fault in the motor drive or sensor circuit.
fixes: In the app's live data, watch the right TGV position voltage from a cold start through warm-up: it should change clearly when the valve opens.
Inspect and clean the right TGV motor connector, and check the harness under the intake manifold for damage.
Check the motor drive and sensor circuits with a multimeter and compare with the service manual values.
Check that the TGV shaft moves freely (easiest with the intake manifold removed) and clean carbon from the valve and shaft if it sticks.
Replace the TGV motor and sensor assembly (or the whole TGV body) if it still does not move correctly.

P1091.meaning: When the ECU commanded tumble generator valve (TGV) 1 on the right side (bank 1, cylinders 1 and 3) to close, the position sensor did not confirm that it closed. A TGV that stays open mainly affects cold idle quality and cold-start emissions; the car is generally safe to drive.
causes: TGV shaft or flap sticking from carbon and oil build-up in the intake runner.
Failing TGV motor, or worn gears in the motor assembly.
Corroded or loose connector at the TGV motor under the intake manifold.
Faulty position sensor reporting the wrong position even though the valve moves.
Wiring fault in the motor drive or sensor circuit.
fixes: In the app's live data, watch the right TGV position voltage from a cold start through warm-up: it should change clearly when the valve closes.
Inspect and clean the right TGV motor connector, and check the harness under the intake manifold for damage.
Check the motor drive and sensor circuits with a multimeter and compare with the service manual values.
Check that the TGV shaft moves freely (easiest with the intake manifold removed) and clean carbon from the valve and shaft if it sticks.
Replace the TGV motor and sensor assembly (or the whole TGV body) if it still does not move correctly.

P1092.meaning: When the ECU commanded tumble generator valve (TGV) 2 on the left side (bank 2, cylinders 2 and 4) to open, the position sensor did not confirm that it opened. P1094.meaning: The ECU found an open circuit in the drive signal to the tumble generator valve (TGV) 1 motor on the right side (bank 1, cylinders 1 and 3). The valve can no longer be moved and stays where it is, which can mean a rough cold idle or less power at high load; it is usually safe to drive gently.
causes: Unplugged, corroded or loose connector at the TGV motor under the intake manifold.
Broken wire in the harness to the TGV motor.
Open (burnt out) winding in the TGV motor.
TGVs removed or deleted without the ECU being tuned to disable the TGV codes.
Rarely, a failed driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Check the connector at the right TGV motor for corrosion, oil and a secure latch.
Measure the TGV motor resistance at its connector and compare with the service manual value; an infinite reading means an open motor.
Check continuity of the drive wires from the ECU to the motor connector.
Repair the harness if a wire is broken, or replace the TGV motor assembly if the motor is open.
Clear and re-test after the repair, watching the TGV position in live data.

P1095.meaning: The ECU found a short circuit in the drive signal to the tumble generator valve (TGV) 1 motor on the right side (bank 1, cylinders 1 and 3). The ECU stops driving the valve, which then stays where it is, so expect a rough cold idle or less power at high load; it is usually safe to drive gently.
causes: Drive wire shorted to ground or to another circuit (chafed harness under the intake manifold).
Shorted winding inside the TGV motor.
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the TGV motor connector.
Seized TGV making the motor draw excessive current.
Rarely, a failed driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Check the connector at the right TGV motor for water, corrosion and bridged pins.
Measure the TGV motor resistance and compare with the service manual value; a very low reading means a shorted motor.
With the ECU and motor unplugged, check the drive wires for a short to ground and to each other.
Check that the TGV is not seized, as a stuck valve can overload the motor.
Repair the harness or replace the TGV motor assembly, then clear and re-test.

P1096.meaning: The ECU found an open circuit in the drive signal to the tumble generator valve (TGV) 2 motor on the left side (bank 2, cylinders 2 and 4). The valve can no longer be moved and stays where it is, which can mean a rough cold idle or less power at high load; it is usually safe to drive gently.

Repair the harness if a wire is broken, or replace the TGV motor assembly if the motor is open.

The ECU stops driving the valve, which then stays where it is, so expect a rough cold idle or less power at high load; it is usually safe to drive gently.

P1102.meaning: On older Subarus the manifold pressure sensor also measures outside air pressure, using a pressure source switching solenoid valve that switches the sensor between manifold vacuum and outside air; the ECU found this solenoid's circuit reading low. Altitude compensation can be off, but the car is usually safe to drive.
causes: Open or shorted pressure source switching solenoid coil.
Unplugged, corroded or loose connector at the pressure source switching solenoid.
Control wire open, or shorted to ground.
Blown fuse in the pressure source switching solenoid supply.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the pressure source switching solenoid for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the supply wire.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for a short to ground.
Also check the small vacuum hoses between the solenoid, the pressure sensor and the manifold for cracks, then replace the solenoid if it tests bad.

P1110.meaning: The atmospheric (barometric) pressure sensor signal is below its normal range. The ECU uses this reading to correct fuelling (and boost on turbo models) for altitude, so running may be affected; on many Subaru ECUs the sensor is built into the ECU itself.
causes: Faulty atmospheric pressure sensor (on many models it is inside the ECU, so this can mean an ECU fault).
On models with a separate sensor: open signal wire or a short to ground.
Lost 5 V reference to the sensor.
Poor ECU power or ground connections.
Water ingress into the ECU or its connectors.
fixes: In the app's live data, check the atmospheric pressure reading with the engine off: it should match local air pressure, roughly 101 kPa (14.7 psi) at sea level and lower at altitude.
Compare it with the manifold pressure reading with the key on and engine off: the two should be almost the same.
Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Clean and tighten the ECU grounds.
On models with a separate sensor, check its connector, 5 V reference and signal wire.
If the sensor is inside the ECU and power and grounds are good, the ECU needs repair or replacement.

P1111.meaning: The atmospheric (barometric) pressure sensor signal is above its normal range. The ECU uses this reading to correct fuelling (and boost on turbo models) for altitude, so running may be affected; on many Subaru ECUs the sensor is built into the ECU itself.
causes: Faulty atmospheric pressure sensor (on many models it is inside the ECU, so this can mean an ECU fault).
On models with a separate sensor: signal wire shorted to voltage, or an open sensor ground.
Poor ECU ground connections.
Water ingress into the ECU or its connectors.
fixes: In the app's live data, check the atmospheric pressure reading with the engine off: it should match local air pressure, roughly 101 kPa (14.7 psi) at sea level and lower at altitude.
Compare it with the manifold pressure reading with the key on and engine off: the two should be almost the same.
Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Clean and tighten the ECU grounds.
On models with a separate sensor, check its connector, ground and signal wire for a short to voltage.
If the sensor is inside the ECU and power and grounds are good, the ECU needs repair or replacement.

P1112.meaning: The atmospheric (barometric) pressure reading is implausible, for example it does not agree with the manifold pressure reading while the engine is off. The ECU uses it to correct fuelling (and boost on turbo models) for altitude, so running may be affected.
causes: Atmospheric pressure sensor drifting out of calibration (inside the ECU on many models).
Faulty manifold pressure sensor giving the wrong comparison value.
On older models that use a pressure source switching solenoid, a stuck solenoid or cracked hose.
Blocked sensor port on models with a separate sensor.
Poor ECU power or ground connections.
fixes: In the app's live data, check the atmospheric pressure reading with the engine off: it should match local air pressure, roughly 101 kPa (14.7 psi) at sea level and lower at altitude.
Compare it with the manifold pressure reading with the key on and engine off: the two should be almost the same.
If only one of the two readings is wrong, focus on that sensor.
On older models, check the pressure source switching solenoid and its small vacuum hoses.
Check ECU power and grounds; if the sensor is inside the ECU and everything else is good, the ECU needs repair or replacement.

P1122.meaning: On older Subarus the manifold pressure sensor also measures outside air pressure, using a pressure source switching solenoid valve that switches the sensor between manifold vacuum and outside air; the ECU found this solenoid's circuit reading high. Altitude compensation can be off, but the car is usually safe to drive.
causes: Pressure source switching solenoid control wire shorted to a power wire.
Shorted pressure source switching solenoid coil (very low resistance).
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the connector.
Harness damage where wires rub or run near hot parts.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the pressure source switching solenoid for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the solenoid and ECU unplugged and the key on, check the control wire for voltage where there should be none.
Inspect the harness for chafing or melted insulation.
Also check the small vacuum hoses between the solenoid, the pressure sensor and the manifold for cracks, then replace the solenoid if it tests bad.

P1130.meaning: The ECU found an open circuit in the front air/fuel (A/F) sensor (bank 1, sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinder boxers the single front sensor is reported as bank 1; on six-cylinders bank 1 is the right side, cylinders 1, 3 and 5). Without it the ECU cannot trim the mixture accurately, so economy and emissions suffer; it is usually safe to drive short-term.
causes: Unplugged, corroded or loose A/F sensor connector.
Wiring broken by heat or road debris near the exhaust.
Failed A/F sensor (internal open circuit).
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: In the app's live data, check the A/F sensor reading: a faulty sensor circuit often sits fixed at one value and does not react to throttle changes or a coasting fuel cut.
Inspect the sensor connector and the harness along the exhaust for melted, chafed or pinched wires.
Unplug the sensor and check continuity of its wires back to the ECU.
Measure the sensor heater resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Replace the front A/F sensor with the correct part if the wiring is good, then clear and re-test.

P1131.meaning: The ECU found a short circuit in the front air/fuel (A/F) sensor (bank 1, sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinder boxers the single front sensor is reported as bank 1; on six-cylinders bank 1 is the right side, cylinders 1, 3 and 5). Without it the ECU cannot trim the mixture accurately, so economy and emissions suffer; it is usually safe to drive short-term.
causes: Sensor wires melted together or shorted to the exhaust or body.
Failed A/F sensor (internal short).
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the connector.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: In the app's live data, check the A/F sensor reading: a faulty sensor circuit often sits fixed at one value and does not react to throttle changes or a coasting fuel cut.
Inspect the sensor connector and the harness along the exhaust for melted, chafed or pinched wires.
Unplug the sensor and check its wires for shorts to ground, to each other and to the heater supply.
Measure the sensor heater resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Replace the front A/F sensor with the correct part if the wiring is good, then clear and re-test.

P1134.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in its own air/fuel (A/F) sensor control circuitry, the part of the ECU that drives and reads the front wideband sensor. Mixture control may fall back to less accurate values; the car is usually drivable, but emissions and economy suffer.
causes: Internal fault in the ECU's A/F sensor control circuit.
Shorted A/F sensor or wiring overloading the ECU circuit.
Low or unstable supply voltage, or poor ECU grounds.
Water ingress into the ECU or its connectors.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Clean and tighten the ECU ground connections and check the ECU connectors for corrosion.
Inspect the A/F sensor wiring and connector for shorts, melted insulation or water.
Clear and re-test; if a sensor circuit code (such as P1130 or P1131) appears instead, repair the sensor side first.
If power, grounds and the sensor circuit are good and the code returns, the ECU needs repair or replacement.

P1135.meaning: The ECU found an open circuit in the front air/fuel (A/F) sensor (bank 2, sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; bank 2 front sensors are found mainly on six-cylinder EZ30/EZ36 engines, where bank 2 is the left side, cylinders 2, 4 and 6). Without it the ECU cannot trim the mixture accurately, so economy and emissions suffer; it is usually safe to drive short-term.
causes: Unplugged, corroded or loose A/F sensor connector.
Wiring broken by heat or road debris near the exhaust.
Failed A/F sensor (internal open circuit).
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: In the app's live data, check the A/F sensor reading: a faulty sensor circuit often sits fixed at one value and does not react to throttle changes or a coasting fuel cut.
Inspect the sensor connector and the harness along the exhaust for melted, chafed or pinched wires.
Unplug the sensor and check continuity of its wires back to the ECU.
Measure the sensor heater resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Replace the front A/F sensor with the correct part if the wiring is good, then clear and re-test.

P1136.meaning: The ECU found a short circuit in the front air/fuel (A/F) sensor (bank 2, sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; bank 2 front sensors are found mainly on six-cylinder EZ30/EZ36 engines, where bank 2 is the left side, cylinders 2, 4 and 6). Without it the ECU cannot trim the mixture accurately, so economy and emissions suffer; it is usually safe to drive short-term.
causes: Sensor wires melted together or shorted to the exhaust or body.
Failed A/F sensor (internal short).

Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: In the app's live data, check the A/F sensor reading: a faulty sensor circuit often sits fixed at one value and does not react to throttle changes or a coasting fuel cut.
Inspect the sensor connector and the harness along the exhaust for melted, chafed or pinched wires.
Unplug the sensor and check its wires for shorts to ground, to each other and to the heater supply.

P1137.meaning: The front air/fuel (A/F) sensor (bank 1, sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinder boxers the single front sensor is reported as bank 1; on six-cylinders bank 1 is the right side, cylinders 1, 3 and 5) is stuck at a mid value equal to lambda 1 (about 14.7:1) and does not respond to real mixture changes. The ECU cannot trim fuel properly, so economy and emissions may suffer; it is usually safe to drive short-term.
causes: Worn-out or contaminated A/F sensor that has stopped responding.
Sensor heater not working, so the sensor never gets hot enough to read.
Open circuit in the sensor wiring that makes the signal float at the mid value.
Corroded or loose connector.
fixes: In the app's live data, watch the A/F sensor during a throttle snap and a coasting fuel cut: it should swing rich and then very lean, not stay at lambda 1.00.
Check the sensor heater fuse, and measure the heater resistance against the service manual value.
Inspect the connector and the harness near the exhaust.
Replace the front A/F sensor if it still does not respond, then clear and re-test.

P1139.meaning: The heater in the front air/fuel (A/F) sensor (bank 1, sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinder boxers the single front sensor is reported as bank 1; on six-cylinders bank 1 is the right side, cylinders 1, 3 and 5) is not performing as expected, for example drawing too little or too much current. A cold sensor reads poorly, so closed-loop fuel control starts late and emissions rise; it is usually safe to drive.
causes: Heater element inside the A/F sensor failing.
Blown heater fuse or a faulty heater relay.
Heat-damaged wiring or a corroded connector.
Low battery or charging voltage.
Rarely, a faulty heater driver in the ECU.
fixes: Check the fuse for the A/F sensor heater.
Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Measure the heater resistance at the sensor connector and compare with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the heater supply wire at the connector.
Replace the front A/F sensor if the heater is out of spec, then clear and re-test.

P1140.meaning: The heater in the front air/fuel (A/F) sensor (bank 2, sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; bank 2 front sensors are found mainly on six-cylinder EZ30/EZ36 engines, where bank 2 is the left side, cylinders 2, 4 and 6) is not performing as expected, for example drawing too little or too much current. A cold sensor reads poorly, so closed-loop fuel control starts late and emissions rise; it is usually safe to drive.
causes: Heater element inside the A/F sensor failing.
Blown heater fuse or a faulty heater relay.
Heat-damaged wiring or a corroded connector.
Low battery or charging voltage.
Rarely, a faulty heater driver in the ECU.
fixes: Check the fuse for the A/F sensor heater.
Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Measure the heater resistance at the sensor connector and compare with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the heater supply wire at the connector.
Replace the front A/F sensor if the heater is out of spec, then clear and re-test.

P1141.meaning: The mass air flow (MAF) sensor reading is lower than the ECU expects for the current engine speed and throttle. This can cause hesitation, a lean mixture or poor running; on turbo models, avoid full boost until it is fixed.
causes: Dirty or contaminated MAF sensor element (often from over-oiled aftermarket air filters).
Unmetered air leaking in after the MAF: cracked intake boot, loose clamps, or cracked PCV and breather hoses (common on EJ turbos).
On turbo models, a leaking turbo inlet hose or blow-off valve.
Aftermarket intake or MAF housing that changes the airflow reading.
Wiring or connector fault (poor ground or high resistance on the signal).
fixes: In the app's live data, check MAF g/s at warm idle (usually about 2.5 to 5 g/s on a 2.0 to 2.5 litre engine) and check that it rises smoothly with rpm.
Check fuel trims: large positive trims at idle point to an air leak after the MAF.
Inspect the intake boot, clamps, PCV and breather hoses, and on turbo models the turbo inlet and blow-off valve. A smoke test finds leaks fastest.
Clean the MAF element with dedicated MAF cleaner only, and reseat its connector.
Replace the MAF sensor if the readings stay low with no leaks found.

P1142.meaning: The throttle position sensor (TPS) reading is lower than expected, or does not agree with other signals such as airflow. You may notice a poor idle, hesitation or erratic shifting on automatics; it is usually safe to drive carefully.
causes: Worn TPS with a dead spot in its track.
TPS out of adjustment (older cable-throttle models).
Corroded or loose TPS connector.
Weak 5 V reference, or signal wire shorted to ground.
Throttle stop screw that has been tampered with.
fixes: In the app's live data, watch throttle position while slowly opening the throttle: it should rise smoothly from closed to wide open without dropouts.
Inspect the TPS connector for corrosion and a secure fit.
With the key on, check the 5 V reference and ground at the sensor connector.
On cable-throttle models, check the closed-throttle TPS voltage against the service manual and adjust the sensor if it is adjustable.
Replace the TPS if the reading is erratic or out of spec.

P1143.meaning: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor reading is lower than expected for the current engine conditions. Fuel and boost calculations can be affected, so on turbo models avoid hard boost until it is fixed.
causes: Faulty MAP sensor.
Blocked or kinked hose to the MAP sensor.
Wiring fault: weak 5 V reference, open signal wire or short to ground.
On turbo models, a boost leak or underboost that keeps manifold pressure lower than expected.
Restricted air intake, such as a blocked air filter or collapsed intake hose.
fixes: In the app's live data, compare manifold pressure with atmospheric pressure, key on and engine off: they should be almost the same.
At warm idle the manifold should show strong vacuum, roughly 25 to 40 kPa absolute, and the reading should rise smoothly when you blip the throttle.
Inspect the hose to the sensor and its connector.
Check the 5 V reference, ground and signal wire at the sensor.
On turbo models, pressure test the intake for boost leaks, then replace the MAP sensor if the readings are still implausible.

P1144.meaning: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor reading is higher than expected for the current engine conditions. Fuel and boost calculations can be affected, so on turbo models avoid hard boost until it is fixed.
causes: Cracked, loose or disconnected hose to the MAP sensor (the sensor then sees near atmospheric pressure).
Faulty MAP sensor.
Signal wire shorted to voltage, or an open sensor ground.
On turbo models, genuine overboost from a stuck wastegate or boost control fault.
Large vacuum leak, or low engine vacuum from a mechanical problem.
fixes: In the app's live data, compare manifold pressure with atmospheric pressure, key on and engine off: they should be almost the same.
At warm idle the manifold should show strong vacuum, roughly 25 to 40 kPa absolute, and the reading should rise smoothly when you blip the throttle.
Inspect the hose to the sensor and its connector.
Check the 5 V reference, ground and signal wire at the sensor.
On turbo models, log boost against target to rule out overboost, then replace the MAP sensor if the readings are still implausible.

P1146.meaning: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor reading is higher than expected for the current engine conditions (some models log this number instead of P1144 for the same fault). Fuel and boost calculations can be affected, so on turbo models avoid hard boost until it is fixed.
causes: Cracked, loose or disconnected hose to the MAP sensor (the sensor then sees near atmospheric pressure).
Faulty MAP sensor.
Signal wire shorted to voltage, or an open sensor ground.
On turbo models, genuine overboost from a stuck wastegate or boost control fault.
Large vacuum leak, or low engine vacuum from a mechanical problem.
fixes: In the app's live data, compare manifold pressure with atmospheric pressure, key on and engine off: they should be almost the same.
At warm idle the manifold should show strong vacuum, roughly 25 to 40 kPa absolute, and the reading should rise smoothly when you blip the throttle.
Inspect the hose to the sensor and its connector.
Check the 5 V reference, ground and signal wire at the sensor.
On turbo models, log boost against target to rule out overboost, then replace the MAP sensor if the readings are still implausible.

P1152.meaning: The front air/fuel (A/F) sensor (bank 1, sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinder boxers the single front sensor is reported as bank 1; on six-cylinders bank 1 is the right side, cylinders 1, 3 and 5) is reporting values below the range the ECU expects, or is responding too weakly to mixture changes. Economy and emissions can suffer; it is usually safe to drive short-term.
causes: Aged or contaminated A/F sensor (oil, coolant or silicone contamination).
Wiring or connector fault in the sensor circuit.
A genuine mixture problem, such as incorrect fuel pressure or a leaking injector.
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor, such as a leaking up-pipe or header gasket on EJ turbos or a cracked header.
fixes: In the app's live data, watch the A/F sensor: it should swing quickly between rich and lean with throttle changes and read very lean during a coasting fuel cut.
Check fuel trims at idle and cruise; large trims point to a real mixture problem rather than the sensor.
Check for exhaust leaks ahead of the sensor (ticking noise, soot marks at gaskets).
Inspect the sensor connector and the harness near the exhaust.
Replace the front A/F sensor if it is slow or stuck and the other checks are good, then clear and re-test.

P1153.meaning: The front air/fuel (A/F) sensor (bank 1, sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; on four-cylinder boxers the single front sensor is reported as bank 1; on six-cylinders bank 1 is the right side, cylinders 1, 3 and 5) is reporting values above the range the ECU expects, or is responding too weakly to mixture changes. Economy and emissions can suffer; it is usually safe to drive short-term.
causes: Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor, such as a leaking up-pipe or header gasket on EJ turbos or a cracked header.
Aged or contaminated A/F sensor.
A genuine lean condition, such as a vacuum leak, cracked PCV hose or weak fuel pump.
Wiring or connector fault in the sensor circuit.
fixes: In the app's live data, watch the A/F sensor: it should swing quickly between rich and lean with throttle changes and read very lean during a coasting fuel cut.
Check fuel trims at idle and cruise; large trims point to a real mixture problem rather than the sensor.
Check for exhaust leaks ahead of the sensor (ticking noise, soot marks at gaskets).
Inspect the sensor connector and the harness near the exhaust.
Replace the front A/F sensor if it is slow or stuck and the other checks are good, then clear and re-test.

P1154.meaning: The front air/fuel (A/F) sensor (bank 2, sensor 1, before the catalytic converter; bank 2 front sensors are found mainly on six-cylinder EZ30/EZ36 engines, where bank 2 is the left side, cylinders 2, 4 and 6) is reporting values below the range the ECU expects, or is responding too weakly to mixture changes. Economy and emissions can suffer; it is usually safe to drive short-term.
causes: Aged or contaminated A/F sensor (oil, coolant or silicone contamination).
Wiring or connector fault in the sensor circuit.
A genuine mixture problem, such as incorrect fuel pressure or a leaking injector.
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor, such as a leaking up-pipe or header gasket on EJ turbos or a cracked header.
fixes: In the app's live data, watch the A/F sensor: it should swing quickly between rich and lean with throttle changes and read very lean during a coasting fuel cut.

Check for exhaust leaks ahead of the sensor (ticking noise, soot marks at gaskets).
