P1160.meaning: On models with an electronic throttle, the ECU checks that the return spring pulls the throttle plate back to its default position, and it found the throttle not returning as expected. The ECU may limit throttle opening (limp mode); drive gently and get it checked, as throttle response can be unpredictable.
causes: Carbon build-up making the throttle plate stick.
Weak or broken return spring inside the throttle body.
Ice in the throttle body in freezing weather.
Worn throttle motor or gears.
Throttle position sensor or wiring fault giving a wrong reading.
fixes: Check for other throttle codes, which help narrow the fault down.
In the app's live data, compare throttle position with its target if available: they should track each other closely.
With the ignition off, inspect the throttle plate for carbon and clean it with throttle body cleaner; do not force the plate or spray into the motor or sensor.
Check the throttle body connector for corrosion and a secure latch.
After cleaning, turn the ignition on and wait a few seconds before starting so the throttle can relearn; replace the throttle body if the code returns.

P1199.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the differential pressure sensor measures the pressure drop across the diesel particulate filter (DPF) to judge how full it is, and the ECU found its signal faulty or implausible. Without it the ECU cannot manage DPF regeneration properly, so get it fixed soon before the DPF clogs and the engine goes into limp mode.
causes: Cracked, disconnected, soot-blocked or swapped hoses between the sensor and the DPF.
Failed differential pressure sensor.
Corroded connector or damaged wiring near the exhaust.
A genuinely blocked DPF giving a very high reading.
Water freezing in the sensor hoses in cold weather.
fixes: Inspect the two hoses from the sensor to the DPF for splits, soot blockage and correct routing (the two sides must not be swapped).
Check the sensor connector and harness for heat damage and corrosion.
If the app shows DPF differential pressure, it should read near zero with the engine off and rise with rpm.
Compare the sensor output with the service manual values and replace it if it is out of spec.
If the DPF itself is blocked, a forced regeneration or DPF cleaning is needed.

P1201.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, each injector has a correction code (printed on the injector) that must be stored in the ECU so it can fine-tune that injector's fuel delivery, and the ECU reports that no codes have been written. The engine may run rougher, smoke or knock more, and may go into limp mode.
causes: Injector or injectors replaced without coding them into the ECU.
ECU replaced or reprogrammed without the injector codes being entered.
Coding procedure interrupted, for example by a battery voltage drop.
Rarely, an ECU memory fault.
fixes: Read the correction code from each injector and note which cylinder it is fitted to.
Connect a battery charger or support unit so the voltage stays stable during coding.
Write the codes with a scan tool that supports Subaru diesel injector coding (such as the dealer's Subaru Select Monitor).
Clear and re-test after coding.
If the codes will not stay stored, the ECU needs further diagnosis.

P1202.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the injector correction codes stored in the ECU are invalid or corrupted. The ECU cannot correct each injector's fuel delivery accurately, so the engine may run rougher, smoke or knock more, and may go into limp mode.
causes: Codes entered incorrectly (typo) or for the wrong cylinders.
Code data corrupted by a voltage drop or interruption during coding or reprogramming.
Injector replaced but its new code not entered.
Rarely, an ECU memory fault.
fixes: Read the correction code from each injector and compare it with what is stored in the ECU.
Connect a battery charger or support unit so the voltage stays stable during coding.
Re-enter the codes carefully for the correct cylinders. Write the codes with a scan tool that supports Subaru diesel injector coding (such as the dealer's Subaru Select Monitor).
Clear and re-test after coding.
If the data corrupts again, the ECU needs further diagnosis.

P1203.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the ECU reports a failure while injector correction codes were being entered, so the codes may not have been accepted. The engine may run rougher, smoke or knock more until the coding is completed correctly.
causes: Invalid code entered (typo or wrong format).
Scan tool communication dropped during coding.
Low battery voltage during the coding procedure.
Scan tool or software that does not fully support Subaru diesel coding.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Re-read the correction code from each injector carefully.
Connect a battery charger or support unit so the voltage stays stable during coding.
Write the codes with a scan tool that supports Subaru diesel injector coding (such as the dealer's Subaru Select Monitor).
Clear and re-test after coding.
If coding keeps failing with a known-good tool, the ECU needs further diagnosis.

P1213.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the ECU's injector driver charges up a high voltage to open the injectors quickly, and it did not reach its target charge. Expect rough running, power loss or a no-start, and the ECU may enter limp mode.
causes: Low battery voltage or a charging system problem.
Shorted injector or injector wiring loading the drive circuit.
Chafed injector harness shorting to ground.
Poor ECU power or ground connections.
Fault in the ECU's injector driver.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Clean and tighten the battery terminals, engine grounds and ECU grounds.
Inspect the injector connectors and harness for chafing, oil ingress and shorts to ground.
Measure each injector's resistance and compare with the service manual value and with the other injectors.
If the wiring and injectors are good, the ECU needs repair or replacement.

P1214.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the ECU's injector driver charges up a high voltage to open the injectors quickly, and the charge went above its target. Expect rough running or power loss, and the ECU may enter limp mode.
causes: Open injector circuit or an unplugged injector.
Charging system overvoltage.
Corroded injector connector with high resistance.
Fault in the ECU's injector driver.
fixes: Check charging voltage with the engine running: 13.5 to 14.7 V is normal.
Check that every injector connector is fully plugged in and free of corrosion.
Measure each injector's resistance and compare with the service manual value and with the other injectors.
Check the injector harness for broken wires.
If the wiring and injectors are good, the ECU needs repair or replacement.

P1230.meaning: Many later Subarus (especially turbo models from about 2005) use a fuel pump control unit that varies fuel pump speed, and the ECU found a fault in that control circuit. The pump may run at the wrong speed and cause lean running or stalling under load, so avoid hard driving and boost until it is fixed.
causes: Failed fuel pump control unit, often from corrosion or water at its location.
Corroded or loose connector at the control unit.
Blown fuse or a faulty fuel pump relay.
Wiring fault between the ECU, control unit and pump.
Worn fuel pump drawing too much current.
fixes: Check the fuel pump fuses and relay.
With the key on, listen for the fuel pump priming for a moment.
Inspect the fuel pump control unit and its connector for corrosion and water damage.
With the key on, check power and ground at the control unit: battery voltage and a good ground.
In the app's live data, check the A/F sensor and fuel trims under load for lean running, then replace the control unit (or the pump if it draws excessive current).

P1232.meaning: The ECU detected that the fuel pump is not working correctly, based on its control or feedback signal. A failing pump can cause hesitation, lean running, stalling or a no-start, so treat it as urgent, especially on turbo models under boost.
causes: Worn or failing fuel pump.
Corroded or loose connector at the top of the fuel pump.
Faulty fuel pump control unit or relay.
Blown fuse in the pump circuit.
Very low fuel level or a clogged pump inlet strainer.
fixes: Check the fuel level and the fuel pump fuses and relay.
With the key on, listen for the fuel pump priming for a moment.
Check the voltage at the pump connector (reached from under the rear seat on many Subarus) while the pump should be running.
Measure fuel pressure with a gauge and compare with the service manual value.
In the app's live data, check the A/F sensor and fuel trims under load, then replace the pump if pressure or delivery is low.

P1233.meaning: The ECU found fuel pressure outside its expected range and blames the fuel pump (detection pattern 1); on the EE20 diesel and direct-injection engines this is the high-pressure rail, otherwise the supply pressure. Low fuel pressure can cause lean running, misfires and limp mode, so avoid hard driving until it is fixed.
causes: Low fuel level or a clogged fuel filter (on the diesel, also water in the fuel filter).
Weak electric fuel pump or a faulty fuel pump control unit.
On the EE20 diesel and direct-injection engines, a worn high-pressure pump or faulty suction control valve.
Faulty fuel pressure sensor giving a wrong reading.
Fuel leak or air getting into the fuel lines.
fixes: Check the fuel level and inspect the fuel lines for leaks.
Replace the fuel filter if it is due; on the diesel, drain water from the filter.
With the key on, listen for the pump priming and check its fuses, relay and connector.
Measure fuel pressure, or compare actual and target rail pressure in live data where available, against the service manual values.
Replace the faulty pump, suction control valve or pressure sensor once identified.

P1234.meaning: The ECU found fuel pressure outside its expected range and blames the fuel pump (detection pattern 2, a different test condition than P1233); on the EE20 diesel and direct-injection engines this is the high-pressure rail, otherwise the supply pressure. Low fuel pressure can cause lean running, misfires and limp mode, so avoid hard driving until it is fixed.
causes: Low fuel level or a clogged fuel filter (on the diesel, also water in the fuel filter).
Weak electric fuel pump or a faulty fuel pump control unit.
On the EE20 diesel and direct-injection engines, a worn high-pressure pump or faulty suction control valve.
Faulty fuel pressure sensor giving a wrong reading.
Fuel leak or air getting into the fuel lines.
fixes: Check the fuel level and inspect the fuel lines for leaks.
Replace the fuel filter if it is due; on the diesel, drain water from the filter.
With the key on, listen for the pump priming and check its fuses, relay and connector.
Measure fuel pressure, or compare actual and target rail pressure in live data where available, against the service manual values.
Replace the faulty pump, suction control valve or pressure sensor once identified.

P1235.meaning: The ECU found the circuit of the intake control valve solenoid reading low; on JDM two-stage (sequential) twin-turbo EJ20 models this solenoid works the valve that lets the second turbo feed the engine. The car may stay on one turbo or have a flat spot, but it is safe to drive gently.
causes: Open or shorted intake control valve solenoid coil.
Unplugged, corroded or loose connector at the intake control valve solenoid.
Control wire open, or shorted to ground.
Blown fuse in the intake control valve solenoid supply.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the intake control valve solenoid for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the supply wire.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for a short to ground.
Replace the solenoid if it tests bad. While there, check the many small vacuum and pressure hoses around the turbos for splits and correct routing.

P1236.meaning: The ECU found the circuit of the intake control valve solenoid reading high; on JDM two-stage (sequential) twin-turbo EJ20 models this solenoid works the valve that lets the second turbo feed the engine. The car may stay on one turbo or have a flat spot, but it is safe to drive gently.
causes: Intake control valve solenoid control wire shorted to a power wire.
Shorted intake control valve solenoid coil (very low resistance).
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the connector.
Harness damage where wires rub or run near hot parts.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the intake control valve solenoid for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the solenoid and ECU unplugged and the key on, check the control wire for voltage where there should be none.
Inspect the harness for chafing or melted insulation.
Replace the solenoid if it tests bad. While there, check the many small vacuum and pressure hoses around the turbos for splits and correct routing.

P1237.meaning: On JDM two-stage (sequential) twin-turbo EJ20 models, the exhaust control valve (ECV) that brings in the second turbo is worked by pressure and vacuum switched by solenoids, and the ECU found the circuit of the positive-pressure (boost side) ECV solenoid reading low. The car may stay on one turbo and feel flat at high rpm, but it is safe to drive gently.
causes: Open or shorted ECV solenoid coil.
Unplugged, corroded or loose connector at the ECV solenoid.
Control wire open, or shorted to ground.
Blown fuse in the ECV solenoid supply.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the ECV solenoid for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the supply wire.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for a short to ground.
Replace the solenoid if it tests bad. While there, check the many small vacuum and pressure hoses around the turbos for splits and correct routing.

The car may stay on one turbo and feel flat at high rpm, but it is safe to drive gently.
causes: ECV solenoid control wire shorted to a power wire.

Water or corrosion bridging pins in the connector.
Harness damage where wires rub or run near hot parts.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the ECV solenoid for corrosion, water and a secure latch.

With the solenoid and ECU unplugged and the key on, check the control wire for voltage where there should be none.
Inspect the harness for chafing or melted insulation.
Replace the solenoid if it tests bad. While there, check the many small vacuum and pressure hoses around the turbos for splits and correct routing.

The car may stay on one turbo and feel flat at high rpm, but it is safe to drive gently.
causes: Open or shorted ECV solenoid coil.

Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for a short to ground.
Replace the solenoid if it tests bad. While there, check the many small vacuum and pressure hoses around the turbos for splits and correct routing.

The car may stay on one turbo and feel flat at high rpm, but it is safe to drive gently.
causes: ECV solenoid control wire shorted to a power wire.
Shorted ECV solenoid coil (very low resistance).
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the connector.
Harness damage where wires rub or run near hot parts.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the ECV solenoid for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the solenoid and ECU unplugged and the key on, check the control wire for voltage where there should be none.
Inspect the harness for chafing or melted insulation.
Replace the solenoid if it tests bad. While there, check the many small vacuum and pressure hoses around the turbos for splits and correct routing.

P1241.meaning: On JDM two-stage (sequential) twin-turbo EJ20 models, the ECU found the turbo system not behaving as expected while running on the primary turbo only (single mode). Boost may be abnormal at low to mid rpm, and the ECU may reduce boost to protect the engine.
causes: Split, perished or misrouted vacuum and pressure hoses (very common on these cars).
Exhaust control valve or relief valve leaking or stuck partly open.
Failed control solenoid (ECV, intake control or relief valve).
Leaking actuator diaphragm.
Boost leak or a worn primary turbo.
fixes: In the app's live data, log boost against rpm: it should build smoothly on the primary turbo and then change over cleanly.
Inspect every vacuum and pressure hose around the turbos and the solenoid group; replace any that are hard, cracked or misrouted (compare with the routing diagram in the service manual).
Test each valve actuator with a hand vacuum or pressure pump: it should move and hold without leaking down.
Check the control solenoids for a click when switched and measure their resistance against the service manual values.
Pressure test the intake system for boost leaks, and have the turbos checked if the controls are all good.

P1242.meaning: On JDM two-stage (sequential) twin-turbo EJ20 models, the ECU found the turbo system not behaving as expected while running on both turbos (twin mode), often because the second turbo is not coming in properly. Expect a loss of power at higher rpm; the ECU may reduce boost to protect the engine.
causes: Split, perished or misrouted vacuum and pressure hoses (very common on these cars).
Exhaust control valve stuck closed or intake control valve not opening.
Failed control solenoid (ECV, intake control or relief valve).
Leaking actuator diaphragm.
Worn or failed secondary turbo, or a boost leak.
fixes: In the app's live data, log boost against rpm: look for boost dropping or stalling at the changeover instead of carrying on to full boost.
Inspect every vacuum and pressure hose around the turbos and the solenoid group; replace any that are hard, cracked or misrouted (compare with the routing diagram in the service manual).
Test each valve actuator with a hand vacuum or pressure pump: it should move and hold without leaking down.
Check the control solenoids for a click when switched and measure their resistance against the service manual values.
Pressure test the intake system for boost leaks, and have the turbos checked if the controls are all good.

P1244.meaning: The ECU found that boost control through the wastegate (boost control) solenoid is not performing as expected, with boost running lower than the target. The car will feel down on power but is generally safe to drive; do not ignore it, as it can also point to a boost leak.
causes: Boost leak at the intercooler couplers, turbo outlet, throttle body coupler or blow-off valve.
Boost control solenoid stuck or with a restricted port.
Cracked or wrongly routed hoses between the turbo, solenoid and wastegate actuator.
Wastegate actuator or flap sticking open.
Exhaust leak before the turbo (up-pipe or header gasket), or a worn turbo.
fixes: In the app's live data, log boost against target (and wastegate duty cycle if available) during a gentle pull.
Inspect the hoses between the turbo, boost control solenoid and wastegate actuator for cracks and correct routing.
Pressure test the intake and intercooler system for boost leaks.
Check the boost control solenoid for a click and measure its resistance against the service manual value.
With the engine cold, check that the wastegate arm moves freely, and check turbo shaft play.

P1245.meaning: The ECU detected a boost control problem serious enough to put boost control into a fail-safe mode, usually limiting boost to protect the engine; this often follows overboost or a boost control solenoid fault. Expect reduced power and avoid full throttle until the cause is found.
causes: Boost control solenoid stuck, causing overboost.
Wastegate actuator hose disconnected or split, causing overboost.
Wastegate flap stuck closed.
Aftermarket boost controller or tune fault.
Large boost leak or underboost.
fixes: In the app's live data, log boost against target and look for overboost spikes.
Also check knock correction and IAM: a falling IAM means the engine has been knocking, so stay out of boost until it is fixed.
Inspect the wastegate actuator hose and the boost control solenoid hoses.
Check the boost control solenoid for a click and measure its resistance against the service manual value.
With the engine cold, check that the wastegate arm moves freely; review any aftermarket boost controller or tune.

P1247.meaning: On JDM two-stage (sequential) twin-turbo EJ20 models, relief valves vent pressure from the second turbo while it pre-spools before the changeover, and the ECU found the circuit of relief valve control solenoid 1 reading low. The turbo changeover may be rough or boost may be off, but it is safe to drive gently.
causes: Open or shorted relief valve solenoid coil.
Unplugged, corroded or loose connector at the relief valve solenoid.
Control wire open, or shorted to ground.
Blown fuse in the relief valve solenoid supply.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the relief valve solenoid for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the supply wire.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for a short to ground.
Replace the solenoid if it tests bad. While there, check the many small vacuum and pressure hoses around the turbos for splits and correct routing.

P1248.meaning: On JDM two-stage (sequential) twin-turbo EJ20 models, relief valves vent pressure from the second turbo while it pre-spools before the changeover, and the ECU found the circuit of relief valve control solenoid 1 reading high. The turbo changeover may be rough or boost may be off, but it is safe to drive gently.
causes: Relief valve solenoid control wire shorted to a power wire.
Shorted relief valve solenoid coil (very low resistance).
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the connector.
Harness damage where wires rub or run near hot parts.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the relief valve solenoid for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the solenoid and ECU unplugged and the key on, check the control wire for voltage where there should be none.
Inspect the harness for chafing or melted insulation.
Replace the solenoid if it tests bad. While there, check the many small vacuum and pressure hoses around the turbos for splits and correct routing.

P1249.meaning: On JDM two-stage (sequential) twin-turbo EJ20 models, relief valves vent pressure from the second turbo while it pre-spools before the changeover, and the ECU found the circuit of relief valve control solenoid 2 reading low. The turbo changeover may be rough or boost may be off, but it is safe to drive gently.
causes: Open or shorted relief valve solenoid coil.
Unplugged, corroded or loose connector at the relief valve solenoid.
Control wire open, or shorted to ground.
Blown fuse in the relief valve solenoid supply.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the relief valve solenoid for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the supply wire.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for a short to ground.
Replace the solenoid if it tests bad. While there, check the many small vacuum and pressure hoses around the turbos for splits and correct routing.

P1250.meaning: On JDM two-stage (sequential) twin-turbo EJ20 models, relief valves vent pressure from the second turbo while it pre-spools before the changeover, and the ECU found the circuit of relief valve control solenoid 2 reading high. The turbo changeover may be rough or boost may be off, but it is safe to drive gently.
causes: Relief valve solenoid control wire shorted to a power wire.
Shorted relief valve solenoid coil (very low resistance).
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the connector.
Harness damage where wires rub or run near hot parts.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the relief valve solenoid for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the solenoid and ECU unplugged and the key on, check the control wire for voltage where there should be none.
Inspect the harness for chafing or melted insulation.
Replace the solenoid if it tests bad. While there, check the many small vacuum and pressure hoses around the turbos for splits and correct routing.

P1282.meaning: The ECU monitors the crankcase ventilation (PCV) system, on some later models through a detection circuit at the PCV hose connection, and found that circuit open, which usually means the hose or its detection connector is disconnected. A disconnected PCV hose lets unmetered air in and oil vapour out, so fix it soon.
causes: PCV hose disconnected or not fully seated.
Cracked PCV hose or fitting.
Detection connector unplugged or corroded.
Broken wire in the detection circuit.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the PCV hose and make sure both ends are fully seated and latched.
Check the detection connector for corrosion and a secure fit.
In the app's live data, check fuel trims: large positive trims at idle suggest a vacuum leak at the PCV system.
Check continuity of the detection circuit and compare with the service manual.
Replace the PCV hose assembly if it is cracked or its detection contact is damaged.

P1301.meaning: The ECU detected misfires at a rate high enough to overheat the exhaust and catalytic converter, and the check engine light may flash. This is serious: reduce load and get it fixed promptly, because unburnt fuel can quickly destroy the catalytic converter and, on turbo models, harm the turbo.
causes: Worn spark plugs or a failed ignition coil (or plug wires on older EJ25s).
Clogged or failed fuel injector.
Vacuum or boost leak causing a lean misfire, or low fuel pressure.
Low compression, for example from a head gasket problem or burnt valve.
On EJ turbos, piston ringland damage.
fixes: Check which cylinders are affected with the companion codes P0301 to P0304 (P0306 on six-cylinders).
In the app's live data, check misfire counts, fuel trims, IAM and knock correction.
Inspect the spark plugs and swap coils between cylinders to see whether the misfire follows the coil.
Check the injector on the affected cylinder (resistance against the service manual value, or swap it) and smoke test the intake.
Do a compression and leak-down test if ignition and fuel are good.

P1306.meaning: The ECU found an open circuit in the drive signal to oil control valve (OCV) 1, the AVCS (variable cam timing) solenoid, usually for bank 1 (right side, cylinders 1 and 3). Cam timing on that side falls back to its default position, so the engine loses some power and smoothness; it is safe to drive gently.
causes: Unplugged, loose or oil-soaked connector at the oil control valve.
Connector pins pushed back or damaged after timing belt or engine work.
Broken wire in the harness to the OCV.
Open coil inside the OCV.
Rarely, a failed driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Inspect the OCV connector for oil, corrosion and a secure latch.
Measure the OCV coil resistance at its terminals and compare with the service manual value; an infinite reading means an open coil.
Check continuity of the wires from the ECU to the OCV connector.
Replace the OCV if the coil is open, and inspect the AVCS oil filter screens while you are there.
After the repair, check in the app's live data that the AVCS cam advance follows its target.

P1307.meaning: The ECU found a short circuit in the drive signal to oil control valve (OCV) 1, the AVCS (variable cam timing) solenoid, usually for bank 1 (right side, cylinders 1 and 3). Cam timing on that side falls back to its default position, so the engine loses some power and smoothness; it is safe to drive gently.
causes: OCV drive wire shorted to ground or to another circuit.
Shorted coil inside the OCV.
Oil or water bridging pins in the OCV connector.
Harness damaged during timing belt or engine work.
Rarely, a failed driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Inspect the OCV connector for oil, water and bridged pins.
Measure the OCV coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; a very low reading means a shorted coil.
With the ECU and OCV unplugged, check the drive wires for a short to ground and to other circuits.
Replace the OCV or repair the harness as needed.
After the repair, check in the app's live data that the AVCS cam advance follows its target.

P1308.meaning: The ECU found an open circuit in the drive signal to oil control valve (OCV) 2, the AVCS (variable cam timing) solenoid, usually for bank 2 (left side, cylinders 2 and 4). Cam timing on that side falls back to its default position, so the engine loses some power and smoothness; it is safe to drive gently.
causes: Unplugged, loose or oil-soaked connector at the oil control valve.
Connector pins pushed back or damaged after timing belt or engine work.
Broken wire in the harness to the OCV.
Open coil inside the OCV.
Rarely, a failed driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Inspect the OCV connector for oil, corrosion and a secure latch.
Measure the OCV coil resistance at its terminals and compare with the service manual value; an infinite reading means an open coil.
Check continuity of the wires from the ECU to the OCV connector.
Replace the OCV if the coil is open, and inspect the AVCS oil filter screens while you are there.
After the repair, check in the app's live data that the AVCS cam advance follows its target.

P1309.meaning: The ECU found a short circuit in the drive signal to oil control valve (OCV) 2, the AVCS (variable cam timing) solenoid, usually for bank 2 (left side, cylinders 2 and 4). Cam timing on that side falls back to its default position, so the engine loses some power and smoothness; it is safe to drive gently.
causes: OCV drive wire shorted to ground or to another circuit.
Shorted coil inside the OCV.
Oil or water bridging pins in the OCV connector.
Harness damaged during timing belt or engine work.
Rarely, a failed driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Inspect the OCV connector for oil, water and bridged pins.
Measure the OCV coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; a very low reading means a shorted coil.
With the ECU and OCV unplugged, check the drive wires for a short to ground and to other circuits.
Replace the OCV or repair the harness as needed.
After the repair, check in the app's live data that the AVCS cam advance follows its target.

P1312.meaning: The exhaust gas temperature (EGT) sensor reading is faulty or implausible. On the EE20 boxer diesel these sensors help control DPF regeneration, so a fault can stop regeneration and eventually clog the DPF; on turbo petrol models that have one, it protects the turbo and catalytic converter, so get it fixed soon.
causes: EGT sensor failed from heat (a common wear item on diesels).
Wiring near the exhaust melted or chafed.
Corroded or loose connector.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: If the app shows exhaust temperature, check it on a cold engine: it should read close to outside temperature and rise steadily as the engine warms.
Inspect the sensor wiring along the exhaust for heat damage.
Check the connector for corrosion and a secure latch.
Measure the sensor resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Replace the EGT sensor if it is out of spec, then clear and re-test.

P1313.meaning: The ECU monitors a separate misfire detection signal line, used on some Subaru engines (typically from the ignition module), and found it stuck at a high voltage. Misfire detection may not work properly; the engine may still run normally, but confirm there is no real misfire.
causes: Signal wire shorted to a voltage source.
Open ground at the module that sends the signal.
Corroded or loose connector.
Faulty ignition module (igniter).
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check for real misfire symptoms such as a rough idle, shaking or a flashing check engine light.
Inspect the connectors at the ignition module and ECU for corrosion.
Check the signal wire for a short to voltage with both ends unplugged.
Check the ignition module's power and ground.
Replace the ignition module if the wiring is good.

P1314.meaning: The ECU monitors a separate misfire detection signal line, used on some Subaru engines (typically from the ignition module), and found it stuck at a low voltage. Misfire detection may not work properly; the engine may still run normally, but confirm there is no real misfire.
causes: Signal wire shorted to ground.
Open signal wire or unplugged connector.
Loss of power to the module that sends the signal.
Faulty ignition module (igniter).
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check for real misfire symptoms such as a rough idle, shaking or a flashing check engine light.
Inspect the connectors at the ignition module and ECU for corrosion.
Check the signal wire for continuity and for a short to ground with both ends unplugged.
Check the ignition module's power and ground.
Replace the ignition module if the wiring is good.

P1380.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the glow plug relay (glow control) circuit reads low, so the glow plugs may not heat. Expect hard starting, white smoke and rough running in cold weather; the engine usually runs fine once warm.
causes: Failed glow relay or glow control unit.
Control wire open or shorted to ground.
Corroded or loose connector at the relay.
Blown fuse in the glow system.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the glow system fuse.
Inspect the relay or glow control unit connector for corrosion and a secure fit.
With the key on from cold, check for the control signal and supply voltage at the relay.
Measure each glow plug's resistance (very low, compare with the service manual value) to find any failed plugs.
Replace the relay or glow control unit if the wiring is good.

P1382.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the glow plug relay (glow control) circuit reads high, which usually means a short to voltage or a relay stuck on. Glow plugs that stay powered can burn out, so get it fixed soon; cold starting may also suffer.
causes: Control wire shorted to a voltage source.
Relay contacts welded or glow control unit stuck on.
Water or corrosion in the relay connector.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check whether the glow system stays powered after the engine warms up (measure voltage at the glow plug feed).
Inspect the relay or glow control unit connector for water and corrosion.
With the relay unplugged and the key on, check the control wire for voltage where there should be none.
Measure each glow plug's resistance and compare with the service manual value, as a stuck relay may have damaged them.
Replace the relay or glow control unit if the wiring is good.

P1400.meaning: The circuit of the fuel tank pressure control solenoid valve, part of the EVAP system that manages pressure in the fuel tank, is reading low. This does not affect how the engine runs, but the EVAP system cannot work properly and the car may fail an emissions test.
causes: Open or shorted fuel tank pressure control solenoid valve coil.
Unplugged, corroded or loose connector at the fuel tank pressure control solenoid valve.
Control wire open, or shorted to ground.
Blown fuse in the fuel tank pressure control solenoid valve supply.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the fuel tank pressure control solenoid valve for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the supply wire.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for a short to ground.
The valve sits near the fuel tank and is exposed to road spray, so clean the connector well; replace the valve if it tests bad.

P1410.meaning: The secondary air injection system blows fresh air into the exhaust after a cold start to heat the catalytic converter quickly, and the ECU found a combination (switching) valve stuck open. Engine performance is normally unaffected, but exhaust gas and moisture can flow back and destroy the air pump, so do not leave it for long.
causes: Combination valve stuck open by carbon or corrosion (a known weak point on Subarus with secondary air).
Moisture in the valve freezing it open in cold weather.
Wiring fault keeping the valve energised.
Faulty secondary air pressure sensor giving a false reading.
fixes: Inspect the hoses between the air pump and the valves: soot or water inside means exhaust has been flowing back.
Check the valve connectors and wiring for corrosion and damage.
Remove and inspect the combination valves; they should seal fully when not powered.
Replace the stuck valve or valves, and check the air pump too, since backflow often damages it.
Clear and re-test with a cold start.

P1418.meaning: The ECU found a short in the secondary air pump control circuit (the pump or its relay); the pump blows air into the exhaust after cold starts to heat the catalytic converter. The engine runs normally, but warm-up emissions rise and the car may fail an emissions test.
causes: Pump motor seized or shorted, often after water or exhaust got into it.
Failed or stuck secondary air pump relay.
Wiring shorted to ground or to power.
Blown fuse in the pump circuit.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the pump fuse and swap the pump relay with an identical one.
After a cold start, listen for the pump running for a short time.
Inspect the pump wiring and connector for chafing and water.
Measure the pump motor resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Replace the pump if it is seized or shorted, and check the combination valves too, since a stuck-open valve often kills the pump.

P1420.meaning: The circuit of the fuel tank pressure control solenoid valve, part of the EVAP system that manages pressure in the fuel tank, is reading high. This does not affect how the engine runs, but the EVAP system cannot work properly and the car may fail an emissions test.
causes: Fuel tank pressure control solenoid valve control wire shorted to a power wire.
Shorted fuel tank pressure control solenoid valve coil (very low resistance).
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the connector.
Harness damage where wires rub or run near hot parts.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the fuel tank pressure control solenoid valve for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the solenoid and ECU unplugged and the key on, check the control wire for voltage where there should be none.
Inspect the harness for chafing or melted insulation.
The valve sits near the fuel tank and is exposed to road spray, so clean the connector well; replace the valve if it tests bad.

P1442.meaning: The ECU saw the fuel level reading stay the same even though the car has covered enough distance that it should have dropped. The engine runs normally, but the fuel gauge may be wrong and EVAP tests may not run, so keep an eye on actual fuel use.
causes: Fuel level sender float or arm sticking.
Worn resistance track in the sender.
On AWD models with a saddle-shaped tank, a fault in the main or sub-tank sender.
Corroded connector or wiring fault at the senders.
On some models, a combination meter fault (the level signal may pass through the meter).
fixes: Compare the fuel gauge with how much fuel goes in at the next fill-up.
If the app shows fuel level, watch it during a drive and while refuelling: it should change smoothly.
Check the connectors at the fuel level senders (reached from under the rear seat on many Subarus) for corrosion.
Measure the sender resistance as the float moves from empty to full and compare with the service manual.
Replace the sticking sender; on AWD models check both the main and sub-tank senders.

P1443.meaning: The EVAP canister vent control solenoid did not open or close as expected during the ECU's EVAP self-test. The engine runs normally, but the EVAP system cannot be checked for leaks, and a vent stuck closed can make refuelling difficult.
causes: Vent solenoid stuck from dirt, spider webs or water.
Clogged vent hose or EVAP air (drain) filter.
Corroded connector or wiring fault.
Failed solenoid coil.
fixes: Check that the fuel cap is tight and its seal is intact.
Inspect the vent hose and EVAP air filter for blockage.
Apply 12 V to the solenoid: it should click and change whether air can pass.
Measure the coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Replace the vent solenoid if it sticks or tests bad, then clear and re-test.

P1446.meaning: The circuit of the fuel tank sensor control valve, a small EVAP solenoid valve used during the ECU's leak test to control what the fuel tank pressure sensor sees, is reading low. The engine runs normally, but the EVAP self-test cannot run and the car may fail an emissions test.
causes: Open or shorted fuel tank sensor control valve coil.
Unplugged, corroded or loose connector at the fuel tank sensor control valve.
Control wire open, or shorted to ground.
Blown fuse in the fuel tank sensor control valve supply.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the fuel tank sensor control valve for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the supply wire.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for a short to ground.
The valve is mounted under the car near the fuel tank, so clean road grime from the connector; replace the valve if it tests bad.

P1447.meaning: The circuit of the fuel tank sensor control valve, a small EVAP solenoid valve used during the ECU's leak test to control what the fuel tank pressure sensor sees, is reading high. The engine runs normally, but the EVAP self-test cannot run and the car may fail an emissions test.
causes: Fuel tank sensor control valve control wire shorted to a power wire.
Shorted fuel tank sensor control valve coil (very low resistance).
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the connector.
Harness damage where wires rub or run near hot parts.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the fuel tank sensor control valve for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the solenoid and ECU unplugged and the key on, check the control wire for voltage where there should be none.
Inspect the harness for chafing or melted insulation.
The valve is mounted under the car near the fuel tank, so clean road grime from the connector; replace the valve if it tests bad.

P1448.meaning: The fuel tank sensor control valve, a small EVAP solenoid valve used during the ECU's leak test to control what the fuel tank pressure sensor sees, is not working as expected. The engine runs normally, but the EVAP self-test cannot run and the car may fail an emissions test.
causes: Valve sticking from dirt or water.
Cracked, disconnected or blocked hoses at the valve.
Faulty fuel tank pressure sensor giving misleading readings.
Corroded connector or wiring fault.
fixes: Check that the fuel cap is tight and its seal is intact.
Inspect the hoses at the valve and the tank pressure sensor for cracks and blockages.
Apply 12 V to the valve: it should click and switch the air path.
Measure the coil resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Replace the valve (or the tank pressure sensor if that is at fault), then clear and re-test.

P1449.meaning: The ECU found the EVAP system's air filter (the drain or vent filter that lets clean air into the charcoal canister) restricted. The engine runs normally, but the tank may not breathe properly: refuelling can be slow with the nozzle clicking off early, and you may hear a rush of air when opening the fuel cap.
causes: Air filter clogged with dirt, mud or insects (common on cars used on dirt roads).
Vent hose kinked or blocked.
Vent control solenoid stuck closed.
Charcoal canister saturated with fuel from topping off the tank.
fixes: Locate the EVAP air (drain) filter and vent hose and inspect them for dirt, mud or insect nests.
Blow gently through the vent line from the filter end to check it is clear.
Replace the filter if it is clogged.
Check the vent control solenoid opens (it should pass air when not powered on most systems; compare with the service manual).
Stop filling once the nozzle first clicks off, and replace the canister if it is saturated.

P1451.meaning: The ECU found a malfunction in the evaporative emission (EVAP) system, which stores fuel vapour from the tank and burns it in the engine. It does not affect how the engine runs, but the car can fail an emissions test and may smell of fuel.
causes: Loose fuel cap or a worn cap seal (the most common cause).
Cracked or disconnected EVAP hose.
Purge control solenoid valve stuck open or closed.
Vent control solenoid stuck.
Damaged charcoal canister or a faulty fuel tank pressure sensor.
fixes: Check the fuel cap: tighten it until it clicks and inspect the seal and filler neck.
Inspect the EVAP hoses in the engine bay and under the car for cracks.
Test the purge valve: it should hold vacuum when not powered.
Check the vent control solenoid and EVAP air filter.
Have a smoke test done to find small leaks, then clear and re-test.

P1458.meaning: Some Subarus, mainly turbo models, have a second canister purge solenoid valve so fuel vapour can still be purged under boost, and the ECU found this valve's circuit reading low. The engine runs normally, but the EVAP system cannot purge properly and the car may fail an emissions test.
causes: Open or shorted purge control solenoid valve 2 coil.
Unplugged, corroded or loose connector at the purge control solenoid valve 2.
Control wire open, or shorted to ground.
Blown fuse in the purge control solenoid valve 2 supply.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Inspect the connector at the purge control solenoid valve 2 for corrosion, water and a secure latch.
Measure the coil resistance at the solenoid and compare with the service manual value.
With the key on, check for battery voltage on the supply wire.
Check the control wire back to the ECU for continuity and for a short to ground.
Replace the valve if it tests bad, and check its hoses for cracks, then clear and re-test.

P1459.meaning: The ECU sees a high (open or shorted-to-power) signal in the control circuit of purge control solenoid valve 2. On turbo models this second purge valve handles fuel vapour purge while the engine is in boost. The car is safe to drive, but EVAP purge will not work correctly and the check engine light stays on.
causes: Control wire between the ECU and purge control solenoid valve 2 shorted to a battery-voltage wire.
Open circuit in the solenoid wiring or a loose, corroded connector at the valve.
Failed solenoid coil (open winding).
Missing power feed to the solenoid because of a blown fuse or broken wire.
Rarely, a faulty output driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Locate purge control solenoid valve 2 (see the service manual for your model; on turbo models it sits in the purge line near the intake or turbo inlet) and check that its connector is fully seated and free of corrosion or oil.
Unplug the valve and measure the coil resistance. Compare with the service manual value: an open reading (OL) means the valve is faulty.
With the ignition on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the power side of the valve connector.
With the ECU and valve unplugged, check the control wire for continuity back to the ECU and make sure it shows no voltage with the ignition on (which would mean a short to power).
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P1462.meaning: The signal from the high-pressure fuel pressure sensor on a direct-injection engine (the sensor that measures fuel pressure going to the in-cylinder injectors) is below its normal range. The ECU usually limits power or runs a fail-safe fuel pressure, so drive gently and get it checked soon.
causes: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground.
Open circuit or poor contact on the sensor's 5 V reference wire.
Loose, corroded or oil-soaked connector at the fuel pressure sensor on the high-pressure rail.
Failed fuel pressure sensor.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the connector at the high-pressure fuel pressure sensor on the fuel rail for a proper click, bent pins and corrosion.
With the ignition on and the sensor plugged in, back-probe the reference wire: it should read about 5 V. Also check the sensor ground.
Measure the signal voltage with the engine off and running and compare with the service manual value. A signal near 0 V in both cases points to a short to ground or a dead sensor.
If your ECU reports fuel rail pressure in live data, compare it at warm idle with the service manual value; a reading pinned at or near zero while the engine runs points to the circuit or sensor.
Inspect the harness around the fuel rail and intake for chafing or heat damage, and repair as needed.
Replace the sensor if the wiring checks good. Never open the high-pressure fuel system with the engine running or right after shutdown: it can hold very high pressure.

P1463.meaning: The signal from the high-pressure fuel pressure sensor on a direct-injection engine (the sensor that measures fuel pressure going to the in-cylinder injectors) is above its normal range. The ECU usually limits power or runs a fail-safe fuel pressure, so drive gently and get it checked soon.
causes: Sensor signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage.
Open circuit on the sensor ground wire.
Loose, corroded or oil-soaked connector at the fuel pressure sensor on the high-pressure rail.
Failed fuel pressure sensor.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the connector at the high-pressure fuel pressure sensor on the fuel rail for a proper click, bent pins and corrosion.
With the ignition on and the sensor plugged in, back-probe the reference wire (about 5 V) and check for a good ground: less than about 0.1 V between the sensor ground and battery negative.
Measure the signal voltage with the engine off and running and compare with the service manual value. A signal stuck near 5 V points to an open ground, a short to the reference, or a dead sensor.
If your ECU reports fuel rail pressure in live data, compare it at warm idle with the service manual value; an impossibly high, unchanging reading points to the circuit or sensor.
Inspect the harness around the fuel rail and intake for chafing or heat damage, and repair as needed.
Replace the sensor if the wiring checks good. Never open the high-pressure fuel system with the engine running or right after shutdown: it can hold very high pressure.

P1465.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the ECU calculates that the diesel particulate filter (DPF) holds more soot than it can safely burn off in a normal regeneration. The DPF light may come on and power may be reduced. Act on it soon: if soot keeps building, a forced regeneration may no longer be possible and the DPF may need replacing.
causes: Mostly short trips, so automatic regenerations never get to finish.
Regenerations repeatedly interrupted by switching the engine off mid-regeneration.
Excess soot from the engine: sticking EGR valve, boost leak, dirty intake, or worn or leaking injectors.
Faulty DPF differential pressure sensor, or split or blocked sensor hoses, giving a falsely high soot reading.
Other stored faults (sensors, EGR, glow plugs) that stop the ECU from starting a regeneration.
fixes: Read and fix any other stored codes first: the ECU will not regenerate while sensor, EGR or temperature faults are active.

If power is not limited, drive for about 15 to 20 minutes at a steady speed above about 60 km/h (for example on a motorway, in a gear that keeps the revs up) so the ECU can complete a regeneration. Do not switch off during the drive.
Inspect the DPF differential pressure sensor hoses for splits, loose ends or soot blockage.
If the soot load is too high for a driving regeneration, have a forced (stationary) regeneration done with a Subaru dealer tool or a capable diesel scan tool.
If a forced regeneration is refused or fails, the DPF needs professional cleaning or replacement. Check the oil level afterwards, as repeated regenerations dilute the oil with diesel.

P1466.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the ECU sees too little pressure difference across the DPF for the current exhaust flow, which it takes to mean the filter substrate is cracked or melted. Soot can then pass straight through, so the car may smoke and fail an emissions test; it is usually drivable, but get it checked.
causes: Pressure-sensor hose disconnected, split or melted, so the sensor sees too little pressure difference.
Faulty DPF differential pressure sensor reading low.
Cracked or melted DPF substrate, usually after an uncontrolled regeneration with a very heavy soot load.
Exhaust leak between the turbo and the DPF.
DPF removed or gutted (the code is expected in that case).
fixes: Inspect both hoses between the exhaust and the DPF differential pressure sensor: they must be connected to the right ports, uncracked and clear.
Check the exhaust for leaks between the turbo and the DPF (black soot marks at joints and gaskets).
Watch DPF differential pressure in live data if your tool shows it: it should rise clearly with engine speed. A reading that barely changes points to hoses, sensor or a broken filter.
Check the tailpipe after a firm pull: a heavily sooted tailpipe on a DPF car points to a damaged filter.
Replace the DPF if it is confirmed cracked, and fix what caused the uncontrolled regeneration (soot overload, short trips, EGR or injector faults).

P1467.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the ECU's ash counter says the DPF is full of non-combustible ash (from engine oil additives) that regeneration cannot burn off. The filter has reached the end of its service life; the car usually still drives, but the DPF needs cleaning or replacement.
causes: High mileage: ash builds up slowly over the life of the filter.
Higher than normal oil consumption (turbo seals, piston rings, crankcase ventilation).
Engine oil that is not the low-ash (low-SAPS) specification required for DPF engines.
Ash counter not reset after a previous DPF cleaning or replacement.
fixes: Check how much oil the engine uses between services and make sure the oil meets the low-ash specification in the owner's manual.
If the DPF was recently cleaned or replaced, have the ash counter reset with a Subaru dealer tool or capable scan tool before buying parts.
Confirm the ECU's ash and soot values with a capable scan tool.
Have the DPF professionally cleaned (ash cannot be burned out by regeneration) or replaced.
After cleaning or replacement, reset the DPF learning values and ash counter, otherwise the code will come back.

P1468.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the ECU estimates that too much diesel has mixed into the engine oil, a side effect of the extra fuel injected during DPF regeneration. Diluted oil protects the engine poorly and the oil level rises; change the oil soon and avoid hard driving until you do.
causes: Frequent or interrupted DPF regenerations, usually caused by short trips.
Oil change interval exceeded.
Oil dilution counter not reset at the last oil change.
A leaking or dribbling injector adding extra fuel.
Underlying fault causing extra regenerations (sensor, EGR or DPF problem).
fixes: Check the dipstick: a level above the upper mark, thin oil or a smell of diesel confirms dilution. Never run with the level well above the upper mark.
Change the engine oil and filter using the correct low-ash oil.
Reset the oil dilution counter with a Subaru dealer tool or capable scan tool after the oil change; the code will return otherwise.
Where possible, add regular longer runs so regenerations can finish without extra dilution.
If dilution comes back quickly, have the injectors, DPF soot level and regeneration history checked.

P1469.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the ECU has put the engine into limp-home mode to protect the DPF, usually because the soot load is too high or a DPF-related sensor has failed. Power is limited; you can drive gently to a workshop, but avoid long, heavy-load driving.
causes: DPF soot overload (often stored together with P1465).
DPF differential pressure sensor or sensor hose fault.
DPF damage or ash overload.
Exhaust gas temperature sensor fault preventing a safe regeneration.
Other engine faults (EGR, boost, injectors) that block regeneration.
fixes: Read all stored codes: this code is a result, and the other codes point to the actual cause.
Inspect the DPF pressure sensor hoses and the DPF and exhaust temperature sensor connectors.
Fix any sensor or EGR faults first, then have a forced regeneration done with a Subaru dealer tool or capable scan tool if the soot level allows it.
Repair or replace the DPF or sensors as indicated, then clear and re-test with a steady drive.

P1471.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the ECU believes the pipe or hose that carries exhaust pressure from in front of the DPF to the differential pressure sensor is disconnected, leaking or blocked. Without it the ECU cannot judge the soot load, so regenerations may be affected.
causes: Upstream sensor hose slipped off, split or melted.
Metal pipe or hose blocked with soot or condensation.
Upstream and downstream hoses swapped after a repair.
Faulty differential pressure sensor.
fixes: Inspect the upstream hose along its full length; replace it with the correct heat-resistant hose if it is soft, split or burned.
Disconnect the hose and blow through the metal pipe to clear soot. Do not blow into the sensor itself.
Check that each hose goes to the correct sensor port (they are usually marked).

Watch DPF differential pressure in live data if your tool shows it: low at idle and rising clearly with rpm. If the hoses are good and the reading stays flat, replace the sensor, then clear and re-test.

P1472.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the signal from the DPF differential pressure sensor is below its possible range. This is normally a wiring or sensor fault rather than a real pressure reading, and the ECU cannot track soot load, so regenerations may be affected and limp mode may follow.
causes: Signal wire open or shorted to ground.
Loss of the 5 V reference feed to the sensor.
Loose or corroded connector at the sensor, which sees heat and road spray.
Failed differential pressure sensor.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the sensor connector for corrosion, water and bent pins.
With the ignition on and the sensor plugged in, check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground.
Compare the signal voltage with the engine off against the service manual value; near 0 V points to a short to ground or open signal wire.
With the ECU and sensor unplugged, check the signal wire for continuity and for any short to ground.
Replace the sensor if the wiring checks good, then clear and re-test.

P1473.meaning: On the EE20 boxer diesel, the signal from the DPF differential pressure sensor is above its possible range. This is normally a wiring or sensor fault rather than a real pressure reading, and the ECU cannot track soot load, so regenerations may be affected and limp mode may follow.
causes: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage.
Open sensor ground.
Loose or corroded connector at the sensor, which sees heat and road spray.
Failed differential pressure sensor.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the sensor connector for corrosion, water and bent pins.
With the ignition on and the sensor plugged in, check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground (less than about 0.1 V between sensor ground and battery negative).
Compare the signal voltage with the engine off against the service manual value; a signal stuck near 5 V points to an open ground or a short to voltage.
With the ECU and sensor unplugged, check the signal wire for continuity and for any short to a power wire.
Replace the sensor if the wiring checks good, then clear and re-test.

P1475.meaning: The ECU sees a low signal in the control circuit of the exhaust by-pass valve solenoid, usually an open circuit or a short to ground. This solenoid switches a valve that diverts exhaust flow on the models that have one; the car normally drives, but power, noise or emissions may be affected.
causes: Open circuit in the solenoid wiring or its power feed.
Control wire shorted to ground.
Loose or corroded connector at the solenoid.
Solenoid coil open or shorted internally.
Rarely, a faulty output driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Locate the exhaust by-pass valve solenoid using the service manual for your model and check its connector for corrosion and a firm fit.
Unplug the solenoid and measure its coil resistance; compare with the service manual value. Open (OL) or near 0 ohms means a faulty solenoid.
With the ignition on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the power side of the solenoid connector.
With the ECU and solenoid unplugged, check the control wire for continuity and make sure it has no continuity to body ground.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P1476.meaning: The ECU sees a high signal in the control circuit of the exhaust by-pass valve solenoid, usually a short to a power wire. This solenoid switches a valve that diverts exhaust flow on the models that have one; the car normally drives, but power, noise or emissions may be affected.
causes: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage wire.
Solenoid coil shorted internally.
Loose or corroded connector at the solenoid.
Harness damage near hot exhaust parts.
Rarely, a faulty output driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Locate the exhaust by-pass valve solenoid using the service manual for your model and check its connector for corrosion and a firm fit.
Unplug the solenoid and measure its coil resistance; compare with the service manual value. A reading well below spec means a shorted coil.
With the ECU and solenoid unplugged and the ignition on, check the control wire for voltage: it should read 0 V. Any voltage means a short to power in the harness.
Inspect the harness where it runs near the exhaust for melted or chafed insulation.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P1477.meaning: The ECU commanded the exhaust by-pass valve to move but did not see the expected result, so the valve is probably stuck or not being actuated. The car normally drives, but power, noise or emissions may be affected.
causes: Vacuum hose to the valve actuator cracked, disconnected or routed to the wrong port.
Valve or shaft seized by carbon or rust.
Torn actuator diaphragm.
Solenoid not switching vacuum, or a leaking vacuum source or check valve.
Linkage between the actuator and valve bent or disconnected.
fixes: Inspect the vacuum hoses between the vacuum source, solenoid and actuator for cracks and correct routing.
Apply vacuum to the actuator with a hand vacuum pump: the rod should move and the gauge should hold steady.
Check that the solenoid clicks when commanded and passes vacuum when energised.
With the engine off and cold, check the valve moves freely by hand; free it with penetrating oil if it is sticky.
Replace the actuator or valve if it is seized or leaks vacuum, then clear and re-test.

P1480.meaning: The ECU sees an abnormal high signal on the control circuit of radiator fan relay 1, usually a short to power or a failed relay. The fan controlled by this relay may not run correctly, so watch coolant temperature, especially in traffic and with the A/C on.
causes: Faulty radiator fan relay 1.
Relay control wire shorted to a battery-voltage wire.
Loose relay or corroded terminals in the relay box.
Blown fuse or broken feed on the relay circuit.
Rarely, a faulty output driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Watch coolant temperature in the app. At operating temperature it normally sits roughly between 85 and 100 °C and the fans should cut in as it climbs; if it passes about 105 °C, stop and let the engine cool.
Check the fan fuses, then swap fan relay 1 with an identical relay from the same box and see if the code or fan behaviour changes.
Turn the A/C on at idle: on most models both fans should run. A fan that never runs points to its relay, fuse, wiring or motor.
Measure the relay coil resistance and compare it with a known-good relay or the service manual value.
With the relay and ECU unplugged, check the control wire for continuity and for voltage with the ignition on (there should be none). Repair wiring or replace the relay, then clear and re-test.

P1491.meaning: The ECU has detected a problem in the crankcase ventilation (PCV, blow-by) system, usually a disconnected or leaking hose. Unmetered air can enter the intake and make the engine run lean, and oil vapour can escape, so fix it soon.
causes: PCV or breather hose disconnected, cracked or split, which is very common on older EJ engines where the rubber gets brittle.
PCV valve stuck open or closed.
Oil filler cap loose or its seal missing, or dipstick not fully seated.
Intake leak near the PCV connection to the manifold or turbo inlet.
On models that monitor the PCV hose connection electrically, a fault in that detection wiring or connector.
fixes: Check that the oil filler cap is tight with its seal in place and the dipstick is fully seated.
Inspect every PCV and breather hose, including the undersides and the elbows at the valve covers and intake. Squeeze them: cracks often only open when flexed.
Check fuel trims in the app at warm idle: combined short and long term trims above about +10 % that improve when you raise the revs point to a vacuum leak.
Remove the PCV valve and shake it: it should rattle freely. Replace it if it is stuck or oily and sticky.
If nothing is visible, have a smoke test done on the intake and crankcase, then clear and re-test after the repair.

P1492.meaning: The ECU sees an abnormally low voltage on signal line 1 of the stepper-motor EGR valve, one of the four coils that step the valve open and closed. This usually means an open circuit or a short to ground. The EGR valve may stop moving: stuck closed it can cause pinging (knock) under load, stuck open it can cause a rough idle or stalling.
causes: Open circuit in the signal 1 wire or in the EGR valve's power feed.
Signal 1 wire shorted to ground through chafed insulation.
Loose, corroded or heat-damaged connector at the EGR valve.
Open or shorted coil 1 inside the EGR valve stepper motor.
Rarely, a faulty output driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Inspect the EGR valve connector for corrosion, bent or pushed-back pins and heat damage, and make sure it clicks fully home.

Unplug the valve and measure the resistance of each of the four coils (power pin to each signal pin). All four should read about the same and match the service manual value; an open (OL) or near 0 ohm reading on coil 1 means the valve is faulty.
With the ignition on and the valve unplugged, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the EGR valve's power pin. No voltage points to a fuse, relay or power-feed wiring fault.
With the ECU and valve unplugged, check the signal 1 wire for continuity end to end and make sure it has no continuity to body ground.
Replace the EGR valve if a coil is faulty, or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test at idle and during a short drive.

The EGR valve may stop moving: stuck closed it can cause pinging (knock) under load, stuck open it can cause a rough idle or stalling.

Harness damage where it runs near hot or sharp engine parts.
Rarely, a faulty output driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Inspect the EGR valve connector for corrosion, bent or pushed-back pins and heat damage, and make sure it clicks fully home.

P1507.meaning: The ECU could not hold idle speed at its target and has switched idle control to a fail-safe mode. Idle may be too high, too low or hunting, and the engine may stall when you stop; the car is usually drivable, but take care in traffic.
causes: Carbon build-up in the throttle body or idle air control (ISC) passages.
Vacuum leak (cracked PCV or breather hoses, intake gasket, brake booster hose) that the ECU cannot compensate for.
Sticking or failed ISC valve, or on drive-by-wire models a sticking electronic throttle.
Idle learning lost after a battery disconnection or throttle cleaning.
Wiring or connector fault at the ISC valve or throttle body.
fixes: Warm the engine fully and check idle rpm in the app with the A/C and lights off; compare with the target idle in the service manual.
Clean the throttle body and idle air passages with throttle cleaner. On drive-by-wire throttles, do it with the ignition off and never force the throttle plate.
Check fuel trims at idle: combined trims above about +10 % point to a vacuum leak. Inspect hoses and do a smoke test if needed.
After cleaning or a battery disconnection, let the warm engine idle for about 10 minutes without touching the pedal so the ECU can relearn idle.
Check the ISC valve or throttle body connector and wiring; replace the ISC valve or throttle body if idle still cannot be controlled, then clear and re-test.

P1510.meaning: The ECU sees an abnormally low voltage on signal line 1 of the idle speed control (ISC) valve, one of the four coils that step the valve open and closed. This usually means an open circuit or a short to ground. Idle speed may be too high, too low or hunting, and the engine may stall when you come to a stop.
causes: Open circuit in the signal 1 wire or in the ISC valve's power feed.
Signal 1 wire shorted to ground through chafed insulation.
Loose, corroded or heat-damaged connector at the ISC valve.
Open or shorted coil 1 inside the ISC valve stepper motor.
Rarely, a faulty output driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Inspect the ISC valve connector for corrosion, bent or pushed-back pins and heat damage, and make sure it clicks fully home.

Unplug the valve and measure the resistance of each of the four coils (power pin to each signal pin). All four should read about the same and match the service manual value; an open (OL) or near 0 ohm reading on coil 1 means the valve is faulty.
With the ignition on and the valve unplugged, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the ISC valve's power pin. No voltage points to a fuse, relay or power-feed wiring fault.
With the ECU and valve unplugged, check the signal 1 wire for continuity end to end and make sure it has no continuity to body ground.
While the valve is off, clean its air passage and the throttle body with throttle cleaner so a new or refitted valve is not fighting carbon build-up.
Replace the ISC valve if a coil is faulty, or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test at idle and during a short drive.
