fixes: Inspect the ISC valve connector for corrosion, bent or pushed-back pins and heat damage, and make sure it clicks fully home.

Unplug the valve and measure the resistance of each of the four coils (power pin to each signal pin). All four should read about the same and match the service manual value; an open (OL) or near 0 ohm reading on coil 2 means the valve is faulty.
With the ECU and valve unplugged and the ignition on, check the signal 2 wire for voltage. It should read 0 V; any voltage means it is shorted to a power wire somewhere in the harness.
While the valve is off, clean its air passage and the throttle body with throttle cleaner so a new or refitted valve is not fighting carbon build-up.
Replace the ISC valve if a coil is faulty, or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test at idle and during a short drive.

P1514.meaning: The ECU sees an abnormally low voltage on signal line 3 of the idle speed control (ISC) valve, one of the four coils that step the valve open and closed. This usually means an open circuit or a short to ground. Idle speed may be too high, too low or hunting, and the engine may stall when you come to a stop.
causes: Open circuit in the signal 3 wire or in the ISC valve's power feed.
Signal 3 wire shorted to ground through chafed insulation.
Loose, corroded or heat-damaged connector at the ISC valve.
Open or shorted coil 3 inside the ISC valve stepper motor.
Rarely, a faulty output driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Inspect the ISC valve connector for corrosion, bent or pushed-back pins and heat damage, and make sure it clicks fully home.

Unplug the valve and measure the resistance of each of the four coils (power pin to each signal pin). All four should read about the same and match the service manual value; an open (OL) or near 0 ohm reading on coil 3 means the valve is faulty.
With the ignition on and the valve unplugged, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the ISC valve's power pin. No voltage points to a fuse, relay or power-feed wiring fault.
With the ECU and valve unplugged, check the signal 3 wire for continuity end to end and make sure it has no continuity to body ground.
While the valve is off, clean its air passage and the throttle body with throttle cleaner so a new or refitted valve is not fighting carbon build-up.
Replace the ISC valve if a coil is faulty, or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test at idle and during a short drive.

P1515.meaning: The ECU sees an abnormally high voltage on signal line 3 of the idle speed control (ISC) valve, one of the four coils that step the valve open and closed. This usually means the line is shorted to a power wire or the coil is not being pulled to ground. Idle speed may be too high, too low or hunting, and the engine may stall when you come to a stop.
causes: Signal 3 wire shorted to a battery-voltage wire in the harness.
Coil 3 inside the ISC valve stepper motor shorted or damaged.
Loose, corroded or heat-damaged connector at the ISC valve.
Harness damage where it runs near hot or sharp engine parts.
Rarely, a faulty output driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Inspect the ISC valve connector for corrosion, bent or pushed-back pins and heat damage, and make sure it clicks fully home.

Unplug the valve and measure the resistance of each of the four coils (power pin to each signal pin). All four should read about the same and match the service manual value; an open (OL) or near 0 ohm reading on coil 3 means the valve is faulty.
With the ECU and valve unplugged and the ignition on, check the signal 3 wire for voltage. It should read 0 V; any voltage means it is shorted to a power wire somewhere in the harness.
While the valve is off, clean its air passage and the throttle body with throttle cleaner so a new or refitted valve is not fighting carbon build-up.
Replace the ISC valve if a coil is faulty, or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test at idle and during a short drive.

P1516.meaning: The ECU sees an abnormally low voltage on signal line 4 of the idle speed control (ISC) valve, one of the four coils that step the valve open and closed. This usually means an open circuit or a short to ground. Idle speed may be too high, too low or hunting, and the engine may stall when you come to a stop.
causes: Open circuit in the signal 4 wire or in the ISC valve's power feed.
Signal 4 wire shorted to ground through chafed insulation.
Loose, corroded or heat-damaged connector at the ISC valve.
Open or shorted coil 4 inside the ISC valve stepper motor.
Rarely, a faulty output driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Inspect the ISC valve connector for corrosion, bent or pushed-back pins and heat damage, and make sure it clicks fully home.

Unplug the valve and measure the resistance of each of the four coils (power pin to each signal pin). All four should read about the same and match the service manual value; an open (OL) or near 0 ohm reading on coil 4 means the valve is faulty.
With the ignition on and the valve unplugged, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the ISC valve's power pin. No voltage points to a fuse, relay or power-feed wiring fault.
With the ECU and valve unplugged, check the signal 4 wire for continuity end to end and make sure it has no continuity to body ground.
While the valve is off, clean its air passage and the throttle body with throttle cleaner so a new or refitted valve is not fighting carbon build-up.
Replace the ISC valve if a coil is faulty, or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test at idle and during a short drive.

P1517.meaning: The ECU sees an abnormally high voltage on signal line 4 of the idle speed control (ISC) valve, one of the four coils that step the valve open and closed. This usually means the line is shorted to a power wire or the coil is not being pulled to ground. Idle speed may be too high, too low or hunting, and the engine may stall when you come to a stop.
causes: Signal 4 wire shorted to a battery-voltage wire in the harness.
Coil 4 inside the ISC valve stepper motor shorted or damaged.
Loose, corroded or heat-damaged connector at the ISC valve.
Harness damage where it runs near hot or sharp engine parts.
Rarely, a faulty output driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Inspect the ISC valve connector for corrosion, bent or pushed-back pins and heat damage, and make sure it clicks fully home.

Unplug the valve and measure the resistance of each of the four coils (power pin to each signal pin). All four should read about the same and match the service manual value; an open (OL) or near 0 ohm reading on coil 4 means the valve is faulty.
With the ECU and valve unplugged and the ignition on, check the signal 4 wire for voltage. It should read 0 V; any voltage means it is shorted to a power wire somewhere in the harness.
While the valve is off, clean its air passage and the throttle body with throttle cleaner so a new or refitted valve is not fighting carbon build-up.
Replace the ISC valve if a coil is faulty, or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test at idle and during a short drive.

P1518.meaning: The ECU does not see the starter signal (the wire that tells it the engine is cranking) when it expects it. The engine usually still starts, but cold starts may be harder because the ECU may not apply its cranking fuel and timing strategy.
causes: Open or high-resistance wire in the starter signal circuit to the ECU.
Poor connection at the starter relay, inhibitor switch (automatic) or clutch start switch (manual).
Blown fuse in the starter signal circuit.
Worn start contacts in the ignition switch.
Rarely, a faulty ECU input.
fixes: Check the fuses related to the starter and ignition circuits.
Check the starter signal switch in the app's switch data if available: it should turn on only while cranking.
Back-probe the ECU starter signal wire: it should show close to battery voltage while cranking and near 0 V otherwise.
Inspect the connectors at the starter relay, inhibitor switch or clutch switch, and at the starter solenoid.
Repair the wiring or replace the ignition switch or faulty switch, then clear and re-test with a few cold starts.

P1519.meaning: The ECU detected that the intake manifold runner control (IMRC, variable intake) valve is staying closed when it should open. On engines with a variable intake manifold, such as some six-cylinder models, this mainly costs power at higher rpm; it is safe to drive.
causes: Vacuum hose to the IMRC actuator cracked, disconnected or misrouted.
Valve or shaft sticking from carbon and oil build-up.
Actuator diaphragm leaking.
IMRC control solenoid not switching.
Vacuum reservoir or check valve leaking.
fixes: Inspect the vacuum lines between the vacuum source, IMRC solenoid and actuator.
Apply vacuum to the actuator with a hand vacuum pump: it should move the valve and hold vacuum.
With the engine off, check that the valve linkage moves freely by hand.
Check that the solenoid clicks when commanded and passes vacuum when energised.
Clean the valve or replace the actuator or solenoid as needed, then clear and re-test with a drive to high rpm.

P1520.meaning: The ECU detected an electrical fault in the intake manifold runner control (IMRC, variable intake) solenoid circuit. The variable intake stops switching, which mainly costs power at some engine speeds; it is safe to drive.
causes: Open circuit or short in the IMRC solenoid wiring.
Loose or corroded connector at the solenoid.
Solenoid coil open or shorted.
Blown fuse or missing power feed.
Rarely, a faulty output driver inside the ECU.
fixes: Locate the IMRC solenoid (see the service manual for your engine) and check the connector for corrosion and a firm fit.
Unplug it and measure the coil resistance; compare with the service manual value.
With the ignition on, check for battery voltage (about 12 V) on the power side of the connector.
With the ECU and solenoid unplugged, check the control wire for continuity and for shorts to ground or to power.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P1521.meaning: The ECU sees the brake switch signal stay on (high) when it should be off, for example while you are accelerating. Cruise control will not work, and on some drive-by-wire models engine power may be reduced. Check that your brake lights are not stuck on.
causes: Brake light switch out of adjustment, or the rubber stop pad on the pedal missing so the switch stays closed.
Failed brake light switch with stuck contacts.
Wiring shorted to the brake light feed.
Aftermarket wiring (trailer module, LED bulbs, extra brake light) feeding voltage back into the circuit.
fixes: Have someone check that the brake lights go off completely when the pedal is released.
Check the pedal stop pad and brake switch adjustment behind the pedal.
Watch the brake switch status in the app's switch data: it should change only when you press the pedal.
Unplug the switch and check its contacts with a multimeter in the pressed and released positions.
Disconnect any trailer or aftermarket lighting modules to rule out backfeed, replace the switch if needed, then clear and re-test.

P1530.meaning: The signal from the battery current sensor (fitted at the negative battery terminal on later models with alternator charge control) is below its normal range. The ECU falls back to a default charging strategy; it is not urgent, but battery charging may be less efficient.
causes: Loose or corroded sensor connector at the negative battery terminal.
Sensor wiring open or shorted to ground.
Failed battery current sensor.
Battery terminal loose or corroded.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Clean and tighten the battery terminals and check the sensor connector at the negative terminal is fully seated.
Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
With the ignition on, back-probe the sensor connector and compare its supply and signal voltages with the service manual values.
With the ECU and sensor unplugged, check the sensor wires for continuity and shorts to ground.
Replace the sensor (on some models it comes as part of the negative battery cable), then clear and re-test.

P1531.meaning: The signal from the battery current sensor (fitted at the negative battery terminal on later models with alternator charge control) is above its normal range. The ECU falls back to a default charging strategy; it is not urgent, but battery charging may be less efficient.
causes: Loose or corroded sensor connector at the negative battery terminal.
Sensor signal wire shorted to a voltage source, or open sensor ground.
Failed battery current sensor.
Battery terminal loose or corroded.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Clean and tighten the battery terminals and check the sensor connector at the negative terminal is fully seated.
Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
With the ignition on, back-probe the sensor connector and compare its supply and signal voltages with the service manual values.
With the ECU and sensor unplugged, check the sensor wires for continuity and for any short to a power wire.
Replace the sensor (on some models it comes as part of the negative battery cable), then clear and re-test.

P1532.meaning: The ECU's alternator charge control is not working as expected: the charging it measures does not match what it commanded. Watch for a battery warning light, dim lights or a battery that goes flat.
causes: Worn or faulty alternator (voltage regulator, brushes or diodes).
Weak or failing battery.
Battery current sensor faulty, or aftermarket accessories grounded directly to the battery negative post so their current bypasses the sensor.
Loose or corroded battery, alternator or ground connections.
Slipping or worn drive belt.
Wiring fault between the ECU and the alternator control terminal.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Watch battery voltage in the app while switching on headlights, blower and rear demister.
Clean and tighten battery terminals and the engine and body ground straps, and check the alternator belt for glazing and correct tension.
Make sure any aftermarket accessory grounds go to the body or the vehicle side of the current sensor, not directly to the battery negative post.
Have the battery load-tested and the alternator output tested.
Check the alternator control wiring for continuity back to the ECU, repair or replace parts as needed, then clear and re-test.

P1540.meaning: The ECU sees little or no vehicle speed signal while engine speed and load say the car is moving. Speedometer, cruise control, idle control and fuel cut logic may misbehave, and on automatics shifting may be affected.
causes: Faulty vehicle speed sensor, or a failed wheel speed sensor on models that take road speed from the ABS/VDC system.
Damaged wiring or a corroded connector in the speed signal circuit.
Fault in the instrument cluster or ABS/VDC module that passes the speed signal on to the ECU.
CAN communication fault on models that share speed over the data bus.
Rarely, an ECU input fault.
fixes: Check whether the speedometer works. If it does not, the fault is upstream of the cluster (sensor or ABS side).
Read ABS/VDC and transmission codes too, and look at the ABS warning light.
Watch vehicle speed in the app while driving and compare with GPS speed: it should rise smoothly with no dropouts.
Inspect the speed sensor connector and wiring at the transmission or wheel for damage and corrosion.
Test or replace the faulty sensor and repair wiring as needed, then clear and re-test with a drive.

P1544.meaning: An exhaust gas temperature (EGT) sensor reported a temperature above the ECU's safe limit. This mainly applies to the EE20 boxer diesel. The ECU will reduce power to protect the turbocharger, catalyst and DPF; ease off, because sustained high exhaust temperatures can damage those parts.
causes: Very hard, sustained driving or towing at high load.
Uncontrolled DPF regeneration with a very heavy soot load.
Boost leak, blocked air filter or restricted intake upsetting the air-fuel ratio.
Leaking or overfuelling injector.
Faulty EGT sensor reading too high.
Aftermarket tuning with more fuelling than stock limits allow.
fixes: After hard driving, let the engine idle for a minute before switching off so the turbo can cool.
Read all stored codes; DPF, boost, EGR and injector codes often explain the high temperature.
If your tool shows EGT in live data, check it on a cold engine: every EGT sensor should read close to outside air temperature. One that does not is suspect.
Inspect the air filter, intake ducts and intercooler hoses for blockages or boost leaks.
Replace a faulty EGT sensor or repair the fuelling or DPF fault, then clear and re-test with a normal drive.

P1545.meaning: The signal from exhaust gas temperature (EGT) sensor 2 is below its possible range. On the EE20 boxer diesel these sensors control DPF regeneration and protect the turbo, so regeneration may be blocked and power may be limited until it is fixed.
causes: EGT sensor 2 signal wire shorted to ground.
Heat-damaged or corroded connector (the connectors sit close to the hot exhaust).
Failed EGT sensor 2.
Harness melted or chafed against the exhaust.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Find EGT sensor 2 using the service manual for your model and check its connector for heat damage, corrosion and a firm fit.
Inspect the sensor lead and harness along the exhaust for melted insulation.
Unplug the sensor and measure its resistance at room temperature; compare with the service manual value (open or near 0 ohms means it is faulty).
With the ECU and sensor unplugged, check both wires for continuity and for any short to ground.
Replace the sensor if faulty (use anti-seize on the threads), then clear and re-test.

P1546.meaning: The signal from exhaust gas temperature (EGT) sensor 2 is above its possible range, which usually means an open circuit. On the EE20 boxer diesel these sensors control DPF regeneration and protect the turbo, so regeneration may be blocked and power may be limited until it is fixed.
causes: Open circuit in the EGT sensor 2 wiring, or signal wire shorted to a voltage source.
Heat-damaged or corroded connector (the connectors sit close to the hot exhaust).
Failed EGT sensor 2 (broken internal element).
Harness melted or chafed against the exhaust.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Find EGT sensor 2 using the service manual for your model and check its connector for heat damage, corrosion and a firm fit.
Inspect the sensor lead and harness along the exhaust for melted or broken wires.
Unplug the sensor and measure its resistance at room temperature; compare with the service manual value (open means it is faulty).
With the ECU and sensor unplugged, check both wires for continuity end to end and for voltage with the ignition on (there should be none on the signal wire).
Replace the sensor if faulty (use anti-seize on the threads), then clear and re-test.

P1547.meaning: An exhaust gas temperature (EGT) sensor is giving a reading the ECU finds implausible, for example one that does not match the other sensors or does not change as the engine warms up. On the EE20 boxer diesel this can block DPF regeneration and limit power.
causes: EGT sensor degraded or drifting with age and heat.
Poor connection or high resistance in the sensor connector or wiring.
Sensors swapped between positions after a repair.
Exhaust leak near the sensor affecting its reading.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: If your tool shows EGT values, compare all sensors on a cold engine (they should all read close to outside air temperature) and watch that each one rises as the engine warms.
Check the sensor connectors for heat damage, corrosion and loose pins.
Check that each sensor is in its correct position and that there are no exhaust leaks near them.
Measure the suspect sensor's resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Replace the sensor that reads out of line, then clear and re-test.

P1559.meaning: The ECU detected that intake air flow or pressure does not match what it expects for the current engine state, which points to a leak, blockage or disconnection in the air intake. Expect rough running or reduced power; fix it soon, because unmetered air can make a petrol engine run lean and a turbo engine lose boost.
causes: Loose or split intake duct, turbo inlet hose or intercooler hose, a common failure on turbo models.
Clogged air filter or blocked intake snorkel.
Dirty or faulty MAF sensor.
Cracked PCV or breather hoses on EJ engines.
On the EE20 diesel, an intake throttle, boost control or EGR fault.
fixes: Inspect the whole intake path from the air box to the throttle body, including every clamp, coupler and the turbo inlet.
Check the air filter and air box for blockage.
Check MAF g/s at warm idle in the app and compare with the service manual value; unusually low or erratic readings point to a leak or a dirty MAF.
Check fuel trims (combined above about +10 % suggests unmetered air) and, on turbo models, whether boost reaches its usual target.
Clean the MAF with MAF-safe cleaner, have a smoke or boost-leak test done, repair what you find, then clear and re-test.

P1560.meaning: The ECU's constant (back-up) battery supply, which keeps learned values and fault memory alive with the ignition off, dropped too low or was interrupted. The engine usually runs normally, but learned idle and fuel trims may reset and the car may idle poorly for a while.
causes: Battery disconnected or run flat; this code often appears after battery work.
Blown back-up or memory fuse feeding the ECU.
Corroded or loose battery terminals.
Open or high-resistance wire in the ECU back-up supply.
Weak battery dipping very low during cranking.
fixes: If the battery was recently disconnected or replaced, clear the code and see whether it returns.
Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running, and not dropping below about 9.5 to 10 V while cranking.
Clean and tighten the battery terminals and check the engine and body ground straps.
Check the ECU back-up fuse and confirm battery voltage is present at the ECU back-up supply with the ignition off (see the service manual wiring diagram).
Load-test the battery and replace it if weak, then clear and re-test.

P1570.meaning: The immobilizer could not communicate properly through its antenna coil around the ignition key barrel. The engine may crank but not start, or start and then stall after a few seconds.
causes: Other transponder keys, key fobs or large metal objects on the key ring interfering with the signal.
Damaged or unplugged antenna coil or connector at the key cylinder.
Faulty transponder chip in the key.
Wiring fault between the antenna and the immobilizer module.
Faulty immobilizer module.
fixes: Take the key off a crowded key ring, keep other car keys and fobs away from the ignition, and try again.
Try the spare key. If the spare works, the first key's transponder is faulty.
Remove the steering column trim and check the antenna coil connector at the key cylinder.
Check the wiring from the antenna to the immobilizer module for damage.
If neither key works and the wiring is fine, replace the antenna or immobilizer module; new parts and keys must be registered with a Subaru dealer tool.

P1571.meaning: The immobilizer data stored in the ECU does not match the immobilizer system. This is typical after fitting a used ECU or immobilizer module from another car. The engine will not start, or will start and stall immediately.
causes: ECU replaced or swapped from another car without being registered to this car's immobilizer.
Immobilizer module or instrument cluster replaced without registration.
Rarely, corrupted immobilizer data in the ECU or immobilizer module.
Communication wiring fault between the ECU and immobilizer module garbling the code exchange.
fixes: If a different ECU or module was fitted recently, refit the original if you still have it.
Otherwise have the ECU, immobilizer and keys registered together with a Subaru dealer tool or a locksmith with Subaru immobilizer capability.
Check the connectors and wiring between the ECU and immobilizer module.
Check battery voltage (about 12.6 V engine off): low voltage can disrupt the code exchange during starting.

P1572.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the immobilizer system circuits other than the key antenna, usually the communication line between the ECU and the immobilizer module or that module's power supply. The engine may not start.
causes: Open or shorted communication wire between the ECU and immobilizer module.
Blown fuse or poor power or ground at the immobilizer module.
Loose or corroded connector at the immobilizer module or ECU.
Faulty immobilizer module.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check battery voltage (about 12.6 V engine off) and the fuses that feed the immobilizer and ECU.
Check the connectors at the immobilizer module and ECU for corrosion and a firm fit.
Check the immobilizer module's power and ground with a multimeter.
Check the communication wire between the ECU and immobilizer module for continuity and shorts.
Replace the faulty module if wiring is good; new modules must be registered with a Subaru dealer tool.

P1574.meaning: The immobilizer could not read or verify the code from the key's transponder chip. The engine will not start, or will start and stall after a few seconds.
causes: Key not registered to the car, for example a newly cut spare that was never programmed.
Damaged transponder chip in the key (after a drop or water damage).
Other transponder keys or fobs on the key ring interfering.
Faulty antenna coil around the key cylinder.
Faulty immobilizer module.
fixes: Remove other keys and fobs from the key ring and try again.
Try the spare key. If it starts the car, the first key is faulty or unregistered.
Check the antenna coil connector at the key cylinder.
Have the keys registered, or a replacement key cut and programmed, with a Subaru dealer tool or a capable locksmith.

P1576.meaning: The engine control module (EGI ECU) detected an error in its own EEPROM memory, which stores immobilizer and other permanent data. The engine may not start; this nearly always means an ECU repair or replacement.
causes: Internal ECU memory fault.
Voltage spike or very low voltage while the ECU was writing to memory (jump starting, welding, a failing battery).
Water or corrosion damage to the ECU.
Poor ECU power or ground connections.
fixes: Check battery voltage (about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running) and the ECU grounds.
Check the ECU connectors and the ECU itself for water ingress or corrosion.
Clear the code and re-test; if it returns immediately, the ECU memory is faulty.
Replace the ECU; a replacement must be registered to the immobilizer and keys with a Subaru dealer tool.

P1577.meaning: The immobilizer control module detected an error in its own EEPROM memory, where key and ECU codes are stored. The engine may not start until the module is replaced.
causes: Internal immobilizer module memory fault.
Voltage spike or very low voltage during operation (jump starting, a failing battery).
Water or corrosion damage to the module.
Poor power or ground at the module.
fixes: Check battery voltage (about 12.6 V engine off) and the immobilizer fuse and ground.
Check the immobilizer module connector for corrosion.
Clear the code and re-test; if it returns immediately, the module memory is faulty.
Replace the immobilizer module and have it registered to the ECU and keys with a Subaru dealer tool.

P1578.meaning: The ECU reports a fault with the combination meter (instrument cluster), which on some Subarus contains the immobilizer control. The engine may not start, and gauges or warning lights may misbehave.
causes: Internal fault in the instrument cluster.
Blown fuse or poor power or ground at the cluster.
Loose or corroded cluster connector.
Communication wiring fault between the cluster and ECU.
Cluster replaced or swapped without immobilizer registration.
fixes: Check whether the gauges and warning lights work normally.
Check the cluster fuses and battery voltage (about 12.6 V engine off).
Remove the cluster and check its connectors for corrosion or pushed-back pins.
Check the communication wiring between the cluster and ECU.
Repair or replace the cluster; a replacement must be registered to the immobilizer with a Subaru dealer tool.

P1579.meaning: The ECU detected a fault in the remote engine starter system, fitted as a factory or dealer accessory in some markets. Normal key starting usually still works, but remote start may be disabled.
causes: Faulty remote engine starter module.
Loose connector or damaged wiring to the remote starter module.
Aftermarket remote starter or immobilizer bypass module interfering with the factory system.
Low battery voltage.
Faulty bonnet (hood) switch or other safety input the remote starter checks.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off.
Check the remote starter module connectors (usually under the dash).
If an aftermarket remote starter or bypass module is fitted, disconnect it and re-test.
Check the bonnet switch and other inputs the remote starter uses, following the installation or service manual.
Repair or replace the remote starter module, then clear and re-test.

P1590.meaning: The ECU sees the neutral position signal from the automatic transmission's inhibitor switch stuck high, so the signal does not match the selected gear. This can upset idle control and may affect starting in P or N.
causes: Inhibitor switch out of adjustment, often after transmission or shift cable work.
Worn or contaminated inhibitor switch contacts.
Neutral signal wire shorted to a voltage source.
Loose or corroded connector at the inhibitor switch on the transmission.
Shift cable out of adjustment.
fixes: Check that the engine starts only in P and N, the reverse lights come on only in R, and the dash gear indicator matches the lever.
Watch the neutral switch status in the app's switch data while moving the lever: it should change only in P and N.
Inspect the inhibitor switch connector on the transmission for corrosion and a firm fit.
Measure switch continuity in each lever position and compare with the service manual table.
Adjust the shift cable or inhibitor switch, or replace the switch, then clear and re-test.

P1591.meaning: The ECU sees the neutral position signal from the automatic transmission's inhibitor switch stuck low, so the signal does not match the selected gear. This can upset idle control and may affect starting in P or N.
causes: Inhibitor switch out of adjustment, often after transmission or shift cable work.
Worn or contaminated inhibitor switch contacts.
Neutral signal wire open or shorted to ground.
Loose or corroded connector at the inhibitor switch on the transmission.
Shift cable out of adjustment.
fixes: Check that the engine starts only in P and N, the reverse lights come on only in R, and the dash gear indicator matches the lever.
Watch the neutral switch status in the app's switch data while moving the lever: it should change only in P and N.
Inspect the inhibitor switch connector on the transmission for corrosion and a firm fit.
Measure switch continuity in each lever position and compare with the service manual table.
Adjust the shift cable or inhibitor switch, or replace the switch, then clear and re-test.

P1592.meaning: The ECU sees a neutral position switch signal from the manual gearbox that does not make sense, for example showing neutral while the car is driving in gear. It uses this switch for idle control and other logic, so idle may dip or behave oddly; it is safe to drive.
causes: Faulty neutral position switch on the gearbox.
Corroded or loose connector at the switch (exposed to road spray under the car).
Damaged wiring between the switch and ECU.
Switch misadjusted after gearbox work.
Rarely, an ECU input fault.
fixes: Watch the neutral position switch in the app's switch data while moving the gear lever with the engine off: it should change state only in neutral.
Inspect the switch connector on the gearbox for corrosion and water.
Unplug the switch and check its continuity in neutral and in gear with a multimeter.
Check the wiring between the switch and ECU for damage.
Replace the switch or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test.

P1593.meaning: The ECU cannot communicate properly with the automatic transmission control module (TCM). Engine and transmission may fall back to default strategies, so expect harsher shifts or limp mode, and the AT OIL TEMP light may flash at start-up.
causes: Blown fuse or poor power or ground at the TCM.
Open or shorted communication wiring between the ECU and TCM.
Loose or corroded connector at the TCM or ECU.
Low battery voltage.
Faulty TCM, or rarely the ECU.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Check the TCM fuses and look for TCM codes (on many Subarus the AT OIL TEMP light flashes at start-up when the TCM has a fault).
Check the TCM and ECU connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
Check the communication wiring between the ECU and TCM for continuity and shorts.
Replace the TCM if its power, ground and wiring check good, then clear and re-test.

P1594.meaning: The ECU monitors a signal line from the automatic transmission control module (TCM) that reports transmission faults, and that signal is abnormal. It often appears alongside a real transmission fault, so read the TCM codes as well.
causes: TCM has a stored fault of its own.
Open or shorted wire between the TCM and ECU on the diagnostic signal line.
Loose or corroded connector at the TCM or ECU.
Poor power or ground at the TCM.
Faulty TCM, or rarely the ECU.
fixes: Read the TCM codes. On many Subarus the AT OIL TEMP light flashes at start-up when the TCM has a stored fault.
Fix any TCM faults first, then clear and re-test.
Check the TCM and ECU connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
Check the diagnostic signal wire between the TCM and ECU for continuity and shorts.
Check TCM power and ground; replace the TCM only if the wiring checks good.

P1595.meaning: The ECU sees the diagnostic signal line from the automatic transmission control module (TCM) stuck low. It often appears alongside a real transmission fault, so read the TCM codes as well.
causes: Diagnostic signal wire between the TCM and ECU shorted to ground or open.
TCM has a stored fault of its own.
Loose or corroded connector at the TCM or ECU.
Loss of power or ground at the TCM.
Faulty TCM, or rarely the ECU.
fixes: Read the TCM codes. On many Subarus the AT OIL TEMP light flashes at start-up when the TCM has a stored fault.
Check the TCM fuse and TCM power and ground.
Check the TCM and ECU connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
With both modules unplugged, check the diagnostic signal wire for continuity and for any short to ground.
Repair the wiring or replace the TCM if the wiring checks good, then clear and re-test.

P1596.meaning: The ECU sees the diagnostic signal line from the automatic transmission control module (TCM) stuck high. It often appears alongside a real transmission fault, so read the TCM codes as well.
causes: Diagnostic signal wire between the TCM and ECU shorted to a voltage source.
TCM has a stored fault of its own.
Loose or corroded connector at the TCM or ECU.
Faulty TCM output.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Read the TCM codes. On many Subarus the AT OIL TEMP light flashes at start-up when the TCM has a stored fault.
Check the TCM and ECU connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
With both modules unplugged and the ignition on, check the diagnostic signal wire for voltage: it should read 0 V.
Check the wire for continuity end to end and repair any damage.
Replace the TCM if the wiring checks good, then clear and re-test.

P1597.meaning: The signal line from the traction control (TCS/VDC) module, which asks the ECU to cut engine torque when wheels spin, is reading low. Traction control may not reduce power properly, or the ECU may cut power when it should not.
causes: Signal wire between the VDC/TCS module and ECU open or shorted to ground.
Loose or corroded connector at the VDC module or ECU.
Fault in the VDC/TCS module (check for VDC warning lights and codes).
Poor power or ground at the VDC module.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check for VDC, TCS or ABS warning lights and read that module's codes.
Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Check the VDC module and ECU connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
With both modules unplugged, check the signal wire for continuity and for any short to ground.
Repair the wiring or have the VDC module diagnosed, then clear and re-test.

P1598.meaning: The signal line from the traction control (TCS/VDC) module, which asks the ECU to cut engine torque when wheels spin, is reading high. Traction control may not reduce power properly, or the ECU may cut power when it should not.
causes: Signal wire between the VDC/TCS module and ECU shorted to a voltage source.
Loose or corroded connector at the VDC module or ECU.
Fault in the VDC/TCS module (check for VDC warning lights and codes).
Harness damage where it runs through the engine bay.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check for VDC, TCS or ABS warning lights and read that module's codes.
Check the VDC module and ECU connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
With both modules unplugged and the ignition on, check the signal wire for voltage: it should read 0 V.
Check the wire for continuity end to end and repair any damage.
Have the VDC module diagnosed if the wiring checks good, then clear and re-test.

P1600.meaning: The ECU has found problems communicating with other modules (transmission, ABS/VDC, instrument cluster) on the CAN data bus. Depending on which messages are missing you may see warning lights, harsh shifts or limp mode.
causes: Low battery voltage, or a voltage dip after jump starting or battery work.
Loose or corroded connector on a module on the CAN network.
Damaged CAN wiring (chafed, pinched or water in a connector).
A failed module disturbing the bus.
Aftermarket devices tapped into the CAN wires or plugged into the OBD port.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Unplug any aftermarket OBD dongles, gauges or CAN taps and re-test.
Read codes in the other modules to see which one the ECU is not hearing from, and check that module's fuse, power, ground and connectors first.

With the battery disconnected, measure resistance between the CAN high and CAN low pins at the OBD port (pins 6 and 14 on cars that bring CAN to the port): about 60 ohms is normal, about 120 ohms means one terminating resistor or a wire is open, near 0 ohms means a short.
Repair the wiring or the faulty module, then clear and re-test.

P1601.meaning: The ECU is not receiving the expected messages from the automatic transmission control module (TCM), usually over the CAN data bus. Engine and transmission may fall back to default strategies: expect harsher shifts or limp mode, and the AT OIL TEMP light may flash at start-up.
causes: Blown fuse or poor power or ground at the TCM.
Open or shorted CAN wiring between the ECU and TCM.
Loose or corroded connector at the TCM or ECU.
Low battery voltage.
Faulty TCM, or rarely the ECU.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Check the TCM fuses and read the TCM codes if the TCM responds.
Check the TCM and ECU connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
Check the CAN wiring between the ECU and TCM, and measure CAN resistance at the OBD port (about 60 ohms with the battery disconnected on cars that bring CAN to the port).
Replace the TCM if its power, ground and wiring check good, then clear and re-test.

P1602.meaning: The ECU found that its programming (software or calibration data) is incomplete or corrupted, for example after an interrupted reflash. The engine may not start, or may run in a fail-safe mode.
causes: Reflash interrupted: cable unplugged, laptop went to sleep, or battery voltage dropped during flashing.
Wrong ROM or calibration flashed for this ECU.
Incomplete dealer software update.
Internal ECU memory fault.
fixes: Connect a battery charger or power supply so voltage stays steady (about 12.5 to 14 V) before any flashing.
Reflash the correct ROM for the ECU (the stock ROM or a known-good tune that matches the ECU ID) with your flashing tool, or have a dealer reprogram it.
Verify the flash completed and the ROM ID reads back correctly.
If reflashing fails or the code returns, the ECU memory is faulty and the ECU must be replaced and registered to the immobilizer.

P1607.meaning: The ECU's internal self-check (a monitoring processor that watches the main processor, mainly for electronic throttle safety) found a problem. The ECU may limit throttle opening or enter a fail-safe mode; have it checked before relying on the car.
causes: Internal ECU fault.
Unstable supply voltage from a weak battery, loose terminals or poor ECU grounds.
Water ingress or corrosion in the ECU or its connectors.
Corrupted or mismatched ECU software after reflashing.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running, and clean and tighten the terminals.
Check the engine and body ground straps and the ECU ground connections.
Inspect the ECU connectors for corrosion or water.
If the ECU was reflashed, reflash the stock ROM and see if the code returns.
Clear and re-test; if it returns with good power and grounds, replace the ECU and register it to the immobilizer.

P1616.meaning: The ECU sees a low signal in the start relay lock circuit, the circuit it uses to allow or block the starter (for example with the immobilizer or starter interlock). The engine may not crank, or the starter may not be blocked when it should be.
causes: Open circuit or short to ground in the start relay control wiring.
Faulty starter cut or start relay.
Blown fuse in the starter circuit.
Loose or corroded relay socket or connector.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Check the starter-related fuses.
Swap the start relay with an identical relay and see whether the behaviour changes.
Check the relay socket and connectors for corrosion and loose terminals.
Check the relay control wire between the ECU and relay for continuity and shorts to ground (see the service manual wiring diagram for your model).
Repair the wiring or replace the relay, then clear and re-test.

P1698.meaning: The signal line the automatic transmission control module (TCM) uses to ask the ECU for a brief torque reduction during gear changes is reading low. Shifts may feel harsh until it is fixed; the car is otherwise drivable.
causes: Torque cut signal wire between the TCM and ECU open or shorted to ground.
Loose or corroded connector at the TCM or ECU.
Faulty TCM output.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Read the TCM codes as well; related transmission faults help narrow it down.
Check the TCM and ECU connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
With both modules unplugged, check the signal wire for continuity and for any short to ground.
Repair the wiring or replace the faulty module, then clear and re-test with several shifts.

P1699.meaning: The signal line the automatic transmission control module (TCM) uses to ask the ECU for a brief torque reduction during gear changes is reading high. Shifts may feel harsh until it is fixed; the car is otherwise drivable.
causes: Torque cut signal wire between the TCM and ECU shorted to a voltage source.
Loose or corroded connector at the TCM or ECU.
Faulty TCM output.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Read the TCM codes as well; related transmission faults help narrow it down.
Check the TCM and ECU connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
With both modules unplugged and the ignition on, check the signal wire for voltage: it should read 0 V.
Repair the wiring or replace the faulty module, then clear and re-test with several shifts.

P1700.meaning: The automatic transmission control module (TCM) is not receiving a valid throttle position signal. Without it, shift points and line pressure go to default values, so expect harsh or late shifts, and the AT OIL TEMP light may flash at start-up.
causes: Faulty throttle position sensor (check for engine TPS codes too).
Open or shorted wiring between the ECU or TPS and the TCM.
Loose or corroded connector at the TPS, ECU or TCM.
Faulty TCM, or rarely the ECU.
fixes: Read engine codes for throttle position faults and fix those first.
Watch throttle position in the app while slowly pressing the pedal (engine off, ignition on): it should rise smoothly from closed to wide open with no jumps or dropouts.
Check the TPS, ECU and TCM connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
Check the throttle signal wire to the TCM for continuity and shorts.
Repair the wiring or replace the TPS, then clear and re-test.

P1701.meaning: The automatic transmission control module (TCM) sees an abnormal signal from the cruise control system, which tells it cruise is active so it can adjust shift behaviour. Shifting on cruise may feel busier; it is not urgent.
causes: Open or shorted wire between the cruise control module or ECU and the TCM.
Loose or corroded connector.
Fault in the cruise control module or switches.
Faulty TCM.
fixes: Check that cruise control sets, holds and cancels normally.
Check for engine or cruise-related codes.
Check the connectors on the cruise control signal path for corrosion and a firm fit.
Check the cruise signal wire to the TCM for continuity and shorts, repair as needed, then clear and re-test.

P1703.meaning: The transmission control module (TCM) detected an electrical fault in the low clutch timing solenoid inside the 4EAT automatic, which controls how the low clutch engages during shifts. Expect harsh shifts or limp mode (stuck in one gear); avoid hard driving until fixed.
causes: Solenoid coil open or shorted.
Damaged internal harness inside the transmission.
Loose, oily or corroded connector at the transmission.
Wiring fault between the transmission and TCM.
Rarely, a faulty TCM.
fixes: Check the ATF level and condition: it should be red, not dark and burnt-smelling.
Check the transmission connector and the TCM connector for corrosion, oil and a firm fit.
Measure the solenoid resistance through the connector and compare with the service manual value.
Check the wiring between the transmission and TCM for continuity and shorts.
If the fault is inside the transmission, replace the solenoid or internal harness (valve body access), then clear and re-test.

P1706.meaning: The transmission control module (TCM) is not getting a valid signal from the rear vehicle speed sensor on the automatic transmission's rear or transfer housing. Shift timing and AWD torque control depend on it, so expect erratic shifting, limp mode or binding in tight turns.
causes: Faulty rear speed sensor.
Metal debris on the sensor's magnetic tip.
Loose or corroded sensor connector.
Damaged wiring between the sensor and TCM.
Rarely, a faulty TCM.
fixes: Check the speed sensor connector at the rear of the transmission for corrosion and a firm fit.
Remove the sensor and clean any metal debris from its tip.
Measure the sensor resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the wiring between the sensor and TCM for continuity and shorts.
Replace the sensor if faulty, then clear and re-test with a drive.

P1707.meaning: The transmission control module (TCM) detected an electrical fault in the AWD (transfer) solenoid valve, which controls how much torque goes to the rear wheels through the transfer clutch. The car may drive as front-wheel drive or bind (shudder or hop) in tight, slow turns; avoid prolonged driving with binding.
causes: AWD transfer solenoid coil open or shorted.
Damaged internal harness in the transmission.
Loose, oily or corroded connector at the transmission.
Wiring fault between the transmission and TCM.
Rarely, a faulty TCM.
fixes: Check the ATF level and condition.
Check the transmission and TCM connectors for corrosion, oil and a firm fit.
Measure the AWD solenoid resistance through the connector and compare with the service manual value.
Check the wiring between the transmission and TCM for continuity and shorts.
Replace the solenoid or repair the wiring, then clear and re-test with some slow full-lock turns.

P1708.meaning: The throttle position signal used by the automatic transmission control module (TCM) is below its normal range. The TCM falls back to default shift points and line pressure, so expect harsh or late shifts.
causes: Throttle position sensor signal wire open or shorted to ground.
Loss of the TPS 5 V reference.
Faulty throttle position sensor.
Loose or corroded connector at the TPS, ECU or TCM.
Rarely, a faulty TCM or ECU.
fixes: Read engine codes for throttle position faults (such as P0122) and fix those first.
Watch throttle position in the app with the ignition on, engine off, while slowly pressing the pedal: it should rise smoothly with no dropouts.
Check for about 5 V on the TPS reference wire and a good ground.
Check the TPS signal wire to the TCM for continuity and shorts to ground.
Repair the wiring or replace the TPS, then clear and re-test.

P1709.meaning: The throttle position signal used by the automatic transmission control module (TCM) is above its normal range. The TCM falls back to default shift points and line pressure, so expect harsh or late shifts.
causes: Throttle position sensor signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage.
Open TPS ground.
Faulty throttle position sensor.
Loose or corroded connector at the TPS, ECU or TCM.
Rarely, a faulty TCM or ECU.
fixes: Read engine codes for throttle position faults (such as P0123) and fix those first.
Watch throttle position in the app with the ignition on, engine off, while slowly pressing the pedal: it should rise smoothly and read near closed with the pedal released.
Check the TPS ground: less than about 0.1 V between the sensor ground and battery negative.
Check the TPS signal wire to the TCM for continuity and shorts to voltage.
Repair the wiring or replace the TPS, then clear and re-test.

P1710.meaning: The transmission control module (TCM) is not getting a valid signal from turbine speed sensor 2, which measures transmission input speed on the 5EAT automatic. Shifts may be harsh and the transmission may go into limp mode.
causes: Faulty turbine speed sensor 2.
Loose or corroded sensor connector.
Damaged wiring between the sensor and TCM.
Metal debris on the sensor tip.
Rarely, a faulty TCM.
fixes: Check the ATF level and condition.
Check the sensor and TCM connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
Measure the sensor resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Check the wiring between the sensor and TCM for continuity and shorts.
Replace the sensor if faulty, then clear and re-test with a drive through all gears.

P1711.meaning: The engine torque control signal 1 between the ECU and the automatic transmission control module (TCM) is abnormal. This signal coordinates engine torque with gear changes, so shifts may feel harsh or flare; the car is otherwise drivable.
causes: Open or shorted wire on torque control signal line 1.
Loose or corroded connector at the ECU or TCM.
Faulty TCM or ECU output.
Low battery voltage.
fixes: Read both engine and TCM codes.
Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Check the ECU and TCM connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
Check signal line 1 for continuity and shorts to ground or voltage, repair as needed, then clear and re-test.

P1712.meaning: The engine torque control signal 2 between the ECU and the automatic transmission control module (TCM) is abnormal. This signal coordinates engine torque with gear changes, so shifts may feel harsh or flare; the car is otherwise drivable.
causes: Open or shorted wire on torque control signal line 2.
Loose or corroded connector at the ECU or TCM.
Faulty TCM or ECU output.
Low battery voltage.
fixes: Read both engine and TCM codes.
Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Check the ECU and TCM connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
Check signal line 2 for continuity and shorts to ground or voltage, repair as needed, then clear and re-test.

P1714.meaning: The 5 V supply that feeds the throttle position sensor is out of range. Other sensors sharing the same 5 V supply may also set codes, and the transmission and engine may both fall back to default strategies.
causes: TPS 5 V reference wire shorted to ground or to battery voltage.
Another sensor on the same 5 V supply shorted internally and pulling the supply down.
Loose or corroded connector at the TPS.
Faulty throttle position sensor.
Rarely, an ECU fault.
fixes: Read all engine codes; several sensor codes at once point to a shared 5 V supply problem.
With the ignition on, check for about 5 V at the TPS reference wire.
Unplug sensors that share the 5 V supply one at a time; if the voltage recovers, the last one unplugged is shorted.
Check the reference wire for shorts to ground or voltage along the harness.
Repair the wiring or replace the faulty sensor, then clear and re-test.

P1716.meaning: The signal from ATF temperature sensor 2 (a second transmission fluid temperature sensor fitted on some Subaru automatics, such as the 5EAT) is below its normal range, which usually means a short to ground (the sensor reads very hot). The TCM uses a default temperature, so shift quality and lock-up may suffer.
causes: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground.
Sensor shorted internally.
Damaged internal harness in the transmission.
Loose, oily or corroded connector at the transmission.
Rarely, a faulty TCM.
fixes: Check the ATF level and condition.
Compare ATF temperature in live data with engine coolant temperature on a cold engine: both should read close to outside air temperature.
Check the transmission and TCM connectors for corrosion, oil and a firm fit.
Measure the sensor resistance through the connector and compare with the service manual value for the current temperature.
Repair the wiring or replace the sensor (usually inside the transmission), then clear and re-test.

P1717.meaning: The signal from ATF temperature sensor 2 (a second transmission fluid temperature sensor fitted on some Subaru automatics, such as the 5EAT) is above its normal range, which usually means an open circuit (the sensor reads very cold). The TCM uses a default temperature, so shift quality and lock-up may suffer.
causes: Open circuit in the sensor wiring.
Sensor open internally.
Damaged internal harness in the transmission.
Loose, oily or corroded connector at the transmission.
Rarely, a faulty TCM.
fixes: Check the ATF level and condition.
Compare ATF temperature in live data with engine coolant temperature on a cold engine: both should read close to outside air temperature.
Check the transmission and TCM connectors for corrosion, oil and a firm fit.
Measure the sensor resistance through the connector and compare with the service manual value for the current temperature.
Repair the wiring or replace the sensor (usually inside the transmission), then clear and re-test.

P1718.meaning: The automatic transmission control module (TCM) has a fault on its CAN communication circuit, so it is not exchanging data properly with the ECU and other modules. Expect default shifting or limp mode, and the AT OIL TEMP light may flash at start-up.
causes: Open or shorted CAN wiring to the TCM.
Loose or corroded TCM connector.
Poor power or ground at the TCM.
Low battery voltage.
Faulty TCM.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Check the TCM fuse, power and ground.
Check the TCM connector for corrosion and a firm fit.
Measure CAN resistance at the OBD port with the battery disconnected (about 60 ohms is normal on cars that bring CAN to the port) and check the CAN wires to the TCM for continuity.
Repair the wiring or replace the TCM, then clear and re-test.

P1719.meaning: The automatic transmission control module (TCM) cannot communicate properly with the engine ECU. Without engine data the TCM uses default shift strategies, so expect harsh shifts or limp mode.
causes: Open or shorted communication wiring between the TCM and ECU.
Loose or corroded connector at the TCM or ECU.
ECU not powering up properly (check ECU fuses and grounds).
Low battery voltage.
Faulty TCM or ECU.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Confirm the ECU responds to the app; if it does not, check the ECU fuses, power and grounds first.
Check the TCM and ECU connectors for corrosion and a firm fit.
Check the communication wiring between the TCM and ECU for continuity and shorts.
Repair the wiring or replace the faulty module, then clear and re-test.

P1720.meaning: The Driver Controlled Centre Differential (DCCD) controller on the STI is not receiving the expected data over the CAN bus. The DCCD may fall back to a default lock setting and its indicator may flash; the car is drivable but may handle differently.
causes: Open or shorted CAN wiring to the DCCD controller.
Loose or corroded connector at the DCCD controller.
Fault in another module on the bus (ECU, ABS/VDC).
Low battery voltage.
Faulty DCCD controller.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running.
Read codes in the ECU and ABS/VDC modules to see whether a module is missing from the bus.
Check the DCCD controller connector for corrosion and a firm fit.
Measure CAN resistance at the OBD port with the battery disconnected (about 60 ohms is normal on cars that bring CAN to the port) and check the CAN wires to the DCCD controller.
Repair the wiring or replace the faulty module, then clear and re-test.

P1721.meaning: The Driver Controlled Centre Differential (DCCD) controller on the STI is not receiving a valid engine speed signal, which it uses to decide how much to lock the centre differential. It may fall back to a default setting and its indicator may flash.
causes: Open or shorted engine speed signal wire from the ECU to the DCCD controller.
Missing engine speed message on the CAN bus on models that share it there.
Engine-side crank signal fault (check ECU codes).
Loose or corroded connector at the DCCD controller or ECU.
Faulty DCCD controller.
fixes: Check that the tachometer works normally; on many models it uses the same engine speed source.
Read ECU codes for crank sensor or communication faults.
Check the DCCD controller and ECU connectors.
Check the engine speed signal wire or CAN wiring to the DCCD controller for continuity and shorts.
Repair the wiring or replace the DCCD controller, then clear and re-test.

P1723.meaning: The signal from ATF temperature sensor 2 (a second transmission fluid temperature sensor fitted on some Subaru automatics, such as the 5EAT) is within range but implausible, for example not rising as the car warms up or not matching the other temperature readings. Shift quality and lock-up may suffer.
causes: ATF temperature sensor 2 drifting or faulty.
Poor connection or high resistance in the sensor circuit.
ATF level very low or fluid badly degraded.
Transmission cooling problem.
Rarely, a faulty TCM.
fixes: Check the ATF level and condition.
Watch ATF temperature in live data from a cold start: it should start near outside air temperature and rise steadily with driving.
Check the transmission and TCM connectors for corrosion, oil and a firm fit.
Measure the sensor resistance at a known temperature and compare with the service manual value.
Replace the sensor if faulty, then clear and re-test.

P1759.meaning: A fault was detected in the lateral G (side acceleration) sensor circuit. This sensor is used by the VDC stability control and, on some models, by the ABS and DCCD, so those systems may be switched off and their warning lights may come on. Normal braking still works.
causes: Loose or corroded sensor connector (the sensor usually sits under the centre console, where spilled drinks can reach it).
Damaged wiring between the sensor and the VDC/ABS module.
Faulty lateral G sensor.
Sensor mounting loose.
Faulty VDC/ABS module.
fixes: Read the VDC/ABS module codes to confirm which sensor signal is at fault.
Check the sensor connector and the carpet around it for moisture or corrosion.
Check that the sensor is mounted firmly and level.
Check the sensor wiring for continuity and shorts.
After replacing or refitting the sensor, perform the zero-point calibration with a Subaru dealer tool or capable scan tool, with the car on level ground.

P1760.meaning: The lateral acceleration (side G) sensor is giving readings that do not match what the car is doing, for example showing side force while driving straight. VDC and, on some models, ABS or DCCD functions may be switched off with warning lights on. Normal braking still works.
causes: Sensor mounting loose or not level.
Sensor out of calibration after replacement or a battery disconnection.
Faulty lateral acceleration sensor.
Poor connection in the sensor circuit.
Steering angle or wheel speed sensor problem making the comparison fail.
fixes: Read the VDC/ABS module codes and look for related steering angle or wheel speed codes.
Check that the sensor is mounted firmly, level and not disturbed.
Check the sensor connector for corrosion or moisture.
After replacing or refitting the sensor, perform the zero-point calibration with a Subaru dealer tool or capable scan tool, with the car on level ground.
Replace the sensor if it still reads wrong after calibration, then clear and re-test with a drive.

P1761.meaning: The signal from the lateral acceleration (side G) sensor is below its normal range, usually a wiring or sensor fault. VDC and, on some models, ABS or DCCD functions may be switched off with warning lights on. Normal braking still works.
causes: Signal wire open or shorted to ground.
Loss of the sensor's supply voltage.
Loose or corroded sensor connector (spilled drinks in the centre console area are a common cause).
Faulty lateral acceleration sensor.
Rarely, a faulty VDC/ABS module.
fixes: Check the sensor connector and surrounding carpet for moisture or corrosion.
With the ignition on, check the sensor's supply voltage and ground and compare with the service manual values.
Check the signal wire for continuity and for any short to ground.
Replace the sensor if the wiring checks good.
After replacing or refitting the sensor, perform the zero-point calibration with a Subaru dealer tool or capable scan tool, with the car on level ground.

P1762.meaning: The signal from the lateral acceleration (side G) sensor is above its normal range, usually a wiring or sensor fault. VDC and, on some models, ABS or DCCD functions may be switched off with warning lights on. Normal braking still works.
causes: Signal wire shorted to a voltage source.
Open sensor ground.
Loose or corroded sensor connector (spilled drinks in the centre console area are a common cause).
Faulty lateral acceleration sensor.
Rarely, a faulty VDC/ABS module.
fixes: Check the sensor connector and surrounding carpet for moisture or corrosion.
With the ignition on, check the sensor's supply voltage and ground and compare with the service manual values.
Check the signal wire for continuity and for any short to a voltage source.
Replace the sensor if the wiring checks good.
After replacing or refitting the sensor, perform the zero-point calibration with a Subaru dealer tool or capable scan tool, with the car on level ground.

P1764.meaning: A fault was detected in the yaw rate sensor circuit. The yaw rate sensor measures how fast the car rotates and is central to the VDC stability control, so VDC will be switched off with its warning light on. Normal braking still works.
causes: Loose or corroded sensor connector (the sensor usually sits under the centre console).
Damaged wiring between the sensor and the VDC module.
Faulty yaw rate sensor (often combined with the lateral G sensor in one unit).
Sensor mounting loose.
Faulty VDC module.
fixes: Read the VDC module codes to confirm the fault.
Check the sensor connector and surrounding carpet for moisture or corrosion.
Check that the sensor is mounted firmly and level.
Check the sensor wiring for continuity and shorts.
After replacing or refitting the sensor, perform the zero-point calibration with a Subaru dealer tool or capable scan tool, with the car on level ground.

P1765.meaning: A fault was detected in the reference (supply) circuit shared by the yaw rate and lateral G sensors. Both signals become unreliable, so VDC and, on some models, ABS or DCCD functions will be switched off with warning lights on. Normal braking still works.
causes: Reference or supply wire to the sensor unit open or shorted.
Loose or corroded sensor connector.
Faulty combined yaw rate and lateral G sensor.
Poor ground at the sensor.
Faulty VDC module supplying the reference.
fixes: Read the VDC module codes; several sensor codes at once point to the shared supply.
Check the sensor connector and surrounding carpet for moisture or corrosion.
With the ignition on, check the sensor's supply and reference voltages and ground and compare with the service manual values.
Check the reference and ground wires for continuity and shorts.
Replace the sensor or repair the wiring, then perform the zero-point calibration with a Subaru dealer tool or capable scan tool on level ground.

P1767.meaning: The DCCD control unit (the driver controlled center differential on the STI) is not getting a valid signal from the steering angle sensor, which it uses to ease center diff lock in tight turns. The DCCD falls back to a default setting and its indicator may flash; the car is safe to drive gently, but AWD behavior will not be optimal.
causes: The steering angle sensor needs a zero-point calibration, for example after a wheel alignment, steering work or a battery disconnect.
Loose or damaged connector at the steering angle sensor at the base of the steering column.
Faulty steering angle sensor.
CAN communication problem between the steering angle sensor, the VDC unit and the DCCD unit.
Low battery voltage during cranking causing a false fault.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units. Also look for VDC or CAN (U-code) faults stored at the same time.
Make sure the steering wheel is straight when the wheels point straight ahead; an off-center wheel after an alignment can upset the sensor.
Inspect the steering angle sensor connector at the base of the steering column for a loose fit, damage or corrosion.
Have the steering angle sensor zero point calibrated with a scan tool that supports Subaru VDC (Subaru Select Monitor or equivalent), then clear and re-test.
If the fault returns after calibration and the wiring is good, replace the steering angle sensor.

P1769.meaning: The DCCD system sees an implausible signal from the yaw rate and lateral G sensor, the combined sensor that measures how fast the car rotates and how hard it corners. The center differential control falls back to a default mode; the car can be driven, but stability and AWD control may be reduced.
causes: Loose or tilted sensor mounting, for example after interior work (the sensor sits near the middle of the car, usually under the center console).
Damaged or corroded connector or wiring to the sensor, often after water got into the cabin.
The sensor needs a zero-point calibration after replacement or a battery disconnect.
Faulty yaw rate and lateral G sensor.
CAN communication fault between the sensor, the VDC unit and the DCCD unit.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units. Also look for VDC, ABS or CAN codes and fix those first.
Check that the sensor is bolted down firmly and sits level; a loose or tilted sensor gives false readings.
Inspect the connector and wiring to the sensor for corrosion, especially if the carpet has ever been wet.
Have the sensor calibrated with a scan tool that supports Subaru VDC, then clear and re-test.
Replace the sensor if the fault persists with good wiring and power.

P1798.meaning: The transmission control detected a fault in the 1st-gear engine braking function, where a clutch or brake inside the automatic gearbox holds 1st gear so the engine slows the car on overrun (manual mode 1st or the 1 range). The gearbox may go into a fail-safe mode; drive gently and have it checked soon.
causes: Low, old or wrong ATF.
Sticking valve or solenoid in the valve body that controls 1st-gear engine braking.
Wiring or connector fault in the transmission solenoid harness.
Worn clutch or brake (such as the low and reverse brake) inside the transmission.
Transmission control unit fault (rare).
fixes: Check the ATF level with the engine warm and idling, using the dipstick marks. Dark, burnt-smelling fluid or debris on the dipstick points to internal wear.
Read all transmission codes, and note whether the AT OIL TEMP light flashes after start-up (Subaru's way of signaling a stored transmission fault).
Inspect the transmission harness connectors for oil intrusion, corrosion and bent or loose pins.
If the fluid is old, have it changed (a drain and fill, possibly repeated), then clear and re-test with some gentle engine braking in manual 1st.
If the code returns, have the valve body, solenoids and clutches checked by a transmission specialist.

P1799.meaning: The transmission control detected an interlock condition: two clutches or brakes inside the automatic gearbox appear to be applied at the same time, which can make the transmission bind. Expect a fail-safe mode (often held in one gear); avoid hard driving and have it checked soon.
causes: Sticking shift or pressure control solenoid or valve in the valve body.
Low, old or contaminated ATF making valves hang up.
Faulty transmission fluid pressure switch giving a false reading (see P1840 to P1844).
Wiring or connector fault in the transmission harness.
Internal clutch or brake damage.
fixes: Check the ATF level with the engine warm and idling, using the dipstick marks. Dark, burnt-smelling fluid or debris on the dipstick points to internal wear.
Read all transmission codes; pressure switch or solenoid codes stored alongside this one usually point to the root cause.
Inspect the transmission harness connectors for oil intrusion, corrosion and bent or loose pins.
Change the ATF if it is old, then clear and re-test with gentle driving through all gears.
If the code returns, have the valve body, solenoids and pressure switches inspected by a transmission specialist.

P1817.meaning: The transmission control sees an implausible signal from the manual mode (SportShift) switch in the gear selector, which tells the gearbox the lever is in the manual gate. Manual shifting may not work or may act strangely; normal driving in D usually still works.
causes: Worn or dirty manual mode switch inside the selector lever assembly.
Spilled drink or debris in the shifter.
Damaged wiring or loose connector under the center console.
Selector lever or cable out of adjustment.
Transmission control unit fault (rare).
fixes: Move the lever into and out of the manual gate and watch the dash: the manual mode indicator should switch on and off every time.
Remove the shifter trim and look for spilled liquid, debris or a loose connector.
Check the selector cable adjustment so the lever sits correctly in each position.
Check the switch with a multimeter: continuity should switch cleanly in and out of the manual gate with no flicker when you wiggle the lever.
Replace the switch or selector assembly if it is faulty, then clear and re-test.

P1840.meaning: The transmission control sees a wrong or implausible signal from fluid pressure switch A in the automatic transmission's valve body. These switches confirm which clutch or brake is applied; the gearbox may go into fail-safe (harsh shifts or held in one gear), so drive gently until it is fixed.
causes: Low, old or contaminated ATF, so pressure does not build as expected.
Oil-soaked, corroded or loose connector at the transmission, or a chafed harness.
Faulty pressure switch A in the valve body.
Sticking valve or solenoid, so the related clutch does not get pressure.
Transmission control unit fault (rare).
fixes: Check the ATF level with the engine warm and idling, using the dipstick marks. Dark, burnt-smelling fluid or debris on the dipstick points to internal wear.
Read all transmission codes; a solenoid code stored at the same time may be the real cause.
Inspect the transmission harness connectors for oil intrusion, corrosion and bent or loose pins.
Check the pressure switch A circuit for continuity and shorts to ground; compare with the service manual values.
Replacing the switch means removing the oil pan and working on the valve body, usually a job for a transmission specialist.

P1870.meaning: The ECU or transmission control is getting a wrong or missing wheel speed signal from the front left ABS sensor (usually passed on from the ABS/VDC unit). Expect the ABS and VDC warning lights, and shift quality or AWD control may be affected; normal braking still works, but ABS and stability control may be switched off.
causes: Dirt, rust or metal debris on the front left wheel speed sensor tip or tone ring.
Damaged sensor wire, often chafed or pulled near the suspension.
Cracked, rusted or damaged tone ring (the toothed sensor ring on the front hub).
Worn wheel bearing letting the gap between sensor and ring change.
Faulty wheel speed sensor.
ABS/VDC unit fault (rare).
fixes: Check the ABS and VDC warning lights and read ABS codes if your tool supports it; they confirm which wheel is affected.
Inspect the front left sensor wire from the wheel to the body connector for chafing, breaks or loose clips.
Remove the sensor, clean its tip and mounting bore, and check the tone ring for rust, cracks or missing teeth.
Check the wheel bearing for play by rocking the wheel at the top and bottom.
Compare the sensor's resistance or signal with the other wheels and the service manual value; replace it if it is out of spec, then clear and re-test with a drive above about 20 km/h.

P1875.meaning: The control unit found an electrical fault in the circuit that controls the center differential: the DCCD electromagnetic clutch on STIs, or the transfer clutch solenoid on AWD automatics. The AWD torque split falls back to a default setting; the car can be driven, but avoid tight turns on dry pavement if you feel binding.
causes: Damaged wiring or corroded connector at the transmission, which sits low and gets road spray.
Blown fuse for the DCCD or AWD control circuit.
Open or shorted coil in the DCCD electromagnetic clutch or transfer clutch solenoid.
DCCD or transmission control unit fault.
fixes: Check the related fuse, and note whether the DCCD or AWD indicator flashes on the dash.
Inspect the connector and harness at the transmission for corrosion, damage or oil contamination.
Measure the coil or solenoid resistance at the connector and compare with the service manual value; also check for shorts to ground.
Repair any wiring faults, then clear and re-test.
If the coil is open or shorted, the center differential clutch or transfer solenoid needs replacing, usually a workshop job.

P2004.meaning: The ECU commanded the right-hand tumble generator valve (TGV, runner 1, bank 1 side, cylinders 1 and 3) to close, but its position sensor says it stayed open. TGVs mainly help cold-start idle and emissions, so the car is safe to drive, but cold idle may be rough and emissions higher.
causes: Carbon and oily sludge (from PCV blow-by) binding the right-hand TGV shaft or butterflies.
Failed TGV motor on the right-hand side of the intake manifold.
Loose, corroded or unplugged TGV connector under the intake manifold.
TGV position sensor misreading, so the ECU thinks the valve did not close.
TGVs deleted or disconnected without the ECU tune disabling TGV monitoring.
fixes: Check whether the TGVs have been removed or unplugged (a common modification on EJ turbos); if so, the ECU tune must have TGV monitoring disabled or these codes will keep coming back.
Inspect the right-hand TGV motor and position sensor connectors for corrosion and broken locking tabs.

From a cold start, watch the right-hand TGV position voltage in live data if your ECU supports it: it should change when the ECU switches the TGVs. You can also watch or listen to the motor cycle at key on.
Remove the TGV assembly and clean carbon and oil from the shaft and butterflies until it moves freely by hand.
Replace the TGV motor or TGV assembly if it still does not move as commanded, then clear and re-test from a cold start.

P2005.meaning: The ECU commanded the left-hand tumble generator valve (TGV, runner 2, bank 2 side, cylinders 2 and 4) to close, but its position sensor says it stayed open. TGVs mainly help cold-start idle and emissions, so the car is safe to drive, but cold idle may be rough and emissions higher.
causes: Carbon and oily sludge (from PCV blow-by) binding the left-hand TGV shaft or butterflies.

P2006.meaning: The ECU commanded the right-hand tumble generator valve (TGV, runner 1, bank 1 side, cylinders 1 and 3) to open, but its position sensor says it stayed closed. A TGV stuck closed restricts airflow to those cylinders, so power may drop at higher load; it is drivable, but get it fixed.
causes: Carbon and oily sludge (from PCV blow-by) binding the right-hand TGV shaft or butterflies.
Failed TGV motor on the right-hand side of the intake manifold.
Loose, corroded or unplugged TGV connector under the intake manifold.
Seized TGV shaft or broken linkage between motor and shaft.
TGVs deleted or disconnected without the ECU tune disabling TGV monitoring.
fixes: Check whether the TGVs have been removed or unplugged (a common modification on EJ turbos); if so, the ECU tune must have TGV monitoring disabled or these codes will keep coming back.

From a cold start, watch the right-hand TGV position voltage in live data if your ECU supports it: it should change when the ECU switches the TGVs. You can also watch or listen to the motor cycle at key on.

From a cold start, watch the left-hand TGV position voltage in live data if your ECU supports it: it should change when the ECU switches the TGVs. You can also watch or listen to the motor cycle at key on.
Remove the TGV assembly and clean carbon and oil from the shaft and butterflies until it moves freely by hand.
