P2008.meaning: The ECU sees an open circuit in the motor drive circuit for the right-hand tumble generator valve (TGV, runner 1, bank 1 side, cylinders 1 and 3). The TGV cannot be moved, so cold idle and emissions suffer; the car is safe to drive.
causes: Unplugged, loose or corroded connector at the right-hand TGV motor (it sits under the intake manifold and is easy to miss).
Broken wire in the harness near the intake manifold.
TGV motor with an open winding.
TGVs removed or unplugged without the ECU tune disabling TGV monitoring.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check whether the TGVs have been removed or unplugged (a common modification on EJ turbos); if so, the ECU tune must have TGV monitoring disabled or these codes will keep coming back.
Inspect the right-hand TGV motor connector for a loose fit, corrosion or a broken lock tab.
Measure the TGV motor resistance at its connector and compare with the service manual value; OL on the meter means an open motor.
Check continuity of each motor wire between the TGV connector and the ECU, wiggling the harness while you measure.
Replace the TGV motor or assembly if it is open, then clear and re-test.

P2009.meaning: The ECU sees a low voltage (usually a short to ground) in the motor drive circuit for the right-hand tumble generator valve (TGV, runner 1, bank 1 side, cylinders 1 and 3). The ECU stops driving the TGV, so cold idle and emissions suffer; the car is safe to drive.
causes: Chafed wire shorting to ground on the intake manifold or engine.
Water or corrosion in the right-hand TGV motor connector.
TGV motor with an internal short.
TGVs removed or unplugged without the ECU tune disabling TGV monitoring.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check whether the TGVs have been removed or unplugged (a common modification on EJ turbos); if so, the ECU tune must have TGV monitoring disabled or these codes will keep coming back.
Inspect the harness to the right-hand TGV motor for chafing or melted insulation where it runs under the manifold.
Unplug the TGV motor and check each wire for a short to ground (continuity to the engine block).
Measure the TGV motor resistance and compare with the service manual value; far below spec means an internal short.
Repair the wiring or replace the TGV motor, then clear and re-test.

P2010.meaning: The ECU sees a higher voltage than expected in the control circuit of the swirl control valve (on the EE20 diesel, the valve that varies intake swirl; on petrol engines with TGVs, the right-hand runner 1 TGV motor circuit), usually a short to power or an actuator fault. The valve may not move, which affects emissions and low-speed running, but the car is normally safe to drive.
causes: Control wire shorted to battery voltage or another powered wire.
Corroded or water-damaged connector at the swirl control valve actuator.
Faulty actuator with an internal short.
Valve blanked off or removed (swirl flap or TGV delete) without the ECU tune disabling monitoring.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check whether the swirl valves or TGVs have been removed or blanked; if so, the tune must have the monitoring disabled.
Inspect the actuator connector for corrosion, water and bent pins.
Check the harness for chafing against other powered wires, especially where it runs over the engine.
Unplug the actuator and measure its resistance; compare with the service manual value. Also check the control wire for battery voltage with the actuator unplugged (there should be none).
Repair the wiring or replace the actuator, then clear and re-test.

causes: Chafed wire shorting to ground on the intake manifold or engine.
Water or corrosion in the left-hand TGV motor connector.
TGV motor with an internal short.
TGVs removed or unplugged without the ECU tune disabling TGV monitoring.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Check whether the TGVs have been removed or unplugged (a common modification on EJ turbos); if so, the ECU tune must have TGV monitoring disabled or these codes will keep coming back.

P2016.meaning: The position sensor for the right-hand tumble generator valve (TGV, runner 1, bank 1 side, cylinders 1 and 3) reads below its normal voltage range, usually a wiring or sensor fault. The ECU cannot confirm TGV position; the car is safe to drive, but cold idle and emissions may suffer.
causes: Open 5 V reference wire or signal wire to the right-hand TGV position sensor.
Signal wire shorted to ground.
Corroded or loose connector at the position sensor under the intake manifold.
Faulty TGV position sensor.
TGVs removed or unplugged without the ECU tune disabling TGV monitoring.
fixes: Check whether the TGVs have been removed or unplugged (a common modification on EJ turbos); if so, the ECU tune must have TGV monitoring disabled or these codes will keep coming back.
Inspect the right-hand TGV position sensor connector and wiring for corrosion, broken locks or chafing.
Watch the right-hand TGV position voltage in live data if available: it should stay inside its normal range and change smoothly when the TGV moves. Wiggle the harness and look for dropouts or spikes.
With the key on and the sensor unplugged, check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground; no reference voltage points to wiring or the ECU.
Replace the position sensor (or TGV assembly, depending on the part supply) if wiring checks out, then clear and re-test.

P2017.meaning: The position sensor for the right-hand tumble generator valve (TGV, runner 1, bank 1 side, cylinders 1 and 3) reads above its normal voltage range, usually a wiring or sensor fault. The ECU cannot confirm TGV position; the car is safe to drive, but cold idle and emissions may suffer.
causes: Open ground wire to the right-hand TGV position sensor.
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage.
Corroded or loose connector at the position sensor under the intake manifold.
Faulty TGV position sensor.
TGVs removed or unplugged without the ECU tune disabling TGV monitoring.
fixes: Check whether the TGVs have been removed or unplugged (a common modification on EJ turbos); if so, the ECU tune must have TGV monitoring disabled or these codes will keep coming back.
Inspect the right-hand TGV position sensor connector and wiring for corrosion, broken locks or chafing.
Watch the right-hand TGV position voltage in live data if available: it should stay inside its normal range and change smoothly when the TGV moves. Wiggle the harness and look for dropouts or spikes.
With the key on and the sensor unplugged, check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground (near 0 ohms to the block); an open ground is the classic cause of a high reading.
Replace the position sensor (or TGV assembly, depending on the part supply) if wiring checks out, then clear and re-test.

P2021.meaning: The position sensor for the left-hand tumble generator valve (TGV, runner 2, bank 2 side, cylinders 2 and 4) reads below its normal voltage range, usually a wiring or sensor fault. The ECU cannot confirm TGV position; the car is safe to drive, but cold idle and emissions may suffer.
causes: Open 5 V reference wire or signal wire to the left-hand TGV position sensor.
Signal wire shorted to ground.
Corroded or loose connector at the position sensor under the intake manifold.
Faulty TGV position sensor.
TGVs removed or unplugged without the ECU tune disabling TGV monitoring.
fixes: Check whether the TGVs have been removed or unplugged (a common modification on EJ turbos); if so, the ECU tune must have TGV monitoring disabled or these codes will keep coming back.
Inspect the left-hand TGV position sensor connector and wiring for corrosion, broken locks or chafing.
Watch the left-hand TGV position voltage in live data if available: it should stay inside its normal range and change smoothly when the TGV moves. Wiggle the harness and look for dropouts or spikes.
With the key on and the sensor unplugged, check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground; no reference voltage points to wiring or the ECU.
Replace the position sensor (or TGV assembly, depending on the part supply) if wiring checks out, then clear and re-test.

P2022.meaning: The position sensor for the left-hand tumble generator valve (TGV, runner 2, bank 2 side, cylinders 2 and 4) reads above its normal voltage range, usually a wiring or sensor fault. The ECU cannot confirm TGV position; the car is safe to drive, but cold idle and emissions may suffer.
causes: Open ground wire to the left-hand TGV position sensor.
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage.
Corroded or loose connector at the position sensor under the intake manifold.
Faulty TGV position sensor.
TGVs removed or unplugged without the ECU tune disabling TGV monitoring.
fixes: Check whether the TGVs have been removed or unplugged (a common modification on EJ turbos); if so, the ECU tune must have TGV monitoring disabled or these codes will keep coming back.
Inspect the left-hand TGV position sensor connector and wiring for corrosion, broken locks or chafing.
Watch the left-hand TGV position voltage in live data if available: it should stay inside its normal range and change smoothly when the TGV moves. Wiggle the harness and look for dropouts or spikes.
With the key on and the sensor unplugged, check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground (near 0 ohms to the block); an open ground is the classic cause of a high reading.
Replace the position sensor (or TGV assembly, depending on the part supply) if wiring checks out, then clear and re-test.

P2032.meaning: The signal from exhaust gas temperature sensor 2 is below its normal range. On the EE20 diesel the ECU uses this sensor to monitor the catalytic converter and DPF during regeneration, so regeneration may be blocked and the DPF can clog if this is ignored; the car is drivable, but fix it soon.
causes: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground, often where the insulation melted against the hot exhaust.
Water or corrosion in the sensor connector.
Faulty EGT sensor with an internal short.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the sensor wiring along the exhaust for melted, chafed or pinched insulation and check the clips that keep it away from hot parts.
Unplug the connector and look for water, green corrosion or pushed-back pins.
After the car has sat overnight, compare EGT readings in live data: all exhaust temperatures should read close to air temperature.
Measure the sensor resistance at room temperature and compare with the service manual value; check the signal wire for a short to ground.
Replace the sensor (loosen it with penetrating oil, ideally with the exhaust warm), then clear and re-test and let a DPF regeneration complete if the soot load is high.

P2033.meaning: The signal from exhaust gas temperature sensor 2 is above its normal range. On the EE20 diesel the ECU uses this sensor to monitor the catalytic converter and DPF during regeneration, so regeneration may be blocked and the DPF can clog if this is ignored; the car is drivable, but fix it soon.
causes: EGT sensor failed open, common from repeated heat cycling.
Unplugged connector or broken wire near the hot exhaust.
Corroded or loose connector pins.
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the sensor wiring along the exhaust for breaks, melted insulation and loose clips.
Unplug the connector and look for corrosion or pushed-back pins; make sure it clicks fully home.
After the car has sat overnight, compare EGT readings in live data: all exhaust temperatures should read close to air temperature.
Measure the sensor resistance at room temperature and compare with the service manual value; an open reading (OL) means the sensor is dead.
Replace the sensor (loosen it with penetrating oil, ideally with the exhaust warm), then clear and re-test and let a DPF regeneration complete if the soot load is high.

P2088.meaning: The ECU sees an open circuit in the control circuit of the intake camshaft oil control valve (OCV) for AVCS on bank 1 (right side, cylinders 1 and 3). Cam timing on that side stays at its default position, so expect less power and possibly a rough idle; it is safe to drive short-term, but get it repaired.
causes: Unplugged, loose or corroded connector at the intake OCV on the right cylinder head.
Broken wire in the harness to the OCV, often where it flexes or runs near the timing belt cover.
OCV coil failed open.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the OCV connector on the right side of the engine (front of the cylinder head) for a loose fit, broken lock tab or corrosion.
Measure the OCV coil resistance at the valve and compare with the service manual value; OL on the meter means the valve has failed open.
Check continuity of both wires between the OCV connector and the ECU, wiggling the harness while you measure.
If the other bank uses the same OCV part number, swap the two valves: if the code moves to the other bank, the valve is faulty.
Replace the OCV (with new O-rings), then clear and re-test; in live data the AVCS cam advance should follow its target.

P2089.meaning: The ECU sees a short circuit in the control circuit of the intake camshaft oil control valve (OCV) for AVCS on bank 1 (right side, cylinders 1 and 3) and stops driving it to protect itself. Cam timing on that side stays at its default position, so expect less power and possibly a rough idle; it is safe to drive short-term, but get it repaired.
causes: OCV wire chafed through and shorting to ground or to a powered wire.
Water or corrosion in the intake OCV connector on the right cylinder head.
OCV coil shorted internally.
ECU driver fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the harness to the intake OCV on the right side for chafing against brackets, the timing cover or the engine.
Unplug the OCV and look for water or green corrosion in the connector.
Measure the OCV coil resistance and compare with the service manual value; a reading far below spec means an internal short.
With the OCV and ECU unplugged, check each wire for a short to ground and to battery voltage.
If the other bank uses the same OCV part number, swap the valves to confirm, then replace the faulty OCV or repair the wiring and clear and re-test.

Cam timing on that side stays at its default position, so expect less power and possibly a rough idle; it is safe to drive short-term, but get it repaired.

Cam timing on that side stays at its default position, so expect less power and possibly a rough idle; it is safe to drive short-term, but get it repaired.

P2096.meaning: The rear oxygen sensor (sensor 2, after the catalytic converter) keeps reading lean on bank 1 (right side, cylinders 1 and 3, plus 5 on six-cylinders; on four-cylinders with one rear sensor this covers the whole engine), and the ECU's fine-tuning correction based on it has hit its limit. Safe to drive short-term, but it often points to an exhaust leak or an ageing front A/F sensor.
causes: Exhaust leak before or near the rear O2 sensor (cracked flex pipe, leaking downpipe or catalytic converter gasket) drawing in outside air.
Ageing or biased front A/F sensor, so the engine actually runs leaner than the ECU thinks.
Real lean running from an intake leak, a cracked PCV or breather hose, or low fuel pressure.
Lazy or contaminated rear O2 sensor.
Aftermarket downpipe, test pipe or tune that changes how the rear sensor behaves.
fixes: In live data, watch the rear O2 sensor voltage and fuel trims at warm idle and steady cruise. A steady rear reading of roughly 0.5 to 0.8 V is typical with a healthy warm catalytic converter; a reading stuck low (around 0.1 to 0.2 V) means lean or an exhaust leak.
With the engine cold, check for exhaust leaks at the downpipe joints, flex section and converter flanges: look for soot marks and listen for ticking at start-up.
Check the intake tract, PCV and breather hoses for cracks, and look at long-term fuel trims: large positive trims confirm a real lean condition.
Compare the front A/F sensor with the fuel trims: a slow or biased front sensor should be replaced.
Replace the rear O2 sensor if it responds slowly or stays flat, then clear and re-test with a mix of idle and cruise.

P2097.meaning: The rear oxygen sensor (sensor 2, after the catalytic converter) keeps reading rich on bank 1 (right side, cylinders 1 and 3, plus 5 on six-cylinders; on four-cylinders with one rear sensor this covers the whole engine), and the ECU's fine-tuning correction based on it has hit its limit. Safe to drive short-term, but it often points to an exhaust leak or an ageing front A/F sensor.
causes: Ageing or biased front A/F sensor, so the engine actually runs richer than the ECU thinks.
Leaking fuel injector or excessive fuel pressure.
Purge valve stuck open, or fuel-diluted oil feeding extra vapor through the PCV system.
Degraded or contaminated catalytic converter (oil or coolant burning).
Faulty rear O2 sensor reading high.
Aftermarket tune or exhaust changes.
fixes: In live data, watch the rear O2 sensor voltage and fuel trims at warm idle and steady cruise. A reading stuck high (around 0.9 V) with negative fuel trims confirms the engine runs rich.
Check the purge solenoid: it should hold closed when not commanded; pinch the purge hose briefly and see if the trims and rear sensor change.
Check the oil for a fuel smell and look for signs of oil or coolant consumption that can poison the catalytic converter.
Compare the front A/F sensor with the fuel trims: a slow or biased front sensor should be replaced.
Check fuel pressure and injectors for leaks, and replace the rear O2 sensor if it is lazy, then clear and re-test.

P2098.meaning: The rear oxygen sensor (sensor 2, after the catalytic converter) keeps reading lean on bank 2 (left side, cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders; only engines that monitor each exhaust side separately set this code), and the ECU's fine-tuning correction based on it has hit its limit. Safe to drive short-term, but it often points to an exhaust leak or an ageing front A/F sensor.
causes: Exhaust leak before or near the rear O2 sensor (cracked flex pipe, leaking downpipe or catalytic converter gasket) drawing in outside air.
Ageing or biased front A/F sensor, so the engine actually runs leaner than the ECU thinks.
Real lean running from an intake leak, a cracked PCV or breather hose, or low fuel pressure.
Lazy or contaminated rear O2 sensor.
Aftermarket downpipe, test pipe or tune that changes how the rear sensor behaves.
fixes: In live data, watch the rear O2 sensor voltage and fuel trims at warm idle and steady cruise. A steady rear reading of roughly 0.5 to 0.8 V is typical with a healthy warm catalytic converter; a reading stuck low (around 0.1 to 0.2 V) means lean or an exhaust leak.
With the engine cold, check for exhaust leaks at the downpipe joints, flex section and converter flanges: look for soot marks and listen for ticking at start-up.
Check the intake tract, PCV and breather hoses for cracks, and look at long-term fuel trims: large positive trims confirm a real lean condition.
Compare the front A/F sensor with the fuel trims: a slow or biased front sensor should be replaced.
Replace the rear O2 sensor if it responds slowly or stays flat, then clear and re-test with a mix of idle and cruise.

P2099.meaning: The rear oxygen sensor (sensor 2, after the catalytic converter) keeps reading rich on bank 2 (left side, cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders; only engines that monitor each exhaust side separately set this code), and the ECU's fine-tuning correction based on it has hit its limit. Safe to drive short-term, but it often points to an exhaust leak or an ageing front A/F sensor.
causes: Ageing or biased front A/F sensor, so the engine actually runs richer than the ECU thinks.
Leaking fuel injector or excessive fuel pressure.
Purge valve stuck open, or fuel-diluted oil feeding extra vapor through the PCV system.
Degraded or contaminated catalytic converter (oil or coolant burning).
Faulty rear O2 sensor reading high.
Aftermarket tune or exhaust changes.
fixes: In live data, watch the rear O2 sensor voltage and fuel trims at warm idle and steady cruise. A reading stuck high (around 0.9 V) with negative fuel trims confirms the engine runs rich.
Check the purge solenoid: it should hold closed when not commanded; pinch the purge hose briefly and see if the trims and rear sensor change.
Check the oil for a fuel smell and look for signs of oil or coolant consumption that can poison the catalytic converter.
Compare the front A/F sensor with the fuel trims: a slow or biased front sensor should be replaced.
