P2100.meaning: The ECU found an open circuit in the electronic throttle motor circuit, so it cannot move the throttle plate. The ECU switches to limp mode with the throttle held slightly open, so power is very limited; drive only to get the car home or to a workshop.
causes: Loose, corroded or damaged connector at the throttle body.
Broken wire between the ECU and the throttle motor.
Faulty electronic throttle control relay or blown fuse, so the motor circuit has no power.
Throttle motor winding open.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units.
Check the electronic throttle control relay and its fuse in the engine bay fuse box; swap the relay with an identical one to test.
Inspect the throttle body connector for corrosion, bent pins or a broken lock, and wiggle the harness with the engine idling to see if the fault appears.
Measure the throttle motor resistance at the throttle body and compare with the service manual value; check both motor wires for continuity to the ECU.

Replace the throttle body if the motor is open. After cleaning or replacing the throttle body, let the ECU relearn it: switch the ignition on for about 10 seconds without starting, then start and idle with all loads off for a few minutes (follow the service manual if it gives a procedure).

P2101.meaning: The electronic throttle is not reaching the position the ECU commands, or not quickly enough, even though the circuit is not fully open or shorted. The ECU switches to limp mode with the throttle held slightly open, so power is very limited; drive only to get the car home or to a workshop.
causes: Carbon buildup making the throttle plate stick or drag.
Ice in the throttle body in freezing, humid weather.
Weak throttle motor or worn gears inside the throttle body.
Low battery voltage or poor engine grounds.
Faulty electronic throttle control relay or poor connection at the throttle body connector.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units. Also check the battery terminals and engine-to-body ground strap.
With the ignition off, remove the intake duct and clean carbon from the throttle bore and plate with throttle body cleaner on a cloth. Do not force the plate or soak the motor housing.
In live data, compare target throttle opening with actual throttle opening: they should track closely with no lag or jumps.

Check the electronic throttle control relay and its fuse in the engine bay fuse box; swap the relay with an identical one to test. Inspect the throttle body connector for corrosion, bent pins or a broken lock, and wiggle the harness with the engine idling to see if the fault appears.

Replace the throttle body if it still lags or sticks. After cleaning or replacing the throttle body, let the ECU relearn it: switch the ignition on for about 10 seconds without starting, then start and idle with all loads off for a few minutes (follow the service manual if it gives a procedure).

P2102.meaning: The ECU sees a low voltage in the throttle motor circuit, usually no power supply or a short to ground. The ECU switches to limp mode with the throttle held slightly open, so power is very limited; drive only to get the car home or to a workshop.
causes: Faulty electronic throttle control relay or blown fuse feeding the motor circuit.
Throttle motor wire chafed and shorting to ground.
Corroded or loose throttle body connector.
Low battery voltage or poor grounds.
Throttle motor internal fault, or ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units.
Check the electronic throttle control relay and its fuse in the engine bay fuse box; swap the relay with an identical one to test.
Inspect the throttle body connector for corrosion, bent pins or a broken lock, and wiggle the harness with the engine idling to see if the fault appears.
Unplug the throttle body and ECU and check both motor wires for a short to ground; measure the motor resistance and compare with the service manual value.

Repair the wiring or replace the throttle body. After cleaning or replacing the throttle body, let the ECU relearn it: switch the ignition on for about 10 seconds without starting, then start and idle with all loads off for a few minutes (follow the service manual if it gives a procedure).

P2103.meaning: The ECU sees a high voltage or excessive current in the throttle motor circuit, usually a short to power or a shorted or binding motor. The ECU switches to limp mode with the throttle held slightly open, so power is very limited; drive only to get the car home or to a workshop.
causes: Throttle motor wire shorted to battery voltage or another powered wire.
Throttle motor with an internal short.
Throttle plate binding from carbon or ice, making the motor draw too much current.
Electronic throttle control relay stuck on.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units.
With the ignition off, remove the intake duct and clean carbon from the throttle bore and plate with throttle body cleaner on a cloth. Do not force the plate or soak the motor housing.
Inspect the throttle body connector for corrosion, bent pins or a broken lock, and wiggle the harness with the engine idling to see if the fault appears.

Measure the motor resistance and compare with the service manual value; far below spec means a shorted motor. Check the motor wires for battery voltage with everything unplugged (there should be none).

Replace the throttle body or repair the wiring. After cleaning or replacing the throttle body, let the ECU relearn it: switch the ignition on for about 10 seconds without starting, then start and idle with all loads off for a few minutes (follow the service manual if it gives a procedure).

P2109.meaning: When the ECU checked the throttle's fully closed position (minimum stop) it found it outside the expected range. The ECU may limit power or set limp mode, and idle can be unstable; drive carefully and have it checked.
causes: Carbon buildup stopping the throttle plate from closing fully.
Throttle body replaced, cleaned or disturbed without the ECU relearning its closed position.
Throttle stop screw tampered with.
Worn throttle position sensor A inside the throttle body.
Ice in the throttle body, or a corroded connector.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units.
With the ignition off, remove the intake duct and clean carbon from the throttle bore and plate with throttle body cleaner on a cloth. Do not force the plate or soak the motor housing.
With the key on and the engine off, read throttle position in live data: at rest it should be the same low value every time, and it should not jump or drift.

After cleaning or replacing the throttle body, let the ECU relearn it: switch the ignition on for about 10 seconds without starting, then start and idle with all loads off for a few minutes (follow the service manual if it gives a procedure).
If the closed position still reads wrong, replace the throttle body (the position sensors are built in), then clear and re-test.

P2111.meaning: The ECU commanded the throttle to close but it stayed more open than commanded. Engine speed may hang high and the ECU usually enters limp mode; take care as the engine may not slow down as expected, and drive only to get it checked.
causes: Heavy carbon buildup or debris jamming the throttle plate.
Ice in the throttle body in freezing weather.
Weak return spring, damaged plate or shaft inside the throttle body.
Worn gears or a failing throttle motor.
Connector or wiring fault giving a false position reading.
fixes: Look inside the throttle body for debris, ice or heavy carbon.
With the ignition off, remove the intake duct and clean carbon from the throttle bore and plate with throttle body cleaner on a cloth. Do not force the plate or soak the motor housing.
In live data, compare target throttle opening with actual throttle opening at idle: actual should drop to the target within a moment.
Inspect the throttle body connector for corrosion, bent pins or a broken lock, and wiggle the harness with the engine idling to see if the fault appears.

Replace the throttle body if it still sticks. After cleaning or replacing the throttle body, let the ECU relearn it: switch the ignition on for about 10 seconds without starting, then start and idle with all loads off for a few minutes (follow the service manual if it gives a procedure).

P2122.meaning: The accelerator pedal position sensor D (the main pedal sensor) signal is below its normal range. The ECU cannot fully trust the pedal, so it limits throttle response (limp mode); drive carefully to a safe place.
causes: Open 5 V reference or signal wire, or signal wire shorted to ground.
Corroded or loose connector at the accelerator pedal.
Faulty pedal position sensor (built into the pedal assembly).
Aftermarket throttle response controller (pedal box) fitted between the pedal and the ECU.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the connector at the top of the accelerator pedal for corrosion, looseness or bent pins, and wiggle the harness while watching live data.
Remove any aftermarket pedal box and reconnect the original plug, then re-test.

In live data, watch the accelerator pedal sensor voltages: released they should sit at a low steady value, and they should rise smoothly to a high value as you press the pedal slowly, with no jumps or dropouts.
With the key on and the pedal connector unplugged, check for about 5 V on the sensor D reference wire and a good ground.
Replace the accelerator pedal assembly (the sensors are built in and not sold separately), then clear and re-test.

P2123.meaning: The accelerator pedal position sensor D (the main pedal sensor) signal is above its normal range. The ECU cannot fully trust the pedal, so it limits throttle response (limp mode); drive carefully to a safe place.
causes: Open ground wire, or signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage.
Corroded or loose connector at the accelerator pedal.
Faulty pedal position sensor (built into the pedal assembly).
Aftermarket throttle response controller (pedal box) fitted between the pedal and the ECU.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the connector at the top of the accelerator pedal for corrosion, looseness or bent pins, and wiggle the harness while watching live data.
Remove any aftermarket pedal box and reconnect the original plug, then re-test.

In live data, watch the accelerator pedal sensor voltages: released they should sit at a low steady value, and they should rise smoothly to a high value as you press the pedal slowly, with no jumps or dropouts.
With the key on and the pedal connector unplugged, check for about 5 V on the sensor D reference wire and a good ground (near 0 ohms to body ground).
Replace the accelerator pedal assembly (the sensors are built in and not sold separately), then clear and re-test.

P2125.meaning: The ECU found a fault in the accelerator pedal position sensor E (the second, backup pedal sensor) circuit: the signal is missing, erratic or not plausible. The ECU cannot fully trust the pedal, so it limits throttle response (limp mode); drive carefully to a safe place.
causes: Intermittent connection at the accelerator pedal connector.
Damaged wiring between the pedal and the ECU.
Worn or faulty pedal position sensor (built into the pedal assembly).
Aftermarket throttle response controller (pedal box) fitted between the pedal and the ECU.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the connector at the top of the accelerator pedal for corrosion, looseness or bent pins, and wiggle the harness while watching live data.
Remove any aftermarket pedal box and reconnect the original plug, then re-test.

In live data, watch the accelerator pedal sensor voltages: released they should sit at a low steady value, and they should rise smoothly to a high value as you press the pedal slowly, with no jumps or dropouts.
With the key on and the pedal connector unplugged, check for about 5 V on the sensor E reference wire and a good ground.
Replace the accelerator pedal assembly (the sensors are built in and not sold separately), then clear and re-test.

P2127.meaning: The accelerator pedal position sensor E (the second, backup pedal sensor) signal is below its normal range. The ECU cannot fully trust the pedal, so it limits throttle response (limp mode); drive carefully to a safe place.
causes: Open 5 V reference or signal wire, or signal wire shorted to ground.
Corroded or loose connector at the accelerator pedal.
Faulty pedal position sensor (built into the pedal assembly).
Aftermarket throttle response controller (pedal box) fitted between the pedal and the ECU.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the connector at the top of the accelerator pedal for corrosion, looseness or bent pins, and wiggle the harness while watching live data.
Remove any aftermarket pedal box and reconnect the original plug, then re-test.

In live data, watch the accelerator pedal sensor voltages: released they should sit at a low steady value, and they should rise smoothly to a high value as you press the pedal slowly, with no jumps or dropouts.
With the key on and the pedal connector unplugged, check for about 5 V on the sensor E reference wire and a good ground.
Replace the accelerator pedal assembly (the sensors are built in and not sold separately), then clear and re-test.

P2128.meaning: The accelerator pedal position sensor E (the second, backup pedal sensor) signal is above its normal range. The ECU cannot fully trust the pedal, so it limits throttle response (limp mode); drive carefully to a safe place.
causes: Open ground wire, or signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage.
Corroded or loose connector at the accelerator pedal.
Faulty pedal position sensor (built into the pedal assembly).
Aftermarket throttle response controller (pedal box) fitted between the pedal and the ECU.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the connector at the top of the accelerator pedal for corrosion, looseness or bent pins, and wiggle the harness while watching live data.
Remove any aftermarket pedal box and reconnect the original plug, then re-test.

In live data, watch the accelerator pedal sensor voltages: released they should sit at a low steady value, and they should rise smoothly to a high value as you press the pedal slowly, with no jumps or dropouts.
With the key on and the pedal connector unplugged, check for about 5 V on the sensor E reference wire and a good ground (near 0 ohms to body ground).
Replace the accelerator pedal assembly (the sensors are built in and not sold separately), then clear and re-test.

P2135.meaning: The two throttle position sensors inside the throttle body (A and B) disagree with each other. The ECU cannot be sure where the throttle is, so it sets limp mode with very limited power; drive only to get the car checked.
causes: Worn or dirty sensor track inside the throttle body.
Corroded or loose throttle body connector causing a voltage offset.
Damaged wiring or high resistance in one sensor wire or the shared 5 V reference or ground.
Water ingress into the throttle body connector.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units.
Inspect the throttle body connector for corrosion, bent pins or a broken lock, and wiggle the harness with the engine idling to see if the fault appears.
With the key on and engine off, press the pedal slowly and watch both throttle position signals in live data: they should change smoothly and in step with each other.
Check the 5 V reference (about 5 V) and ground at the throttle body connector, and check each wire for continuity to the ECU.

Replace the throttle body (the sensors are built in). After cleaning or replacing the throttle body, let the ECU relearn it: switch the ignition on for about 10 seconds without starting, then start and idle with all loads off for a few minutes (follow the service manual if it gives a procedure).

P2138.meaning: The two accelerator pedal position sensors (D and E) disagree with each other. The ECU cannot fully trust the pedal, so it limits throttle response (limp mode); drive carefully to a safe place.
causes: Worn sensor track in the accelerator pedal assembly.
Corroded or loose connector at the pedal causing a voltage offset.
Damaged wiring or high resistance in one sensor wire or the shared ground.
Aftermarket throttle response controller (pedal box) fitted between the pedal and the ECU.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the connector at the top of the accelerator pedal for corrosion, looseness or bent pins, and wiggle the harness while watching live data.
Remove any aftermarket pedal box and reconnect the original plug, then re-test.
In live data, press the pedal slowly and watch both pedal sensor voltages: they should both rise smoothly and stay in the same relationship all the way.
Check the 5 V reference and ground at the pedal connector, and each wire for continuity to the ECU.
Replace the accelerator pedal assembly (the sensors are built in and not sold separately), then clear and re-test.

P2146.meaning: The ECU detected an open circuit in injector power supply A, the high-voltage feed for one group of injectors. On the EE20 diesel (and direct-injection petrol engines) the injectors in that group cannot fire, so the engine runs very roughly or will not start; do not keep driving.
causes: Damaged or corroded injector harness connector, or an injector connector not fully seated.
Broken wire in the injector supply circuit, often where the harness flexes or runs under the intake manifold.
Injector with an open coil or internal fault in group A.
ECU injector driver fault.
fixes: Injector circuits on the EE20 diesel run at high voltage when the engine runs: only measure with the ignition off and the battery disconnected.
Check which cylinders are misfiring or dead (misfire counters in live data, or a rough-running check) to identify the affected group.
Inspect every injector connector and the harness on the affected side for damage, oil contamination and corrosion.
Measure injector resistance at each injector connector and compare with the service manual value, and check continuity of the supply wire from the ECU to each injector in the group.
If wiring and injectors are good, the ECU injector driver may be faulty; have the ECU tested before replacing it.

P2147.meaning: The ECU detected that an injector drive circuit is shorted to ground. On the EE20 diesel (and direct-injection petrol engines) the ECU shuts off the affected injector group, so the engine runs very roughly or stalls; do not keep driving.
causes: Injector wire chafed through and touching the engine or a bracket.
Water or oil in an injector connector.
Injector with an internal short to its body.
ECU injector driver fault.
fixes: Injector circuits on the EE20 diesel run at high voltage when the engine runs: only measure with the ignition off and the battery disconnected.
Check which cylinders are misfiring or dead to narrow down the affected injector.
Inspect the injector harness for chafing, melted insulation or pinched wires, especially near brackets and the intake manifold.
Unplug the injectors one at a time and check each circuit for a short to ground; measure each injector's resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Repair the wiring or replace the shorted injector (on the diesel, new injectors need their correction codes entered into the ECU), then clear and re-test.

P2148.meaning: The ECU detected that an injector drive circuit is shorted to a positive voltage. On the EE20 diesel (and direct-injection petrol engines) the ECU shuts off the affected injector group, so the engine runs very roughly or stalls; do not keep driving.
causes: Injector wire chafed and touching another powered wire.
Water or corrosion bridging pins in an injector connector.
Injector with an internal short.
ECU injector driver fault.
fixes: Injector circuits on the EE20 diesel run at high voltage when the engine runs: only measure with the ignition off and the battery disconnected.
Check which cylinders are misfiring or dead to narrow down the affected injector.
Inspect the injector harness for chafing and for wires melted together, and check the connectors for water or corrosion.
With injectors and ECU unplugged, check each injector wire for a short to any other wire or to battery voltage; measure each injector's resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Repair the wiring or replace the faulty injector (on the diesel, new injectors need their correction codes entered into the ECU), then clear and re-test.

P2149.meaning: The ECU detected an open circuit in injector power supply B, the high-voltage feed for one group of injectors. On the EE20 diesel (and direct-injection petrol engines) the injectors in that group cannot fire, so the engine runs very roughly or will not start; do not keep driving.
causes: Damaged or corroded injector harness connector, or an injector connector not fully seated.
Broken wire in the injector supply circuit, often where the harness flexes or runs under the intake manifold.
Injector with an open coil or internal fault in group B.
ECU injector driver fault.
fixes: Injector circuits on the EE20 diesel run at high voltage when the engine runs: only measure with the ignition off and the battery disconnected.
Check which cylinders are misfiring or dead (misfire counters in live data, or a rough-running check) to identify the affected group.
Inspect every injector connector and the harness on the affected side for damage, oil contamination and corrosion.
Measure injector resistance at each injector connector and compare with the service manual value, and check continuity of the supply wire from the ECU to each injector in the group.
If wiring and injectors are good, the ECU injector driver may be faulty; have the ECU tested before replacing it.

P219A.meaning: The ECU detected that the cylinders on bank 1 (right side, cylinders 1 and 3, plus 5 on six-cylinders) are not getting the same air-fuel mixture: one cylinder runs noticeably richer or leaner than the others. It can cause rough running and higher emissions, and a rich cylinder can overheat the catalytic converter over time.
causes: Clogged, dirty or leaking fuel injector on bank 1.
Intake leak at one cylinder, such as a leaking intake manifold gasket, injector O-ring or split vacuum hose near one runner.
TGV stuck on the right side (EJ engines with TGVs), or heavy carbon in one intake port.
Weak ignition coil or worn spark plug on one cylinder.
Exhaust leak before the front A/F sensor.
Slow or faulty front A/F sensor.
fixes: Check misfire counts per cylinder and fuel trims in live data; a misfire on one cylinder points straight at the problem.
Inspect spark plugs and coils on bank 1; swap a coil to another cylinder and see if the problem follows it.
Smoke-test or spray-test the intake for leaks around the manifold gasket, injector O-rings and vacuum lines on the right side.
Check the injectors on bank 1: listen for even clicking, measure resistance and compare with the service manual value, or swap injectors between cylinders to see if the fault follows.
Check the exhaust for leaks before the A/F sensor, and replace the sensor if its reading is slow or stuck; then clear and re-test.

P219B.meaning: The ECU detected that the cylinders on bank 2 (left side, cylinders 2 and 4, plus 6 on six-cylinders) are not getting the same air-fuel mixture: one cylinder runs noticeably richer or leaner than the others. It can cause rough running and higher emissions, and a rich cylinder can overheat the catalytic converter over time.
causes: Clogged, dirty or leaking fuel injector on bank 2.
Intake leak at one cylinder, such as a leaking intake manifold gasket, injector O-ring or split vacuum hose near one runner.
TGV stuck on the left side (EJ engines with TGVs), or heavy carbon in one intake port.
Weak ignition coil or worn spark plug on one cylinder.
Exhaust leak before the front A/F sensor.
Slow or faulty front A/F sensor.
fixes: Check misfire counts per cylinder and fuel trims in live data; a misfire on one cylinder points straight at the problem.
Inspect spark plugs and coils on bank 2; swap a coil to another cylinder and see if the problem follows it.
Smoke-test or spray-test the intake for leaks around the manifold gasket, injector O-rings and vacuum lines on the left side.
Check the injectors on bank 2: listen for even clicking, measure resistance and compare with the service manual value, or swap injectors between cylinders to see if the fault follows.
Check the exhaust for leaks before the A/F sensor, and replace the sensor if its reading is slow or stuck; then clear and re-test.

P2227.meaning: The ECU's atmospheric (barometric) pressure reading does not agree with what it expects, for example with the manifold pressure at key-on engine-off. The ECU uses it for fuel, ignition, boost and altitude correction, so running may be slightly off; normally safe to drive.
causes: MAP sensor reading wrong, so the two readings no longer agree (look for MAP sensor codes too).
Faulty atmospheric pressure sensor. On many Subarus the atmospheric pressure sensor is built into the ECU; others use a separate sensor.
Moisture or corrosion in the ECU or sensor connector.
Blocked vent or port on a separately mounted sensor.
ECU fault.
fixes: With the key on and the engine off, compare atmospheric pressure and manifold pressure in live data: they should match within a few kPa (about 101 kPa at sea level, lower at altitude).
Compare the atmospheric reading with the local weather-station pressure, corrected for your altitude.
If manifold pressure is the odd one out, check the MAP sensor, its connector and its vacuum hose first.
Check the ECU (usually under the dash) and its connectors for water damage or corrosion.
If the barometric sensor is inside the ECU and reads wrong, the ECU needs repair or replacement.

P2228.meaning: The atmospheric (barometric) pressure signal is below its normal range, usually an electrical fault in the sensor or its circuit. The ECU substitutes a default value, so fuel, boost and altitude correction may be off, especially in the mountains; normally safe to drive.
causes: Open 5 V reference or signal wire, or signal shorted to ground (on models with a separate sensor).
Faulty atmospheric pressure sensor. On many Subarus the atmospheric pressure sensor is built into the ECU; others use a separate sensor.
Corroded or loose sensor connector.
ECU internal fault, when the sensor is built into the ECU.
fixes: With the key on and the engine off, compare atmospheric pressure and manifold pressure in live data: they should match within a few kPa (about 101 kPa at sea level, lower at altitude).
If your car has a separate sensor, inspect its connector and wiring, and check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground with the key on.
Check the ECU and its connectors for water damage or corrosion.
Replace the separate sensor if its wiring is good; if the sensor is built into the ECU, the ECU needs repair or replacement.
After the repair, clear and re-test, and confirm the atmospheric reading matches local pressure.

P2229.meaning: The atmospheric (barometric) pressure signal is above its normal range, usually an electrical fault in the sensor or its circuit. The ECU substitutes a default value, so fuel, boost and altitude correction may be off, especially in the mountains; normally safe to drive.
causes: Open ground wire, or signal shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage (on models with a separate sensor).
Faulty atmospheric pressure sensor. On many Subarus the atmospheric pressure sensor is built into the ECU; others use a separate sensor.
Corroded or loose sensor connector.
ECU internal fault, when the sensor is built into the ECU.
fixes: With the key on and the engine off, compare atmospheric pressure and manifold pressure in live data: they should match within a few kPa (about 101 kPa at sea level, lower at altitude).
If your car has a separate sensor, inspect its connector and wiring, and check for about 5 V on the reference wire and a good ground with the key on.
Check the ECU and its connectors for water damage or corrosion.
Replace the separate sensor if its wiring is good; if the sensor is built into the ECU, the ECU needs repair or replacement.
After the repair, clear and re-test, and confirm the atmospheric reading matches local pressure.

P2401.meaning: The ECU sees a low voltage (short to ground or open) in the control circuit of the EVAP leak detection pump, part of the leak check module mounted near the charcoal canister under the rear of the car. The EVAP leak test cannot run; the car drives normally, but it may fail an emissions inspection.
causes: Corroded or water-filled connector at the leak check module, which gets road spray.
Damaged wiring to the module (under the car near the fuel tank).
Faulty pump motor in the leak check module.
Blown fuse for the module.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check the fuse for the EVAP leak check module.
Inspect the leak check module connector for water, mud and green corrosion; clean it and apply dielectric grease.
Check the wiring from the module forward for chafing or damage where it runs along the body.
Check the pump circuit for a short to ground and continuity to the ECU, and measure the pump motor resistance against the service manual value.
Replace the leak check module if its pump is faulty, then clear and let the car complete an EVAP test (usually after a key-off soak of several hours).

P2402.meaning: The ECU sees a high voltage (usually a short to power) in the control circuit of the EVAP leak detection pump, part of the leak check module mounted near the charcoal canister under the rear of the car. The EVAP leak test cannot run; the car drives normally, but it may fail an emissions inspection.
causes: Control wire shorted to battery voltage or another powered wire.
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the leak check module connector.
Faulty leak check module (internal short).
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the leak check module connector for water, mud and green corrosion; clean it and apply dielectric grease.
Check the wiring from the module forward for chafing or damage where it runs along the body.
With the module and ECU unplugged, check the pump control wire for battery voltage (there should be none).
Measure the pump motor resistance and compare with the service manual value.
Replace the leak check module if faulty, then clear and let the car complete an EVAP test (usually after a key-off soak of several hours).

P2404.meaning: The pressure sensor inside the EVAP leak check module gave readings outside the expected range during the leak test. The EVAP leak test cannot run; the car drives normally, but it may fail an emissions inspection.
causes: Blocked vent filter or vent hose (mud, water, insects) between the module and the atmosphere.
Kinked, cracked or disconnected hose between the canister and the leak check module.
Water inside the leak check module.
Faulty pressure sensor in the leak check module.
Connector corrosion or wiring fault.
fixes: As a general EVAP first step, check that the fuel cap seal is intact and the cap clicks when tightened.
Inspect the vent hose and filter at the leak check module for mud, water or insect nests; they must flow freely.
Check the hoses between the canister, module and fuel tank for kinks, cracks and loose fittings.
Inspect the leak check module connector for water, mud and green corrosion; clean it and apply dielectric grease.
Replace the leak check module if it has water inside or the sensor still reads wrong, then clear and let the car complete an EVAP test.

P2413.meaning: The ECU saw that the EGR valve did not move to the commanded position, usually because soot has built up and it is sticking. On the EE20 diesel expect reduced power, hesitation or smoke and possibly limp mode; drivable gently, but get it cleaned or replaced.
causes: Soot and carbon buildup on the EGR valve and seat, common on diesels used for short trips.
Worn or failing EGR valve motor or position sensor.
Connector or wiring fault at the EGR valve.
Heavy carbon buildup in the EGR passages or intake.
On petrol engines with EGR, carbon in the valve or passages.
fixes: Inspect the EGR valve connector and wiring for damage or corrosion.
In live data, compare actual EGR position with the target: it should follow closely with no lag or sticking.
Remove the EGR valve and clean soot from the valve, seat and passage with a suitable cleaner; fit a new gasket.
Check the intake and EGR passages for heavy carbon buildup and clean if needed; regular longer drives at motorway speed help keep it clean.
Replace the EGR valve if it still sticks or the motor is weak, then run the EGR learning procedure if the service manual requires one and clear and re-test.

P2419.meaning: The ECU sees a low voltage (short to ground or open) in the control circuit of the EVAP switching valve, the change-over valve inside the leak check module mounted near the charcoal canister under the rear of the car. The EVAP leak test cannot run; the car drives normally, but it may fail an emissions inspection.
causes: Corroded or water-filled connector at the leak check module.
Damaged wiring to the module under the car.
Faulty switching valve (solenoid) inside the leak check module.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the leak check module connector for water, mud and green corrosion; clean it and apply dielectric grease.
Check the wiring from the module forward for chafing or damage.
Check the switching valve circuit for a short to ground and continuity to the ECU, and measure the solenoid resistance against the service manual value.
Replace the leak check module if the valve is faulty (it is usually not sold separately).
Clear and let the car complete an EVAP test (usually after a key-off soak of several hours).

P2420.meaning: The ECU sees a high voltage (usually a short to power) in the control circuit of the EVAP switching valve, the change-over valve inside the leak check module mounted near the charcoal canister under the rear of the car. The EVAP leak test cannot run; the car drives normally, but it may fail an emissions inspection.
causes: Control wire shorted to battery voltage or another powered wire.
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the leak check module connector.
Faulty switching valve (internal short) in the leak check module.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the leak check module connector for water, mud and green corrosion; clean it and apply dielectric grease.
Check the wiring from the module forward for chafing or damage.
With the module and ECU unplugged, check the valve control wire for battery voltage (there should be none), and measure the solenoid resistance against the service manual value.
Replace the leak check module if the valve is faulty (it is usually not sold separately).
Clear and let the car complete an EVAP test (usually after a key-off soak of several hours).

P2431.meaning: During the secondary air check after a cold start (when a pump blows fresh air into the exhaust ports to heat the catalytic converter quickly), the ECU saw a pressure reading that does not match what it expects from the pump. The engine runs normally; this only affects cold-start emissions, but it can lead to other secondary air codes.
causes: Secondary air pump weak or full of water (it draws air from low at the front of the car and often ingests water).
Faulty secondary air pressure sensor or its connector.
Leaking, cracked or disconnected hose between the pump and the combination valves.
Combination (air switching) valve stuck or corroded.
Wiring fault in the pump or sensor circuit.
fixes: On a cold start (engine sat for several hours), listen for the secondary air pump: it should whir loudly for a short while after start-up and then stop.
Inspect the hoses from the pump to the combination (air switching) valves on each cylinder head for cracks, loose clamps and signs of water.
Check the pump inlet and filter for dirt or water; water in the pump outlet hose means the pump has sucked it in and is likely damaged.
With the key on and the engine off, compare the secondary air pressure reading with atmospheric pressure in live data if available: they should be close.
Replace the faulty pressure sensor, pump or valves. Clear and re-test from a true cold start; the system only runs its check after the engine has cooled for several hours.

P2432.meaning: The ECU sees a low voltage in the secondary air monitoring circuit (listed here as the pump circuit), the pressure sensor that confirms the pump is blowing air into the exhaust after a cold start. The engine runs normally; this only affects cold-start emissions.
causes: Open 5 V reference or signal wire, or signal shorted to ground.
Corroded or water-filled connector at the secondary air pressure sensor.
Faulty secondary air pressure sensor.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the secondary air pressure sensor connector and wiring for corrosion, water and chafing.
With the key on, check for about 5 V on the sensor reference wire and a good ground.
With the key on and the engine off, compare the secondary air pressure reading with atmospheric pressure in live data if available: they should be close and steady.
Replace the pressure sensor if the wiring is good.
Clear and re-test from a true cold start; the system only runs its check after the engine has cooled for several hours.

P2433.meaning: The ECU sees a high voltage in the secondary air monitoring circuit (listed here as the pump circuit), the pressure sensor that confirms the pump is blowing air into the exhaust after a cold start. The engine runs normally; this only affects cold-start emissions.
causes: Open ground wire, or signal shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage.
Corroded or water-filled connector at the secondary air pressure sensor.
Faulty secondary air pressure sensor.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Inspect the secondary air pressure sensor connector and wiring for corrosion, water and chafing.
With the key on, check for about 5 V on the sensor reference wire and a good ground.
With the key on and the engine off, compare the secondary air pressure reading with atmospheric pressure in live data if available: they should be close and steady.
Replace the pressure sensor if the wiring is good.
Clear and re-test from a true cold start; the system only runs its check after the engine has cooled for several hours.

P2440.meaning: After a cold start the secondary air system pumps fresh air into the exhaust to heat the catalytic converter, and the ECU found that combination (air switching) valve 1 on the right cylinder head (bank 1) stays open when it should be closed. Hot exhaust can then flow back toward the pump and damage it, so get it fixed soon; the engine itself runs normally.
causes: Corrosion or carbon holding the right combination valve open.
Valve solenoid or its wiring keeping the valve energized.
Faulty secondary air pressure sensor giving a false reading.
Secondary air pump relay stuck on (check for P2444 too).
fixes: Check for other secondary air codes; P2444 or pressure sensor codes change the diagnosis.
Inspect the hose at the right combination valve for heat damage or soot inside, a sign that exhaust has been flowing back.
Check the valve connector and wiring for corrosion or damage.
Test the valve per the service manual: it should block air when unpowered and open when powered.
Replace the combination valve and check the pump for heat damage. Clear and re-test from a true cold start; the system only runs its check after the engine has cooled for several hours.

P2441.meaning: After a cold start the secondary air system pumps fresh air into the exhaust to heat the catalytic converter, but the ECU found that combination (air switching) valve 1 on the right cylinder head (bank 1) does not open, so no air reaches that side. The engine runs normally; it only affects cold-start emissions.
causes: Combination valve on the right side seized by corrosion or carbon.
Open circuit in the valve solenoid or its wiring, or a corroded connector.
Blocked, kinked or disconnected hose to the valve.
Weak or dead secondary air pump (the ECU can see this as a closed valve).
Faulty secondary air pressure sensor.
fixes: On a cold start (engine sat for several hours), listen for the secondary air pump: it should whir loudly for a short while after start-up and then stop.
Inspect the hoses from the pump to the combination (air switching) valves on each cylinder head for cracks, loose clamps and signs of water.
Check the right valve connector for corrosion and measure the solenoid resistance against the service manual value.
Test the valve per the service manual: it should block air when unpowered and open when powered.
Replace the seized valve or repair the wiring. Clear and re-test from a true cold start; the system only runs its check after the engine has cooled for several hours.

P2442.meaning: After a cold start the secondary air system pumps fresh air into the exhaust to heat the catalytic converter, and the ECU found that combination (air switching) valve 2 on the left cylinder head (bank 2) stays open when it should be closed. Hot exhaust can then flow back toward the pump and damage it, so get it fixed soon; the engine itself runs normally.
causes: Corrosion or carbon holding the left combination valve open.
Valve solenoid or its wiring keeping the valve energized.
Faulty secondary air pressure sensor giving a false reading.
Secondary air pump relay stuck on (check for P2444 too).
fixes: Check for other secondary air codes; P2444 or pressure sensor codes change the diagnosis.
Inspect the hose at the left combination valve for heat damage or soot inside, a sign that exhaust has been flowing back.
Check the valve connector and wiring for corrosion or damage.
Test the valve per the service manual: it should block air when unpowered and open when powered.
Replace the combination valve and check the pump for heat damage. Clear and re-test from a true cold start; the system only runs its check after the engine has cooled for several hours.

P2443.meaning: After a cold start the secondary air system pumps fresh air into the exhaust to heat the catalytic converter, but the ECU found that combination (air switching) valve 2 on the left cylinder head (bank 2) does not open, so no air reaches that side. The engine runs normally; it only affects cold-start emissions.
causes: Combination valve on the left side seized by corrosion or carbon.
Open circuit in the valve solenoid or its wiring, or a corroded connector.
Blocked, kinked or disconnected hose to the valve.
Weak or dead secondary air pump (the ECU can see this as a closed valve).
Faulty secondary air pressure sensor.
fixes: On a cold start (engine sat for several hours), listen for the secondary air pump: it should whir loudly for a short while after start-up and then stop.
Inspect the hoses from the pump to the combination (air switching) valves on each cylinder head for cracks, loose clamps and signs of water.
Check the left valve connector for corrosion and measure the solenoid resistance against the service manual value.
Test the valve per the service manual: it should block air when unpowered and open when powered.
Replace the seized valve or repair the wiring. Clear and re-test from a true cold start; the system only runs its check after the engine has cooled for several hours.

P2444.meaning: The secondary air pump keeps running when it should be off, usually because its relay is stuck on. The pump is only meant to run briefly after a cold start, so it can overheat and fail, and a pump that runs with the key off drains the battery; fix it promptly.
causes: Secondary air pump relay with welded (stuck) contacts.
Relay control wire shorted to ground, keeping the relay energized.
Faulty secondary air pressure sensor giving a false reading.
Wiring fault in the pump circuit.
fixes: With the engine warm (or the key off), listen near the pump: it should be silent. If it runs, pull the secondary air pump relay and confirm it stops.
Swap the relay with an identical one or fit a new relay.
Check the relay control wire for a short to ground with the ECU unplugged.
Check the pump for heat damage or noise after it has been running continuously, and replace it if needed.
Clear and re-test from a true cold start; the system only runs its check after the engine has cooled for several hours.

P2503.meaning: The ECU measured system voltage below the normal charging range while the engine was running. The battery is not being charged properly; left alone the car may stall or fail to start, and low voltage can set other odd codes.
causes: Loose, glazed or worn alternator belt.
Failing alternator or voltage regulator.
Loose or corroded battery terminals, or a poor engine-to-body ground strap.
Blown alternator fuse or fusible link.
Worn-out battery that cannot hold a charge.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units.
Check the alternator belt for tension, cracks and glazing; a squeal at start-up is a hint.
Clean and tighten the battery terminals and check the ground straps from the engine and battery to the body.
Have the battery and alternator load tested (many parts stores do this for free).
Replace the alternator or battery as indicated by the test, then clear and re-test and watch battery voltage in live data.

P2504.meaning: The ECU measured system voltage above the normal charging range while the engine was running. Overcharging can boil the battery and damage electronics, so have it checked soon and watch for a hot, swollen or smelly battery.
causes: Failed voltage regulator in the alternator.
Poor connection or ground at the alternator, so the regulator senses the wrong voltage.
Battery charger or jump pack connected while the engine runs.
Aftermarket electrical add-ons interfering with the charging circuit.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units. Above about 15 V running is too high.
Disconnect any charger, jump pack or aftermarket device and re-check the voltage.
Clean and tighten the alternator connections, the battery terminals and the ground straps.
Have the alternator tested; a faulty regulator usually means replacing the alternator.
Check the battery for swelling or electrolyte loss after the repair, then clear and re-test.

P2610.meaning: The ECU's internal timer that measures how long the engine has been switched off did not count correctly. It uses this timer for self-tests such as the EVAP leak check, so those tests may not run; the engine itself runs normally.
causes: Battery recently disconnected, flat or weak.
Poor ECU backup power supply or ground.
Blown or loose ECU memory (backup) fuse.
ECU software issue or internal fault.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units.
Check the ECU backup power fuse and the ECU ground connections.
After the battery and power checks, clear the code and let the car sit switched off for several hours, then see if it returns.
Ask a Subaru dealer whether an ECU software update exists for your model.
If it keeps returning with good power and grounds, the ECU needs repair or replacement.

P2633.meaning: The ECU sees a low voltage in the control circuit of the sub fuel pump relay, which switches the second fuel pump (or a second pump stage) on some Subaru models. Fuel delivery may be reduced at high load or the pump may run when it should not, so avoid hard acceleration until it is fixed.
causes: Faulty sub fuel pump relay.
Relay control wire open or shorted to ground.
Blown fuse in the relay circuit.
Corroded relay socket or connector.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check the fuel pump fuses in the fuse boxes.
Swap the sub fuel pump relay with an identical one, or fit a new relay, and re-test.
With the key on, check the relay socket: one side should have battery voltage, and the ECU control wire should switch when the ECU commands the relay.
Check the control wire for continuity to the ECU and for shorts to ground or battery voltage.
Inspect the fuel pump connector (usually under the rear seat) for corrosion, then clear and re-test.

P2634.meaning: The ECU sees a high voltage in the control circuit of the sub fuel pump relay, which switches the second fuel pump (or a second pump stage) on some Subaru models. Fuel delivery may be reduced at high load or the pump may run when it should not, so avoid hard acceleration until it is fixed.
causes: Faulty sub fuel pump relay (for example stuck on or internally shorted).
Relay control wire shorted to battery voltage.
Corroded relay socket or connector.
ECU fault (rare).
fixes: Check the fuel pump fuses in the fuse boxes.
Swap the sub fuel pump relay with an identical one, or fit a new relay, and re-test.
With the key on, check the relay socket: one side should have battery voltage, and the ECU control wire should switch when the ECU commands the relay.
Check the control wire for continuity to the ECU and for shorts to ground or battery voltage.
Inspect the fuel pump connector (usually under the rear seat) for corrosion, then clear and re-test.

P2635.meaning: The ECU detected that the suction control valve (SCV) on the EE20 diesel's high-pressure fuel pump is sticking, so rail pressure does not follow its target. Expect hesitation, stalling, hard starting or limp mode; fix it before driving far.
causes: Contaminated fuel or water in the fuel making the valve stick.
Clogged fuel filter or air in the fuel system.
Worn or sticking suction control valve.
Wiring or connector fault at the valve.
Wear inside the high-pressure pump, or the wrong fuel (petrol in the tank).
fixes: Drain the water separator on the fuel filter and look for water or debris in what comes out.
Replace the fuel filter and bleed the fuel system as described in the service manual.
In live data, compare actual rail pressure with target rail pressure at idle and while revving: actual should follow closely.
Inspect the SCV connector and wiring, and measure the valve resistance against the service manual value.
Replace the suction control valve (or the pump if the valve is not sold separately); if metal debris is found, have the whole high-pressure system inspected.

P2707.meaning: The transmission control detected that shift solenoid F is not giving the expected result (the shift or clutch engagement it controls), although its electrical circuit looks OK. The gearbox may go into fail-safe (held in one gear, harsh shifts) and the AT OIL TEMP light may flash; drive gently.
causes: Low, old or contaminated ATF.
Solenoid F or its valve sticking from debris or varnish.
Intermittent wiring or connector fault.
Worn clutch or brake inside the transmission.
Transmission control unit fault (rare).
fixes: Check the ATF level with the engine warm and idling, using the dipstick marks. Dark, burnt-smelling fluid or debris on the dipstick points to internal wear.
Read all transmission codes, and note whether the AT OIL TEMP light flashes after start-up (Subaru's way of signaling a stored transmission fault).
Inspect the transmission harness connectors for oil intrusion, corrosion and bent or loose pins.
Change the ATF if it is old or dark (a drain and fill, possibly repeated), then clear and re-test.
If the code returns, have the valve body and solenoid F checked or replaced by a transmission specialist.

P2709.meaning: The transmission control found an electrical fault (open or short) in the shift solenoid F circuit. The gearbox usually goes into fail-safe (held in one gear) and the AT OIL TEMP light may flash; drive gently and have it fixed soon.
causes: Oil-soaked, corroded or loose connector at the transmission.
Damaged wiring in the external or internal transmission harness.
Shift solenoid F with an open or shorted coil.
Transmission control unit fault (rare).
fixes: Read all transmission codes, and note whether the AT OIL TEMP light flashes after start-up (Subaru's way of signaling a stored transmission fault).
Inspect the transmission harness connectors for oil intrusion, corrosion and bent or loose pins.
Measure solenoid F resistance at the transmission connector and compare with the service manual value; also check for a short to ground.
Check the wiring between the transmission connector and the TCM for continuity.
Replace solenoid F or the internal harness (valve body work, usually a specialist job), then clear and re-test.

U0073.meaning: The control unit found that the CAN communication bus went into a 'bus off' state: it could not send or receive messages reliably. Other systems (transmission, VDC, gauges) may show warnings at the same time; the car may run but with limited functions, so diagnose it soon.
causes: CAN wiring shorted or open, for example a chafed harness or water in a connector.
Low battery voltage or poor grounds.
A failing module disturbing the bus.
Aftermarket devices spliced into the CAN wiring or plugged into the diagnostic port.
Corroded connector at one of the modules on the bus.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units.
Unplug any aftermarket devices on the diagnostic port or spliced into the wiring (alarms, remote start, gauges, OBD dongles) and re-test.

On cars with CAN at the diagnostic port (pins 6 and 14), measure resistance between those pins with the battery disconnected: about 60 ohms is normal, about 120 ohms means one end of the bus is disconnected, and near 0 ohms means a short.
Check for water in the footwells or around modules, and inspect connectors for corrosion.
Unplug modules one at a time while watching whether communication returns, to find the one pulling the bus down; then repair and clear and re-test.

U0101.meaning: The engine ECU stopped receiving messages from the automatic transmission control unit (TCM) over the CAN bus. Shift quality, torque reduction during shifts and AWD control may be affected, and the transmission may be in fail-safe; drive gently.
causes: TCM is not powered: blown fuse, poor ground or low battery voltage.
Loose or corroded connector at the TCM.
CAN wiring fault between the ECU and the TCM.
ECU or ROM set up for a different equipment level (for example after an engine or ECU swap), so it expects a module the car does not have.
Internal failure of the TCM.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units.
Check the fuses feeding the TCM and look for other U-codes that point to a shared wiring fault.
Try to talk to the TCM with a scan tool: if it does not respond at all, focus on its power, ground and connector.
Inspect the TCM connector for corrosion and bent pins, and check the CAN wires between ECU and TCM for continuity.

On cars with CAN at the diagnostic port (pins 6 and 14), measure resistance between those pins with the battery disconnected: about 60 ohms is normal, about 120 ohms means one end of the bus is disconnected, and near 0 ohms means a short.

U0122.meaning: The engine ECU stopped receiving messages from the VDC unit (the ABS and stability control unit in the engine bay) over the CAN bus. ABS, VDC and traction control warning lights will usually be on and those systems may be off; normal braking still works, but drive with extra care.
causes: VDC unit is not powered: blown fuse, poor ground or low battery voltage.
Loose or corroded connector at the VDC unit.
CAN wiring fault between the ECU and the VDC unit.
ECU or ROM set up for a different equipment level (for example after an engine or ECU swap), so it expects a module the car does not have.
Internal failure of the VDC unit.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units.
Check the fuses feeding the VDC unit and look for other U-codes that point to a shared wiring fault.
Try to talk to the VDC unit with a scan tool: if it does not respond at all, focus on its power, ground and connector.
Inspect the VDC unit connector in the engine bay for water, corrosion and bent pins, and make sure it is fully latched.

On cars with CAN at the diagnostic port (pins 6 and 14), measure resistance between those pins with the battery disconnected: about 60 ohms is normal, about 120 ohms means one end of the bus is disconnected, and near 0 ohms means a short.

U0140.meaning: The engine ECU stopped receiving messages from the BIU (body integrated unit, the body control module under the dash that handles functions such as the immobilizer, lights and A/C requests) over the CAN bus. Body functions, the A/C request or the immobilizer handshake may be affected, and the car may not start if the immobilizer is involved.
causes: BIU is not powered: blown fuse, poor ground or low battery voltage.
Loose or corroded connector at the BIU.
CAN wiring fault between the ECU and the BIU.
Water in the cabin (leaking windscreen, door seal or sunroof drain) reaching the BIU or its connectors.
Internal failure of the BIU.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units.
Check the fuses feeding the BIU and look for other U-codes that point to a shared wiring fault.
Try to talk to the BIU with a scan tool: if it does not respond at all, focus on its power, ground and connector.
Inspect the BIU connectors under the dash for water, corrosion and loose fit, and look for damp carpet in the footwells.

On cars with CAN at the diagnostic port (pins 6 and 14), measure resistance between those pins with the battery disconnected: about 60 ohms is normal, about 120 ohms means one end of the bus is disconnected, and near 0 ohms means a short.

U0402.meaning: The engine ECU receives messages from the automatic transmission control unit (TCM), but their content is invalid or implausible. The ECU ignores the bad data, so shift quality and torque control may suffer; drive gently.
causes: The TCM has its own fault and is flagging its data as invalid (check TCM codes).
Mismatched software between the ECU and the TCM, for example after replacing or reflashing one of them or fitting a used unit.
Low battery voltage or poor grounds causing corrupted data.
Electrical noise on the CAN bus from damaged wiring or aftermarket devices.
Internal fault in the TCM.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units.
Read the TCM's own codes and fix those first; they usually explain why its data is invalid.
Unplug any aftermarket devices on the diagnostic port or spliced into the wiring (alarms, remote start, gauges, OBD dongles) and re-test.
If the TCM or ECU was recently replaced or reflashed, confirm the part and software match the car and are registered correctly.
Inspect the CAN wiring and connectors at the TCM, then clear and re-test.

U0416.meaning: The engine ECU receives messages from the VDC unit (ABS and stability control), but their content is invalid or implausible. ABS, VDC or traction warning lights may be on and those systems may be limited; normal braking still works.
causes: The VDC unit has its own fault, such as a wheel speed sensor or steering angle sensor problem (check VDC codes).
Mismatched software between the ECU and the VDC unit, for example after replacing or reflashing one of them or fitting a used unit.
Low battery voltage or poor grounds causing corrupted data.
Electrical noise on the CAN bus from damaged wiring or aftermarket devices.
Internal fault in the VDC unit.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units.
Read the VDC codes and fix those first; also have the steering angle and yaw sensors calibrated if they were disturbed.
Unplug any aftermarket devices on the diagnostic port or spliced into the wiring (alarms, remote start, gauges, OBD dongles) and re-test.
If the VDC unit or ECU was recently replaced or reflashed, confirm the part and software match the car and are registered correctly.
Inspect the CAN wiring and connectors at the VDC unit, then clear and re-test.

U0422.meaning: The engine ECU receives messages from the BIU (body integrated unit), but their content is invalid or implausible. Functions that depend on the BIU, such as the A/C request, immobilizer or dash signals, may act up.
causes: The BIU has its own fault or is set up for a different equipment level (check BIU codes).
Mismatched software between the ECU and the BIU, for example after replacing or reflashing one of them or fitting a used unit.
Low battery voltage or poor grounds causing corrupted data.
Electrical noise on the CAN bus from damaged wiring or aftermarket devices.
Internal fault in the BIU.
fixes: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.5 to 14.7 V running. Low voltage can set false faults in control units.
Read the BIU codes if your tool supports it and fix those first.
Unplug any aftermarket devices on the diagnostic port or spliced into the wiring (alarms, remote start, gauges, OBD dongles) and re-test.
If the BIU or ECU was recently replaced or reflashed, confirm the part and software match the car and are registered correctly.
Inspect the CAN wiring and connectors at the BIU, then clear and re-test.
